stories.Headline: Faculty member addresses artificial intelligence practically and theoretically - The Pennsylvania State University
stories.Summary:
Penn State associate professor Heather Shoenberger, of the Donald P. Bellisario College of Communications, has been working on artificial intelligence both in the classroom and in research. Shoenberger co-created a three-credit undergraduate course, COMM 200N Generative AI for All, with Mehrdad Mahdavi, an associate professor of computer science and engineering. She has taught the course since the fall semester of 2024, and it is cross-listed in the Bellisario College and the College of Engineering, with sections taught in both colleges. The course reaches its enrollment cap each semester.

The course is designed to explain how generative AI works, along with the ethical, sociopolitical and other issues it raises. Shoenberger said the material must be kept current because the technology keeps changing, and she said she prepares well ahead of each class. Her research has produced a published article introducing the human-AI asymmetric relationship theory, or HAART. The article appeared in a special AI-focused issue of the Journal of Advertising, which Shoenberger described as the most prestigious journal in her field. She wrote it with four colleagues from King's College London, CQUniversity, Old Dominion University and the University of Amsterdam.

According to Shoenberger, the theory holds that conversational AI can display relational characteristics, such as simulated emotional responsiveness, commitment, attachment and intimacy, but it cannot experience relational benefits or commitment. Users may perceive a mutual relationship that does not actually exist, which she said could leave consumers vulnerable to dependence, risk and control. She said the framework could eventually encourage more transparency about these interactions and possibly regulation, and that she and her co-authors hope it will aid future advertising research. The articles do not describe any specific next steps beyond that.

Articles.Title: Faculty member addresses artificial intelligence practically and theoretically - The Pennsylvania State University

stories.Headline: Ulster County Bans Government Use of AI Surveillance
stories.Summary:
Ulster County Executive Jen Metzger issued an executive order on October 22 banning the use of Flock cameras and other AI-assisted video surveillance technologies in county government. The order, titled "Prohibiting the Use of Flock Cameras and other AI-Assisted Video Surveillance Technologies" and designated Executive Order No. 5, took effect immediately upon its announcement. It bars any department or employee under the county executive's office from buying or deploying such systems, from helping to develop them, and from aiding private individuals or corporations in implementing them. Flock systems, made by Flock Safety, include security cameras, license plate readers and data-sharing networks, many of which use generative AI and machine learning to identify people, track them and build databases.

The ban covers buildings and property under the county executive's authority, including the Ulster County Courthouse, the Sheriff's Office, UCAT public transit facilities, county public works departments and public recreational areas such as rail trails. It does not reach facilities controlled by towns and villages, such as the New Paltz Town Hall, the New Paltz Courthouse or the New Paltz Police Headquarters, and it does not apply to private individuals or businesses. In her order, Metzger argued that protecting public safety and individual rights go hand in hand in a democracy and that the rapid, unregulated growth of the AI sector threatens that balance. She wrote that tech companies dominate AI development without independent oversight, that multiple security breaches have occurred in these companies' systems, and that collected information could be shared outside county government without authorization.

New Paltz Town Supervisor Tim Rogers said he agrees with Metzger's assessment that unregulated AI in security matters can weaken public safety and democratic principles, and he warned that civil liberties could be trampled if for-profit companies are left to operate without limits. He also said the town has no current plan to adopt Flock technology, citing its high cost, and that to his knowledge the New Paltz Police Department does not use it. Rogers acknowledged that surveillance can deliver local benefits, arguing that cameras like those Lowe's operates on Route 299 help deter shoplifting and theft. The New Paltz Oracle reports that the town has three AI surveillance systems in and around its territory, two of them Flock cameras owned by Lowe's facing its parking lot, and that the owner of the third remains undisclosed. Rogers said Lowe's is not required to register these cameras with the town and that no site plan or building review involves Flock cameras, so private companies remain outside local regulation, just as they do at the county level.

Articles.Title: Ulster County Bans Government Use of AI Surveillance - The New Paltz Oracle

stories.Headline: Hands-on experience prepares Wayne State engineers for Michigan’s AI-powered manufacturing future
stories.Summary:
Wayne State University is giving engineering students hands-on experience with robots, conveyor systems, machine vision and generative AI, and that experience is already helping graduates land jobs in the field. The work takes place in part in IntelliMake, a new research hub and pilot-scale factory being developed in partnership with Kyndryl to advance AI-driven manufacturing. Students at the James and Patricia Anderson College of Engineering learn to make manufacturing smarter, more flexible and more efficient. The article was published on November 10, 2026.

The initiative addresses a workforce challenge for Michigan, where manufacturing remains central to the economy. According to the state's AI and Workforce Plan, an estimated 75% of manufacturing jobs will require some form of upskilling as artificial intelligence and automation become more prevalent. The state estimates that responsible AI adoption could generate up to $70 billion in economic impact and support 130,000 jobs. Wayne State says preparing that workforce means giving students chances to experiment with these technologies, understand their limits and apply them to real engineering problems.

Dr. Ratna Babu Chinnam, professor and chair of industrial and systems engineering and co-director of IntelliMake, said the university is trying to create a pipeline of students who can address that need. Raj Sohmshetty, co-director of IntelliMake and instructor of IE 6000: Digital Automation, redesigned the course to combine classroom learning with hands-on work in the IntelliMake lab. Chinnam said computer science students may understand AI but do not know how to think about the real need, and that the lab bridges that gap. The article notes that traditional industrial robots follow programmed instructions and may fail when a part's position or geometry varies slightly.

The article reports that about 10 students spent substantial time in the lab during fall 2025, and several subsequently secured positions with leading companies. One recent graduate of the artificial intelligence master's program, Gokula Kumaran Kiruthiga Gopal, became an AI engineer with Panasonic. Kiruthiga Gopal said the IntelliMake experience was part of the reason she landed that position, and that Panasonic was especially interested in a factory-monitoring system her team developed. Chinnam said that in one recent class about 70% of students were already working engineers or other professionals, including people employed by automotive companies.

Sushant Lingras, an operations manager for PHINA, formerly Delphi Technologies, is pursuing a master's in artificial intelligence. He said he developed an AI-powered agent that helps employees quickly access plant information, standard work and operational knowledge, which eliminated several manual data-entry tasks. Derek Stringfellow, an applications analyst at Great Lakes Water Authority and a Wayne State graduate student in AI, said the class shows how such systems are built, how they fail and how a person still has a significant role. The article says that at IntelliMake students can test ideas and refine solutions in a controlled environment, which is impractical at a production plant. As the facility develops, Wayne State plans to extend the approach to quality control, production control, facilities design and operational optimization.

Articles.Title: Hands-on experience prepares Wayne State engineers for Michigan’s AI-powered manufacturing future

stories.Headline: Stony Brook FinTech Workshop Explores AI’s Impact on Finance, Announces New Industry Partnership
stories.Summary:
Stony Brook University held its FinTech Workshop on November 6 in the New Computer Science Building, where researchers and industry leaders discussed how artificial intelligence is changing financial analysis, software development and investment decisions. The event was organized by Karina Torres Castro, manager of research and innovation and assistant research professor in mechanical engineering, and it included the announcement of a new AI Innovation Lab in partnership with the financial technology company Broadridge. Students and faculty will work alongside industry experts in the lab to tackle challenges in AI and finance. The workshop included academic research presentations, industry perspectives and a panel discussion, and it was sponsored by the College of Engineering and Applied Sciences, the Long Island Manufacturing Extension Partnership, the Center of Excellence in Wireless and Information Technology and the AI Innovation Institute.

Amy Erickson, executive director of the Long Island Manufacturing Extension Partnership, said AI-driven financial modeling can help small and mid-sized manufacturers reduce waste and make better investment decisions without replacing skilled workers. She described the workshop as the first of several AI-focused programs her organization is rolling out for regional manufacturers. Andrew C. Singer, dean of the college, welcomed participants and introduced keynote speaker Robert J. Frey, research professor and founder of the university's Quantitative Finance Program. Frey, who has held leadership roles at Renaissance Technologies and other financial firms, compared the rise of AI with earlier technological advances that disrupted industries, saying some adjustments can be painful in the short term. He argued that stagnation is not the answer.

At Broadridge, AI is taking on more complex software development tasks, including some once assigned to entry-level employees. Roger Burkhardt, the company's chief technology officer of capital markets and AI, said the career ladder is changing and that new employees may be expected to define problems, evaluate AI-generated code and recognize security vulnerabilities. He encouraged students to experiment with AI development tools while learning to assess their output, and he said critical thinking and communicating with users are lasting skills. Jill Scher, managing director at CBIZ Advisors, began her accounting career in 1994 working with paper ledgers and red pencils, and she now uses AI to analyze financial statements and prepare for client meetings. Frey said that when AI is used properly, students will see it as a force multiplier that increases productivity rather than replacing them.

Pawel Polak, a faculty member in the Department of Applied Mathematics and Statistics, presented research on an international competition that attracted more than 1,000 registered participants to develop AI agents capable of writing code, forecasting financial trends and simulating markets. Some agents significantly improved the speed of existing software, but others struggled with unfamiliar problems. Teams that incorporated financial knowledge and agents required to explain their predictions generally performed better on new tasks, and Polak said human involvement definitely helps. Lav Varshney, professor of electrical and computer engineering and inaugural director of the AI Innovation Institute, argued that opaque "black box" AI may be less helpful because its inner workings are unknown. He described research using explicit, verifiable rules, with one possible application being financial transactions that fail to settle as expected, a context where traceability matters in regulated industries.

The afternoon panel, moderated by Yvette Wohn, inaugural chair of the Department of Technology, AI and Society, included Polak, Burkhardt, Scher and Melissa Brown, managing director of investment decision research at SimCorp. Brown said her team helps investors understand how unexpected economic developments might affect their portfolios, and she described an exercise considering what could happen if the Federal Reserve lost its independence. She said that work once took hours of searching historical data but now can be done by asking AI to identify similar past circumstances, which "takes five minutes rather than a day." Scher said some clients arrive with AI-generated tax analyses and ask her to confirm them, even when those analyses may overlook changing regulations or individual circumstances. Samir Das, chair of the Department of Computer Science, closed the workshop by announcing the AI Innovation Lab, which he said will focus on experiential learning and on how universities and industry can work together.

Articles.Title: Stony Brook FinTech Workshop Explores AI’s Impact on Finance, Announces New Industry Partnership

stories.Headline: Quectel Wireless Solutions: Quectel SP900BF-AP Smart Module Sets the Pace for Edge AI with 100 TOPS of Computing Power
stories.Summary:
Quectel Wireless Solutions announced the SP900BF-AP on November 11, 2026, in Munich, describing it as a smart module that lets robots, inspection systems and edge gateways run large AI models on the device itself. The module is built on the Qualcomm Dragonwing IQ-9075 Processor and delivers up to 100 TOPS of on-device AI compute. Industrial OEMs can use it to integrate advanced AI directly into their products, which the company says reduces latency, bandwidth costs and data privacy risks tied to cloud-based processing. Quectel presented the module as the product of close collaboration with Qualcomm Technologies, combining modular design with system-level optimisation.

By processing data locally, manufacturers can support real-time robotics, automated inspection and other demanding industrial applications while keeping greater control over sensitive production data. The module also offers long-term hardware availability to meet the extended product lifecycles that industrial customers require. Quectel commits to a product lifecycle of up to 10 years, which it says helps customers reduce inventory, maintenance and upgrade costs. The module is designed to run Ubuntu and Yocto Linux, with support for those systems described as currently in development. Its PCIe, USB 3.1, UART, SPI and I²C interfaces let OEMs add 4G/5G or Wi-Fi to suit each deployment.

Raymond Wang, Product Head, Smart at Quectel Wireless Solutions, said that the value of AI must ultimately be proven on the industrial front line. He said the company is providing a complete, ready-to-use edge intelligence solution that helps customers avoid complex low-level development. The module supports autonomous mobile robots with four-camera support, 3D perception and on-device navigation. It also supports production-line inspection with real-time defect detection, and edge AI gateways that run large language and vision-language models such as Qwen, DeepSeek, Gemma and LLaVA locally.

The module combines an octa-core Qualcomm Kryo CPU running at up to 2.36 GHz with an Adreno 663 GPU, a Hexagon DSP and a dedicated NPU. Memory options reach up to 36 GB LPDDR5X and 256 GB UFS, and the module supports real-time multi-stream video processing and multiple displays. The Dragonwing IQ-9075 processor's support for industrial real-time control and low-power design is described as helping balance performance with energy use. The company says the SP900BF-AP has completed key technical validation.

Engineering samples are now available to selected customers for solution evaluation and joint development. The articles state that attendees at Electronica can find the module and the complete Quectel IoT solutions portfolio on stand C2.601 at the show. Quectel describes itself as a global end-to-end IoT solutions provider with a worldwide team of over 10,000 professionals. The company's portfolio spans cellular, GNSS, satellite, Wi-Fi and Bluetooth modules, high-performance antennas, value-added services and turnkey offerings including ODM services and system integration. stories.Headline: A.I.Matics' AIM-T1 Named CES Innovation Awards® 2027 Honoree in Two Categories
stories.Summary:
A.I.Matics, a South Korean vision AI company, announced that its AIM-T1 AI vision inspection platform has been named a CES Innovation Awards 2027 Honoree in two categories, Artificial Intelligence and Construction & Industrial Tech. The award was announced on November 9 and 10, 2026, and the platform is aimed at electronics manufacturers that need to identify defects and adapt inspections to new products. The company says the system is built for quality, process and manufacturing engineers who work with camera modules, semiconductor packages and printed circuit board assemblies. Its recognition comes from the Consumer Technology Association, which organizes the program.

The announcement presents AIM-T1 as a response to a recurring problem in electronics production, where inspection has to stay consistent even as product designs and manufacturing requirements change. Introducing a new product can require manufacturers to gather defect images, revise inspection criteria and adjust imaging equipment, tasks that place extra demands on experienced inspectors and AI engineers. According to the company, AIM-T1 pairs modular imaging hardware with software-defined inspection so teams can adapt workflows on a common platform. The system uses reference samples of acceptable products to set inspection criteria and flag deviations that may signal defects. Its optical system uses liquid lens technology and electronic focus stacking to capture images at several focal planes without mechanical Z-axis movement, and camera resolution, lens magnification, lighting and inspection settings can be adjusted for different applications.

A.I.Matics is the party responsible for these claims, and the company describes the platform's aim as making inspection knowledge easier to reuse so that each product changeover depends less on specialized expertise. It says this matters for manufacturers reshoring production or adding regional capacity, since transferring inspection know-how helps new facilities come online. The company also plans to showcase AIM-T1 at CES 2027, taking place January 6 to 9 in Las Vegas, and to meet with manufacturers, automation equipment integrators and potential distribution partners. The CES notice adds that its awards are based on materials submitted to judges, that CTA did not verify the accuracy of submissions or claims, and that CTA did not test the product. Booth and meeting details are to be announced once confirmed.

A.I.Matics is a subsidiary of Dreamtech and began as an in-house venture at Hyundai Motor Company in 2000, before being incorporated in 2003. The company built its expertise by supplying lane departure warning systems to automakers and now develops AI solutions for transportation, logistics and manufacturing. Its portfolio also includes AI-powered driver safety cameras, the aid fleet management platform, intelligent process and operations management tools, and AI chatbots for logistics call centers. The company says it will continue pursuing industry partnerships at the show, and further product information is available on its vision website.

stories.Headline: Kyndryl Uses Agentic AI to Accelerate Enterprise Modernization with AWS
stories.Summary:
Kyndryl, a provider of mission-critical enterprise technology services, announced on November 5, 2026 an integrated agentic modernization solution with Amazon Web Services. The solution pairs Kyndryl Agentic Modernization services-as-software with AWS Transform to help customers modernize applications quickly, reduce transformation risk and build AI-ready technology foundations. Kyndryl's services-as-software capability, AI-enabled workflows and engineering expertise are combined with AWS Transform so organizations can assess, plan and carry out modernization at scale. The approach is meant to let customers modernize applications, infrastructure and core systems faster, with more consistency and lower risk. Shawn D'Souza, Global Modernization Leader at Kyndryl, said many organizations still treat modernization as a destination when it should be an ongoing business capability.

He said organizations that can keep modernizing will be better placed to adopt AI and adapt to change. Kyndryl's first global modernization report found that nearly 50% of respondents were behind schedule on their modernization goals. Early adopters that deployed agentic AI in production reported stronger results, with 67% saying they were ahead of or on track, compared with 51% of other organizations. Through the solution, joint customers can accelerate projects by taking a continuous approach to modernization, build resilient and AI-ready architectures, and reduce technical debt while improving operational efficiency. Kyndryl describes services-as-software as an emerging model that delivers services through software-driven automation and scalable digital workflows.

Built on the Kyndryl Agentic Framework and scaled through Kyndryl Bridge, it lets companies run complex modernization programs on compressed timelines and at lower cost by reusing pre-built agentic workflows. Customers also gain access to Kyndryl's expertise in cloud, security, compliance, FinOps and mission-critical operations. Kyndryl is a launch partner for AWS Transform and has worked with AWS to help customers move beyond project-based modernization to a repeatable approach for continuously evolving their technology environments. Kyndryl describes itself as offering advisory, implementation and managed services to thousands of customers in more than 60 countries. The company says it is the world's largest IT infrastructure services provider.

Separately, on November 10, 2026, Denodo announced a multi-year strategic collaboration agreement with AWS focused on helping enterprises scale agentic AI on real-time, governed data across hybrid and multi-cloud environments. Key initiatives include customer workshops, co-marketing, field alignment and co-selling, commercial incentives for evaluations and AWS Marketplace purchases, and solution offerings with systems integrators. Denodo CEO Ángel Viña said the collaboration gives joint customers a unified AI data layer so agents can access live, governed data without moving or replicating it. Allison Johnson, Director of Americas Technology Partners at AWS, said the collaboration helps customers extend the value of their AWS AI investments across their data estate.

stories.Headline: Drug Ads Can Influence AI Treatment Recommendations, Study Finds
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai reported on November 11, 2026, in the online issue of The Lancet Digital Health that a clearly labeled pharmaceutical advertisement can shift which treatment an artificial intelligence model recommends. The team tested 12 AI models from companies including Google, OpenAI and Anthropic. They gave the models physician-written clinical cases, sometimes preceded by a real drug ad and sometimes without one. The study was published in the Nov. 11 online issue of the journal.

Across 33 clinical scenarios, the advertised drug was selected in 47.6% of responses when an ad was present, compared with 35% without one. In four cases, models went from never selecting the advertised drug to selecting it 100% of the time once the ad appeared. The researchers analyzed 258,559 AI responses, assessing both which treatment was chosen and whether it matched clinical guidance. The shift often occurred among options that were all clinically reasonable, which made the influence easy to overlook.

Mahmud Omar, MD, a physician-scientist and lecturer in the Windreich Department of Artificial Intelligence and Human Health, who is first author, said the answers often appeared reasonable and that the influence could be easy to miss in typical research evaluations. Senior author Girish N. Nadkarni, MD, MPH, chair of the department and chief AI officer of the Mount Sinai Health System, said that as AI becomes part of how people get health information, clinical guidance must be distinguished from commercial influence. In a subset of free-text responses, models explicitly mentioned the ad in only 29.9% of responses, though they repeated its claims more often. The investigators cautioned that the ads did not clearly increase recommendations for unsupported supplements or clearly suboptimal drugs.

The researchers did not examine whether the changes in AI recommendations affected prescriptions, patient decisions, costs or health outcomes. They recommended testing AI systems with and without promotional content, clearly disclosing when advertising is presented to an AI system, and keeping promotional material separate from clinical advice. The study may also matter to regulators weighing how existing rules on pharmaceutical advertising apply when promotional content becomes part of AI-generated health information. The Mount Sinai team plans to extend the work through its ongoing evaluation of AI and human-AI interaction in real-world clinical cases.

stories.Headline: GITEX World RobotiX 2026 brings humanoid debuts and next-gen embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI) to Dubai
stories.Summary:
GITEX World RobotiX, a new launch event at GITEX GLOBAL, will take place from 8 to 11 December 2026 at Dubai Exhibition Centre in Expo City Dubai. The event will bring together robotics pioneers and embodied AI leaders to show how machines that perceive, reason and act in the physical world are transforming manufacturing, logistics, healthcare, hospitality and smart infrastructure. GITEX GLOBAL 2026 opens with the GITEX Summit on 7 December at Dubai World Trade Centre, ahead of the exhibition. The event follows reports that more than 22,000 humanoid robots were shipped globally in the first half of 2026, a 300 percent year-on-year increase according to Counterpoint Research. Shipments are expected to exceed 50,000 units by the end of the year.

Dubai is also pursuing robotics through its Robotics and Automation Program, which targets deploying 200,000 robots over 10 years to 2032. Unitree, cited as one of the world's largest humanoid makers with a 31 percent global market share, leads this year's participation. Other headline exhibitors include UBTECH, whose humanoids are deployed in car factories and being tested by Airbus, and AiMOGA, Chery Auto's embodied AI robotics brand. DEEP Robotics, a global leader in quadrupeds, will also attend, along with the UAE's Micropolis Robotics, which provides autonomous patrol robots for Dubai Police.

UAE-based Mangobot, a robotics solutions provider, will present autonomous general-purpose robots, patrol robots, multilingual robot receptionists and live robotic performances. Visitors can also try wearable exoskeleton technology. Mazen El-Kurdi, CTO of Mangobot, said that the focus is on what working alongside robots actually feels like. Making its Middle East debut, MOS 2 from Chinese innovator Lumos Robotics is a wheeled AI Worker with dual arms that can handle payloads of up to 50 kg and operate for more than eight hours. Lumos Robotics says its first-generation MOS robots completed over 1,000 hours of continuous operation at Mitsubishi Electric's Changshu factory.

UAE-based Lootah Robotics will show humanoid, quadruped, service, cleaning and telepresence robots from manufacturers including Unitree, AGIBOT, Pudu Robotics, UBTECH and EngineAI. Its general manager, Hazem Ghazal, said the company is building an integrated robotics ecosystem in which organisations can select different robots for different requirements. China's Light Origins will make its first public appearance of a bunny-shaped robot, with live household demonstrations. Its co-founder and CTO, Tingxiang Fan, said the company believes the robot is ready to enter consumers' homes. Raydiculous, from the Chengdu Humanoid Robot Innovation Centre, will make its Middle East debut with the TP01 humanoid, which can communicate in English and Arabic, and the DINOBOT bipedal walking bionic dinosaur.

Besomi, a UAE technology and robotics education company, will introduce six humanoid and mobile robots called the Besomi Rangers, with Unitree, Seeed Studio, Arduino and Qualcomm joining it on the stand. A live Robotics & AI Lab will offer hands-on training using the Arduino VENTUNO platform, developed with Qualcomm. Its CEO, Mohammad Hani, said the aim is to encourage young engineers to build the next generation of robotics technologies in the UAE. Chinese developer JWIPC will launch robotic controllers built on NVIDIA's Thor module, which the company says delivers up to 2,070 TFLOPS of FP4 computing performance. Nick Zhang, Regional Sales Manager at JWIPC, said the module provides a high-compute edge brain for embodied intelligence.

Songying Technology will demonstrate ORCA OS and ORCA Lab, a connected robotics development environment covering simulation, synthetic data generation, AI training, validation and deployment. Taiwan-based Vecow will unveil rugged Edge AI and robotics platforms and introduce its dedicated UAE team. The GITEX GLOBAL Expo runs for four days at Dubai Exhibition Centre alongside Expand North Star, a startup and investor event. The 46th edition of GITEX GLOBAL, organised by inD, is expected to bring together more than 6,000 enterprise and startup exhibitors and tens of thousands of government leaders, executives, investors and buyers from 180 countries.

stories.Headline: Lafayette City Council rejects proposed new downtown AI bar - KATC
stories.Summary:
The Lafayette City Council met late into the night on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, and voted down a proposed high-tech bar in downtown Lafayette. The decision followed concerns about safety in the downtown area, and the club's owner had planned to use artificial intelligence bartenders to staff it. The proposed venue, called Plush, was to occupy the former Bliss cocktail lounge. Its owner, entrepreneur Quintin Borel, described a model in which patrons would scan a barcode and order from their seats, with a machine preparing the drink and a server delivering it.

Borel argued that the system would reduce disturbance and traffic movement and let him manage the venue as he wished. The Downtown Development Authority opposed the plan, and its board had passed a resolution a couple of weeks earlier asking the council to vote no. Kevin Blanchard, the authority's CEO, said the environment downtown on weekends after midnight was unsafe and cited a lot of chaos and violence on the streets. He said the authority had raised that concern for some time. The articles do not say what Borel plans to do next.

The vote came as one local outlet was reporting unrelated downtown news, but the articles do not connect the two stories. The council's action was the central event, and the articles present it as a response to downtown safety rather than a ruling on the technology itself. Borel's stated goal was to offer a more convenient and better-organized experience for guests. The reporting makes clear that the opposition centered on weekend conditions downtown rather than on the use of automated service.

Acadiana News First, which published the most detailed account, reported the vote in an article posted on November 11, 2026. The coverage describes the council's decision as final for the proposal as submitted, though the articles do not state any further procedural steps. No additional timeline for the venue or any reconsideration is provided in the reporting. The sources agree on the basic outcome and the stated reasons, and they leave Borel's next move unresolved.

stories.Summary:
SAP SE announced on November 10, 2026, in Walldorf, Germany, that AstraZeneca, a global biopharmaceutical company, is migrating to SAP Cloud ERP Private through the RISE with SAP journey. The move expands a relationship between the two companies that spans 20 years. It is described as a full-estate migration that extends one of the largest SAP footprints in life sciences. The articles say the change simplifies and standardizes AstraZeneca's technology landscape, which they describe as helping create a more agile and resilient digital foundation. The stated aim is to let the company move faster, make better-informed decisions and deliver value for its stakeholders.

Through its Axial Business Transformation Programme, AstraZeneca is moving from legacy environments in SAP ERP Central Component to SAP Cloud ERP Private. The articles say this supports more standardized ways of working, harmonized data and connected processes across the enterprise. AstraZeneca is also exploring business AI capabilities from SAP, including the Industry AI portfolio, the Joule solution and agentic use cases across finance, supply chain and manufacturing. The articles say these capabilities could enhance productivity, strengthen data quality and governance, and enable faster decision-making. They add that the SAP Business Data Cloud solution can help build a clean data core, while the SAP Green Ledger solution can connect sustainability and business data across the value chain.

AstraZeneca's Chief Information Officer, Chris Taylor, said that SAP has been a key part of how the company runs its operations for more than two decades. Taylor said the partnership is about more than modernizing technology, and that Axial is intended to simplify operations and create the foundations to move faster and unlock greater value from AI. Thomas Saueressig, SAP's Chief Customer Officer and a member of its Executive Board, said companies across life sciences and healthcare are rethinking how technology can help them manage complexity. He said AstraZeneca's programme shows how cloud, data and AI can create a stronger foundation for innovation at scale. The articles say SAP and AstraZeneca both describe the migration as a means to faster decisions and trusted insights for patients.

AstraZeneca is described as a global, science-led biopharmaceutical company focused on discovering, developing and commercializing prescription medicines. Its areas include oncology, rare disease, cardiovascular, renal and metabolism, respiratory and immunology. SAP's stock is listed on the NYSE under the symbol SAP. stories.Headline: U.S. and China should stay clear-eyed on AI cooperation and competition, says Scott Bessent
stories.Summary:
Scott Bessent, the U.S. Treasury Secretary, said on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, in prepared remarks to the National Committee on U.S.-China Relations in New York, that the United States and China should harbor no illusions about their differences on artificial intelligence. He said the two countries must cooperate to mitigate the technology's risks while competing for AI supremacy. Bessent, who will travel to China next week, said he wanted to build a constructive relationship on the basis of balance and reciprocity. He described the meeting in Shenzhen, to be held on the sidelines of the November 18-19 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders summit, as the place where a new bilateral dialogue on "superintelligence" would advance. The dialogue is meant to guard against shared risks and prevent misunderstanding between the two systems.

Bessent said the two sides expect to exchange best practices for evaluating and testing advanced models before their release, and for keeping human judgment in command of the technology. The two sides had agreed to establish a direct channel for alerting each other to serious incidents. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping agreed on this AI alert system during their previous meeting at the White House in September. At that time, Trump said he was reluctant to add new guardrails because he wanted to preserve U.S. leadership. Bessent said that as superintelligence advances, the need for new areas of risk management will grow as well.

Bessent's remarks did not mention the controversy surrounding Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Nvidia's board is investigating Huang after a New York Times report said he had an affair with a businesswoman suspected by U.S. security services of being a Chinese intelligence asset. China's Foreign Ministry called the spying accusations "groundless" and "a smear." Nvidia has said its board has no reason to believe U.S. national security or company secrets were compromised, and that Huang has committed to cooperating with the internal review. Huang has told employees he was unfaithful to his wife but gave no details about the relationship, and it was unclear whether Trump would bring him to the APEC summit.

Bessent also referred to trade initiatives agreed during the two previous Trump-Xi summits. These include a "Board of Trade" to determine mutual tariff cuts on $30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction, and China's pledged purchases of U.S. farm goods. A similarly structured "Board of Investment" will address market access for American companies in China and what he called increased predictability for Chinese companies. He said the U.S. trade deficit with China remains a source of friction, but the U.S. objective is to de-risk, not to decouple, from trade with China. A fourth Trump-Xi summit this year is expected in December at the U.S.-hosted G20 summit in Miami.

Separately, China became the first of the 38 founding members to approve the World AI Cooperation Organization, a body China proposed and hosts. The approval was made at the 25th session of the Standing Committee of the 14th National People's Congress. Xi unveiled the organization at a July event combining the 2026 World Artificial Intelligence Conference with a high-level meeting on global AI governance. The organization's stated purpose is to help countries benefit from AI's opportunities. China says preparations are continuing ahead of full operations and invites more countries to join.

stories.Headline: Software Transparency Is Changing: Allan Friedman on SBOM, AI BOMs and What Comes Next
stories.Summary:
Allan Friedman, a cybersecurity policy expert who helped drive early government and industry work on the Software Bill of Materials, discussed the evolution of software transparency on the SecurityWeek Podcast, hosted by Brian Schleifer. The conversation covered SBOMs, AI Bills of Materials, vulnerability management and the Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange. Friedman described software as assembled rather than written, noting that what it is assembled from is more software. The interview was reported in articles published on November 10 and November 11, 2026.

Friedman said producing an SBOM is not the end goal, since the real value lies in what organizations and their suppliers do with the information. He argued that a supplier able to generate an accurate SBOM shows an early sign of supply chain maturity. During a Log4j-style vulnerability or a malicious update, that capability lets suppliers determine exposure quickly and shortens response time for customers. He also said SBOM data should feed vulnerability management, asset management, procurement and continuous risk management instead of sitting as a static document.

Friedman identified the Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange as a companion to the SBOM, providing a machine-processable way to say whether a vulnerability actually affects a product. He said this helps separate the presence of a vulnerable component from an exploitable condition, which matters as security teams face growing volumes of vulnerability data. He also described the emergence of AI BOMs, which would document the model, its supporting data, external data sources and the infrastructure used to operate the system. Friedman argued that transparency should favour defenders, because attackers can already identify components through reverse engineering while defenders need visibility across thousands of systems.

Friedman suggested that the different transparency mechanisms, including cryptographic and hardware bills of materials, could eventually converge, which he jokingly called an "omnibomb." The articles note that interoperability remains a challenge, since two quality SBOM tools analyzing the same software may produce different dependency graphs. Friedman pointed to continuing work among governments, cybersecurity agencies, industry and the open source community to define expectations for the SBOM ecosystem. The articles state that the stated goal is continuous software transparency that supports rapid risk decisions.

stories.Headline: Cloud engineering teams must protect AI agent data in use
stories.Summary:
Cloud engineering teams at financial companies are facing a security problem that encryption alone cannot solve, as AI agents move into production on Kubernetes. Container orchestration has become the default foundation for AI workloads, and the data those agents use is now the main target. Payment networks feel this pressure more than most because every transaction carries customer data and regulatory exposure. Protecting data while it is being processed, not just while it is stored or moving, has become central to running agents at scale, according to Krishna Mayuram, senior principal engineer and vice president of cloud engineering at Mastercard Inc. He spoke with theCUBE Research's John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA during an exclusive broadcast.

Mayuram described confidential computing as launching applications in highly secure, virtualized or confidential containers, which lets a company protect data in use. He said his company has already protected data at rest and data in motion, and asked what happens to data in use. Mastercard runs its platforms on Red Hat Inc.'s OpenShift, a Kubernetes platform that Red Hat is extending to support AI agents. Red Hat has also brought confidential containers to OpenShift on bare metal. Mayuram explained that agents act much like microservices and need the same elastic infrastructure.

Scale raises the risk, particularly for a company that operates under the laws of many countries. Mastercard recently added trust services for agentic commerce. Internally, Mayuram said the same idea applies, with guardrails at every step from development to deployment. He said the business and the industry are distributed and subject to different laws, so all of these things need to be covered by guardrails. In his view, whether the workload is agents or regular applications, the guardrails and enterprise security remain the same.

The tribal college article reaches a related conclusion for a different set of institutions. Tribal colleges and universities are using artificial intelligence across institutional operations, teaching and learning, and technology initiatives. The tools offer opportunities to expand capacity and improve efficiency, but they also bring responsibilities for protecting institutional and tribal data. The article, written by Chad J. Davis and dated November 10, 2026, says these colleges are building a secure, localized, and culturally informed AI environment. They are doing so through professional and workforce development, training faculty, staff, and students on the responsible and secure use of AI tools.

The American Indian Higher Education Consortium has partnered with the National Institutes of Health through its AIM-AHEAD initiative. Eric Johnson, the consortium's health initiatives communication coordinator, said participants are learning how to use AI responsibly, with an understanding of data sovereignty, privacy, ethics, and community trust. Many programs start with publicly available and practice datasets before participants work with sensitive tribal data. Colleges are also developing policies and establishing AI committees, and Sarah Barott, an English instructor at Red Lake Nation College, described shared governance guided by the seven grandfather values. The article notes that some colleges are strengthening tribal institutional review board protocols for AI-enabled research.

Cybersecurity is treated as equally essential in the tribal college article. Colleges are upgrading their cyberinfrastructure while balancing research data sharing, and the National Science Foundation Tribal Colleges and Universities Program supported Lac Courte Oreilles Ojibwe University and other colleges in enhancing their security. Tristan Stevens, the university's director of information technology, said the strategy and skills training contributed to building a human firewall across campus. Colleges are also classifying institutional data to comply with institutional policies, tribal laws, state and federal regulations, including FERPA, and they apply identity and access management and encryption to restrict sensitive data by role. Some colleges are building on-premises AI capabilities so that sensitive tribal information and Native languages are not used to train public, open-source models.

stories.Headline: Google's $10 million plan to buy Spirit's data and use it to train AI cleared one of its last big hurdles
stories.Summary:
Spirit Airlines shut down in May 2026, and its assets were then put up for auction. Google won the bid to pay $10 million for a large body of company data, including 500 million Microsoft Teams chats, 100 million emails, and other internal documents. Google has said the data would help improve its products and AI models. The sale stalled in bankruptcy court over privacy concerns, and on November 11, 2026, reports said it had cleared one of its last major obstacles.

The breakthrough came after the Association of Flight Attendants and other unions reached a deal with Google to protect the personal data of former Spirit staff, and they then withdrew their objections to the sale. Under the agreement, data covering employees' medical and disability history, drug or alcohol testing records, and payroll records would be excluded. The unions also secured a more rigorous de-identification process than had originally been planned, and Google is barred from trying to re-identify the information. Earlier, a court-appointed privacy ombudsman had recommended approval after personal information about 97 million Spirit customers was excluded.

The union called the agreement a historic win for worker privacy protections. Sara Nelson, international president of the AFA-CWA, said that worker data privacy in the age of AI has become a new worker's rights issue, and that without the union no one would have spoken for workers in the sale. She said the union would now seek similar contractual protections with other employers and urge lawmakers to protect workers through federal and state law. Last month, 121 members of Congress, led by Senator Elizabeth Warren, had raised concerns about the deal. Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment, though it had earlier said it was not looking to buy any personal information from Spirit and that such information would either be excluded or de-identified by an independent third party before Google received any data.

stories.Headline: AI-assisted reverse engineering challenges proprietary software
stories.Summary:
Nishant Tiwari, a software engineer at PayPal, used an AI-assisted reverse-engineering workflow to examine Uber's pricing and inspect the company's web application. His analysis of Uber's client-side code identified scripts that appeared to access battery status and other device information, including browser and hardware attributes. He tested the same ride across four phones, three Android devices and an iPhone, repeating the experiment five to six times. He found a correlation between battery levels and fares. The findings were enabled by open-source tools such as Reverse Engineering Anything, a GitHub project created by a user named morluto, who declined to take part in the story.

The project connects AI agents to reverse-engineering tools that help developers examine software and infer how it works. It has more than 447,000 stars on GitHub, up from about 10,000 in early October, placing it among the platform's five most-starred repositories. Experts say AI makes it simpler for developers to inspect software and infer its functionality, which challenges proprietary software models and raises intellectual property questions. For companies selling proprietary software, the central question is how much of a product's functionality customers can reconstruct from the code and behaviour available to them.

Security researcher Himanshu Anand says reverse engineering once required considerable expertise, including interpreting assembly instructions. He says large language models have lowered that barrier, and estimates a task that once took a month could now take "one or two hours." Abhishek Agarwal, President of Judge India, says AI can help developers identify relevant functions, but much of a product's behaviour may depend on a private service that a recreated feature would not reproduce. Agarwal suggests comparing conventional and AI-assisted reverse engineering under similar conditions, measuring reliability and the human effort required. Anand dismisses fears that the tools will end software as we know it, comparing them to concerns that open source would end Microsoft.

On the legal side, Bharadwaj Jaishankar-Bharadwaj, a partner at CMS INDUSLAW, says copyright protects software code as a literary work but not ideas. Shantanu Sahay, a litigation partner at Anand & Anand, believes recreating a feature does not automatically infringe copyright, since the question depends on what was copied and whether it is protected. Section 52(1)(ac) of India's Copyright Act permits observing, studying or testing a program to determine its underlying ideas, while Section 52(1)(ab) covers acts necessary for interoperability, subject to conditions. These provisions do not grant blanket permission to copy or commercially reproduce software. Sahay adds that licence and non-disclosure agreements can also restrict decompilation.

Agarwal advises companies to treat client applications and binaries as inspectable rather than relying on unpublished source code. He says obfuscation and anti-tampering measures may only delay analysis. He recommends moving core business logic off distributed clients where practical, removing secrets from builds, tightening API boundaries, monitoring for repeated probing, and reviewing binaries and front ends at release. He says the design question should shift to what happens when an AI agent can inspect a product repeatedly and cheaply. For enterprise software companies, the risk is whether AI can produce a reliable substitute for a feature customers pay for.

stories.Headline: Anthropic wants Claude to join your meetings
stories.Summary:
Anthropic has announced Claude Meetings, a feature that lets its Claude AI assistant join video calls as a visible participant and start working on tasks while people are still talking. The announcement came on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, alongside new workplace tools including Claude Whiteboards, Claude Sheets, Claude Data and interactive connectors. During a call, Claude can take notes, draft the plan being discussed, map out a timeline, answer questions in the meeting chat, and pull information from connected work apps. Afterward, notes, action items and other work products are available inside Claude. Claude Meetings is launching in beta for Team and Enterprise customers, while Whiteboards and Sheets are launching in beta for paid subscribers.

Claude Data, previously called Claude Dashboards, lets workers query company data and generate dashboards, written reports and narrated videos, and it is now broadly available with some new features still in beta. Anthropic is also expanding its integrations so users can open full versions of applications from partners including Adobe, Atlassian and HubSpot without leaving Claude. The company has tested Claude Meetings internally for about two months, and according to Nicholas Lin, its product lead for knowledge work, the assistant now takes part in nearly all of its meetings. Lin said Claude can surface information participants don't have on hand, create slides and other materials as people talk, and track action items for follow-up. For now Claude mostly waits for instructions, though Lin said Anthropic expects to make it more proactive over time.

Anthropic's aim is to make Claude as central to knowledge workers as it already is for many software developers. Lin acknowledged that Claude has changed how developers work, while other knowledge workers have not seen the same transformation, and he said Anthropic wants those workers to be able to move just as quickly. The launch comes a few weeks after OpenAI unveiled its own workplace tools for ChatGPT, and the companies are competing to turn their products into office suites that can challenge Microsoft and Google. Meta is also competing in this space with its Muse AI agent, which can build mini-apps on the fly to help users complete specific tasks. The articles do not say how the companies' products will perform against one another or how widely these features will be adopted.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave targets 2028 profitability as AI demand remains strong
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave, the AI cloud company backed by Nvidia, said on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, that it expects to turn a profit on an adjusted basis in the first half of 2028. Executives made the announcement as they tried to reassure investors that strong demand and customer commitments could support the company's debt-fueled expansion. Shares were last up about 5% in volatile extended trading after falling more than 40% over the past month. The slide was driven by fears of an AI bubble, with investors worried about heavy borrowing to build data centers while interest rates rise.

The company's CEO, Mike Intrator, disclosed that CoreWeave holds $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits expected to flow in over the next three months. CoreWeave said it would not tap unsecured debt markets at current yields, relying instead on cash flow from existing customer commitments to repay debt. Its contracted revenue backlog reached $132.5 billion at the end of September, up from $104 billion at the end of June. Quarterly capital spending rose to $14.5 billion from $9.4 billion in the prior quarter. The company had about $46.9 billion in total debt as of the end of September.

Intrator said in a statement that customer contracts come first and investment follows, so lenders have something concrete to lend against and customers typically help fund the buildout. He argued that because CoreWeave's investments are tied to committed demand, its borrowing rests on that demand. The company has never turned a profit, according to data compiled by LSEG. Its customer roster includes Microsoft, Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic.

CoreWeave now expects 2026 revenue of between $13.0 billion and $13.3 billion, up from a previous range of $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion. It also raised the lower end of its annual spending target by $2 billion, now projecting $37 billion to $39 billion. Third-quarter revenue surged nearly 170% to $3.66 billion, beating estimates of $3.55 billion, and its per-share loss of 95 cents was smaller than the $1.16 loss analysts expected. The stock's fall also prompted a wider loss of confidence in the AI trade, which was amplified by Democrats' sweeping win in the US midterm elections and expectations of tighter regulation of data-center construction. Recent earnings reports from large cloud providers also hinted at delays in data-center projects and a slower ramp in spending.

stories.Headline: Cloud native developer population hits 21.2 million globally
stories.Summary:
The Cloud Native Computing Foundation and SlashData reported that the global cloud native developer population reached 21.2 million in the third quarter of 2026. The figure rose from 15.6 million a year earlier and from 19.9 million in the first quarter of 2026. Cloud native developers now make up about 41 per cent of all developers worldwide. The report was published in November 2026 and covered by TechGig and The New Stack. The report found that 75 per cent of cloud native developers use AI coding tools, compared with 55 per cent of non-cloud native developers.

Sixty-seven per cent of cloud native developers are integrating AI into their services, against 38 per cent of their non-cloud native counterparts. Among those integrating AI, 49 per cent reported having agentic systems in production. In North America, 21 per cent of cloud native developers use AI to draft code before reviewing it, while 12 per cent use autonomous agents for coding tasks. Developers who have not yet added AI functionality cited cost, data privacy and security as their primary concerns. The report was produced by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation and SlashData.

Liam Bollmann-Dodd, principal market research consultant at SlashData, said that cloud native maturity is becoming an important indicator of how actively developers engage with AI. The report also shows that 93 per cent of developers now work at organisations using some form of DevOps standardisation or internal developer platform, up from 77 per cent in the third quarter of 2025. Platform engineering is therefore becoming standard practice. Among backend developers, 40 per cent use API gateways, 30 per cent use microservices, 21 per cent use observability tools and 19 per cent use Kubernetes.

The figures come from the same CNCF and SlashData report. The New Stack headlined its coverage with the 75 per cent figure and an explanation from Jonathan Bryce. The articles give no further background on how the survey was conducted. The articles do not say what will happen next.

stories.Headline: The Odds of an AI Bubble-Bursting Event Appear to Be Sharply Rising
stories.Summary:
A Motley Fool piece published Nov. 10, 2026, by analyst Sean Williams argues that the odds of an AI bubble-bursting event are rising, pointing to three developments. The first came on Election Night, when Democrats retook both houses of Congress in the midterms and Democratic candidates flipped at least five governorships previously held by Republicans, with two races still uncalled by the Associated Press as of Nov. 6. The flipped seats include Texas, Georgia and Ohio, all central to data center planning and construction. Williams also points to tightening lending conditions for so-called neoclouds and some large cloud companies, along with a stock market that is historically expensive.

On the numbers, Cleanview data cited in the article says 41% of America's planned data center capacity, or 158.6 GW across nine states, sits in states where the governor backs a pause on development. Texas leads with 88.4 GW, followed by Ohio at 21.9 GW, Georgia at 20.2 GW, New Mexico at 11.0 GW and New York at 9.9 GW. Williams notes that President Donald Trump has pledged to minimize AI regulation and threatened to use his veto to keep the status quo in Congress, but that a veto cannot touch state-level changes made by Democratic governors. He adds that the market entered 2026 at its second-highest valuation in 156 years by the Shiller price-to-earnings ratio. That measure has topped 30 during a continuous bull market six times in the past century, including now, and the previous five were followed by declines of 20% or more in at least one major index.

Several people and groups are named as responsible for the shifts. Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa has vowed to impose a moratorium on new data center approvals until the legislature passes laws covering electricity and water rights, among other issues. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, speaking after the Federal Open Market Committee's Oct. 28 meeting, said interest rates have had an effect and that market participants are discriminating between the kinds of investments they want to make. He said credit spreads for certain assets have widened sharply, which Williams reads as a sign that borrowing is becoming less favorable for neoclouds, a view he says is backed by falling corporate bond prices for those firms and some hyperscalers.

A second article, from the Idaho Dispatch on Nov. 6, looks at the same risk locally, citing an October 2026 report from the Open Markets Institute and Americans for Financial Reform Education Fund that warns heavy, debt-financed AI spending could cause problems well beyond the technology industry. In Idaho, data center projects qualifying with at least $250 million in investment and 30 jobs can receive sales tax exemptions, and bills to cap that break failed in 2025 and 2026. Lawmakers did pass House Bill 911 in 2026 to keep the costs of serving large electricity customers from falling on existing ratepayers, and House Bill 895 to limit certain water use for cooling new data centers. A federal lawsuit filed in September over Idaho's authority to administer federal water rights at Idaho National Laboratory, and a Bannock County moratorium on data center permit applications in unincorporated areas, show the debate there is still unfolding.

stories.Headline: NVIDIA scrutiny, US selloff challenge India's AI cloud boom
stories.Summary:
A selloff in US-listed neocloud companies and growing scrutiny of NVIDIA have raised questions about the financing model behind the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom. Investors have been selling shares of US neocloud companies since September, with CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN seeing sharp corrections. The selling intensified through October and into November, as concerns mounted over the sustainability of AI infrastructure spending and the debt these companies have taken on. These developments could affect India's GPU cloud providers, which face questions about debt exposure, customer commitments and GPU depreciation. Political and regulatory resistance to data centre expansion in the US could also slow infrastructure investment.

Neoclouds provide GPU compute to customers that may not have the scale or resources to build their own infrastructure. Their business models are capital-intensive, and NVIDIA has supported the ecosystem through strategic investments and financing arrangements. India is increasingly part of this buildout, serving subsidised compute under the IndiaAI Mission and commercial workloads. The IndiaAI Mission had onboarded over 45,000 GPUs by June 2026 and approved 237 projects by August, with 93.18 lakh GPU hours sanctioned. Sanctioned hours do not necessarily translate into sustained usage, so Indian neoclouds are betting on commercial customers to justify their spending.

Unlike US peers backed by large hyperscaler customers such as Meta and OpenAI, Indian neoclouds have limited domestic anchor demand. International customers account for 75 to 80 per cent of Yotta's customer base. Yotta plans to spend over $7 billion on AI infrastructure by the end of FY27 and is targeting a $1.5 billion initial public offering. The IndiaAI Mission utilised less than half its FY26 outlay of ₹10,000 crore, which has affected hardware procurement and deployment timelines. Juspay's co-founder and COO Sheetal Lalwani said the company had been told it would wait three to six months to receive GPUs it is buying with its own cash.

NeevCloud said its engagement with NVIDIA covers technical planning, GPU availability and deployment readiness, while procurement and financing are separate arrangements. Narendra Sen, founder of NeevCloud and RackBank Datacenters, said the market correction reinforces the need for discipline in assessing each project's commercial viability. ESDS said it has no direct commercial or financing relationship with NVIDIA and buys systems from Supermicro, Dell, Lenovo and WWT. Piyush Somani, founder of ESDS, said the company commits capital expenditure only after a customer pays at least 35 per cent of the project cost. NVIDIA offered a revenue-sharing and credit-support model to neoclouds globally in July but later paused some deals, The Wall Street Journal reported.

The Government of India has noted that its compute ecosystem relies on globally sourced GPUs, so changes in chip availability, export controls, pricing or allocation could affect deployment schedules and project economics. Lenders and investors are now favouring projects with confirmed customers, predictable revenues and substantial upfront advances. Sen added that older GPUs could face more pricing pressure as newer generations arrive. Closer to home, ESDS closed at about ₹1,147.25 on November 9, against a September 24 high of ₹1,864.35. E2E Networks ended at around ₹490.50, well below its October 14 high of ₹769.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave raises 2026 revenue forecast on AI infrastructure demand; shares surge
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave, the Nvidia-backed cloud provider, raised its full-year 2026 revenue forecast on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, citing stronger demand for its artificial intelligence infrastructure. Its shares rose nearly 13% in extended trading. The company now expects 2026 revenue of $13 billion to $13.3 billion, up from its earlier forecast and analyst consensus of $12.9 billion. It also lifted its adjusted operating income outlook to $1.275 billion to $1.375 billion, a 26% increase at the midpoint from its earlier guidance.

Executives said on an earnings call that they expect CoreWeave to turn profitable on an adjusted basis in the first half of 2028. The company is racing to deploy data center capacity as AI companies and cloud providers compete to secure computing infrastructure. Capital spending jumped to $14.5 billion in the third quarter from $9.4 billion in the prior quarter. CoreWeave raised the lower end of its 2026 capital expenditure forecast to $37 billion from $35 billion, keeping the upper end at $39 billion, and said the higher spending reflects expectations of deploying infrastructure to customers ahead of schedule. It still expects more than 1.85 gigawatts of active power by year-end.

For the third quarter, CoreWeave reported revenue of $3.66 billion, up from $1.37 billion a year earlier and above analyst estimates of $3.54 billion. Its adjusted loss was $1.27 per share, narrower than the expected loss of $1.55 per share. However, the company reported a net loss of $709 million, compared with a loss of $110 million a year earlier. Net interest expense rose to $846 million from $310 million, and the company forecast fourth-quarter interest expense of $1.05 billion to $1.15 billion. Its debt stood at about $47 billion as of September 30.

CoreWeave said it added more than 200 megawatts of active power during the quarter, bringing its total to more than 1.7 gigawatts. Its revenue backlog was approximately $132.5 billion at the end of September. The articles describe the company as sitting at the heart of the AI debt boom, having taken on large amounts of debt to fund its expansion of computing capacity, which leaves it vulnerable to any slowdown in AI development. Before the announcement, its shares had fallen nearly 58% over the past month as investors worried about rising debt levels and signs of an AI bubble.

stories.Headline: DEPDev backs EO to create National AI Council
stories.Summary:
The Philippine Department of Economy, Planning, and Development, known as DEPDev, said on Monday that it hopes the government can issue an executive order this month creating a National Artificial Intelligence Council. Economy Undersecretary Rosemarie G. Edillon told reporters on the sidelines of a briefing that the proposal for the council follows the finalization of the National AI Governance Framework. She said the framework has already been approved by the National Innovation Council. Edillon expressed hope that the order could be issued within two weeks. The report was published on November 10, 2026.

Under the proposal, the council would oversee technical working groups, with one group assigned to each of the six pillars of the AI Governance Framework. Those pillars are enabling resources, research and development and data, capabilities, building expertise in AI, infrastructure support, and demand generation. Edillon said the plan also calls for a private sector representative in each working group. She added that the private sector would have a part in carrying out standards and assurance mechanisms, and she named third-party certification as one example.

Edillon is the official who laid out the proposal, and she was careful to say that the final shape of the order is not yet known. She noted that the government does not yet know how the final executive order will come out, and that what she described is DEPDev's proposal. In her words, the council's job is to make sure the strategies and policies identified in the governance framework are put in place. She described the aim as implementing the framework in a coherent manner, so that its strategies and policies are carried out together rather than separately.

The articles give little further background on the proposal, and no date has been confirmed for the order itself. The next step is the issuance of the executive order that DEPDev is seeking, which Edillon hopes will come within two weeks of her remarks. A separate report from the United Arab Emirates, dated November 9, 2026, covered a meeting of that country's Ministerial Council for Artificial Intelligence and Development, chaired by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed Al Nahyan. That meeting reviewed government initiatives on artificial intelligence and digital transformation, but it is a different matter from the Philippine proposal.

stories.Headline: Samsung SDI's backup battery for AI data centers wins CES award
stories.Summary:
Samsung SDI has won a CES 2027 Innovation Award in the Enterprise Tech category for a battery system meant to provide backup power for AI data centers. The Consumer Technology Association announced the award on Monday, Nov. 9, local time, and Samsung SDI confirmed it on Nov. 10. The winning product is the SDI U8A3-UPS, a prismatic battery solution built for uninterruptible power supply systems. Such systems supply emergency electricity when the main power supply is disrupted, and they can also add power during sudden spikes in demand from AI computing. That extra power helps prevent server outages and data loss.

The SDI U8A3-UPS uses lithium manganese oxide-based prismatic battery cells that combine high power output with improved energy density. Samsung SDI said the system offers 33 percent greater space efficiency than its previous products, so data centers can keep power supplies reliable with fewer batteries. The system also went through an indoor large-scale fire test run by the global safety certification organization UL Solutions. Samsung SDI said it was the first product in the world to meet all the evaluation criteria in that test. CES 2027 is due to be held in Las Vegas in January next year.

A Samsung SDI official said the recognition reflects the technology's potential as a power solution for the AI era. The official added that the company will keep developing products that meet market demands for performance and safety. A Samsung SDI representative quoted by the Kyunghyang Shinmun described the award as recognition of the innovativeness of a core power solution for the AI era. The same representative said the company will keep leading the market with products that combine the performance and safety customers require.

The award is Samsung SDI's third consecutive year of recognition at CES since it began showcasing its products at the event in 2025. At CES 2026, its high-output cylindrical battery, the SDI 25U-Power, received a Best of Innovation Award. Its No Thermal Propagation technology, designed to prevent fires from spreading between battery cells, earned an Innovation Award at the same show. The Korea Herald reported that surging electricity demand from AI data centers is increasing the need for stable power supplies.

Separately, the neural processing unit developer DEEPX said on Tuesday that it has won a CES 2027 Innovation Award in the AI category. Its prize-winning chip, the DX-M2, is an ultra-low-power chip designed to run inference on large language models and vision-language models. It is built on Samsung Electronics' 2-nanometer foundry process and draws around 5 watts. The chip is meant to let robots and industrial devices run generative AI without relying on cloud computing. DEEPX completed the chip's tape-out earlier this month, with initial mass production scheduled for the fourth quarter of 2027 and full-scale production slated to begin in 2028.

stories.Headline: Cribl acquires Tero to accelerate AI-native observability
stories.Summary:
Cribl, a San Francisco-based AI platform for telemetry, has acquired Tero, a company that builds intelligence tools for observability data. The deal was disclosed during the KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 week, and the articles say it is meant to expand Cribl's AI-native observability and first-party monitoring capabilities. Tero's three co-founders, chief executive Ben Johnson, CTO Adam Cohen and COO Nihar Singhal, will join Cribl along with their engineering team. Johnson will take the role of VP of observability and help lead the company's product strategy in the sector. The acquisition is Cribl's third in four months, following CardinalOps in July and Radiant Security's AI SOC technology in August.

Tero's technology helps organisations assess the value of their telemetry data and identifies information that adds little to their observability operations. It is designed to show engineering teams where low-value data is accumulating across their tools, without requiring changes to existing workflows. At Cribl, the team will focus on four areas: host monitoring, application performance monitoring, federated observability and AI-native observability. These capabilities will be built on Cribl's existing open platform, which lets customers collect, route and refine telemetry data. Cribl said Tero brings observability market expertise, established customer and partner relationships, and engineering experience that will help accelerate product development.

Cribl co-founder and CEO Clint Sharp said the best builders in observability are choosing to build with Cribl and that Johnson has spent a decade on the hardest problem in the space. Sharp said the team would help take the next step by building observability directly on the platform customers already trust with their data. Johnson said Tero was started to help engineers understand their telemetry rather than just collect more of it. He said that, rather than compete with Cribl, the team chose to build alongside it. The articles say Cribl's wider strategy is to bring observability and security products together on a shared telemetry platform.

Johnson previously co-founded Timber, the company behind the open source Vector data pipeline, which Datadog acquired in 2021. The articles say his experience building telemetry infrastructure is expected to support Cribl's push toward a broader observability offering. Cribl was founded in 2018 and describes itself as an AI platform for IT and security telemetry. Its infrastructure supports its own security information and event management, observability and AI SOC products, along with applications built by customers and AI agents. The company also provides a control plane for routing and governing AI traffic, protecting sensitive information and monitoring AI usage, costs, performance and risk.

stories.Headline: Israel Plans National AI Model to Reduce Foreign Dependence, Protect Control of Critical Infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Israel plans to build its own national artificial intelligence model to reduce reliance on foreign technology and keep control of critical infrastructure. Brig. Gen. (res.) Erez Askal, head of the National AI Directorate in the Prime Minister's Office, presented the plan on November 9, 2026, at AI Week at Tel Aviv University.

He said the country's AI systems would need to stay under national control, warning that the government would otherwise lose control over essential services. The announcement came as officials worry that AI is becoming central to electricity, water and health care. Askal's concern is that commercial providers may have interests that differ from those of the governments they serve. The proposed infrastructure is large and costly. Askal said Israel would need about 2 gigawatts of electricity capacity to support AI computing facilities, data centers and semiconductor manufacturing.

The plan also calls for roughly 300,000 graphics processing units, with about 100,000 serving domestic needs such as universities, government agencies, the military and startups. A nationally controlled foundation model, the underlying technology behind applications such as chatbots, is also part of the strategy. Askal did not give a budget or timetable for these targets during his presentation. He added that the government has issued a tender for an Israeli-built national quantum computer. Askal framed the effort as a matter of sovereignty, arguing that governments cannot be sure foreign AI services will remain available or aligned with their needs.

He said Israel does not intend to produce every component itself or cut off international markets, only to control the critical elements. He also suggested the country might build its advanced model with allied nations facing similar challenges. Askal said AI could help solve practical problems, and a new body, the National Institute for Impact-Driven Artificial Intelligence, will coordinate ministries, businesses and universities on projects in health care, education and transportation. He also called for workforce retraining and clear rules on cybersecurity and accountability. The strategy comes as countries worldwide grapple with the influence of major technology companies over AI infrastructure and computing resources.

The institute plans 10 to 14 initiatives a year, aiming to move five of its first 10 projects into implementation within one year. Askal's broader five-year framework targets 10 challenges annually, with examples such as improving fourth-grade mathematics and reducing congestion on Highway 6. Whether Israel can secure the electricity, hardware, investment and partnerships needed remains unresolved. Askal summed up his position by saying that countries that act will keep control, and that Israel has decided to act.
