stories.Headline: From teacher workloads to student work, Boise schools navigate AI
stories.Summary:
The Boise School District plans to give its teachers and staff access to ChatGPT for Teachers, a tool built by OpenAI, with a rollout set for spring 2027. The district is weighing how to protect student privacy, review AI-generated materials, and help teachers handle concerns about cheating as the technology spreads through classrooms. Teachers could use the tool to draft practice quizzes, prepare assignments, or turn spoken instructions into lesson plans for substitutes. The story was reported by Riley Shoemaker of Idaho News 6.

Ryan Gravett, the district's chief technology officer, said the tools could ease teachers' workloads. He gave the example of a teacher who wakes up sick and must prepare someone else to teach the day's lessons, saying a teacher could simply dictate what a day would look like. Gravett also said AI-generated materials still need human review before they reach students. Data privacy, he said, was a major part of the agreement with OpenAI, and the district asked who owns the data, what is done with it, and where it is stored.

According to the article, OpenAI says information entered into the district's workspace will not be used to train its AI models. Gravett said parents and students trust the district with the tools it provides, which is why those questions matter. The new workspace is meant for staff, but students are already using AI, so teachers face the question of whether students did their own work. Gravett said teachers can review how a document developed over time, allowing them to see how an essay took shape. He said the district is leaving judgments about possible AI misuse to individual teachers.

The district is also asking parents to share their views on AI in schools through a survey posted on its website. The article does not say how many parents have responded or what the district will do with the results. It also does not describe any incidents, costs, or formal policies beyond what Gravett described. The rollout in spring 2027 is the next milestone the article identifies.

Articles.Title: From teacher workloads to student work, Boise schools navigate AI

stories.Headline: Congress’s Permitting Bill Is a ‘Massive Giveaway’ to the AI Data Center Industry, Critics Warn
stories.Summary:
The Senate voted on Monday to advance a bipartisan bill called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, which is meant to ease the construction of new energy infrastructure. The bill has support from labor leaders, who say it will produce thousands of jobs, and from clean energy advocates, who think it could unlock wind and solar projects. Its sponsors want it passed before the current Congress ends in January. Critics, however, say it would speed up an AI data center buildout that voters rejected in the midterm elections.

BAAJA would force data centers to pay the full cost of the grid upgrades they trigger and includes transmission reforms meant to modernize the grid. It would also weaken some environmental protections and could lead to more gas-powered data centers and more construction on public lands. Its permitting provisions could fast-track projects that are now waiting for approval and limit judges' ability to halt construction over environmental review. One study estimates data centers would pay about $55 billion in transmission charges over ten years, roughly $35 billion more than under current policy. Hundreds of local and national groups, including the Sierra Club and the Natural Resources Defense Council, have urged Congress not to pass the bill as written.

Supporters, including Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, a Democratic sponsor, argue the bill ends data center cost-shifting onto households and businesses. Sierra Club's Holly Bender and Earthjustice's Meg Slattery have warned that gas and fossil fuel investment could rise instead. Oil Change International's Allie Rosenbluth called the bill a massive giveaway to the data center industry. President Donald Trump urged the Senate to pass it, saying China would take any data center the United States does not want. Tribal leaders have written that the bill would weaken their ability to protect historic and cultural sites threatened by federally connected projects.

The vote is a test for Democrats after the midterms, since the bill must still pass a Senate vote to take it up, face amendments, and then pass the House in identical form before reaching Trump. Gas-powered data center projects have grown sharply, from roughly 4 gigawatts in early 2024 to 189 gigawatts in development by mid-2026, according to Global Energy Monitor data reported by Wired. Critics on the left, including Michele Jawando of Omidyar Network, want Democrats to wait for the next Congress, which will include many new House members. Supporters hope to pass it this year as a rare bipartisan win on affordability.

Articles.Title: Congress’s Permitting Bill Is a ‘Massive Giveaway’ to the AI Data Center Industry, Critics Warn - Time Magazine

stories.Headline: Denver, Aurora schools to get $350K for AI tool
stories.Summary:
The DSST Public Schools charter network will receive a $350,000 grant to build AI tools across its 16 campuses in Denver and Aurora. The grant comes from Multilingual by Design, a philanthropic group based in Washington, D.C., which is financially backed by the Bezos Family Foundation and pairs education nonprofits with AI developers. The group picked DSST as one of three grant recipients from applicants across the nation. The announcement was published on November 10, 2026. The Denver Gazette reported the details.

DSST will use the money to pilot a tool called Premo, which helps K-8 teachers plan grade-level math lessons so multilingual students can take on content while building academic English. Premo aligns each lesson to established English language development frameworks and creates teaching strategies matched to each student's English proficiency level. The tool will roll out across all 16 DSST campuses over the coming year, and teachers will receive coaching, technical assistance and support. Throughline Learning, a Rhode Island-based nonprofit, will partner with DSST to implement the tool and help teachers understand how it works in classrooms. More than 65% of students at the 16 campuses are current or former multilingual learners.

Some of those campuses are part of Denver Public Schools and others part of Aurora Public Schools. Sandra Licon, fund director at Multilingual by Design, said teachers are short on time and working hard to help multilingual learners keep up in math and early literacy. She said the three funded teams started with close attention to what students and teachers experience day to day. Angie McPhaul, director of youth success at Gary Community Ventures, a financial backer of the group, said every child deserves a classroom where they are understood and supported. She said the projects center the strengths multilingual students bring to schools.

Both statements praised the grant recipients' focus on students' needs. The grant is part of a broader effort by Multilingual by Design to fund tools that support multilingual learners in classrooms. The articles do not describe how the results of the pilot will be measured or whether the tool will be expanded beyond the 16 campuses after the first year. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Denver, Aurora schools to get $350K for AI tool - Denver Gazette

stories.Headline: Hidden in plain sight: Schools hunt for AI smart glasses ahead of college entrance exam
stories.Summary:
Korean education officials are stepping up inspections and testing detection tools to stop AI-powered smart glasses from being used to cheat on the College Scholastic Ability Test, or CSAT, which is set for Nov. 19. The glasses look almost identical to ordinary eyewear, and one common method involves photographing exam questions and displaying answers on the lenses. The Korea JoongAng Daily reported the effort on Nov. 11, 2026, with just over a week left before the exam. Officials are working to identify the devices and keep them out of exam rooms.

Researchers at Duke University have proposed a way to spot the glasses by their optical features. In their study, smartphone cameras were used to find waveguides, the components that project images onto the lenses, with about 80 percent accuracy. Ordinary glasses should show fairly even lens brightness from different angles, while smart glasses can leak light that makes the area around the eyes appear to glow. Even when the displays are off, light from ceiling fixtures can create rainbow-colored streaks on the waveguides.

In Korea, a separate approach focuses on wireless signals rather than cameras. The Korea Communications Agency issued a tender earlier this month for equipment that can detect Bluetooth and Wi-Fi signals inside exam rooms, which proctors would carry as they walk around. A website called ExamGuard was also released online on Saturday, letting users scan a room through their browser for nearby Bluetooth-enabled devices. Lee Seung-hyun, vice president of the AI company 42Maru and the developer of the website, said the tool could still be a useful reference before the exam.

Yoon Sang-ho, a professor at the Graduate School of Culture Technology at KAIST, said jamming radio signals would be hard to carry out in practice. He also noted that students could modify their glasses with miniature AI memory systems that work without wireless communication, so physical inspection may be the most reliable method for now. He suggested proctors check students' glasses directly and attach security certification stickers. A official at a regional education office said staff would be trained on the devices' physical traits and use metal detectors as an initial screening step this year. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Hidden in plain sight: Schools hunt for AI smart glasses ahead of college entrance exam - Korea JoongAng Daily

stories.Headline: Democratic Congress, Trump and AI investment for SP:SPX by Swissquote
stories.Summary:
The Democratic Party's victory in the US midterm elections triggered selling pressure across the technology sector, particularly among semiconductor stocks. Market participants fear that large planned investments in AI infrastructure could be questioned or delayed by Democratic legislative efforts at the federal and local levels. The new Democratic majority in Congress can influence AI-related regulation, and Democratic officials in individual states and localities may also try to block or slow the physical deployment of AI infrastructure. The article argues that these fears may be exaggerated, since there is no unified Democratic push to undermine AI momentum in the United States. It adds that the Republican minority and the White House still hold significant tools to resist such moves.

The article explains the new balance of power between the White House and the Democratic-led Congress over AI investment. President Donald Trump can veto legislation, and Democrats would need a two-thirds majority in both chambers to override that veto, a threshold the article describes as particularly difficult to reach given their simple majority. Local authorities, by contrast, control urban planning, zoning and building permits, so they can reject projects, impose extra requirements or suspend developments, and a presidential veto cannot overturn such municipal decisions. Environmental limits, water use and heavy electricity demand are also possible sources of opposition. Congress can additionally apply pressure through hearings, investigations into large technology companies and budget debates, which can add regulatory uncertainty without new legislation.

The article identifies the companies most exposed as Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet and Meta, which are the hyperscalers building large data centers. It says these firms could keep their massive investment budgets while facing greater difficulty obtaining permits, securing electricity connections and accessing the computing capacity needed for new facilities. The analysis distinguishes between a broad federal blockade, which presidential powers constrain, and operational delays to individual infrastructure projects, which are the more realistic risk. The author, Vincent Ganne writing for Swissquote, concludes that the political shift adds a risk to the timeline for deploying AI infrastructure but does not necessarily undermine the structural investment momentum in the sector.

The article does not describe specific next steps beyond this assessment. The main issue for equity markets, according to the article, is the gap between the capital spending announced by hyperscalers and the actual commissioning of new computing capacity. Investors are therefore advised to watch that gap rather than focus solely on the election result. The article is framed as market commentary for informational purposes and is not investment advice.

Articles.Title: Democratic Congress, Trump and AI investment for SP:SPX by Swissquote - TradingView

stories.Headline: From principles to practice: Rewriting the rules of AI
stories.Summary:
Japan and the United States are moving AI governance from concepts to practice, with each country adopting a soft-law approach that has no legal binding force. On Aug. 25, the Japanese government published the Principle Code for Protection of Intellectual Property and Transparency for the Appropriate Use of Generative AI. In the United States, an executive order and a presidential memorandum on AI were released in June, and in July the National Institute of Standards and Technology released a draft of guidance and documentation templates for AI datasets and models. The two countries differ, however, in what they aim to protect and what they hope to develop. The U.S. executive order links advanced AI capabilities to national security while keeping private-sector development moving.

Washington envisions quick and confidential government assessments of frontier models, with government and industry working together on cybersecurity vulnerability discovery and remediation. The government does not plan any mandatory preclearance or permitting requirements, and it will focus on frontier models that could launch cyberattacks on critical infrastructure. On Sept. 29, top executives from leading U.S. AI developers agreed with President Donald Trump that the industry would police itself. In September the United States also revealed methods for assessing systems, including adversarial red-teaming. Japan's code also has no legal binding force and takes a "comply-or-explain" approach, meaning businesses must either follow the principles or explain why they cannot.

Under the code, generative AI developers and providers must ensure they do not violate intellectual property rights and that their operations are transparent. Information about the models used, their training data and measures for protecting IP must be made public. After the government released its draft in December 2025, some expressed the view that regulations should not be too restrictive, and the final version reflected this view to a considerable extent. As a result, research and development not provided to the public, and systems with limited data and users, are in general not subject to the code.

The article's author says the revisions are commendable, but identifies remaining problems. Compliance pressure from business partners, investors and the public could become a barrier to entry for small and medium-sized enterprises with limited capital and personnel. Foreign businesses serving Japan can still decline to follow the code by explaining instead, and the article asks whether it can be equally effective for domestic and foreign companies. The author also raises a question about consistency with Article 30-4 of Japan's Copyright Law, which generally allows AI models to be trained on copyrighted works without permission from rights holders.

The author argues that the burden on AI businesses should be commensurate with company size, applications, capabilities and the risk of rights infringement. The article concludes that the code is a first step from concept to implementation and that its true value depends on whether it can reduce IP disputes, build trust and expand domestic research, development and investment. It says Japan should move toward governance that accelerates AI use while safeguarding confidential information and IP rights, as the United States does. The author is Shigeru Kitamura, who joined the National Police Agency in 1980 after graduating from the University of Tokyo, became Director of Cabinet Intelligence in 2011, and served as Secretary General of the National Security Secretariat from 2019 to 2021.

Articles.Title: From principles to practice: Rewriting the rules of AI - Asia News Network

stories.Headline: OpenAI and Georgia county leaders hit with Mafia-style RICO racketeering lawsuit over $30 billion AI data center
stories.Summary:
A residents' group in Effingham County, Georgia, has filed a Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act lawsuit against county commissioners, county leaders, OpenAI and its affiliates over the proposed "Project Camellia" data center. The plaintiffs are Dr. Michelle Finch-Mincey, Lehman Mincey Jr. and Raymond Carver, who are seeking civil damages. They say the project has harmed their property values and that purchase offers for nearby residential properties have dropped or been withdrawn since the data center was announced. The filing reported by the Effingham Herald alleges a conspiracy to advance the project through confidential negotiations and closed-door decisions.

The lawsuit names all six Effingham County Commissioners as defendants, including Chairperson Damon Rahn, Forrest Floyd, Roger Burdette, Jamie DeLoach, Elizabeth Helmly and Phil Kieffer. It also names County Manager Tim Callanan, Effingham County Industrial Development Authority CEO Brandt Herndon, and the IDA itself. The defendants further include OpenAI, Octans GA LLC, which operates the data center on OpenAI's behalf, and Savannah Industrial Development LLC, which was involved in the sale of IDA property to Octans and OpenAI. The plaintiffs allege fraud and concealment through non-disclosure agreements and misleading public statements, along with improper land transactions, zoning violations and civil racketeering.

Project Camellia is one of OpenAI's largest planned data centers in Effingham County, with an expected cost between $20 billion and $30 billion. The project is to be built across five phases with a planned compute capacity of 3.2 gigawatts. OpenAI has said it will pay the full cost of all required infrastructure upgrades so the community's utility costs are not affected, and that its closed-loop water system will keep water use minimal. The residents opposing the project contend that the county sought land, tax incentives and zoning approvals without informing the public until key decisions were finalized and contracts signed.

The federal RICO Act was originally designed to counter organized crime, and Georgia's version is less stringent than the federal one. Georgia's statute has been used in the 2023 election racketeering case against Donald Trump and 18 others, and in Young Thug's trial over the alleged YSL Records street gang. Georgia State University criminal justice professor Volkan Topalli, quoted by Atlanta Magazine, said critics consider the state law too encompassing and say it has been used against defendants in more ordinary felony cases. The articles also note that data center developers have used non-disclosure agreements during negotiations, and that an AWS data center in Gilroy, California, drew scrutiny after residents learned of its nature only when construction began.

Articles.Title: OpenAI and Georgia county leaders hit with Mafia-style RICO racketeering lawsuit over $30 billion AI data center

stories.Headline: AI lending surge tests credit insurance capacity as banks seek cover
stories.Summary:
Three of the world's largest banks have recently explored or bought credit insurance to hedge their exposure to AI infrastructure loans, according to the Financial Times. Barclays has been asking insurers about default protection on more than $10 billion of such loans, and HSBC has also looked at using credit insurance on data center debt. JPMorgan Chase considered the approach but ultimately declined it. The moves suggest that the rapid growth in data center financing is pushing against the limits of what bank balance sheets can carry alone.

Concentration limits, which cap how much a bank can lend to a single company, project or sector, are restricting lending at the same time that hyperscalers want ever-larger loan packages. Credit insurance eases that constraint by shifting part of the default risk to insurers. In a typical deal, a bank cedes 20% to 50% of its exposure, which frees capacity to approve bigger facilities or more deals. Azi Larsen of Marsh Specialty told the FT that the rising cost of credit default swaps and the scale of AI debt issuance have led US lenders to look at insurance as a cheaper route to exposure relief.

The number of credit insurance providers for project finance has grown from a handful a decade ago to more than 70, including AIG, Chubb and Axa, according to the FT. Premiums for data center exposure run at 50% to 70% of what banks earn on that part of their loan portfolios, the report says. A Willis Towers Watson survey released in May 2026 found that several non-trade credit insurers were approaching sector limits or were already full on data center exposure. Willis Re also reported that direct credit insurance premium at Lloyd's rose by roughly a quarter in 2025 to about £1.6 billion, after Lloyd's removed premium income limits on credit and financial guarantee business in July 2025.

Charlie Radcliffe of BPL Global, a specialist credit and political risk broker, told the FT that banks will pay premium rates to secure majority lender status or to show support for a client. Willis Re has warned that reinsurers will scrutinize data center concentrations closely at the January 2027 renewals. The specific insurers approached by Barclays and HSBC have not been named, and several of the transactions remain exploratory. Even so, credit risk transfer on AI infrastructure has begun to look like a recurring placement category, where insurer selectivity and capacity management will shape outcomes as much as price.

Articles.Title: AI lending surge tests credit insurance capacity as banks seek cover

stories.Headline: Andhra Pradesh Cabinet clears policy frameworks to attract investments in AI, electronics, renewable energy
stories.Summary:
The Andhra Pradesh Cabinet, chaired by Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu at the Secretariat on Tuesday, approved a series of proposals aimed at drawing investment in artificial intelligence, electronics, renewable energy, pharmaceuticals and manufacturing. The approvals covered the Animation, Visual Effects, Gaming, Comics and Extended Reality policy for 2026 to 2031 and the Robotics and Physical AI policy for 2026 to 2036. The Cabinet also cleared amendments to the Semiconductor and Display Fab Policy for 2024 to 2029. Decisions on infrastructure, education and administration were taken alongside these investment measures.

Among the largest approvals is a ₹31,387 crore investment by AM Intelligence for a 512 MW green integrated AI data centre at Amanam in Bheemunipatnam mandal of Visakhapatnam district. The Cabinet also cleared a ₹4,000.20 crore advanced materials project by Carbon Cosmo at Naidupeta and allotted land in Tirupati to Dixon Technologies for a ₹700 crore investment. About 25 acres were allocated to Reliance Industries for a gigascale AI data centre at Bhogapuram in Vizianagaram district. An ₹570.20 crore Epack unit at Rambilli in Anakapalli district is expected to employ 2,565 people, and Hetero Group received 173.82 acres in the Nakkapalli Bulk Drug Park.

The Cabinet approved the creation of a Directorate of Traffic Management and Road Safety under the Director-General of Police, with its headquarters at Mangalagiri. It also sanctioned a ₹236.92 crore expansion of Ravali Spinners in West Godavari district, expected to employ 1,569 people, and a 30-acre industrial park for women entrepreneurs at Jaggayyapet in NTR district. Compressed biogas plants were approved for NTR, Prakasam and Vizianagaram districts, and the government agreed to study small modular nuclear reactors as an alternative to thermal power. The Cabinet also transferred 5.50 acres of APGENCO land to the Vijayawada Municipal Corporation for a 15 MW waste-to-energy plant.

The articles do not name anyone outside the Cabinet as responsible for the decisions beyond the Chief Minister, who chaired the meeting. The Hindu's report, published on November 11, 2026, attributes the investment figures to sources in the government. Other measures included a 30-year lease of 192.68 acres of Wakf land in Anantapur district for a solar project, a Kendriya Vidyalaya site in the capital region, and the withdrawal of earlier land allotments made to Websol Renewables and Metro Decorative at the Naidupeta Special Economic Zone. The articles do not describe any next steps or timelines for these approvals.

Articles.Title: Andhra Pradesh Cabinet clears policy frameworks to attract investments in AI, electronics, renewable energy

stories.Headline: Taiwan Creative Content Fest Takeaways: ‘Avatar’ VFX House Brings Its AI Ambitions to Taipei as Character IP Booms
stories.Summary:
Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) wrapped its 2026 edition in Taipei with animation and character IP companies moving to the front of the show floor. They made up the largest exhibitor group, at 29 of 107 exhibitors, up from 19 in 2025, according to post-event figures from organizer the Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA). Of this year's exhibitors, 69 were Taiwanese and 38 came from overseas, compared with 117 exhibitors in total last year. Television and media networks rose from 20 to 22 exhibitors, while new media, streaming and entertainment companies grew from six to eight.

Film and TV production and distribution companies dropped from 22 to 16, digital tech, VFX and immersive media fell from 15 to eight, and publishing, comics and webtoons went from 12 to five. The Pitching program presented 93 projects and stories to industry participants from 28 countries, including entries from TAICCA School. TAICCA is still compiling buyer attendance and the value of business done. The headline deal came on opening day, Nov. 6, when New Zealand visual effects company Weta FX signed a memorandum of understanding with TAICCA.

The agreement aims to make Taiwan an AI hub for Asia's content industries. Weta FX will partner with Taiwanese animation and VFX outfit Moonshine Studio and set up a technology platform to back Taiwanese film and TV projects. The deal also includes exchanges and internships for young Taiwanese filmmakers. Weta FX CEO Daniel Seah said studio legal departments had ruled out any use of generative AI on their projects early last year. By the turn of the year, clients were asking about Weta's AI strategy, mostly to find out how much money the technology could save.

Seah said AI had become a national strategy in Taiwan on the back of the island's semiconductor industry, and Moonshine had been moving quickly as a result. Japanese studios also brought their AI work to Taipei. Toei, the studio behind "Kamen Rider" and the Super Sentai series, has adopted rules for generative AI and is already using it for backgrounds, according to president Yoshimura Fumio. At a TCCF panel on AI in animation, OLM Digital board director Yotsukura Tatsuo presented a coloring tool that learns a show's look from three hand-painted frames. Taiwanese technology company imCore Corp. launched Core Studio, an AI filmmaking platform with more than 24 specialized agents, at TCCF on Nov. 7.

Southeast Asia ran through the program. K7 Media's Trang Nguyen presented a study of Indonesia, Southeast Asia's biggest film market with box office revenue of $352.9 million in 2025, and pointed to horror as a natural meeting ground for Taiwanese and Indonesian producers. The top Pitching prize, the $35,000 TAICCA × CNC Feature Film Grand Award, went to "Somewhere in the South," a Malaysian feature written and directed by Tan Ce Ding and produced by Anthony Chen. Grace Chan, a program planner at Taiwan Television Enterprise (TTV), said the broadcaster had seen a significant increase in Vietnamese buyers this year, after Korean buyers had been the largest group last year.

Japan was also looking at Taiwan. Cinematographer Wayne Lo, at TCCF for the first time, met several Japanese teams and found that up-and-coming filmmakers see working directly with TAICCA as a route to getting projects made. Toei's Yoshimura said Japanese films were the most-released titles in Taiwan in 2025 and second only to U.S. films at the box office. Toei is also launching a games label whose first three titles are originals rather than adaptations of its existing IP. Publishing, comics and webtoon exhibitors were down, but Mirror Fiction's "The Three Witches of Shetou" won both the TAICCA Award: Best Story and the friDay Video Original Story Award.

TAICCA presented the slates of its four joint-venture funds, which have backed 27 projects and drawn NT$4.9 billion in private capital alongside NT$740 million from the agency, about $180 million in all. The Chunghwa Digital Cultural and Creative Fund, majority owned by Chunghwa Telecom, totals NT$1 billion ($32 million). Enjoy Entertainment, a partnership with telecom Far EasTone, invested in 15 projects in its first 10 months. "The Rope Curse 4: Kuntilanak," a Taiwan-Indonesia horror collaboration that Toei also invested in, took NT$80 million ($2.6 million) at the Taiwanese box office, a franchise record.

Articles.Title: Taiwan Creative Content Fest Takeaways: ‘Avatar’ VFX House Brings Its AI Ambitions to Taipei as Character IP Booms

stories.Headline: The Pensions Regulator Sets Out Seven Principles for Trustees' Use of AI
stories.Summary:
The Pensions Regulator (TPR) has published guidance on how trustees of pension schemes should use artificial intelligence, dated 10 November 2026. The guidance does not create new legal requirements or change trustees' existing duties. It explains how those duties apply when AI is used by the trustee board or by the scheme's advisers and service providers. It sets out seven principles that TPR expects trustees to follow.

The first principle is to start with the problem rather than the technology, using AI only to solve real problems and improve member outcomes, efficiency and value for money. The second principle keeps human responsibility central, since trustees remain accountable for everything done for the scheme, including outsourced work. For each significant use of AI, trustees should be able to say what it is used for, what data it uses, who is accountable, how its decisions can be challenged by a person, and what happens if it fails. Where AI significantly influences a decision, trustees should be able to explain what service was used, what human checks were made and who made the decision. The guidance also notes that data protection law restricts decisions with significant effects that are made solely by automated means.

The third principle treats governance as ongoing, with AI risks built into the scheme's risk management framework and kept under regular review, with oversight proportionate to the risk. The fourth principle asks trustees to plan for disruption, so that business continuity plans cover AI failing or becoming unavailable. The fifth principle stresses data quality, since AI magnifies the effect of poor data, and warns against "shadow AI", meaning use of unapproved public AI services. The sixth principle covers transparency, noting there is no general duty to tell members about every use of AI, but trustees should consider what members need to understand where AI directly affects them. The seventh principle asks trustees to test outcomes for unfair bias across groups and to consider vulnerable and digitally excluded members.

TPR has also published separate guidance on identifying and managing hidden AI-related investment exposure, prompted by concern that the growing influence of AI companies on global markets could create concentration risks that leave investors more vulnerable in a downturn. That guidance asks trustees to understand their scheme's aggregate exposure and test whether diversification will hold under stressed conditions. The article, written by lawyers at Mayer Brown, advises trustees to review the guidance and check whether their current arrangements for AI meet TPR's expectations, and to act where gaps exist. The article does not describe any enforcement action or deadline.

Articles.Title: The Pensions Regulator Sets Out Seven Principles for Trustees' Use of AI - Mayer Brown

stories.Headline: Softbank loses $3.7 billion on canceled AI data center gas turbine orders days after denying Elon Musk’s claim it was defaulting
stories.Summary:
SoftBank, the Japanese technology investment firm, has taken a $3.7 billion loss after canceling orders for gas turbines meant to power AI data centers, according to a report published by Tom's Hardware on November 11, 2026. The article, citing The Wall Street Journal, says the company had reserved more than 13 gigawatts of turbine capacity, roughly equal to more than six Hoover Dams. The cancellations, which the article says SoftBank made voluntarily, came days after the company denied a claim by Elon Musk that it had defaulted on turbine orders. SoftBank now plans to unwind its remaining reservations with GE Vernova, its turbine supplier, along with contracts for orders that were too far along to cancel.

The turbines were intended for gas-fired power plants supporting data centers. The article reports that SoftBank had planned a 9.2-gigawatt power plant in Ohio, with construction scheduled for early 2027 and a cost of $33 billion, to supply a neighboring eight-gigawatt data center. That data center was to be leased to OpenAI, and the article says Nvidia had entered discussions about guaranteeing around $250 billion of financing for the project. The article says SoftBank initially planned to use the turbines for future gas plants but later changed direction.

SoftBank Chief Financial Officer Yoshimitsu Goto responded to Musk's claim, reportedly saying, "This is simply not correct at all," and "There is no such default." Musk had made his claim in a post on X, which the article identifies as a social network. On an earnings call, SoftBank told investors the orders had been placed to secure power generation equipment in anticipation of shortages. The article attributes the turbine reservation details to unnamed people familiar with the orders.

The article says turbine manufacturers typically charge customers tens of millions of dollars per gigawatt, and that orders must be placed years before the equipment is needed. SoftBank had bet on demand outstripping supply, which the article says would have left it holding valuable orders. By early 2026, the article notes, the company had reserved more power generation capacity than the entire state of Connecticut after securing a large share of global gas turbine production. The article does not say what the cancellations will mean for the Ohio project or the OpenAI lease.

Articles.Title: Softbank loses $3.7 billion on canceled AI data center gas turbine orders days after denying Elon Musk’s claim it was defaulting

stories.Headline: Elon Musk wants to build a s $24 billion gas-powered AI supercomputer in Texas company town
stories.Summary:
Starbase, Texas, which hosts SpaceX's Starship rocket program, has posted notice of a public hearing on a gas-fired power plant and supercomputing facility within the city limits. The project carries an initial cost of $24 billion and will apparently be owned by SpaceX. Tom's Hardware reported the project on November 11, 2026, and described it as a 10 gigawatt site that goes up for approval in December. Bloomberg reports that the project could face resistance from incoming Texas governor Gina Hinojosa.

Hinojosa campaigned against approving new data centers until the state's legislature enacts stronger protections against potential harms from those projects. The $24 billion figure covers only the "initial phases of the projects," and the company says the plan could "include future expansions." Starbase is essentially a company town for SpaceX, since the city mostly sits on land owned by SpaceX and its population mostly comprises the company's own employees. That arrangement may draw less local opposition than the company's Memphis facilities did.

SpaceXSI, the company behind the plan, has been building out its Colossus I and Colossus II data centers near the Mississippi-Tennessee border. Those projects have faced backlash, including a lawsuit from area residents that aims to curb pollutants produced by the large number of gas turbines required to power them. The project appears to be part of SpaceX's push to build 10 gigawatts of compute in 2027 alone. Hinojosa's arrival in the governor's office could override the local regulatory climate the company likely hoped for.

Beyond its terrestrial plans, SpaceX is also working on launching data centers into space. Musk has laid out plans for a first-generation AI1 compute satellite with a 150kW peak compute payload. The company has also submitted a proposal to the FCC to build a 1-million-satellite Orbital Data Center System. Musk wrote in a post on X after the recent U.S. midterm elections that "data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now," and that work could accelerate after data center measures lost big in the polls.

Articles.Title: Elon Musk wants to build a s $24 billion gas-powered AI supercomputer in Texas company town

stories.Headline: CJC recommendations regarding use of AI for preparing court documents
stories.Summary:
On 29 October 2026, the Civil Justice Council published its final report on the use of AI in preparing documents provided to a court in civil proceedings. The report followed an interim report and a consultation process, and it focuses on AI use by legal representatives and expert witnesses. It sets out 15 recommendations in total. The Council took an incremental approach overall, and it proposed a new Practice Direction to codify the court's existing approach to AI use and sanctions for misuse.

The most significant recommendations concern witness statements and expert evidence, and these would be implemented through rules prepared by the Civil Procedure Rule Committee. A witness of fact would have to declare that AI used in preparing a statement has not generated or influenced its substantive content. An expert would have to declare AI use where it has generated or influenced the substantive content of a report, giving enough detail for the other side and the court to scrutinise the evidence. The Council also recommended good practice guidance on AI use by experts. It declined to adopt a technical definition of AI and instead proposed defining the scope of AI use by function.

The commentators at Norton Rose Fulbright note that the Council's final recommendations are more limited than those in the interim report. For example, no new rules were recommended requiring lawyers to declare AI use in statements of case or skeleton arguments, since existing professional duties already protect those documents. The Council also saw no need for new procedural reforms on AI in disclosure, though further rules may follow a separate review of PD57AD, and it kept the requirement that translations be certified by a professional human translator. The firm observes that the line between form and substance in evidence is often unclear, so the draft rules will matter.

The authors suggest that, if the recommendations are implemented, solicitors, experts and clients will need to keep clear records of how they have used AI in producing evidence and of discussions with witnesses about their evidence. They also say AI use should be addressed in the instructions given to any expert witness. The authors state that a basic spell check or accurate transcription does not generate substantive content, but they note that more substantive edits or reorganisation of material may cross the line. The articles do not say when the draft rules will be published or take effect.

Articles.Title: CJC recommendations regarding use of AI for preparing court documents

stories.Headline: Governor's 2027 preview touches Alexandria's asks on housing, solar, and AI, but not transit or school funding
stories.Summary:
Gov. Abigail Spanberger released the first preview of her 2027 legislative agenda on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, at the State Capitol in Richmond. The preview, called "Moving Virginia Forward," was outlined alongside House and Senate Democratic leaders and touches several of Alexandria's requests for the General Assembly, including housing near transit, solar energy, and artificial intelligence. It does not mention transit funding, the state's school funding formula, or immigration enforcement, all of which appear in the city's draft legislative package. The preview landed hours before City Council was scheduled to receive that draft at its Tuesday night meeting.

The release and a two-page summary describe the agenda as a set of select proposals rather than the full program. Spanberger and legislators are expected to travel the state in the coming weeks to announce more. Council plans to hold a public hearing and adopt Alexandria's package on Saturday, November 14. The General Assembly session begins January 13, 2027.

Together, these dates set the timeline for how the city's requests will be weighed against the governor's priorities. The governor's office issued the release, and Spanberger and the Democratic leaders of the House and Senate presented the agenda in person. The Alexandria Brief, a local outlet, reported on the preview and on the city's pending package, which is the document Council will consider. The articles do not describe any response from city officials to the omissions on transit and school funding.

Alexandria's requests on housing, solar, and AI have been met in part by the governor's preview, while transit and school funding remain unaddressed in it. The articles do not say whether those omitted issues will appear in the later announcements. Council's vote on Saturday will determine what the city formally asks the General Assembly to consider. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Governor's 2027 preview touches Alexandria's asks on housing, solar, and AI, but not transit or school funding - The Alexandria Brief

stories.Headline: Digital Health and AI: Key Regulatory, Reimbursement and Policy Developments
stories.Summary:
Last week, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services finalized its 2027 Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment System rule and its Medicare Physician Fee Schedule rule, both of which address digital health and artificial intelligence. In the outpatient rule, CMS coined the term "Software as a Medical Service" for software that supports clinical decisions through algorithmic analysis. CMS also created an interim payment pathway, assigning qualifying services to New Technology Ambulatory Payment Classifications and establishing a new status indicator, O1. The policy does not guarantee separate payment for every AI-enabled tool, since payment still depends on service and coding requirements. CMS also finalized separate payment for certain stand-alone algorithmic analyses of previously completed laboratory data, including secondary analyses of genomic sequencing results.

The physician fee schedule rule did not create an AI-specific payment pathway, but it signals growing attention to how technology affects physician work and quality measurement. CMS issued a Request for Information seeking industry input on technology-enabled primary care and on how Medicare payment might account for clinical AI. The rule cites an estimated 25 percent penetration of AI documentation tools, such as ambient scribes, among U.S. physicians. CMS also said more than 40 percent of U.S. physicians had self-reported using OpenEvidence, an AI application that answers clinical questions from peer-reviewed sources. Many commenters expressed skepticism and urged CMS to ensure that any Medicare-paid AI demonstrates proven clinical value.

CMS said it would consider that feedback in future rulemaking. CMS addressed AI in the Medicare Annual Wellness Visit, stressing that a physician or other health professional must still perform the visit and that clinicians must retain responsibility for clinical decisions. The agency said AI may support components such as administering the Health Risk Assessment, reconciling medications for clinician verification, and drafting a personalized prevention plan for clinician review. CMS said it was not aware of how AI could conduct a cognitive assessment under the current standard.

Beneficiary-facing software used to implement a prevention plan must not constitute the practice of medicine or replace the beneficiary-clinician relationship, and it must comply with fraud and abuse laws, including the Anti-Kickback Statute. CMS may issue further guidance in future rulemaking. CMS also tightened oversight of remote patient monitoring and remote therapeutic monitoring after findings by the Office of the Inspector General about potential fraud, waste and abuse. The rule extends the established-patient requirement to remote therapeutic monitoring, so practitioners must furnish a separately reportable initiating face-to-face visit, in person or via telehealth, before monitoring begins.

CMS also finalized a requirement that clinical staff performing these services be directly employed by the billing practitioner or practice, subject to incident-to requirements. That requirement may materially affect digital health companies that provide outsourced monitoring services. CMS delayed its implementation until Jan. 1, 2029, giving providers and vendors more time to adjust their operating models. Separately, the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology streamlined portions of the federal health IT certification framework, and the American Medical Association released a clinical AI liability framework.

The AMA framework would allocate responsibility among clinicians, AI developers and deploying healthcare organizations based on each party's authority, access to information and ability to control or mitigate risk. It rejects the assumption that keeping a physician "in the loop" automatically shifts responsibility away from developers or health systems. Congress has also extended several Medicare telehealth flexibilities through Dec. 31, 2027, including audio-only telehealth and access from beneficiaries' homes. Pending legislation, including the PATIENT AI Act and Doctors Not AI Act, reflects continued congressional attention to AI reimbursement, oversight and privacy.

Articles.Title: Digital Health and AI: Key Regulatory, Reimbursement and Policy Developments - JD Supra

stories.Headline: TSMC, Microsoft executives debate AI's impact on Day 2 of Nikkei Dialogue
stories.Summary:
TSMC and Microsoft executives were scheduled to speak on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, on the second day of Nikkei's 2026 Global Management Dialogue in Tokyo. The event, which opened its second day in the Japanese capital, was set to keep artificial intelligence at the top of its agenda. Among the participants was a senior executive from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., the world's largest contract chipmaker. Other speakers were also scheduled to take part in the program. The articles describe the session mainly as a forum for discussing AI's broader effects.

The event is the second day of a multi-day gathering organized by Nikkei, and the articles present it as a platform rather than a source of new rules or policy changes. The conference also features speakers from fitness and martial arts, according to the subheading of the coverage. Nikkei's reporting connects the discussion to wider industry concerns, including memory chip prices and AI-driven demand that other coverage in the same publication has covered. The articles do not state any formal requirement, deadline, or change arising from the debate. No specific figures, commitments, or outcomes from the sessions were reported in the material available.

Responsibility for the program rests with Nikkei, which organized the dialogue and commissioned the related content through its Global Business Bureau. The articles do not include direct statements from the TSMC or Microsoft executives in the form of quotations, so their positions on AI are not reported here. The coverage notes that other executives at the event have expressed views on AI, such as the Siemens CEO saying that AI will not take jobs but those who can use it will, and a Foxconn chief downplaying bubble concerns. Those remarks come from separate reports and are not drawn from the TSMC or Microsoft sessions. The articles carry no further information about what will follow the event beyond the conclusion of the dialogue.

Articles.Title: TSMC, Microsoft executives debate AI's impact on Day 2 of Nikkei Dialogue

stories.Headline: More than $5 billion spent by AI giants this year is aimed at implementation
stories.Summary:
The AI giants have spent more than $5 billion this year on implementation, the work of getting artificial intelligence running inside businesses rather than building the models themselves. According to the article, OpenAI, Anthropic and others made these commitments in 2026, with the article published on November 11, 2026. Anthropic, with Blackstone, put $1.5 billion into a venture built around getting AI working inside businesses. Microsoft created Frontier, backed by $2.5 billion and 6,000 people who sit directly inside customer organizations. AWS committed $1 billion to a team that embeds engineers with clients, and OpenAI is buying implementation firms outright to build its own staff.

The article says the spending reflects a shift in where the difficulty lies. Model prices have fallen, but results have not followed, because the slowdown sits in companies' data, their context, and their access to people who can connect the two. The article presents the giants' spending as a sign that the hard part is no longer building the AI model itself. It notes that the announcements reveal the decisions of four companies but not who else is making similar bets. To find that, the article draws on ZoomInfo data tracking hiring surges and AI technology adoption between the end of 2025 and the middle of 2026.

That data shows the share of hiring surges demanding hands-on generative AI skills rose from 5.9% at the end of 2025 to 7.6% by the middle of 2026. Two-thirds of the surges tracked were in engineering and technical teams. Mentions of Claude in surge hiring rose from 33 in the fourth quarter of 2025 to 125 in the second quarter of 2026. Overall adoption of AI and machine learning technology is up 38% in six months, across 1,835 named products. Custom software and IT services firms are adopting faster, up 52%, while construction is up 72%, financial software 87%, insurance 76% and law firms 72%.

The article says these figures point to a market shifting quickly, with the most growth outside technology companies. It advises sellers that a generative AI hiring surge marks a buying window that opens before procurement begins, and that the tools named in job descriptions indicate which stack a company is committing to. It also says the AI software market covers 1,492 vendors in ZoomInfo's technology index, with 92% offering exactly one product. The article notes that the giant announcements are a lagging indicator, since those decisions were made months before they were published.

The article's guidance is aimed at sellers and builders. For those selling AI, data or implementation services, it recommends reviewing target lists, since construction, insurance, legal and financial services are the fastest-growing adopters. It advises that accounts in those industries require longer cycles and that a named reference in the same industry carries more weight than a feature list. For companies building their own AI stacks, it says competitors can access the same models, so first-party data and whether it is current and connected become the differentiators. The article closes its analysis by posing the question of what would have to change for an agent to answer a live customer question using a company's data without human verification.

Articles.Title: More than $5 billion spent by AI giants this year is aimed at implementation

stories.Headline: Infineon, SoluM to Develop HVDC Power Solutions for AI Data Centers
stories.Summary:
Infineon Technologies Korea said on Nov. 5 that it signed a memorandum of understanding with SoluM to jointly develop high-voltage direct current power solutions for AI data centers. The agreement was signed by Adam White, president of Infineon's Power Systems division, and SoluM CEO Jeon Seong-ho. The two companies will cooperate on three product areas: server power supply units, battery backup units and intermediate bus converters. HVDC distributes electricity inside data centers as direct current instead of alternating current, which reduces the number of power conversion stages and so cuts energy losses.

Under the deal, Infineon will take part from the early stages of projects, proposing products, developing reference designs and providing technical support. It will supply silicon, silicon carbide and gallium nitride power semiconductors, along with microcontrollers and sensors. SoluM will design and manufacture the server power solutions and power modules. The companies also agreed to hold regular technical exchanges to develop next-generation technologies. SoluM was set up in 2015 as a spin-off of Samsung Electro-Mechanics' Digital Module division and makes power modules for televisions and servers, as well as electronic shelf labels.

White said AI data centers increasingly need power infrastructure with higher efficiency, reliability and power density, and that SoluM's server power expertise and Infineon's semiconductor knowledge complement each other. Jeon said the collaboration will strengthen SoluM's high-voltage, high-efficiency power design capabilities and open new business in the next-generation AI data center power market. At a press conference the same day at Infineon Korea's Seoul headquarters, White set out the company's "From Grid to Core" strategy and said its chips are used across the whole power supply chain of AI data centers. A report on the event also listed Hyosung and LS Electric among Infineon's expanding partnerships in Korea.

White projected that data centers' share of global electricity generation will rise from 3% today to 7% to 8% by 2030. He said power use per server rack will grow from 100 to 150 kilowatts now to more than 1 megawatt after 2028, as the power draw of each GPU climbs from 1,000 watts to above 2,000 watts. The 800-volt direct current architecture, which Nvidia is promoting, converts incoming power straight to 800V DC and steps it down only once or twice near the GPU, cutting losses, heat and the space taken by cabling and power supplies. Nvidia plans to widen its use alongside shipments of its Kyber racks in 2027. A Simply Wall St article on Nov. 7 noted that the SoluM tie-up gives context to growth assumptions for Infineon, whose shares were at €45.76 and had gained 60.5% over three years, and it judged the stock modestly undervalued on a discounted cash flow basis.

Articles.Title: Vertiv partners with Infineon to scale power semiconductors for AI data centers
