stories.Headline: An analysis of the tech job market in late 2026: product managers seem to be benefiting most in the AI era, demand for engineers is plateauing, and more (Lenny Rachitsky/Lenny's Newsletter)
stories.Summary:
Lenny Rachitsky's newsletter published a report on November 10, 2026, titled "State of the tech job market: late 2026," analyzing hiring trends at tech companies. The report is based on two datasets: TrueUp, which tracks global job openings at more than 9,000 tech companies, and Live Data Technologies, which tracks job changes for 124 million professionals, with hiring figures specific to the United States. Rachitsky said the report is his second of 2026 and the most surprising of the five he has produced over the past few years. Product managers appear to be benefiting most in the AI era, according to the report. Open PM roles are at their highest level in nearly four years, up 75% from the March 2023 low, and PM openings grew 56% since the start of 2023, compared with 43% for engineering.

PM's share of hiring rose from 16% in 2021 to 21% today, even though hiring for every core product role has been flat or declining. Rachitsky wrote that this suggests growing demand for PMs but that landing strong candidates is getting harder. Engineering demand has plateaued, the report says. Open engineering roles grew 29% through 2024, 15% through 2025, and just 2.5% in the past year, and there are fewer open engineering roles today than in March. U.S. companies hired about 113,000 software engineers between May 2025 and April 2026, less than half the 2022 peak of 239,000, and the number has dropped every year since 2022.

Rachitsky pointed to recruiter openings, which are up nearly 300% since mid-2023, as a possible sign that engineering hiring could reaccelerate. He also noted the rise of forward deployed engineer roles, with about 1,500 open globally after a 4.6x increase over the past year. Design and user research roles are declining sharply, according to the report. There are about 1,900 open product design roles at tech companies globally, the lowest since tracking began and down 28% from a year ago, and U.S. companies hired about 12,600 product designers in the past 12 months, less than half the 27,600 hired in 2022. User researcher hiring fell 66% from 5,300 in 2022 to about 1,800 over the past year, and only 108 UXR jobs are open globally.

Rachitsky attributed the decline to faster product development, with teams releasing products earlier and relying more on post-launch iteration, along with better tools that let non-researchers conduct user research. The report also tracks skills and location trends. "LLM" is now the most mentioned skill in PM job descriptions, while "Claude" is the second most mentioned skill in designer job descriptions this spring. Fifteen percent of open tech roles are now based in the Bay Area, up 43% from a year ago, and only 14% offer a remote option, the lowest on record and down from 21% in late 2022. Rachitsky said the report's final takeaway, that the tech job market is growing outside of software roles, was reserved for paid subscribers, so the article's text available here does not describe it.

stories.Headline: AI Opportunity Fund Expands AI Skills Training Across Asia Pacific with 28 Phase Three Local Implementing Partners
stories.Summary:
AVPN, Asia's largest platform for social impact, announced on November 11, 2026 the 28 organisations selected as local implementing partners for phase three of the AI Opportunity Fund: Asia-Pacific, supported by Google.org and the Asian Development Bank. The new cohort extends the Fund's AI skills training into schools, universities and workplaces across 19 markets, including through organisations taking part in AI Ready ASEAN, led by ASEAN Foundation. Most of the new partners will work directly with K-12 teachers, university students and faculty, reaching the educators who shape the next generation of workers. Other partners will reach healthcare workers, agricultural and service-sector workers, and employees of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises. The same day, AVPN also launched the AI Opportunity Learning Platform.

The platform gives learners access to localised AI training and recommended learning pathways in 16 languages, with a pathway suggested after a short assessment. Certification is available on completion of training. A Gemini-powered assistant helps users navigate the platform and provides guided learning. For phase three, AVPN brought on two new strategic partners: the Raspberry Pi Foundation, which will help local partners localise its Experience AI content, and the Ayala Foundation, which will give educators and students in the Philippines access to Google AI learning resources and support local partners there. Among the funded organisations, Pratham Education Foundation in India will train teachers to use AI critically, JA Korea will pair Google's AI training with formal certification for public school educators, and AI Edu Corp in Vietnam will support embedding AI literacy into national teacher standards.

AVPN chief executive Naina Subberwal Batra said that AI tools are already entering classrooms and workplaces across the region, and that the challenge is helping people use them well and know when not to rely on them too heavily. She said local organisations understand the languages and communities they serve and can adapt training in ways a regional programme alone cannot. Marija Ralic, head of Google.org APAC, said access to AI skills depends on whether people can find relevant training in a language and setting that works for them, and that the platform brings training and local partners together in one place. The Fund was launched in 2024 with a USD 15 million commitment, received a further USD 10 million in phase two in May 2025 and another USD 10 million in phase three in May 2026, bringing Google.org's total commitment to USD 35 million. To date, the Fund has trained more than 850,000 workers and 63,000 small businesses through almost 60 local implementing partner organisations, delivering programmes in more than 30 local languages.

stories.Headline: IBM report finds 94% of surveyed enterprises faced a sovereignty challenge, with AI the most common
stories.Summary:
The IBM report, Proof, Not Promises: The Digital Sovereignty Index, was released on November 11, 2026, and it finds that 94% of the enterprises it surveyed faced at least one sovereignty challenge over the previous three years. Those challenges included AI-provider failures, regulatory conflicts, critical vendor disruption, government restrictions such as export controls, and data-access problems. Of the organizations affected, 81% had to supply formal evidence of control to regulators, customers, auditors or internal stakeholders. IBM describes the gap it has found as an "overconfidence gap," in which leaders believe they can prove sovereign control but the evidence often falls short of the Index's highest standards.

The report measures whether an organization can retain and prove control over its critical AI, technology, operations and data, especially when conditions change or dependencies come under pressure. It assesses six areas: responsibility, which asks whether the organization can prove who was accountable; trace, which asks whether it can show exactly what happened; constraint, which asks whether it can prove its controls were working; intervention, which asks whether it can show how it responded and recovered; legitimacy, which asks whether it can explain and justify decisions under scrutiny; and exit, which asks whether it can prove it could change provider or recover operations if needed. The findings suggest that the difficulty is less about control itself than about sovereignty efforts not being built to answer these questions smoothly under pressure. Only a third of respondents, 33%, test their ability to demonstrate sovereignty continuously or as part of regular governance and assurance processes.

IBM's Senior Vice President and Chief Global Affairs Officer, Jonathan Adashek, said that sovereignty should expand future choices rather than restrict them, and that boards need to show how they can adapt, change strategy or change critical provider. He added that the next step is stronger evidence that governance works, including testing exit capabilities, understanding critical dependencies and focusing on where a loss of control would have the greatest impact. Emmanuel Frenehard, Chief Digital Officer at Sanofi, said that digital sovereignty is a business reality rather than a compliance checkbox, and that it is a matter of business continuity as AI becomes embedded across the enterprise. The report itself does not say which organizations or regulators, beyond these two executives, took any position on the findings.

AI emerged as the most common sovereignty problem, with AI-related issues, including incorrect outputs, explainability problems, model or provider failures and governance concerns, cited by 44% of respondents. That figure was ahead of significant provider changes at 35%, formal audit or regulatory events at 38%, data-access or transfer issues at 33%, and government restrictions such as export controls or sanctions at 30%. An average of 82% of respondents said they were very or extremely confident they could provide evidence of sovereign control. However, only 26% of enterprises reached the Index's Leading Digital Sovereignty tier, and enterprises in that tier were more than twice as likely to resolve their most testing challenge without material disruption, at 52% compared with 22% of establishing enterprises.

The research behind the Index combined a review of 27 sources, including legislation, standards, governance frameworks and academic research, with 25 interviews with policymakers, regulators, public-sector officials and policy experts, and perspectives from 17 senior customer leaders across five countries. Its quantitative survey covered 2,003 senior decision-makers at large enterprises in the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, France, Saudi Arabia, India and Japan. Among the barriers that respondents reported to proving sovereignty were manual or time-consuming evidence collection, cited by 56%, and fragmented evidence across teams and systems, dependence on third parties for records, and legacy systems or inconsistent standards, each cited by 53%. Half of respondents, 50%, pointed to untested controls, recovery or exit arrangements. The report does not describe any specific steps that organizations are scheduled to take next.

stories.Headline: Rackspace and Together AI Announce Strategic Agreement to Support Enterprise AI Inference
stories.Summary:
Rackspace and Together AI announced an initial multiyear strategic AI infrastructure agreement on November 10, 2026, in San Antonio. Under the deal, Rackspace expects to provide and operate dedicated NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 infrastructure, connected with NVIDIA Spectrum-X Ethernet networking, to support Together AI inference workloads. Deployment is planned for 2027, subject to certain conditions. The companies also signed a separate, non-binding letter of intent to explore a joint go-to-market approach for enterprise-focused AI solutions. Rackspace is described as the operator of the full enterprise AI stack.

Rackspace expects to supply the dedicated NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra infrastructure, including power, liquid cooling, networking and storage. Together AI expects to provide the managed cloud platform running on that infrastructure, including access to open source models, inference optimizations and developer tools. The parties expect to evaluate additional security, governance and compliance controls for future offerings, depending on customer requirements. Rackspace intends to build a repeatable model to support AI platform companies, systems integrators and enterprises. Its approach is to seek contractual commitments for dedicated capacity and manage related financing with the goal of aligning to expected customer demand and the useful life of the hardware.

Gajen Kandiah, Chief Executive Officer of Rackspace, said that enterprise AI requires more than compute, and that success depends on bringing compute into production and operating it reliably. He said Rackspace brings more than 25 years of experience operating complex enterprise environments. Vipul Ved Prakash, founder and CEO of Together AI, said that scaling in the enterprise requires infrastructure that can grow with the company's ambitions. Raj Mirpuri, Vice President of Global AI Clouds and Infrastructure Ecosystem at NVIDIA, said that Rackspace and Together AI can run inference workloads efficiently with NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra. Rackspace, an NVIDIA Cloud Partner, plans to operate the deployment in a purpose-built, liquid-cooled facility.

Effective November 6, 2026, Rackspace entered into a share purchase agreement with an investor group led by Voss Capital, LP, providing for an aggregate $66 million private placement of common stock. Rackspace expects to use the net proceeds for general corporate purposes, working capital, capital expenditures and growth capital, including GPU-related initiatives. Rackspace expects to seek separate financing for the NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems and is in active discussions with potential lenders. However, no definitive GPU financing commitment had been obtained as of the release date. The release states that Rackspace's obligations to proceed with the deployment are subject to the financing condition and other conditions in the definitive agreement.

Together AI, described as the AI Native Cloud, was founded in 2022 and says it powers over two million developers. The release says the non-binding letter of intent contemplates evaluating how Together AI's inference, post-training and reinforcement learning capabilities could be combined with Rackspace's infrastructure and engineering services. Any joint offerings would depend on further agreement between the parties and applicable customer requirements. The release also says that the availability of any deployment configurations, including data residency and compliance features, would be determined by the specific offering. The release does not say what happens next beyond the planned 2027 deployment and the exploration of joint offerings.

stories.Headline: Norway reins in data centre industry amid AI boom
stories.Summary:
The articles here cover a US story, not Norway, and they are about analysts warning of a regulatory slowdown in the American AI data centre buildout after Democrats won the midterm elections. Forecasters on Wall Street cut their projections for Big Tech infrastructure spending within hours of the vote. They cautioned that a wave of proposed project moratoria and tighter oversight could stall up to 30 per cent of planned US facilities. The pessimism also hit stock prices on Thursday, US time.

The articles say the warned-of measures include proposed project freezes in Texas and federal regulatory pushback. Analysts said these could force developers to shrink their capacity plans. The sources give no specific dates, dollar figures or rule text for these freezes beyond the 30 per cent estimate. They describe the threat as a possible clampdown rather than an enacted policy. Nothing in the articles says what specific rules would take effect or when.

The article attributes the warnings to Wall Street forecasters and analysts rather than to any government body or company. It does not quote a named official or executive responding to the predictions. The reporter, Mia Nurmamat, wrote the piece for the South China Morning Post, published on November 6, 2026. The article describes the reaction as a forecast of pain for the sector, not a confirmed outcome.

The articles do not mention Norway, so they offer nothing on the Norwegian story in the headline. They also do not say what happens next beyond the market reaction and the warnings. The forecasts are the only concrete development reported so far. Further detail on which projects would be affected, or how the federal response would unfold, is not in these sources.

stories.Headline: Tester joins AI, data and surveillance company with MAGA ties
stories.Summary:
Former Montana U.S. Senator Jon Tester has taken a job as a senior advisor at Palantir Technologies, an artificial intelligence, surveillance and data analytics company with ties to the GOP and the Trump administration. The company's software is used by U.S. immigration enforcement and the Israeli military, drawing scrutiny from the American Civil Liberties Union. Palantir was co-founded by billionaire conservative Trump ally Peter Thiel. The Palantir opportunity reached Tester's desk in July.

Tester said working for Palantir is not the same as working for data centers, though the two are connected. He said data centers are "screwed up big time" because they can overload energy grids, and he argued that communities need to be driving the decisions about them. He called for complete transparency from data center operators. He also said there will be congressional hearings, accountability and oversight on AI.

Tester said he hopes to use his experience as a third-generation organic grain and crop farmer to streamline the paperwork-heavy parts of food production with AI. He said AI could let the U.S. Department of Agriculture and crop insurers interact without overlapping paperwork. He pointed to medical record sharing between Veterans Affairs facilities and the private sector, where Palantir is already active. He said his official role is limited to advising on real-world uses of AI and improving efficiency and ease of use.

The Chronicle asked Tester about earlier statements by Palantir CEO Alex Karp that AI could disrupt white-collar jobs such as coding, writing and legal work. Tester said he did not reach his decision overnight and had talked with Karp before accepting the position. He said people at the company he spoke with one-on-one respected civil liberties and privacy. Karp has contended that only vocational or technical workers and neurodivergent individuals with out-of-the-box problem-solving skills can thrive in an AI-driven world.

Tester said Congress needs to put "sideboards" on AI and that it "bears watching." On July 23, Democratic California representative Ted Lieu and Texas Republican Nathaniel Moran introduced an AI Kill Switch Act, which remains in limbo. Polling from The AI Policy Institute found that 86% of voters support legislating a guaranteed shutdown capability. Tester-endorsed Democratic Representative-elect Sam Forstag proposed a kill switch during an Oct. 26 visit to Montana State University, and Tester said he had not compared notes with Forstag but likes him a lot.

stories.Headline: AI hoaxes are deceiving 911 dispatchers, and they're only getting harder to detect
stories.Summary:
In August, a caller made a bomb threat to Wheatland Union High School in Yuba County, California. Police responded overnight, classes were canceled, and no bomb was found and no one was hurt. Authorities said the call was part of a series of hoax calls, also called swatting, made to schools across the country over the summer. What set this incident apart was that the caller's voice was generated by artificial intelligence.

Swatting calls can be placed to 911 or police departments, with callers reporting a bomb threat, mass shooting or another life-threatening emergency in order to set off a large emergency response. According to the FBI, the aim is to harass or retaliate against targets such as public officials. Such calls usually trigger a big, chaotic police response that pulls resources away from real emergencies. Mel Maier, CEO and executive director of APCO International, notes that people have been killed and injured in swatting attacks.

Maier says AI-generated voices have changed these hoaxes. Earlier swatting voices were fairly easy to recognize, but now they sound natural, with pauses and filler words such as "uh" and "um." APCO and NENA: The 9-1-1 Association, which together represent 911 dispatchers, have voiced growing concern about how bad actors could use AI. In June, APCO and the Public Safety Threat Alliance published findings from 766 responses from public safety communications professionals, and about 14% of dispatchers said they had been targeted using AI tools. Maier says he expects that figure to keep rising as the tools improve.

Brandon May, an assistant professor of forensic psychology at the Florida Institute of Technology, says companies such as ElevenLabs offer synthetic voice software that is cheap and easy to get. He says he can clone his own voice on ElevenLabs for less than $20 and change its intonation, pitch and pauses. May says it is no longer simple to tell from a voice or video that it is AI, and he says elaborate fraud callers using AI chatbots are even tricking people out of their life savings. He says the fakes will be nearly impossible for dispatchers to detect during high-stakes calls.

April Heinze, NENA's vice president and chief of 911 operations, says most swatters do not dial 911 directly, because 911 supplies location, a callback number and the phone owner's name, and spoofing a location on 911 is essentially impossible. Swatting calls are usually made to police departments or courthouses and then transferred into 911 centers, which makes them hard to trace. Heinze and Maier both decline to describe their dispatcher training in detail, saying more public information would make it easier to train AI to fool dispatchers. Maier says APCO is developing caller interrogation criteria that ask questions granular enough that an AI could not pull the answers from public databases or social media. Both Maier and Heinze stress that dispatchers will always treat reports of life-threatening situations as real and send emergency resources, with Heinze saying, "if it's a life-or-death situation, you cannot ever take chances on that."

stories.Headline: Testing the new generation of AI-enabled fire-extinguishing drones
stories.Summary:
Fire crews in Aspen, Colorado are training to pilot a new generation of drones made by the California-based company Seneca, and the Aspen Fire Protection District will be the first fire department in the country to operate them independently once training is complete. The drones are about 10 by 12 feet wide, have four large arms with propellers, and are designed to work in a swarm. Five of them can carry 500 to 1,000 gallons of finished fire foam, and firefighters reported they were easy to operate. Andy Fisher, deputy chief of Aspen Fire, said the department's program could launch as early as next year. So far the drones have only been used on prescribed burns in California with support from Seneca's staff.

Fisher wants to send the drones to hard-to-reach fires, such as remote lightning strikes, before firefighters arrive. The city of Aspen is surrounded by dense forests and has few evacuation routes for residents and visitors. Seneca's founder, Stuart Landesberg, said the drones have a range of 5 to 10 miles, double that when empty, and can cross steep or treacherous terrain quickly. Hovering over a fire, an AI-supported sensor suite calculates distance and wind speed, then releases water or retardant at a specific angle and velocity. Landesberg said the drones will not replace air tankers on big fires but can carry tools, monitor fires and help extinguish hot spots.

Landesberg said the drones could make aerial firefighting far cheaper than helicopters, saying they could be "the next best thing at two orders of magnitude less cost." Aspen Fire says it will pay about $2.5 million over the next five years, with private donors covering the bill. Joe Stutler, a firefighter with nearly 60 years of experience who is not affiliated with Aspen Fire or Seneca, said he is a "big proponent of technology" and hopes the drones can fight fires overnight, when manned aircraft are often grounded. He also hopes they will reduce risk to pilots flying helicopters and air tankers. Stutler remains skeptical, saying he has not seen results from real wildfires and that claims need to be backed by data.

The FAA granted Aspen Fire a waiver in late October, allowing the department to fly the drones up to 200 feet in Pitkin County once training is complete. The drones cannot fly over populated areas, and someone must keep eyes on them at all times, including a spotter on a ridgeline who can communicate with the pilots. If the drones prove useful, Aspen Fire hopes to expand the waiver and help fight fires elsewhere in the state. Before other fire departments invest in the technology, many are watching Aspen to see how effective the drones can be.

stories.Headline: Veterans tour Washington war memorials using AI glasses
stories.Summary:
On Tuesday, November 11, 2026, a group of veterans from across the country toured the war memorials in Washington using special AI glasses to help them locate fallen service members. The trip was an honor flight sponsored by Meta, and many of the three-day participants were blind or visually impaired. Each veteran received a pair of Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses to help them move around the memorials built in their honor. The glasses use built-in cameras, microphones and artificial intelligence to sense a wearer's surroundings and describe them aloud.

Meta has committed to donating 130,000 pairs of the glasses to visually impaired and blinded veterans nationwide. John Bockstanz, an Innovation Policy Manager at Meta and an Iraq War veteran, said the glasses help users read menus, navigate busy airports and even match clothing. He described the effort as an ongoing, year-round commitment rather than a single flight. The glasses also let veterans ask questions about the memorials and learn more about what they are looking at. Bockstanz said the company is already hearing how the devices are restoring independence in daily life.

Victor Dunham, a Vietnam veteran from Texas, used the glasses to search for a friend named Anthony, known as Tony, who died while serving beside him. Dunham said he had kept finding a major who died on the same day, but the glasses helped him learn more and pursue the search further. With their help he located Anthony's name on the Vietnam Memorial wall. Dunham said that finding him closed a loop that had stayed open for years. He also said the trip was deeply meaningful, and his son Mark, an Iraq War veteran, joined him on the journey.

stories.Headline: Not funny: US comedians say 'sexualized' AI personas steal jokes
stories.Summary:
Several American stand-up comedians say AI-generated social media personas are copying their jokes, according to an Agence France-Presse report published on November 11, 2026. Julia Jasunas, a Los Angeles-based comedian, said an account called "Aylen Skye" lifted a joke about kissing a roommate that she had spent years developing. AFP found several similar sexualized AI personalities on Instagram and TikTok that were reusing material from real comedians, and it was unclear who was running them. Some of the accounts appeared to drive traffic to subscription services that host pornography.

The Aylen Skye account gathered more than 230,000 Instagram followers and a Meta verified checkmark before it was removed, while the TikTok version still exists and links to Fanvue, a subscription platform with adult content from AI models. New York comedian Olivia Carter said a copycat video used her joke about asking out a personal trainer, a bit she once performed on Jimmy Fallon's show, and she has stopped posting new material online. California comedian George Brett Olson said an account called "Tiffany Sloane," with over 370,000 followers, copied his joke, his outfit and his stage setup. Experts quoted in the report describe the problem as part of a wider pattern in which AI systems take creative work from painters, musicians and others without payment or credit.

The comedians said platform owners should do more to stop this, and Jasunas argued that companies with the money and technology have a duty to tighten their rules. Meta did not immediately comment, while a TikTok spokesperson pointed to community guidelines that bar sharing content that violates another user's intellectual property rights. Meta's head, Adam Mosseri, responded to Olson's complaint by saying that banning AI was not practical but that the company wanted to direct more traffic to original creators. He added that Meta should work out what it could do about wholesale copying, though he said he was not sure what that would be. Olson called the response a "big nothing-burger."

Carnegie Mellon University professor Michael Smith told AFP that comedians once policed one another's jokes informally, but large language models scraping the internet have made that difficult to enforce. Smith warned that the accounts siphon clicks and money from artists who rely on social media to build audiences and win bookings, which could weaken the early stages of comedy careers. stories.Headline: CNCF Welcomes Vultr as a Platinum Member to Advance Open and Sovereign Cloud Infrastructure for AI
stories.Summary:
On November 10, 2026, the Cloud Native Computing Foundation announced that Vultr had upgraded its CNCF membership to Platinum, at a time when cloud native and AI infrastructure are converging on shared, open interoperability. The announcement was made at KubeCon and CloudNativeCon North America, held in Salt Lake City. The upgrade builds on Vultr's deepening partnerships with CNCF projects and on the recently launched Vultr Open Source Alliance. The alliance brings together work across open infrastructure, cloud native technologies, AI, and developer ecosystems.

The move centers on the idea that developers should be able to choose the infrastructure, frameworks, models, tools, and protocols that suit their workloads without being tied to a single technology stack. Vultr contributed both CPU and GPU infrastructure capacity to support CNCF project testing. Its Vultr Kubernetes Engine is a CNCF Certified Kubernetes product. Vultr also serves as a member of the Agentic AI Foundation, a separate Linux Foundation initiative that stewards open standards for the agentic AI stack.

Chris Aniszczyk, CTO of CNCF, said AI factory infrastructure should be open and fungible rather than another walled garden, and he described Platinum membership as a real commitment to building that open future. Kevin Cochrane, Chief Marketing Officer of Vultr, said open source is the foundation of modern AI infrastructure and that developers should be free to choose their frameworks, models, and infrastructure. Cochrane said the Platinum upgrade builds on five years of work alongside the CNCF community. Vultr's engineering team has worked directly with maintainers on CNCF projects including Kubernetes and Kubeflow.

Vultr first joined CNCF as a Silver Member in 2021. Its infrastructure runs heterogeneous GPU and CPU capacity that supports open source frameworks, including PyTorch for model training and Kubernetes for inference. The engineering work includes contributing feedback and improvements upstream rather than only consuming the technology downstream. The CNCF describes itself as hosting critical components of the global technology infrastructure, including Kubernetes, Prometheus, and Envoy. It is supported by nearly 800 members and over 200 startups, and it is part of the nonprofit Linux Foundation.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave Delivers Another Blowout Quarter. Is It Enough To Save the AI Trade?
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave, the largest of the neoclouds, tumbled over the last month and dragged the AI sector down with it after a social media post showed its bond yields had reached as high as 15%. That observation set off another round of concerns that the AI build-out is unsustainable. The worries were magnified after Democrats swept the midterm elections, in part by campaigning on increased regulation for data centers. Against that backdrop, CoreWeave reported third-quarter results on Tuesday afternoon, and the company made clear that demand for its services, which essentially consist of renting AI compute, continues to skyrocket.

Revenue in the quarter jumped 168% to $3.66 billion, ahead of the analyst consensus of $3.54 billion. The revenue backlog improved from $104 billion at the end of the second quarter to $132.5 billion at the end of the third. Its GAAP operating margin rose from 4% to 6%, as GAAP operating income climbed from $52 million to $207 million. Those figures point to strong demand and improving profitability at the operating level.

The bottom line still carries heavy costs. CoreWeave has taken on tens of billions in debt to fund its rapid data center expansion and chip purchases. Interest expense rose from $310 million a year earlier to $846 million, and the company finished the quarter with a GAAP net loss of $709 million, or $1.27 per share, against expectations of a $1.21 loss per share. On a free cash flow basis, it lost $7.7 billion in the quarter, and its debt jumped to $47 billion.

Investors mostly shrugged off the report, with the stock up 2% in after-hours trading before the 5 p.m. ET earnings call. Management said it would not use the unsecured debt market at current interest rates, which offers some encouragement to investors worried about rising bond yields. CoreWeave expects interest expense to reach $1.05 billion to $1.15 billion in the fourth quarter, on $4.7 billion to $5 billion in revenue, and it raised its full-year revenue forecast to $13 billion to $13.3 billion. On the earnings call, CEO Michael Intrator argued that prices for older GPUs had been resilient and were in fact rising, even for Nvidia chips that are three generations old.

The company plans to collect $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits in the fourth quarter, which should offer some reassurance to investors. The Fed is expected to raise interest rates at its next meeting in December after a hot Consumer Price Index report. CoreWeave has a current ratio below 0.5, and its interest expense is more than 20% of its revenue. From CoreWeave's perspective, demand looks set to outstrip supply for years to come, and the company believes it has several levers to pull to fund the build-out.

stories.Headline: Broadcom contributes VM API to CNCF for Kubernetes, AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Broadcom has contributed an application programming interface for virtual machines to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, the body that steers Kubernetes. The move was announced at KubeCon North America 2026 and was reported on November 10, 2026. Its stated purpose is to let virtual machines run as first-class Kubernetes workloads and to simplify the management of AI infrastructure. Alongside it, Broadcom is supporting a newly formed Workload Conformance Working Group, which aims to set objective standards for making Kubernetes workloads portable across environments.

The contribution centers on standardizing APIs so that virtual machines can be provisioned declaratively, whether they are proprietary or open-source projects. Broadcom's diagnostic tool Sonobuoy is central to the certification effort tied to the new standards. The company is also pushing customers to consolidate monolithic, cloud-native and AI workloads on its VMware Cloud Foundation platform, with the aim of lowering IT costs by running diverse workloads on one platform. Broadcom says over 2,600 organizations have licensed VCF 9, spanning more than 24 million processor cores. It has also validated 30 partner offerings to run on the VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service, an optimized Kubernetes distribution for VCF.

Prashanth Shenoy, chief marketing officer for Broadcom's VMware Cloud Foundation division, said the VM API contribution is meant to ensure virtual machines are treated as first-class citizens within cloud-native computing environments. The articles attribute the broader rationale to the Linux Foundation, which reported that virtual machines make up 53 per cent of production applications. It also found that 34 per cent of respondents expect to expand their VM footprint for AI and agentic workloads. Together, these figures are presented as the backdrop for why Broadcom is pressing for tighter integration between VMs and Kubernetes.

The articles frame this as a bid to bring virtual machines into the same orchestration model that governs containers, at a time when AI workloads are driving infrastructure demand. They do not describe timelines for when the working group will publish its standards or how the CNCF will adopt the API. Nor do they report any reaction from competing vendors or open-source maintainers. The coverage stays focused on Broadcom's announcement and the figures it cites.

stories.Headline: After challenging Google's Android with Cyanogen, its co-founder takes aim at Windows for AI era
stories.Summary:
Kora Systems, the company led by Kirt McMaster, the co-founder of Cyanogen, unveiled on Tuesday a Linux-based desktop operating system that builds AI models and autonomous agents directly into the computing experience. The software can work across applications, access files, and keep context between tasks. Kora expects to launch it in 2027 as a free desktop operating system, with support for Intel and AMD PCs as well as machines running Qualcomm's Snapdragon chips. The company is building it with about 50 engineers who use AI coding tools from OpenAI and Anthropic, which McMaster says have sped up development at least fivefold, mostly over the past six months.

The operating system is aimed at people who rely heavily on AI and are willing to pay for access to powerful models and services, not at Windows' entire user base. McMaster estimated that 45 million to 50 million people currently account for much of AI usage and revenue, and he expects that group to exceed 200 million users by 2033. Kora plans to earn money through subscriptions bundling AI models and agentic services. Its Cortex engine is designed to run AI tasks locally when possible and turn to cloud-based models for heavier work. The system is built on Linux and Nix, replacing the Fedora Silverblue base of Playtron's earlier gaming operating system, and Kora says its own Cortex engine and desktop interface will remain proprietary, though it plans to support AI models from different providers.

McMaster said that his time at Cyanogen taught him the risk of depending on the company he was trying to challenge, arguing that Cyanogen stayed reliant on Google Mobile Services and so could not build an independent ecosystem. Kora's engineers did not come from Cyanogen, and McMaster said the company recruited heavily from the Linux gaming community. Kora is also working with Qualcomm for nearly a year to optimize the system for Snapdragon PCs, and with Saudi Arabia's AI company Humain on an enterprise version called Humain OS, expected on Snapdragon laptops in 2027. McMaster did not name any PC manufacturers Kora plans to partner with or give a timeline for those announcements.

The company was previously known as Playtron, a gaming operating-system business that McMaster led, and it rebranded as Kora in July 2025 as it shifted toward AI. McMaster said the change followed moves by companies such as Perplexity and OpenAI into AI-powered browsers, which he believed would not give AI agents enough access to a computer for complex tasks. Windows held about 77% of the worldwide desktop operating-system market in October, compared with nearly 10% for Apple's OS X, according to StatCounter. Kora's investors include Samsung Next, Square Enix, Alumni Ventures, Polychain, VanEck, and Circle, all of which backed Playtron. McMaster said the company has raised more funding since the shift to AI but declined to give the total or its valuation, saying only that Kora has enough money to operate for several years.

stories.Headline: Futures Rise, CoreWeave Jumps In Good News For AI
stories.Summary:
Futures on the Dow Jones, S&P 500 and Nasdaq rose overnight after CoreWeave jumped following its late Tuesday report, a move that lifted neocloud and AI stocks. Investor's Business Daily reported the rise as Wall Street looked ahead, and the earlier session had been hit by a hot CPI inflation report and hawkish comments from Federal Reserve Gov. Christopher Waller that sent Treasury yields soaring. Nvidia kept sliding in the same period over CEO Jensen Huang's espionage affair. Those are the only details the articles give about the overnight move, so the account stops there.

Separately, Cloudflare rose 20% to $293.43 in morning trading after reporting Q3 2026 results on November 5, with revenue up 39% year over year to $782.5 million against a $738.3 million consensus. Its adjusted earnings per share of $0.38 beat the $0.34 consensus, and CEO Matthew Prince called it the company's best quarter ever. Cloudflare raised its full-year revenue outlook to $2.963 billion to $2.964 billion and projected fourth-quarter sales of $845 million to $846 million. Its GAAP net loss, however, widened to $34.1 million from $1.3 million a year earlier, weighed down by $174.1 million in stock-based compensation.

IREN, a GPU cloud provider, rose 15% to $20.81 after reporting Q1 FY2027 results on November 5, when its revenue climbed to $228 million from $137 million in the prior quarter. Sales in its AI Cloud segment jumped to $200 million from $71 million, and its adjusted EBITDA of $66 million exceeded forecasts. Its net loss narrowed to $263 million from $684 million in the previous quarter. Since quarter-end, IREN signed a five-year contract at $22 million per megawatt, with the customer prepaying 90% of the related GPU capital costs, and a separate short-duration contract at $40 million per megawatt.

CoreWeave gained 10% to $48.07 even though its latest earnings report dates to August 11, a gain the article reads as sector-wide rather than company-specific. Over the month through the prior session's close, CoreWeave had fallen 48% as concerns about its debt load pressured its bonds, and IREN had fallen 50%. Cloudflare had been down 17% over the same period. The October jobs report added to risk appetite, with the U.S. adding 165,000 jobs against Bloomberg's expectations and unemployment ticking down to 4.1%. September's job gain was revised up to 60,000 from 29,000.

The articles describe the business models that separate these companies. Cloudflare sells security, networking and developer tools from its global edge network and markets itself as the first "agentic cloud," a subscription model far less capital-intensive than building GPU clusters. IREN owns the land, power and data centers under its business, much of it converted from crypto mining, which management says lets it pace spending to funding conditions. CoreWeave runs a debt-financed GPU cloud for AI labs, hyperscalers and enterprises. For IREN, the key question is whether more than $4 billion in annualized revenue run rate comes online by January 31, 2027, a target that may slip to the end of February.

Bulls point to rising contract prices, customer prepayments and Cloudflare's fastest revenue growth in nearly four years. Bears point to IREN's $6 billion in planned capital spending still to be funded, CoreWeave's heavy debt and Cloudflare's lower free cash flow margin. stories.Headline: E2E Networks unveils Blaze, a pay-per-token inference service for open AI models
stories.Summary:
E2E Networks has launched Blaze, a pay-per-token inference service for open AI models, and the announcement was published on November 10, 2026. Blaze gives developers and enterprises a single endpoint that is compatible with OpenAI's interface, connecting them to leading open models. The service runs on NVIDIA GPU infrastructure and uses open-source components from NVIDIA DSX OS. Customers pay only for the tokens they use.

The launch comes as Indian AI companies move from pilots to production, where the cost and speed of inference increasingly decide whether a product is viable. Rising token consumption from AI agents and growing AI-assisted development costs are adding pressure on chief information officers to use tokens more efficiently. Data sovereignty and keeping computing within India are also key priorities for buyers. Blaze is aimed at inference-heavy products where latency and cost per token matter most, including voice, coding agents, document AI and OCR, image and video generation, and language applications.

E2E Networks' founder and managing director, Tarun Dua, said customers want frontier-class open-weight models running on an NVIDIA Cloud Partner with reference design clusters as sovereign compute, and that Blaze provides this on E2E Cloud in India. He also said Blaze integrates easily with the rest of the E2E Cloud platform services. Vishal Dhupar, managing director for South Asia at NVIDIA, said access to AI computing and inference services is essential to advancing India's AI ecosystem. He added that NVIDIA's accelerated computing platform gives cloud providers such as E2E a foundation for making AI more accessible to developers and enterprises in India.

Blaze works alongside TIR, E2E's AI platform, which supports self-hosted inference and model training on NVIDIA Blackwell GPU clusters through managed Kubernetes. The service uses NVIDIA Dynamo for distributed model serving, along with other NVIDIA components for routing, scheduling and hardware-level isolation between customers. E2E says its AI factory capacity is expanding to about 14.6 MW, including a 1,024-GPU NVIDIA Blackwell cluster that has been live since May 2026. An additional 5.4 MW of Blackwell capacity, including HGX B300 systems, is also being added.

stories.Headline: Fluidstack begins construction on a 99-acre AI data center campus in Wythe County, Virginia
stories.Summary:
Fluidstack, the AI cloud provider building data centers for Anthropic, has begun construction on a 99-acre campus at Progress Park in Wythe County, Virginia, DatacenterDynamics reported on Tuesday. The company expects most of the campus to be finished by the end of 2027, with operations starting in phases, as it told county supervisors last month. The site was first announced in December 2025 by Solis Arx, a new developer led by founder and CEO Rob Noll, which projected a total investment of over $1 billion according to county administrator Stephen Bear. Fluidstack later took over the project, and the county's board approved an amendment renaming it Fluidstack in August. Neither the company nor the county has disclosed the campus's power capacity or building size, and no end customer has been named.

Solis Arx arranged electric service directly with Appalachian Power, and the county said the project would not affect local electricity rates. Fluidstack says it will pay for its own electricity use, the infrastructure it needs and upgrades to the nearby substation. The campus will use a closed-loop cooling system that needs an initial fill of about 400,000 gallons of water, with ongoing use mostly for staff. Fluidstack expects about 1,000 construction workers at peak and 75 permanent jobs once the campus is running, and says it did not seek or accept project-specific tax incentives. The county gave the ungraded lot to the developer at no cost and projects more than $10 million a year in tax revenue by 2028 if the schedule holds.

The project has drawn local opposition, and Wythe County has no zoning outside its two towns. Andy Kegley, leader of the residents' group Preserve Wythe, said at an October 28 open house that the deal was done and grading was already underway. The county is now drafting its first land-use ordinance. Anthropic said in November 2025 that it would invest $50 billion in U.S. computing infrastructure with Fluidstack, starting with sites in Texas and New York. Fluidstack is also the anchor tenant at bitcoin-miner conversions backed by Google, including TeraWulf's Lake Mariner campus in New York and Cipher Mining's 168 MW lease.

She drew on real deployments at Rabobank to describe the changes needed for that move. The talk is about 45 minutes long and is presented as part of the AI, ML and Data Engineering track.

According to the summary, Chu covers several specific practices. She recommends replacing naive OCR with agentic multimodal parsing, so that documents are read in a more capable way. She describes encoding non-textual temporal signals, which helps prevent systems from retrieving outdated information. The summary frames these as necessary for systems to survive in a heavily regulated environment.

Chu's background includes more than seven years building production data and machine learning pipelines and more than three years building generative AI products. She specializes in designing data and AI pipelines and in responsible AI practices, with deep expertise in natural language processing. The talk is one of many at QCon London, a practitioner-driven conference for technical team leads, architects, engineering directors and project managers.
