stories.Headline: PSI is trying to make a business out of AI-driven scientific discovery
stories.Summary:
David Turturean, a recent MIT graduate on the technical staff of the startup lab Physical Superintelligence (PSI), used early access to Anthropic's Fable 5.2 model to solve an 18-year-old problem in quantum computing, the Aaronson-Ambainis conjecture. The reporting was published on November 10, 2026, by TechCrunch. The solution concerns whether quantum computers can solve certain problems faster than classical ones. Scott Aaronson, one of the researchers who posed the problem, said he does not fully follow the proof but believes it is correct because it was autoformalized in Lean and checked by a team of top researchers with whom PSI shared it.

The result appears to rule out one route quantum computers could take to solve some hard problems quickly, though not all of them. PSI held the result until Anthropic's model was nearly ready for release, which gave it time to share the work with relevant experts. Turturean said the academic community will expect him to explain the result. Aaronson wrote that he was surprised the problem was missing from a recent OpenAI batch of solved problems.

PSI CEO Matt Pines said the company's model relies on specialized harnesses, tools, memory systems and simulation infrastructure to tackle scientific problems across breadth and depth. For now, the company earns revenue by using its tools to optimize data centers, simulating heat, power, water and sound. Its longer goal is converting theoretical physics breakthroughs into real technologies, which Pines acknowledged has not yet happened. He noted that AI has claimed solutions in mathematics and computer science, where results can be expressed in validated code, but physics is harder because nature has the final say.

Jim Halverson, a Northeastern University professor who advises PSI, said transparency and contacting experts are emerging best practices, and he will attend an MIT summit next week where leading physicists will discuss the new pace of science. Pines said PSI focuses on validating computational results with experiments as efficiently as possible. The startup Discovered Materials recently released a $1 million grand challenge for AI-driven research on problems such as superconductivity and heat dissipation. Participants in these new "neolabs for science" are still working out what standards will govern this work.

Articles.Title: PSI is trying to make a business out of AI-driven scientific discovery

stories.Headline: Gemini Robotics 2.5 accelerates real-world general dexterity
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind introduced Gemini Robotics 2.5 on November 10, 2026, describing it as its most capable vision-language-action model to date. The model increases both the breadth of skills a robot can learn and the speed at which it can acquire them. The company said the model is meant to help robots move out of the lab and into unstructured, real-world environments, where they can assist people with a wider range of tasks. Gemini Robotics 2.5 is rolling out to robotics partners.

The company tested the model across more than 200 distinct tasks, such as serving food with tongs, tying a bow on a gift box and pipetting a liquid. Compared with previous baselines, the model achieves a 30% to 100% higher success rate depending on the task type, while completing tasks 20% to 30% faster. The model works natively with many robot types, including Apptronik's Apollo 2 humanoid robot, which has a five-finger, 22 degree-of-freedom SharpaWave hand, and the Franka Duo platform with two-fingered parallel grippers. Google DeepMind also said that its robotics models can be extended to many more tasks than the 200 it tested.

In a proof-of-concept, Google DeepMind partnered with Apptronik and Mercedes-Benz to run Apollo 2 humanoid robots on active automotive production lines in Kecskemét, Hungary, and Sindelfingen, Germany. The robots performed automotive kitting, sorting individual parts from bulk bins into organized trays in the order needed for each vehicle. The pilot achieved a 96% success rate, and the company said the models improved dramatically in just a few weeks of post-training and carried over to Mercedes-Benz production with very little drop-off. Apptronik co-founder and CEO Jeff Cardenas said the work is the foundation for bringing humanoid robots to industrial and commercial environments at scale.

For safety, Gemini Robotics 2.5 uses inference-time reasoning guidance to steer around physical hazards in real time. In the company's evaluations, this capability boosted safe task completion around obstacles by 33% and around nearby people by 43%. Google DeepMind is also releasing ASIMOV-Jailbreak, an open-source benchmark containing hundreds of prompts that disguise unsafe requests across dozens of scenes. Its Gemini 4 Argon model achieves a 99.5% jailbreak resistance, compared with 82% for the previous baseline, Gemini Robotics ER 2.

Gemini 4 Argon also helped accelerate development of the model by acting as a simulation engine. It can generate thousands of varied, simulated practice runs from a real-world camera scene and build a realistic digital twin, which combined with real training demonstrations helps robots generalize to new scenes and objects. The company said the model can also help researchers hypothesize why task failures happen from video footage and test improvements in simulation and on real robots. Google DeepMind described Gemini Robotics 2.5 as an important milestone on the path toward solving physical AGI.

Articles.Title: Gemini Robotics 2.5 accelerates real-world general dexterity

stories.Headline: SGLang RCE Exploit Breaches NEAR AI, Steals Data From 18 Agents and About 100 Users
stories.Summary:
An attacker exploited a remote code execution flaw in SGLang, an open-source inference engine, and ran code on one of NEAR AI's inference servers last Sunday. The attacker could also have seen requests processed on that server that day, including requests sent in confidential mode. That mode runs requests inside a trusted execution environment meant to keep them private even from the company. The company said that environment does not protect against flaws in the software running inside it, and SGLang runs there. The attacker then moved further into the company's systems.

The attacker reached an internal system behind Private Chat, a product the company had already deprecated, and downloaded account details for about 100 users, including email addresses and names. For some accounts, plan and balance information was also taken, though the company found no sign that stored conversations or uploaded files were accessed. The attacker also reached 18 AI agents on an older NEAR AI Agents deployment that did not run inside the company's trusted environment, taking chat history, settings and logs. Two customers' NEAR AI Cloud API keys were exposed in logs, and the company has revoked both. After detecting the attack, the company revoked all active sessions and administrator credentials, replaced all agent tokens, and took Private Chat offline.

NEAR AI said it deployed a fix for the SGLang flaw on all its inference servers, rotated remaining credentials, and completed a full forensic review, according to its incident report. It has restored access to its NEAR AI Cloud service and reported the flaw to the SGLang project. The company has not given a CVE number, named the affected SGLang versions, or said whether the project has released a fix. It contacted affected users directly from its security address and advised them to be wary of unexpected messages about their accounts or balances. In a follow-up post, it said users who have not heard from it need take no action.

The company has not said whether people whose requests passed through the affected server last Sunday were among those contacted. Brave, the browser maker, said in an October 15 technical write-up that its Leo assistant runs chats with one model inside a trusted environment operated by NEAR AI. NEAR AI has not said whether the affected server handled any of those chats. The articles do not say whether further disclosures are planned.

Articles.Title: SGLang RCE Exploit Breaches NEAR AI, Steals Data From 18 Agents and About 100 Users

stories.Headline: In age of AI, human touch still matters
stories.Summary:
Prime Sarmiento, a China Daily correspondent based in Hong Kong, wrote a first-person column published on November 10, 2026, after covering the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank in Bangkok, which he reached on October 12. He had expected the event to focus on the IMF's World Economic Outlook, interest rates, inflation and the energy shock, but he found that artificial intelligence came up in most discussions across the week. Some sessions were devoted to AI, including a popular panel featuring Jack Clark, co-founder of the United States company Anthropic. Participants, he wrote, felt a mix of optimism about AI's benefits and unease that its costs could outweigh the economic gains it was expected to bring.

The IMF's World Economic Outlook, released during the meetings, projected global growth of 3.1 percent in 2026 and 3.4 percent in 2027, but the gains are unevenly spread. Economies tied into the AI supply chain are better placed to absorb external shocks, while energy-importing economies outside that chain face higher import bills, exchange rate pressure and tighter fiscal room, and many of them are low-income or vulnerable countries. At a fireside chat with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh gave no clear signal on US interest rates and instead focused on AI, including its potential to fundamentally transform monetary policy and its still-uncertain effect on jobs. Krishna Srinivasan, director of the IMF's Asia and Pacific Department, noted that since ChatGPT's launch, job postings requiring emerging AI skills have grown, roughly twice as fast in occupations highly exposed to the technology.

The author, who said he has used AI to transcribe interviews, do research, process data and copy edit, argued that AI cannot conduct interviews, build relationships with contacts or produce truly in-depth stories. He acknowledged that AI-generated content is widespread online and that producing a news report with a language model is one thing, while whether that report is worth reading is another. He concluded that only human journalists can verify questionable data, supply the context that makes facts meaningful, demand accountability and build understanding with audiences. He wrote that journalists remain relevant and have become more important in the age of AI, though the article does not describe any formal policy or institutional change arising from these discussions.

Articles.Title: In age of AI, human touch still matters

stories.Headline: Celestica Stock: Is AI Growth Worth the Risk in a Retirement Portfolio?
stories.Summary:
Celestica (TSX: CLS), which designs and manufactures networking and computing equipment for data centres, is drawing attention from investors weighing its exposure to artificial intelligence. The Motley Fool Canada analysis, published November 10, 2026, asks whether the stock's growth is worth the risk in a retirement portfolio. The article reports that the stock closed at $330.24 on the day of publication after falling about 9.2% that day. It notes that Celestica's October results showed third-quarter revenue rising 83%. Celestica's 2026 free-cash-flow outlook was reduced from US$600 million to US$460 million, while management lifted its sales outlook.

The company attributes the reduction to working-capital investment for faster growth ahead, including more inventory and receivables. The article explains that free cash flow is money left after the company's defined adjustments and capital spending. It also notes that the company has raised its 2026 revenue outlook to US$20.5 billion, according to a related Motley Fool headline. The author, Amy Legate-Wolfe, writes as a Motley Fool Canada contributor and states she has no position in any of the stocks mentioned. Her view is that Celestica suits a patient, long-term growth role rather than income.

She suggests an initial allocation of 2% of an otherwise diversified retirement portfolio, not a centrepiece holding. She also advises keeping near-term withdrawals in cash or suitable guaranteed investments. The article presents its illustrations as arithmetic, not predictions. It shows that a 40% share-price decline would reduce a whole portfolio by 0.8% at a 2% weighting, 2.0% at 5%, and 4.0% at 10%. It adds that holding the stock inside a Tax-Free Savings Account can generally shelter Canadian tax on gains, provided there is contribution room.

The article also says that Motley Fool's Stock Advisor Canada list of top TSX stocks for 2026 does not include Celestica. The article does not describe any next event for Celestica or set out a timeline for future results. It offers no forecast for the share price. The author's stated conclusion is that customer orders turning into cash would earn her confidence more than another ambitious outlook.

Articles.Title: Celestica Stock: Is AI Growth Worth the Risk in a Retirement Portfolio?

stories.Headline: Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy
stories.Summary:
Apple appears to be developing a new Mac app called Harbor, which is designed to make running local AI models simple. The app was discovered by the leaker Aaron Perris, who shared details in a post on X on November 10, 2026. According to the post, Harbor turns a Mac into a private AI inference server that runs open-weight models on Apple silicon, so data stays on the user's hardware and does not reach the cloud. The report says Harbor is currently in a private preview under Apple's Claris brand.

Harbor is described as offering several features aimed at ease of use and scale. It detects devices connected over Thunderbolt 5 and forms a cluster automatically, without manual configuration or command-line work. Users can browse, download, and load open-weight models from inside the app, which handles model management. Two or more Thunderbolt 5-capable Macs can also be connected so that their unified memory is pooled into a single inference resource, allowing larger models or more concurrent requests than one machine could handle alone.

The information comes from Perris's discovery and his public post, and the article does not report any statement from Apple about the app. The report places Harbor within a wider trend in which the Mac has become more popular as a tool for running AI models locally on machines such as the Mac Studio and Mac mini. The article notes that budget-friendly models like the MacBook Neo have also contributed to that growth. It suggests Apple may be leaning harder into this use case, and it expects a public launch in the weeks or months ahead, though no date has been confirmed.

Articles.Title: Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy

stories.Headline: AI usage generates a fragile codebase
stories.Summary:
Evan X. Merz, a software developer, published an essay on his blog on November 7, 2026, arguing that heavy reliance on AI coding tools produces fragile codebases. He wrote that he was laid off from Meta in May, though he could only speculate that his resistance to adopting AI tools as quickly as some peers played a part. In his final months there he generated at least 90 percent of his code with AI, the minimum for a decent rating, but he said the tools did not multiply his output and that the code his AI-reliant colleagues pushed was brittle. He now works at another large tech company and generates all of his code with AI, which he describes as the current expectation.

Merz names four failure modes. He says AI writes shallow tests, mostly trivial get and set checks and end-to-end tests that cover only already-tested paths and a single type of user, which leaves gaps that line coverage metrics do not reveal. He says AI writes overly complex code, using several helper methods where one would do and applying rules like DRY to excess. He argues that a growing reliance on AI reduces how well human developers understand the codebase, leaving them unable to spot poor abstractions. Finally, he says AI produces pull requests faster than humans can review them, so reviewers skim and small quality problems accumulate into long-term technical debt.

As symptoms of such a codebase, Merz lists more incidents over time, longer recovery times because engineers are working in unfamiliar code, errors that surface only for real users rather than in tests, and a poorer user experience. He concludes that software serving human customers needs human judgment and that the most expensive, well-regarded products will continue to be developed mainly by people. The essay is his opinion and offers no measured data on incident rates or any company's practices. It does not describe any next steps beyond his prediction that many people will come to see AI-heavy development as unsustainable.

Articles.Title: AI usage generates a fragile codebase

stories.Headline: Introducing AlphaProof Code: a breakthrough in verifying complex software at depth
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind researchers announced on November 10, 2026, that they used a new agentic framework called AlphaProof Code to mathematically prove key security properties of the actual code behind the Signal protocol, the technology that protects private messages in apps such as Signal and Google Messages. The work was led by Pushmeet Kohli and Swarat Chaudhuri and is described in a technical paper released alongside the announcement. The company describes the result as a milestone in software security that had long been considered a grand challenge. It is presented as the first time AI has been used to formally verify a widely deployed cryptographic protocol at this depth, and the first time such a protocol's implementation has been formally verified by any method.

The framework splits the work between people and machines. Human researchers worked with a mix of models to turn Signal's security goals into formal mathematical specifications, and each one was reviewed by experts. Agents powered by Gemini Carbon then produced the proofs, generating over six million lines of Lean, a computer language used to mathematically check code. The agents also flagged roughly one percent of the codebase that needed a second look from a human, while Lean checked the rest automatically. The verification process took four weeks, a task the article says historically takes expert teams years.

The researchers also tested whether the system could distinguish correct code from buggy code. They reintroduced two real, previously fixed bugs into an isolated version of Signal's code, and in both cases the system produced a machine-checked proof that the buggy version was insecure. The proofs go beyond design-level analysis to cover the compiled code running on devices, which matters because real-world vulnerabilities often sit in the gap between design and implementation. The researchers say they are open-sourcing their formal verification artifacts for community use.

Ehren Kret, Chief Technology Officer of Signal, said that earlier formal verification work had focused on smaller scopes and that using AI agents to translate live code into valid Lean theorems is a major breakthrough. He said that as AI-driven security threats grow, rigorous verification gives Signal greater confidence in its privacy guarantees. The article also says the approach could be applied to other vital systems, such as medical device firmware and power grid software, though scaling it will require continued research. It further points to related work, including the CodeMender defense agent, as part of a broader effort to counter fast, large-scale cyber threats.

Articles.Title: Introducing AlphaProof Code: a breakthrough in verifying complex software at depth

stories.Headline: S-1: Nvidia plans to invest ~$10B in Anthropic after its IPO, or ~10% of the total new cash Anthropic is expected to raise in November, including in its IPO (Cory Weinberg/New York Times)
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the maker of AI software tools, began courting investors on Tuesday for an initial public offering that could value the company at up to $1.4 trillion. The filing shows that Nvidia, the chipmaker that has become the financial engine of the AI boom, plans to invest about $10 billion in Anthropic immediately after the IPO. That sum would amount to roughly 10 percent of the total new cash Anthropic is expected to raise in November, including through the offering. The deal was reported by Cory Weinberg of The New York Times, based on the investor prospectus. Anthropic said Nvidia would be among a group of AI companies investing alongside the offering.

The arrangement ties together two companies that had long kept their distance from each other despite operating in closely connected parts of the industry. For years they grew into some of the most valuable firms in the world without doing much business together. Their chief executives also publicly sparred over how the U.S. government should regulate AI technology. The new investment changes that picture, since Nvidia is now set to hold a direct financial stake in Anthropic.

Kevin S. Xu, chief investment officer of Interconnected Capital, which invests in publicly traded AI companies, said the two companies' futures are now more intertwined than ever. The article describes the timing as notable, with one company preparing for its public debut while the other faces what it calls a prolonged corporate drama that has shaken the AI industry and left investors on edge. The article does not detail the nature of that drama. It also does not say what conditions, if any, attach to Nvidia's planned investment, or how the stake would be structured beyond the roughly $10 billion figure.

Articles.Title: S-1: Nvidia plans to invest ~$10B in Anthropic after its IPO, or ~10% of the total new cash Anthropic is expected to raise in November, including in its IPO (Cory Weinberg/New York Times)

stories.Headline: The GIGABYTE AI TOP ATOM 64 GB is now available and expands the possibilities of AI development on desktop PCs
stories.Summary:
GIGABYTE has made a 64 GB version of its AI TOP ATOM desktop AI system available as of November 11, 2026, alongside the existing 128 GB model. The announcement was distributed through PR Newswire from Taipei. Both memory versions are built on the NVIDIA DGX Spark platform and share the same compact chassis design. The 64 GB version is offered with either a 1 TB or a 2 TB NVMe M.2 SSD using PCIe 4.0 connectivity, so buyers can match storage to their needs. The system is intended for local AI development, giving developers dedicated AI compute in a desktop form factor.

It supports local model inference, prototyping, data analysis, and application validation in offices, labs, and educational settings. Users can run models and process project data within their own IT environment. For supported distributed AI workloads, up to four AI TOP ATOM systems can be linked into a cluster using the built-in NVIDIA ConnectX-7 networking and NVIDIA Sync's Cluster Assistant. The announcement says this can add storage and compute resources, depending on the application and software setup.

GIGABYTE also bundles its AI TOP Utility software, which supports downloading supported models, running inference, and retrieval-augmented generation for building question-answering tools on a user's own documents. GIGABYTE's announcement says availability, sales channels, pricing, and memory configurations may vary by region. More information is available on the company's AI TOP ATOM product page. The release also notes that GIGABYTE has recently expanded its local AI lineup with the AI TOP AERO, a separate desktop built on NVIDIA's RTX Spark platform.

Articles.Title: The GIGABYTE AI TOP ATOM 64 GB is now available and expands the possibilities of AI development on desktop PCs
