stories.Headline: Cisco Live Melbourne: AI agents will break today’s enterprise network, and Cisco wants to rebuild it
stories.Summary:
At Cisco Live APJC in Melbourne, Cisco Asia Pacific, Japan and Greater China president Ben Dawson said agent token consumption passed human consumption for the first time in February, and agents now consume tokens at roughly seven times the human rate. He said each agent generates far more traffic and data than a human doing the same task. Cisco's focus at the event shifted from GPUs, AI factories and data centers to the campus, the branch and the network that connects everything. Speakers argued that networks built for people will not hold up when thousands of agents work around the clock. The keynote framed the problem as a need to rebuild enterprise networking for agent behavior.

Jeff Schultz, Cisco's SVP of portfolio strategy and marketing, explained that agents still send heavy north-south traffic to reach models and context. They also generate large volumes of east-west traffic as agents talk to other agents across desktops, campuses, branches and data centers. Schultz said the architecture for campus and branch networking needs to be fundamentally reimagined. Dawson said AI will place new demands on wired infrastructure, making it more critical. Cisco's chief sales officer, Oliver Tuszik, cited IDC data showing only 9% of organizations in the region believe their networks are fully ready for new AI and digital initiatives.

He also cited research indicating 85% of organizations globally are experimenting with agents, but only 5% have deployed them to production. Cisco's product announcements covered the data center, campus and operations. Schultz highlighted 102.4 Tbps systems based on the Silicon One G300 for scale-out, and the deep-buffered Silicon One P200 for connecting data centers across metro, long-haul and transcontinental distances. Cisco is integrating ThousandEyes into its Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 access points at no extra cost for customers with eligible Networking Essentials and Advantage licenses. Schultz admitted ThousandEyes has been difficult to license and deploy.

Cisco Cloud Control, the company's unified operations layer, combines cross-domain telemetry, purpose-built models and both Cisco and third-party agents. Schultz said no new Cisco product will ship unless it is integrated with Cloud Control. Cloud Control is currently available only for US-based infrastructure. Cisco scheduled Australia, the EU and the UK for February 2027, followed by Japan, India and Canada in May. Schultz said the line between observing an agent and securing an agent is beginning to blur, citing an agent that suddenly deleted 10,000 files.

Cisco AI Defense is adding Anthropic's Claude Mythos to its adaptive red-teaming engine, limited to targets customers own and have registered. The model will be available to select enterprises soon, with broader availability for qualified customers later. Splunk's Tokenomics feature enters private preview in December, with general availability on AWS Marketplace in early 2027. Customers described their own deployments at the event. John Kelvie, chief digital and information officer at Asahi Beverages, described a Melbourne head office for about 1,000 employees built on Cisco's SD-Access architecture.

Asahi has since brought operational technology on its production floor onto a single IP network. Kelvie said his biggest obstacle is data, not people or technology. Yessie Yosetya, CIO of Indonesian operator XLSmart, inherited two networks after a merger, with security maturity scores of 3.2 and 1.6 on a NIST-based scale. She redesigned around five areas and reduced the company's security tools from 54 to 14. XLSmart put eight agents into production for red, blue and purple teaming, then found it could not scale them without standardization.

Articles.Title: Cisco Live Melbourne: AI agents will break today’s enterprise network, and Cisco wants to rebuild it

stories.Headline: AMD Launches Epyc SP7, Helion as AI Rack Demand Rises
stories.Summary:
AMD said on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, that its sixth-generation Epyc SP7 server processor is now generally available and that hardware makers have begun shipping servers powered by the chip. The company also said the first Helion racks for agentic AI, which hardware vendors build from an AMD blueprint, will become available throughout this month. The SP7 supports up to 256 cores and is the first of four sixth-generation Epyc CPUs to become available. AMD said the other three are expected in 2027. The broader family, much of which is code-named "Venice," is designed for enterprise, cloud, high-performance computing, and AI workloads.

AMD said it is seeing strong demand for the new chip. During the company's third-quarter earnings call last week, AMD Chair and CEO Lisa Su said early demand for Venice is the strongest AMD has seen for any new generation of Epyc processors. Su said AMD began revenue shipments of Venice during the third quarter and that hardware makers have committed to more than 240 Venice platforms, 20% more than the number committed for Turin, AMD's fifth-generation Epyc chip. Su also said Venice delivers significantly better performance per watt, per core, and per dollar than any other x86 or Arm server CPU. AMD said systems based on the SP7 deliver up to 3.7 times the performance of an Nvidia Vera CPU-based system and up to 2.2 times the performance of an Intel Xeon 6980P system.

AMD is working to capture more market share in CPUs, GPUs, and overall AI infrastructure as it competes with rivals amid surging AI demand. It is directly challenging market leader Nvidia in GPUs and rack-scale systems, while Nvidia is taking on AMD with its own CPU. Arm has also introduced an Arm-based CPU to compete with Intel and AMD's x86 processors. Cloud providers AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure have built their own custom AI accelerators and Arm-based CPUs. AMD introduced Helion in October as an open rack-scale design for agentic AI, with partners that include Dell Technologies, Hewlett Packard Enterprise, Lenovo, Supermicro, and Cisco.

AMD said Helion will come in three versions. Helion Liquid is a CPU-only, liquid-cooled rack designed to operate side by side with a Helios rack for large-scale agentic AI deployments. Helion Air is a CPU-only rack designed to expand agent capacity within existing air-cooled data centers. AMD Helion Air Inference is an air-cooled rack that combines CPUs and GPUs for inference. The article notes that Helion racks are built for agentic AI and differ from AMD's Helios racks, which are designed for large-scale inference, frontier model training, and fine-tuning.

Matt Kimball, vice president and principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, said Venice is an important launch for AMD and for enterprises. Kimball said enterprise CIOs have fixed power budgets and need infrastructure that supports traditional workloads today and agentic AI in the years ahead. With up to 256 cores, Venice lets companies run traditional workloads on fewer servers, freeing up space for AI infrastructure. Kimball also said that servers running sixth-generation Epyc processors are well suited to future agentic workloads because of the CPU's high core count and large cache and memory. AMD also said Meta is preparing to deploy sixth-generation Epyc platforms at scale and that Microsoft Azure's HDv2 service for AI data processing is in preview.

Articles.Title: AMD Launches Epyc SP7, Helion as AI Rack Demand Rises

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike Brings Falcon Guardian to Anthropic's Claude Cowork
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike announced on November 3, 2026, that it is bringing its Falcon Guardian AI Detection and Response product natively into Anthropic's Claude Cowork. The announcement was made in Austin, Texas and Barcelona, where CrowdStrike was holding its Fal.Con Europe 2026 event. The integration was delivered in partnership with Anthropic in response to enterprise customer demand. The company described the move as extending Falcon protection to AI agents throughout their lifecycle. The integration places Falcon Guardian protection directly inside Claude Cowork.

The article says the protection secures agents from creation onward. It also places those agents under the Falcon platform's enterprise security control plane. The announcement describes this as an added layer for organizations that already use Claude Cowork to deploy AI agents. CrowdStrike, which trades on the Nasdaq under the ticker CRWD, is the company behind the announcement. Anthropic is the company that makes Claude Cowork and worked with CrowdStrike on the integration.

The article does not give further statements from either company beyond the announcement itself. The article does not provide further background on the history of the partnership or on prior Falcon Guardian releases. It also does not give pricing, availability dates, or the number of customers affected. The articles provide no information on next steps. The available text ends before the full announcement body, so details of the rollout are not given.

Articles.Title: CrowdStrike Brings Falcon Guardian to Anthropic's Claude Cowork

stories.Headline: CrowdStrike Extends the Agentic SOC to Detect and Stop Agent Insider Threats
stories.Summary:
CrowdStrike announced on November 4, 2026 new agentic SOC capabilities aimed at detecting and stopping what it calls agent insider threats, meaning trusted AI agents that operate under a real employee's identity and approved tools. The company says such an agent can drift without tripping an alarm when something upstream changes, such as a tampered tool or an instruction that should not be there. CrowdStrike states that AI agents touch the SOC in two ways, as the new operating unit of the SOC and as a new identity to secure. The article says current tools fall short in different ways. Most agentic SOC tools run a single LLM serially through detections without memory of prior investigations or identity, endpoint, or ownership context.

Standalone AI security tools can inventory agents and flag unusual activity but stop at detection. The article describes Agent Insider Threat Detection, slated for Q4, which is built on CrowdStrike Falcon Next-Gen SIEM. It learns the normal behavior pattern for every AI agent and the person who runs it, including the files it touches, the tools it calls, and where it sends data. It flags deviations even when no policy is violated, which the company says catches an agent that stays within its granted permissions yet is compromised. Dynamic Risk Scoring, also slated for Q4, feeds agent risk into the same 0 to 100 risk score Falcon Next-Gen SIEM builds for the agent's owner and host.

AI Ecosystem Detections, also for Q4, add detection logic for attacks on AI services, including LLM API abuse, stolen API keys, and compromise of coding assistants, MCP servers, and agent frameworks. Federated Search Expansion lets teams search related data in place without re-ingestion, with GovCloud, Dynatrace, Databricks, and Snowflake connectors generally available and Splunk, Elastic, and Cribl Lake connectors following in Q4. CrowdStrike says Multi-Agent Triage and Investigation, generally available and announced at Fal.Con US 2026, has SOC agents investigate detections end to end, with specialist agents working on shared context across endpoint, identity, and the agent's activity. In Q4, triage coverage extends to Falcon Guardian, Falcon Cloud Security, Falcon Shield, Falcon Data Security, and custom detections, including abnormal agent behavior flagged by Falcon Next-Gen SIEM. The company says investigating agents can trace a session back to what the person asked for and separate that from what the agent did on its own.

The Unified Agentic SOAR Experience, generally available and also announced at Fal.Con US 2026, handles response by coordinating stopping the agent, cutting off its access, keeping it from coming back, and documenting what happened. CrowdStrike says it is open by design and connects to any agent, model, or tool through API or MCP. The article's background is that security teams face hundreds of thousands of alerts a month, and agents add more telemetry, while an agent insider threat rarely sounds a loud alarm. CrowdStrike frames the problem as a new insider threat: not an employee, but a trusted agent acting on their behalf. The articles do not say what happens beyond the features described for Q4 and general availability dates.

Articles.Title: CrowdStrike Extends the Agentic SOC to Detect and Stop Agent Insider Threats

stories.Headline: Microsoft buyouts: ‘Concerned workers’ write open letter to management, urge rethink of ‘speed-at-all-costs’ AI push
stories.Summary:
A group of current and former Microsoft employees, calling themselves "Concerned Microsoft Workers," has written an open letter to company management. The letter comes as Microsoft rolls out a buyout offer to around 66,000 of its staff amid an aggressive push into artificial intelligence. According to The New York Times, which first reported it, the letter began circulating before the October 26 buyout announcement. The workers say the timing reflects growing unease inside the company about where its AI effort is heading.

The letter criticizes what the employees describe as a "speed-at-all-costs" approach to developing and deploying AI. It asks Microsoft to involve employees in decisions about how AI is built and used, and to stop tying AI use to rewards or reprimands. The writers also raise concerns about workplace conditions, job security, customer safety and the environment. They point to heavier workloads, frequent restructuring and uncertainty about the future of jobs as the company accelerates its AI investments. The letter also asks for employees to have a greater say in how the technology is developed and deployed.

The buyout itself was announced on October 26 as a Voluntary Exit Offer for eligible employees in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States at level 70 and below, in participating teams. Microsoft says the offer gives eligible workers who may be considering a future outside the company a chance to make that move now, with support. Employees have until December 9 to decide, and those who accept will leave on December 31 with a minimum of eight weeks of base pay, with the amount varying by job level and tenure. The company has also cut jobs repeatedly, laying off 10,000 workers in 2023 and more than 15,000 in 2025, and in the spring offered a retirement-age buyout to about 8,600 US employees, roughly 30 percent of whom accepted.

Microsoft's headcount peaked at 228,000 full-time employees across fiscal years 2024 and 2025 and stood at 223,000 at the end of June, as the company continues a series of workforce reductions and restructuring tied to its shift toward AI. The articles do not report a response from Microsoft management to the open letter. They also do not say whether the group plans further action or whether the company will change its AI policies. The buyout deadline of December 9 is the next date the articles identify.

Articles.Title: Microsoft buyouts: ‘Concerned workers’ write open letter to management, urge rethink of ‘speed-at-all-costs’ AI push

stories.Headline: AI pushes mid-sized IT firms to rethink sales playbook
stories.Summary:
Hexaware Technologies has replaced target-based sales incentives with commissions tied directly to the revenue its employees bring in, according to a Mint report published on 10 November 2026. The company is one of several mid-sized IT services firms changing how they motivate sales teams and reach customers as artificial intelligence reshapes client demand. Hexaware's president, Shantanu Baruah, outlined the change at the company's AI Day on 21 August. Its commission-based plan removes several performance thresholds that previously determined payouts, and the commissions are separate from employees' variable pay.

LTM Ltd is offering separate incentives for AI-native deals, while Coforge Ltd is turning to external deal advisors to access new opportunities. The article says firms with $1-5 billion in annual revenue face the challenge of finding new sources of growth as AI changes technology spending, while competing against larger rivals. Hexaware ended the July-September quarter with $412 million in revenue, up 2% sequentially, and does not disclose its order intake. LTM ended the September quarter with revenue of $4.76 billion, up 1% quarter-on-quarter, and order intake of $1.26 billion, down 25%. Coforge ended its last quarter with $652 million in revenue, up 10%, and order intake that rose 51% to $1.04 billion.

Vikash Kumar Jain, chief financial officer of Hexaware, described the commission shift on a post-earnings analyst call on 29 October and said the company expects it to work out well. Venu Lambu, chief executive of LTM, said on a post-earnings call on 16 October that the company uses different sales commission structures to encourage salespeople to sell AI-native deals, describing it as a change management exercise. John Speight, president and executive director of Coforge, said on a call on 23 October that the company has started using advisory channels that have brought in deals it had never had before. Saurabh Goel, Coforge's chief financial officer, said advisory costs sit under sales or other sales and marketing expenses. An email sent to LTM seeking more detail on its commission structure went unanswered.

Traditionally, Coforge relied on sole-sourced deals rather than competitive bids. The article also notes that larger peers, including Tata Consultancy Services Ltd and Infosys Ltd, said they were investing in their sales processes but did not elaborate. Peter Bendor-Samuel, founder of Everest Group, said a more attractive commission structure helps firms attract better sales teams in what he called a moribund market. Namratha Dharshan, chief business leader for India Research at ISG, said the new incentive systems could also help firms retain key account personnel whose client relationships matter in winning business.

Articles.Title: AI pushes mid-sized IT firms to rethink sales playbook

stories.Headline: AI was supposed to kill this industry. So why is it still growing?
stories.Summary:
The Philippines' outsourcing industry, long expected to be among the first casualties of artificial intelligence, is still growing. According to the IT and Business Process Association of the Philippines, the information technology and business process management sector employed about 1.9 million people and generated US$40 billion in revenues in 2025. Its contact centre and business process management segment added roughly 60,000 workers, bringing that segment's employment to 1.68 million. The figures were reported in June, and the article's author, J.C. Punongbayan, a visiting fellow at ISEAS and an assistant professor at the University of the Philippines School of Economics, argues they do not suggest the industry is being wiped out.

The article notes that growth in headcount does not rule out displacement, since firms can cut some roles while adding others, and totals alone cannot isolate AI's effect. It cites a 2025 study finding that AI assistance raised customer support productivity by 15 per cent, measured by issues resolved per hour, with less experienced workers benefiting most. The author says the Philippines' opportunity lies in more specialised services such as complex customer support, financial analysis, healthcare administration and supervising automated processes. A revised best-case target of 2.14 million workers by 2028 implies annual growth of roughly 4 per cent, close to the 3.7 per cent growth reported for 2025, against the original 2.5 million target that would have required about 9.6 per cent a year.

Punongbayan writes that AI is not the only pressure on future hiring. He points to US initiatives to discourage offshoring, including the bipartisan Keep Call Centers in America Bill and proposals from the US Federal Communications Commission, which he says could lead clients to delay Philippine expansion even before any rules take effect. He also cites an August Stanford study finding that employment among US workers aged 22 to 25 in AI-exposed occupations lagged behind peers in less-exposed jobs, largely because of weaker hiring, which the authors present as early, descriptive indicators rather than causal estimates. The author calls for policymakers, government agencies and the IBPAP to identify the tasks employers need and tie publicly supported training to demonstrated demand, measuring success through placement, retention and earnings. He also urges employers to keep paid apprenticeships and supervised routes into skilled work, warning that automating simpler entry-level tasks could weaken how the industry trains its future workers.

Articles.Title: AI was supposed to kill this industry. So why is it still growing?

stories.Headline: Takaichi seeks international AI cooperation at France-hosted meeting
stories.Summary:
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Monday urged the international community to work together on security issues tied to artificial intelligence. She joined a meeting hosted by the French government online, which started at 10 p.m. that day. French President Emmanuel Macron also attended, along with leaders, government institution representatives and AI-related business officials from interested countries. The article does not state the exact date of the meeting beyond Monday, and it was reported on November 10, 2026.

Takaichi said that advanced AI is creating new security problems, including its use in cyberattacks and the risk of losing control over it. She argued that because the effects of AI cross national borders, international cooperation is essential. She also called for deeper international discussion on how to encourage innovation while managing risks at the same time. The Japanese government, she said, aims to host an AI summit at an early date and hopes to help advance international cooperation under an evolved free and open Indo-Pacific.

Takaichi faced criticism at home for skipping an online summit of the Group of Seven major nations held on Oct. 2. At a news conference on Tuesday, Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said the French government had informed Tokyo of the schedule for Monday's meeting in the second half of the previous week. He said the prime minister chose to take part because it was important to communicate Japan's stance and efforts to the international community. The article does not say whether the French government confirmed any outcomes from the meeting.

Articles.Title: Takaichi seeks international AI cooperation at France-hosted meeting

stories.Headline: Why is Vietnam’s To Lam in Japan? AI, chips and nuclear power
stories.Summary:
Vietnam's leader To Lam visited Tokyo this week to widen trade and investment ties with Japan, with a focus on technology. The trip came as uncertainty continues over the future direction of American policy. After talks with Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Monday, the two leaders pledged to speed up public-private cooperation on critical minerals. A joint statement called economic security a top priority in the relationship and promised deeper cooperation on defence and investment.

The two governments also stressed the need to bring Japanese-funded liquefied natural gas and gas-fired power projects online quickly. They reaffirmed their plan to introduce nuclear power to Vietnam. Hanoi is seeking to build domestic industrial strength through these partnerships. The agenda covers artificial intelligence, semiconductor chips, critical minerals, LNG projects and defence ties. Each of these areas is tied to the broader aim of strengthening Vietnam's economy.

Responsibility for these commitments rests with the leaders of both countries, who issued a joint statement after their meeting. Takaichi and To Lam framed economic security as central to the bilateral relationship. The articles do not give further detail on specific figures or timelines for the projects. Officials from both sides are expected to carry the agreed cooperation forward, though the reporting does not specify who will lead each track.

The visit reflects Vietnam's effort to diversify its partners at a time when its traditional economic ties are being tested by shifting policy in Washington. Japan offers capital, technology and energy expertise that Hanoi wants for its industrial plans. What happens next depends on how quickly the announced projects move from pledges to construction and operation. The articles do not say when specific agreements will be signed.

Articles.Title: Why is Vietnam’s To Lam in Japan? AI, chips and nuclear power

stories.Headline: Japan to create defense research hubs at universities for AI, space tech
stories.Summary:
Japan plans to set up research hubs by fiscal 2031 at universities and other institutions to develop technologies that can be applied to defense equipment. The move was reported by Nikkei Asia on November 10, 2026, and it is aimed at helping the country respond to new forms of warfare in areas such as artificial intelligence and space. The hubs are part of an effort to strengthen Japan's defense research base in fields that are changing quickly. The article notes that Japan has lagged behind the United States and China in next-generation defense research. The initiative represents a shift in how Japan organizes its defense science, with academic institutions being brought more directly into military-related technology work.

Its stated purpose is to give the country a longer-term perspective as the security environment changes rapidly. Japan's government has been under pressure to keep pace with rivals that are advancing in these areas more quickly. The article presents the hubs as a way to build capacity over the coming years rather than respond only to immediate needs. The article attributes the plan to the Japanese government in Tokyo, and reporter Ryota Ogata wrote the report. Its headline frames the initiative as Tokyo's response to rapid changes in the security sector.

The piece does not provide direct quotations from named officials in the portion available. It also links to related Nikkei coverage on Japan's plans to reorganize defense research around AI and cyber issues. Taken together, the report describes a government effort to build long-term defense research capacity inside universities. It points to growing competition in advanced military technology as the backdrop for the decision. The available text does not provide further details on budgets, the specific universities involved, or how the hubs will be governed, so those points remain unclear from this report.

Articles.Title: Japan to create defense research hubs at universities for AI, space tech

stories.Headline: China’s Singles’ Day turns 18: bye coupon math, hello AI tokens
stories.Summary:
Singles' Day, China's annual online shopping festival also known as Double 11, marked its 18th year this season with a noticeably different tone. Shopper Sunny He, a 32-year-old from Shanghai, bought a 12,000-yuan iPhone 18 Pro Max on Alibaba Group Holding's Tmall marketplace, using a 300-yuan voucher to lower the price. He told the South China Morning Post that the event felt less lively than before because she had less spare cash. Her selective approach, the article says, mirrors a wider change in how Chinese consumers are spending during the sale.

The article frames the season around a pivot away from complicated coupon schemes toward simpler, straightforward pricing. Retailers appear to be moving to clearer discounts, and the article notes that the shift is aimed at keeping shoppers in a domestic market that has become increasingly saturated. Newer elements such as AI-driven shopping features are also part of what the headline describes, though the excerpt available here offers limited detail on how they work. Shoppers are generally becoming more cautious, and the article ties this to a sluggish economy. Buyers are choosing to purchase items they had previously avoided at full price rather than spending freely across the board.

The reporting attributes the analysis to unnamed analysts, who link the pricing change to the goal of retaining customers. Ann Cao, the reporter, covered the story from Shanghai and published it on November 10, 2026. The excerpt does not give further figures, company statements, or forecasts for sales results. Readers should look to the full article for any additional data on the scale of the shift or the specific AI tools being introduced.

Articles.Title: China’s Singles’ Day turns 18: bye coupon math, hello AI tokens

stories.Headline: Integration among ASEAN, China, Japan, South Korea boosted by AI boom
stories.Summary:
The artificial intelligence boom is accelerating economic integration across Southeast Asia, China, Japan and South Korea, according to Yasuto Watanabe, director and CEO of the ASEAN+3 Macroeconomic Research Office (AMRO). He made the remarks in Bangkok on Nov. 10, 2026, as reported by Nikkei Asia. He said the technology will boost trade and investment within the region. The report centers on his outlook for regional ties. Watanabe's comments came at a time when the private sector is driving closer links among these economies.

The article says AI demand is pulling companies into deeper cooperation across borders. It does not give specific figures on trade volumes or investment totals in its excerpt. Nor does it set out any new policy requirements or formal agreements tied to his remarks. Watanabe, who leads AMRO, is the source of the outlook described in the report. The article attributes the bullish view to him and does not report any dissenting official view.

He is quoted at an event held during the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings, which the article places in Bangkok on Oct. 14. The photo caption describes him speaking at that gathering. The surrounding coverage points to a region where AI and related supply chains are reshaping business ties, though the excerpt provided does not spell out the details. Other stories listed alongside the article cover electric vehicle competition, chip-related supply chain pressures and regional trade frictions. The articles provided do not say what steps AMRO or governments will take next.

Articles.Title: Integration among ASEAN, China, Japan, South Korea boosted by AI boom

stories.Headline: India's electronics firms face PCB squeeze as AI demand drives up costs
stories.Summary:
India's electronics manufacturers are facing high costs and supply constraints for printed circuit boards as an increasing share of capacity is captured by booming demand for artificial intelligence hardware. Nikkei Asia reporter Ananta Agarwal reported the story from Bengaluru on November 10, 2026. Printed circuit board makers worldwide are diverting more production toward advanced and specialized boards for demanding AI applications. That shift is squeezing India's traditional users in the electronics industry, which rely on more ordinary boards. The article says that prices for these materials have risen by as much as 350 percent.

Manufacturers in India are passing those higher costs on to their customers. The article gives no further figures on the size of the increases or on the period over which they occurred. The article does not name a specific company or official who is responsible for the squeeze. It describes it as a result of market forces, with global board makers choosing to put their output into AI-related work.

The article gives no statement from any named industry figure, government body or board maker on the situation. The article does not describe any policy response or a timeline for relief. Its headline frames the squeeze as the outcome of rising AI demand, and the body text points to the same cause. The piece gives no outlook for how long supply will stay constrained.

Articles.Title: India's electronics firms face PCB squeeze as AI demand drives up costs

stories.Headline: Sakana AI may go public in 2027
stories.Summary:
Sakana AI, a Japanese artificial intelligence company, may go public in 2027, according to media reports. Nikkei broke the news, saying the firm is weighing a listing on the Tokyo Stock Exchange, Nasdaq, or both for its initial public offering. The company's market value could exceed that of Mercari, which is valued at ¥680 billion ($4.3 billion), and would put Sakana AI among Japan's most valuable startup listings. Goldman Sachs has reportedly been hired as an adviser for the process.

Sakana AI responded in an X post on Monday, saying it has no near-term plans for an IPO. The company said its priority is building a generational AI company that serves as Japan's national AI champion. The reports come as AI companies worldwide face problems with valuations, local resistance to data centers, and doubts about how useful the technology is. AI shares fell sharply after the U.S. midterm elections, as investors worried a Democratic-controlled Congress would tighten AI rules and slow data center construction. The Nasdaq is about 9% below its all-time high, partly because of the retreat in AI stocks.

The company has raised ¥32 billion ($200 million) in Series B funding from backers including Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group, Google and Citi, and Nvidia took part in an earlier Series A round. Earlier this year, Sakana AI introduced Sakana Namazu, its first large language model, which was built on Kimi 2.6, an open-weight model from China's Moonshot AI. Concerned about overreliance on Chinese and U.S. models, Japan has made developing its own language models a priority, and it has reportedly invested $6 billion in an AI effort through Noetra, a consortium that includes Sakana AI, SoftBank and Sony. On Oct. 26, Sakana AI said it was training its own model from scratch, and its planned Sakana Sawara series will include a large and a small model.

Articles.Title: Sakana AI may go public in 2027

stories.Headline: Deux revives late Kim Sungjae's voice with AI for new album
stories.Summary:
Legendary Korean hip-hop duo Deux is set to release a full-length album, "4th Deux," on November 21, 2026, and will use artificial intelligence to recreate the vocals of the late Kim Sungjae. The album arrives more than 30 years after the duo's previous record, "Force Deux," which is widely regarded as one of the best albums in K-pop history. The pair split barely three months after that release, and each went on to a solo career. Kim was found dead in a Seoul hotel room in November 1995, one day after his solo debut, and the case remains unsolved.

The upcoming album has nine tracks, and Lee led its production and wrote "The Future," one of two focus tracks. The other main track, "I Want You," features Dynamic Duo, another well-known hip-hop pair. Lee described the song at a pre-listening session in Seoul on Saturday, saying it sounds like what Deux might have produced had it taken a new jack swing number a step further. Under Lee's wishes, a portion of the album's proceeds will go to Kim's family. The articles do not say how the AI was used or how the vocals were produced.

Lee is the person the article ties most directly to the project, as he led production and wrote the focus track. The article reports his remarks at the pre-listening session and his request that proceeds go to Kim's family. It gives no further statements from the duo's partners or from Kim's family. The article also notes that the two musicians parted ways after their last album and later released two albums, a live recording and a best-of set, in 1995 and 1997. It does not report any further developments beyond the album's release plans.

Articles.Title: Deux revives late Kim Sungjae's voice with AI for new album

stories.Headline: When AI writes, what remains human?
stories.Summary:
Philippe Jaenada, who was named winner of France's Prix Goncourt on November 3, 2026, has admitted using AI three times while writing his prize-winning novel, "L'inconnue du quai de Javel." The admission came amid a wider dispute in France over AI in literature, which the opinion piece links to the removal of Haitian Canadian writer Thélyson Orélien from the shortlist in September after allegations of AI use. Orélien denied using AI, while Jaenada acknowledged his actions voluntarily. Social media critics have questioned whether Orélien, a writer of color, was treated more harshly than Jaenada, a white man.

Jaenada said he had inserted a ChatGPT-generated sentence to "play with the reader" and included an AI-generated section to show how unreliable the tool could be on technical questions. The author of the column says his explanations are hard to judge for sincerity. The dispute has also produced a new literary award, the Pascal Prize, which accepts only works created with AI and requires applicants to submit a technical dossier naming the large language models used and the prompts that started the work. Its jury is chaired by futurist Jacques Attali. The organizers first proposed a Goncourt AI Prize, but the Goncourt rejected that idea, saying it honors books written by humans, not machines.

The column draws two lessons for Korea. First, the Goncourt remains France's most prestigious literary award, so an AI controversy there carries real weight. Second, the French debate has split into acceptance of the technology on one side and insistence on purely human authorship on the other, and the writer argues Korea would gain little by copying that rigid division. Publisher L'Observatoire plans a label called "Sanctuaire" to certify fully human-authored works, which the column presents as part of that polarization.

The column argues that AI use is already spreading through Korean writing, translation and research faster than these debates are moving. Lee Eun-hye, head of the publisher Geulhangari, wrote on Facebook that she has received noticeably more translation proposals from master's and doctoral candidates, and that some of the samples are suspiciously polished. She told the columnist she strongly suspects some of those samples were prepared with AI. The column also cites Kim Seong-woo's 2024 book, which describes how AI can let researchers write while relying on machine summaries instead of reading the original papers. The author ends by asking what distinguishes human intellectual work once machines can write, summarize and translate, and says it is time to reconsider what it means for writing to be entirely human.

Articles.Title: When AI writes, what remains human?

stories.Headline: Hitjis and Jenus music videos will be created through an AI video contest
stories.Summary:
MindSpark is running the generative AI video contest "The 3rd Korea AI Advertising Awards," accepting entries from November 9 through midnight on November 30. This year's biggest change is a music video category that uses unreleased new songs from two idol groups, the five-member girl group Hitjis, who debuted in April of last year, and the five-member boy group Jenus, who debuted in April of this year. Entrants can pick a track from either group and make a music video with generative AI. MindSpark will choose one standout work per track and give each winner 1 million KRW.

The category is meant to ease a real burden on rookie idols, since sets, filming crews, and equipment quickly push production costs up. Several creators can interpret the same song through different videos, letting Hitjis and Jenus review multiple versions of a music video for one new track. Entrants also get hands-on experience making videos for newly debuted idols. The organizers present it as a chance to see how far AI video can extend beyond advertising into music content.

Alongside the music category, the contest is running brand advertising briefs from 14 companies across finance, beauty, food, and robotics. Samsung Securities wants ads that make pension products approachable for younger audiences, while JB Financial Group seeks ads that present its group image with an MZ-generation sensibility. Entrants may submit a horizontal AI Video Ad (16:9, 30 seconds) or a vertical AI Short-form Video (9:16, 30 seconds to 1 minute), with one work per category and the option to try several brands. Anyone aged 14 or older can enter individually or as a team, and a new corporate division has been added for production companies and studios.

The contest has grown quickly, with entries rising from 725 in the first edition in May last year to 999 in the second in December, a 38% increase in seven months. The total prize pool has also grown from 47 million KRW to 50 million KRW and now 53 million KRW this year. According to a Ministry of Science and ICT report, 44.5% of people have used generative AI, up 11.2 percentage points in one year. Judging is 80% expert panel and 20% public YouTube vote, and some winning works will be shown on the M-CITY billboard at the Euljiro-ipgu Station intersection in Seoul. A MindSpark representative said AI advertising is no longer an experiment but a production method that brands actually use.

Articles.Title: Hitjis and Jenus music videos will be created through an AI video contest

stories.Headline: Enticed by massive GPU sales···The AI chip ‘backdoor’ market reexamined amid the Jensen Huang affair
stories.Summary:
Reporting from Korea's Kyunghyang Shinmun on November 10, 2026, describes how an adultery scandal involving Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang has drawn renewed attention to a practice in which China has reportedly obtained advanced AI chips through Southeast Asia despite US export controls. The woman involved, Alice Huang, is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singaporean firm suspected of illicitly exporting graphics processing units. According to industry sources cited in the article, Megaspeed has grown into the largest buyer of Nvidia GPUs in Southeast Asia. Bloomberg reported that from 2023 through November 2025 the company procured at least 4.6 billion dollars in Nvidia equipment and leased computing capacity to Chinese companies, including Alibaba.

The article also reports that the US Commerce Department had been investigating allegations that Megaspeed illegally exported GPUs, citing the New York Times. In August of last year, Nvidia's top legal officer reportedly asked to meet Commerce officials and said he had secured the approval of a deputy secretary, after which the inquiry was halted. This has prompted allegations that Nvidia tried to influence the probe to protect its GPU sales. US short seller Culper Research estimated in May that more than 20 percent of Nvidia's computing revenue in fiscal 2026 came from Chinese demand routed through Southeast Asia and other regions, and its founder, Christian Lamarco, said he had identified at least six more firms with similar warning signs. Separately, Bain & Company reported that data center capacity in Southeast Asia rose 45 percent in half a year, from 4 gigawatts at the end of last year to 5.8 gigawatts in the first half of this year, and the Institute for Progress estimated that about 75 percent of AI compute Chinese firms access remotely from overseas is concentrated in the region.

The article explains that US policy has largely allowed remote leasing of chips while blocking physical smuggling. The Biden administration's AI Proliferation Rule, which would have restricted exports to places such as Malaysia and Singapore, was rescinded by the Trump administration two days before it was to take effect after industry objections. More recently, Nvidia has required overseas cloud providers to sell at least 51 percent of their services to customers outside China, and on the 4th it emerged that Oracle, under US government pressure, canceled a GPU leasing deal with Tencent. On the 9th, Republican Representative Jim Banks and Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren called for tougher export controls on AI chips bound for China, and supporters of a Chip Security Act pressed for mandatory location tracking of GPUs overseas. A domestic AI industry source quoted in the article said that chip purchases through routes such as Malaysia had long been an open secret, and that confirmed violations could cause serious damage to the industry.

Articles.Title: Enticed by massive GPU sales···The AI chip ‘backdoor’ market reexamined amid the Jensen Huang affair

stories.Headline: Dot-Com lessons for the AI bubble
stories.Summary:
Chi Onwurah, a Labour Party member of the U.K. Parliament and chair of the House of Commons Science, Innovation and Technology Committee, published an opinion piece on November 10, 2026, in The Korea Times, distributed by Project Syndicate, arguing that the current artificial intelligence investment boom may be a bubble and that the late-1990s dot-com crash offers warnings. Drawing on her own experience as an engineer at a telecoms infrastructure company that collapsed in the early 2000s, she describes how that boom ended with the loss of her job and visa. She notes that firms such as Global Crossing and WorldCom filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, while Nortel Networks and Lucent lost about 99 percent of their stock value. She says the infrastructure providers of that era relied heavily on debt and on "vendor financing," in which suppliers helped their own customers pay for products, and she sees similar circular arrangements in today's AI sector.

Onwurah points to specific examples of this circularity. She cites Anthropic buying compute capacity powered by Nvidia chips from a company in which Nvidia is a major investor, and Microsoft investing more than $13 billion in OpenAI while also selling it cloud services through its Azure division. She also writes that justifying the trillions of dollars being spent on AI infrastructure would require more than $2.5 trillion in annual revenue by 2030, and that this revenue would likely have to come from customers cutting costs, mainly salaries. Her view is that such cuts could cause societal upheaval, and that a financial crash could follow either from that process or from markets concluding that AI firms cannot repay their debts. She argues that today's scale of debt is far larger than in 2001 and closer to the run-up to the 2008 financial crisis, and that the technology, media, and telecommunications sector now accounts for nearly half of the broader U.S. large-cap equity market, up from one-fifth during the 2008 crisis.

Onwurah says booms end when lenders stop funding them, pointing to American Express suspending her former company's credit cards months before its bankruptcy filing. She asks whether money withdrawn from AI could flow into productive investment elsewhere, such as in Newcastle or in youth unemployment, or instead into safe assets like gold, and says she does not know the answer. She concludes that with the U.K. placing AI at the center of its ambitions during its 2027 G20 presidency, the country's agenda should include security, standards and planning for a possible crash. The article does not describe any formal government action or response to her arguments.

Articles.Title: Dot-Com lessons for the AI bubble

stories.Headline: Inside AI-powered fight against digital sex crimes
stories.Summary:
The National Center for Digital Sexual Crime Response in Korea is using artificial intelligence to detect suspected child sexual exploitation material and speed up takedown requests. The center's AI system collects posts around the clock using about 220 keywords, analyzes text and images together, and presents its findings to staff for review. Once a staff member approves a report, the system prepares the information the relevant platform or authority needs, and each takedown request now takes about a minute or less to process. The center's director, Kim Mi-soon, said the system handles most of the process without human intervention at every step, and she said it is also detecting deepfakes that are hard to spot with the naked eye. The Korea Times reported these details in a November 10, 2026 article.

The center says the AI has greatly increased its output. The average number of cases each worker processes per day rose from 20.8 in 2025 to 202.1, roughly a 9.7-fold increase. From April to September 2026, the center processed 96,210 cases, more than twice the 45,438 handled in all of 2025. Automation also limits staff exposure to disturbing images, since images are now blurred by default and revealed only when needed for a reporting decision.

The center plans to expand monitoring from 14 platforms to 139 by 2027. It is also developing technology that looks at how conversations unfold, in order to detect online grooming, and an AI chatbot that will send vulnerable young people information about support services. Officials at the center described the grooming problem in plain terms. A staff member at a demonstration for reporters on Tuesday said comments on a teenager's video, such as compliments or questions about age, can look harmless but may be used to build trust and move a child toward private contact.

The center's official said keyword searches alone cannot catch this because individual words are not suspicious by themselves. Kim Mi-soon said she hopes these tools will curb digital sex crimes, which fall most heavily on teenagers and people in their 20s. The center supported 10,637 victims in 2025, up from 4,973 in 2020, and that group made up 77.6 percent of those supported last year. Park Kwang-soo, head of the Women's Human Rights Institute of Korea, which oversees the center, credited the gains to staff expertise and said that people remain necessary at many points in victim support.

Faster detection does not guarantee removal, and the center reported that 28.5 percent of its takedown requests went unfulfilled in 2025. Among websites whose server locations it could identify, at least 95.5 percent were hosted overseas, which complicates enforcement. Officials said technical gains must be paired with international cooperation, stronger platform accountability, and efforts to cut off the revenue that sustains illegal sites. The article does not describe any specific steps scheduled to address these gaps beyond the planned expansion and new tools.

Articles.Title: Inside AI-powered fight against digital sex crimes

stories.Headline: Harvey Partners with Djøf Forlag to Add Danish Legal Sources
stories.Summary:
Harvey, the legal AI company, announced on November 11, 2026, a partnership with Danish legal publisher Djøf Forlag to add licensed Danish legislation, executive orders and preparatory works to its platform. Jurabibliotek licensees will be able to research and draft from those materials alongside their own documents. The Jurabibliotek legislative content is scheduled to become available in Harvey at the start of 2027 at no additional charge. Access requires a license to Djøf Forlag's digital platform, and the collection will sit alongside Danish public sources already available in Harvey.

The collection covers consolidated acts, the executive orders issued under them, amendments and preparatory documents. Lawyers will be able to move from a statutory provision to the regulations implementing it and to material showing legislative intent, with each answer citing its source. Harvey gives examples such as checking what preparatory works said when a provision was introduced and drafting Danish-law advice from the licensed sources together with a firm's prior work. The content can be used in Harvey Assistant, Agents, Vault, Workflows and the Word Add-in, next to a team's own notes and matter documents.

Djøf Forlag Digital Director Bjarke Madsen said the publisher has supplied Danish legal sources for more than 65 years, and that customer demand for making them available in AI-powered legal tools motivated the partnership. The agreement follows Harvey's data partnership with Gyldendal Rettsdata in Norway and builds on its work with Danish firms including Kromann Reumert, which went live with Harvey across the firm in 2026. At Accura, Executive AI Officer and Head of AI Christian Høyer Ørum described a regulatory-advice process that starts with the act, checks executive orders and returns to preparatory works when interpretation matters. He said the integration will let Accura perform those steps in the tool it already uses, making the work faster and more consistent.

For Danish firms, the practical significance lies in linking licensed authority with internal work product. Because each answer cites its source, an AI-assisted draft can be traced back to the act, executive order or preparatory document supporting it. This keeps legal verification attached to the research and drafting process. The articles do not describe further rollout timelines beyond the January 2027 availability date for the legislative content.

Articles.Title: Harvey Partners with Djøf Forlag to Add Danish Legal Sources - Unite.AI

stories.Headline: Delegation by default: should UK justice reverse its drift to private AI?
stories.Summary:
The NFJO report, Delegated by Default?, by Dr Natalie Byrom, argues that UK justice has handed much of its digital work to private AI vendors by default, and it calls this "a policy choice." The report sets out 26 recommendations grouped under four themes. It appeared days after the Civil Justice Council published 15 recommendations on how parties should use AI in civil court documents, on 29 October. The CJC's remit covered what lawyers and witnesses file, but not the AI judges use, and the NFJO finds little public information on that. The report does not ask government to stop buying from private vendors.

Its author says it is not an argument against digital or AI-mediated justice, or against private-sector involvement. What it wants reversed is the default, not the market. According to the NFJO summary, the handover covers online legal information, dispute resolution and software that justice agencies run internally. The summary attributes the shift to money pressures, the troubled court modernisation effort and the speed of generative AI's arrival. The Law Society Gazette reports that Byrom sees the turn to the market as an understandable consequence of the HMCTS court reform programme failing to achieve its aims.

The central concern is accountability for tools already in use. Judges now have a locked-down edition of Microsoft Copilot, yet the report finds limited public information on how it was judged safe, what it is meant for, who checks its use and what a litigant can do to object. David Lammy told a Microsoft AI Tour event in London in February that the Ministry of Justice had been one of the fastest growing government users of Copilot, as The Register reported. He also said AI was helping some judges hearing immigration and asylum cases draft notes and remarks. The April 2025 judicial guidance described Copilot Chat on judges' devices, but the October 2025 guidance that replaced it does not mention Copilot.

The NFJO warns that general-purpose models can get facts wrong, invent material and introduce subtle shifts in meaning, and that in family work this could flatten what the report calls justified asymmetry. It argues that judges acting as a human in the loop is unreliable, because fluent outputs make users less likely to scrutinise them. It asks the ministry, the courts service and the judiciary to publish the evidence behind disregarding Microsoft's own advice against using Copilot where it could affect legal status or rights. The current judicial guidance says judges are not generally obliged to describe the preparatory work behind a judgment, which sits awkwardly with calls for litigants to be able to contest AI use.

The CJC's final report, chaired by Sir Colin Birss, recommends a Practice Direction for civil proceedings and a declaration from witnesses of fact that AI did not generate or influence the substance of their statements. It excluded judicial use of AI and the use by unrepresented parties from its remit, though it asked the CJC and the procedure rule committee to consider guidance for unrepresented parties as a matter of urgency. The NFJO says litigants in person are turning to generative AI for advice and documents, with limited redress when it gets the law wrong. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Delegation by default: should UK justice reverse its drift to private AI? - Resultsense

stories.Headline: Obsidian expands AI agent security with runtime policy enforcement
stories.Summary:
Obsidian Security announced its Runtime Policy Decision Engine, which gives security teams centralized control over AI agent actions before they run. The engine uses context about who is behind an agent, its access and the third-party applications involved to allow or block an action, or require human approval where supported. Context from apps, identity systems and customer labels feeds one Policy Decision Engine, and each enforcement point applies its decision before the agent's action reaches the app. The announcement was published on November 11, 2026, and the source given is Obsidian.

Enterprises face agent risk from employees using platforms to write code and start workflows, and from third-party vendors embedding agents in their products. Obsidian's discovery and governance coverage spans platforms including Codex, Claude Code, Cowork, Cursor, Microsoft Copilot, Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex and n8n. It also covers agents built into Snowflake, Databricks, ServiceNow and Workday. Security teams can identify agents, understand their access and address risky configurations. The new MCP Security Proxy checks agent tool calls before they reach business applications, and the new Policy Decision API extends the decision to customer-operated gateways and custom agent tools.

Hasan Imam, CEO of Obsidian Security, said an agent can hold valid credentials, use an approved tool and still take an action that costs the business millions. He said policies are defined once and enforced at the moment of action. Avivah Litan, a former Distinguished Gartner Analyst, said most enterprise agents act across SaaS applications, data platforms and developer tools, and that Obsidian's coverage of Workday, ServiceNow, Snowflake and Databricks addresses a real gap. Kenny Johnson, Principal Product Manager, Security at Cloudflare, said Obsidian's Policy Decision API lets customers apply decisions informed by who is behind an agent at the point where agent traffic already flows.

Obsidian said developers are adopting coding agents faster than guardrails can be put in place, often across several vendors at once. Runtime policy enforcement now extends to OpenAI Codex, so security teams can apply the same policies to Codex, Claude Code, Cowork and Microsoft Copilot from one console. Obsidian also said AI features often arrive switched on in applications, and users can build agents in the app, frequently without a security review. Its in-app agent discovery now maps the identities, tools and data those agents can reach and flags risky configurations.

The MCP Security Proxy gives employees and agents a governed layer between the AI client and supported apps such as Salesforce, Slack, Google Drive and Snowflake. It keeps the app's token out of the AI client and checks each tool call against policy before it runs. Obsidian is partnering with Cloudflare and its MCP Server Portal to provide policies for agentic access into third-party applications through the Obsidian MCP Proxy. Security teams can also supply their own context, such as data classification labels, which Obsidian evaluates alongside identity, HR and application data.

Articles.Title: Obsidian expands AI agent security with runtime policy enforcement - Help Net Security

stories.Headline: Microsoft Warns a New Trade Crackdown Could Derail America's AI Boom
stories.Summary:
Microsoft has urged the Trump administration to drop a planned restriction on Chinese-made optical transceivers, according to a November 10 Reuters report cited by GuruFocus and Yahoo Finance. The company has lobbied administration officials against an import ban being developed by the Federal Communications Commission. The move was reported on November 10, 2026. The dispute centers on components that connect servers, networking switches and other equipment through high-speed fiber-optic cables.

The proposed ban would restrict these devices because the administration worries that Chinese-made components could enable espionage, malware installation or disruptions to critical American infrastructure. The article notes that China accounts for roughly two-thirds of the global optical transceiver market, according to Counterpoint Research. American manufacturers Coherent and Lumentum offer competing products but currently lack sufficient production capacity to replace Chinese suppliers. One possible compromise would restrict only advanced transceivers capable of transmitting 3.2 terabits per second, which are not expected to enter large-scale production until 2028. The article identifies the FCC's final decision as the most important near-term catalyst.

Microsoft is the company pressing the issue, and the article says it raised supply-chain concerns during September meetings with White House and National Security Council officials. The company has 35 data centers under construction across the United States and another 134 planned, according to market intelligence firm Cleanview. Microsoft's position is that a broad ban could increase construction costs and delay AI deployments. The administration's stated concern, as described in the article, is national security.

The article places the dispute within a broader vulnerability, since large technology companies' AI investments still depend on Chinese components that domestic manufacturers cannot quickly replace. Investors are told to watch whether restrictions target existing products or future generations, and how Azure revenue growth and data center utilization respond. The article suggests a narrowly targeted restriction could preserve Microsoft's expansion plans while broader restrictions could leave expensive AI processors underutilized. The FCC's final decision on the matter is still pending, and the article does not say when it will be issued.

Articles.Title: Microsoft Warns a New Trade Crackdown Could Derail America's AI Boom

stories.Headline: Commvault CEO on AI security, Nvidia, data recovery
stories.Summary:
Commvault CEO Sanjay Mirchandani appeared on CNBC's "Power Lunch" on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, in an interview that ran from 2:42 p.m. Eastern time. The segment covered AI agents that have gone rogue, the company's partnerships with Nvidia, and data recovery. The video listing identifies the interview only by these topics and does not describe any specific incident or event involving the company.

The article gives no further detail on what the rogue AI agents did or how Commvault's Nvidia partnership works, so those points cannot be filled in from the material provided. The listing also includes a list of other videos from the same program, mostly featuring executives from utility and energy companies discussing electricity demand and data center growth. Those related segments are not about Commvault and do not add facts about its products or customers. No new requirements, dates for changes, or regulatory actions are stated in the article.

Mirchandani is responsible for the remarks in the interview, and the article presents him as speaking for Commvault. The listing does not include any paraphrased or quoted statements from him, so his specific views on AI security or recovery are unavailable here. The CNBC description frames the discussion as a conversation about AI agents and data protection, rather than reporting a confirmed breach or outage. More to follow.
