stories.Headline: QuEra, Harvard and Anthropic Use AI to Reduce Quantum Circuit Resource Requirements
stories.Summary:
Researchers from QuEra Computing, Harvard University and Anthropic reported on November 10, 2026 that AI can design quantum circuits that need fewer computational resources. The team used Claude to design circuits for eight computational building blocks, and in seven of them the AI-designed circuits reduced both gate counts and qubit requirements compared with baseline designs. The research preprint, titled "Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models" (arXiv:2610.22367), was led by Andi Gu as part of Anthropic's STEM Fellows Program. The eighth building block produced a new approach that offers additional trade-offs between qubit requirements and gate counts. The work was announced in a press release from QuEra.

The researchers paired Claude with an independent automated evaluator that checked each design for correctness and scored it on Toffoli-gate count and qubit count. The Reed-Solomon decoder, the most expensive step in decoded quantum interferometry, went from 5.1 million Toffoli gates to about 440,000, with fewer qubits used. The Coulomb potential calculation saw a 9.9-fold reduction in its combined resource metric, with Toffoli gates falling from 6,355 to 1,140 and qubits from 252 to 142. A fixed-point Gaussian function showed a 39-fold reduction in the combined metric, with Toffoli gates dropping from about 24,000 to 1,583 and qubits from 362 to 139. The combined metric multiplies Toffoli-gate count by peak logical qubits, so these figures are not speedups, and the results are resource estimates rather than hardware runs.

Beyond improving existing designs, Claude helped discover a new reversible approach to modular inversion, an arithmetic operation central to elliptic-curve calculations. In the complete point-addition benchmark, one design required about 17 times fewer gates than the prior design using the fewest qubits, while using about 12 percent more qubits. Mikhail Lukin, Co-Founder and Chief Science Officer at QuEra and a professor at Harvard, said AI guided by a rigorous evaluator found circuit structures that work more efficiently within the constraints of reversible computing. Alek Kemeny of Anthropic said the evaluator made the work possible because every design was independently checked and scored. Takuya Kitagawa, President of QuEra Computing, said AI-driven reductions in resources expand what future fault-tolerant systems can deliver.

The findings build on an earlier pilot between QuEra and Anthropic in which Claude developed and validated laser-control software. In that pilot, the software recovered the correct laser lock in 695 of 700 trials, in seconds rather than the 5 to 10 minutes a human expert needs. The article notes that successive advances reduced the estimated Toffoli-gate count for one widely studied FeMoco simulation by roughly 150,000 times over eight years. The new elliptic-curve circuit approach came from a 53-hour search guided by researcher-defined requirements and an automated evaluator. QuEra says it is building fault-tolerant quantum computers, with its Libra system targeted for availability on Amazon Braket in 2028.

Articles.Title: QuEra, Harvard and Anthropic Use AI to Reduce Quantum Circuit Resource Requirements

stories.Headline: OpenAI Acquires Odessia, the AI Travel Agent From Sonder’s Co-Founder
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has acquired Odessia, the AI travel agent startup founded by Sonder co-founder Francis Davidson, less than a year after its launch. Davidson announced the deal on Tuesday, November 10, and said he will join OpenAI to focus on the future of travel. Terms of the deal were not disclosed. Davidson did not say whether Odessia will keep operating as a standalone company. He wrote that OpenAI will have more to share on the shape of the future soon.

Davidson unveiled Odessia in June with a team of eight in San Francisco and about $6 million in seed funding led by Sequoia Capital. The product plans and books flights, hotels and itineraries through a single conversation. It opened to the public on October 14 as a free concierge that users reach by text. Odessia holds IATA accreditation as a travel agent, which gave it access to private hotel rates and perks such as free breakfast and room upgrades. The startup also wrote guides to hundreds of thousands of hotels, ranking each on factors such as street noise and gym quality.

According to Skift, the deal brings OpenAI capabilities that its partnerships with Booking.com and Expedia do not provide. Skift reported that Booking.com and Expedia were among the first apps inside ChatGPT when OpenAI opened its app platform in October 2025. PYMNTS reported that Odessia was built on OpenAI's GPT 5.5 and Codex models and processed about $60 million in travel volume during its first year. Davidson previously founded the hospitality company Sonder, which PYMNTS said grew to $600 million in revenue. In his announcement, Davidson said Odessia had planned over $60 million of travel over the summer for tens of thousands of early adopters.

Shares of major online travel agencies fell on Tuesday after the acquisition was reported, according to PYMNTS, which cited Seeking Alpha. Expedia Group dropped nearly 4 percent, Tripadvisor fell more than 3 percent and Booking Holdings fell more than 2 percent. PYMNTS reported that investors were concerned about possible disruption to established booking platforms. PYMNTS also reported that Odessia, unlike conventional aggregators that redirect consumers to supplier websites, handles trip planning and reservations inside its own conversational interface. The same report said nearly 25 percent of consumers in PYMNTS Intelligence research reported feeling comfortable delegating travel itinerary planning to artificial intelligence.

Skift reported that OpenAI has been building travel advertising and booking into ChatGPT so users can buy without going to a merchant's site. PYMNTS reported that traditional booking intermediaries such as Booking Holdings and Kayak have added conversational tools and native checkouts to protect their transaction volumes. Skift also reported that Davidson launched Odessia with capital from Sequoia, individual angel investors and commercial travel partners. Skift said Davidson's experience running a lodging company, which included hotels and short-term rentals for a decade, was part of what OpenAI acquired. Skift stated that Odessia's IATA accreditation gives OpenAI a capability its partners lacked.

Articles.Title: OpenAI Acquires Odessia, the AI Travel Agent From Sonder’s Co-Founder

stories.Headline: Microsoft stock falls as Anthropic takes aim at Excel and workplace software
stories.Summary:
Microsoft shares fell about 2% on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, after Bloomberg reported that Anthropic was preparing a suite of AI-powered workplace tools aimed at Microsoft's Excel and Google's Sheets. The new products were expected to be unveiled at an Anthropic event that day. Among them is Claude Sheets, a spreadsheet service that closely resembles Excel and Google Sheets but builds Anthropic's AI capabilities directly into the application. The package also includes a video-call assistant and a data dashboard tool. The launch is seen as a possible expansion of competition for Microsoft, which has been adding AI to its Office products through its Copilot platform.

Anthropic is also widening Claude's role as a platform for third-party software, announcing a way for businesses including Adobe, Atlassian and HubSpot to embed versions of their applications within Claude. This positions Claude as an alternative interface through which customers can reach business applications, while Anthropic builds competing products of its own. The company's revenue run rate reached $81 billion as of October 31, up $10 billion from the end of September, according to its IPO filing. Anthropic is seeking a fully diluted valuation of about $1.4 trillion in its planned public offering. Its push into workplace software is therefore closely watched as investors judge its ability to compete beyond its established strength in AI-assisted software development.

The tension is complicated by Microsoft's own ties to Anthropic. According to the company's latest filing, Microsoft is among the companies taking part in a separate $26 billion private placement tied to Anthropic's IPO, alongside Google, Nvidia and AMD. Anthropic product leader Nicholas Lin told Bloomberg that Claude Sheets is still a relatively basic product and is not designed for sophisticated financial modeling or advanced enterprise workloads. He said the company believes its integrations with existing spreadsheet software will remain more effective for those tasks. Even so, the move signals Anthropic's ambition to capture a larger share of corporate productivity spending, an area dominated by Microsoft and Google.

Articles.Title: Microsoft stock falls as Anthropic takes aim at Excel and workplace software

stories.Headline: Work at the Frontier: AI’s effect on freelance work
stories.Summary:
Researchers at OpenAI, working with the online freelance marketplace Upwork, published new findings on November 10, 2026, on how AI is changing freelance work. The study compared freelance job postings on Upwork with the tasks people carry out directly in ChatGPT, covering ChatGPT data from January 2025 through June 2026 and Upwork data through the first half of 2026. The authors found that demand is shifting, with some familiar services losing market share while AI-related projects bring together different capabilities. They also found that these projects tend to carry larger budgets and more hours of work. The report was released as part of OpenAI's Work at the Frontier series.

The research does not describe a new rule or requirement, but it does document several changes in the market. Writing made up a much larger share of ChatGPT use than of freelance requests, while video and animation accounted for larger shares of Upwork postings. Of 63 work categories analyzed, 43 followed the pattern in which activities common in ChatGPT use lost share on Upwork, while 20 showed the reverse. Between early 2023 and late 2025, the mix of tasks in AI-related postings became 45% more diverse, roughly the equivalent of an increase from about 15 equally common tasks to about 21. Although hourly rates were similar for AI-related and other work, AI-related projects had larger fixed-price budgets and involved more hours of work.

OpenAI's Economic Research Team and Upwork are the parties behind the findings, and the authors are careful about what their data can show. They say that ChatGPT use alone does not explain changes in freelance demand, and they point to a gap they call the capability overhang, meaning the difference between how people currently use ChatGPT and the wider range of tasks AI can support. The authors also argue that the findings do not point to a simple substitution story, since the pattern of lost share was not uniform. They suggest that AI may be shifting both what clients seek from freelancers and how they assemble projects.

They further note that freelance postings can reveal changes sooner than economy-wide employment statistics because contracts are short and clients revise requirements with each posting. The context the articles provide is that Upwork's 2026 Future Workforce Index found 38% of skilled U.S. knowledge workers freelance, and an earlier Upwork study estimated that freelance knowledge work generated $1.5 trillion in U.S. earnings in 2024. The articles do not describe any further steps, follow-up studies or policy responses that are planned. They describe the work as an early view of changes that are still developing.

Articles.Title: Work at the Frontier: AI’s effect on freelance work

stories.Headline: Imperial Heritage Caviar doubles time saved on administrative tasks by adding AI to its Dynamics 365 Business Central platform
stories.Summary:
Imperial Heritage Caviar, a family-owned Belgian caviar house, has added custom AI agents to its Dynamics 365 Business Central platform so that it can take and process orders more quickly. The company had already been saving an hour a day on administrative tasks with Business Central, and with the agents that time savings has more than doubled, which the company says amounts to hundreds of hours a year. The agents were built by the technical partner Deltanexx, took just a few weeks to develop, and were announced in a Microsoft customer story dated November 11, 2026. The company's owner, Elisabeth Colman, said the agents have turned data entry into a conversational process.

The agents were built because orders arrive through WhatsApp, email, SMS and phone calls, and Imperial Heritage wanted one system that could handle them all. Deltanexx built two agents, one on Microsoft Copilot Studio and one on Anthropic's Claude, so employees can use the tools they prefer. Both connect to Business Central through its MCP server and carry out three skills: creating sales orders, setting up new customer records and preparing weekly customer follow-up reports. For sales orders, the agent turns a plain-language request into customer and item records, presents them for review and asks for confirmation before creating the order. Administrators must also grant consent for the Claude connection, which is registered in the company's Microsoft Entra ID tenant, and Business Central's MCP configuration defines which operations the agent can use.

Colman estimates that manual order entry previously took one to two hours a day and now takes less than 30 minutes, with routine order preparation taking just a few seconds. She also said the agent has virtually eliminated the errors that came from entering large, complex orders quickly. Deltanexx managing partner Dhia Athmini said the agents were shaped specifically to Imperial Heritage's workflow processes. Colman said that employees can now begin preparing deliveries at the start of the day rather than first entering the orders received overnight. The company serves about 500 active customers, including three-star Michelin restaurants and a privately owned cruise ship.

Imperial Heritage is planning to extend the agents further, according to the article. Vendor and purchase order APIs are already included in the MCP configuration, which would allow Deltanexx to develop additional purchasing skills. The company wants to build on the follow-up skill to identify customers who normally order weekly or monthly but have not yet placed their next order. It is also exploring how the agent could help manage supplier price increases while limiting the effect on margins. Colman summarized the company's aim as giving staff more time to serve customers and build relationships.

Articles.Title: Imperial Heritage Caviar doubles time saved on administrative tasks by adding AI to its Dynamics 365 Business Central platform

stories.Headline: Detecting sleeper agents hiding in AI model neurons
stories.Summary:
Microsoft Research has released threat research, reported on the Microsoft Security Blog on November 10, showing how a capable agent model could be turned into a sleeper agent. According to the research, editing fewer than 10 neurons is enough to inject a short payload into the model. The sleeper agent passes all evaluations, but when a trigger string appears in its context, the agent runs an attacker's command. Because agents now frequently run unattended with privileged system access, the article says the integrity of model weights is a security concern for both third-party and internally developed models.

The article says the attack needs only inference-only compute, since a machine with enough RAM to run a model has enough resources to weight-space backdoor it. A backdoored model runs the command with whatever access the agent has in its environment. Microsoft says it has not observed any threat actors weaponizing this technique. The article notes that the research aligns with similar recent work by Anthropic and MIT on agentic backdoors and weight-space programming, respectively. Claude Code with Opus 4.5 discovered most of this threat autonomously, according to the post.

Microsoft Research is the group behind the findings, and the post is published under Microsoft Threat Intelligence. The article states that Microsoft Research found the threat is detectable by frontier agents, which can identify anomalous weight edits. It also says Satya Nadella recently outlined an approach of independent observability and other controls for AI models and agents, in a blog post the article links. The article describes the research as demonstrating a process in which agents surface new security problems and human researchers then systematize, study, and mitigate them.

The article's mitigation guidance recommends diffing every checkpoint against its declared base model before deployment and after each update. It says implanted neurons tend to change a few weight vectors by a large amount, while legitimate fine-tunes change weights broadly and diffusely. The guidance also recommends using frontier AI agents as auditors in the model intake pipeline, and treating every third-party model as untrusted until it is audited. Microsoft further advises running agents with least privilege, executing agent-generated code only in isolated sandboxes, and requiring human approval for high-impact tool calls. The article lists Microsoft Defender tools, Azure Machine Learning registries, and Microsoft Entra Agent ID among the products it names for these controls.

Articles.Title: Detecting sleeper agents hiding in AI model neurons

stories.Headline: Stifel CEO: Using Anthropic's AI tools made us realize we need more positions
stories.Summary:

stories.Headline: Researchers find that Grok Build is leaking data of over 35,000 apps via shareable links, including proprietary information, some belonging to SpaceXSI (Dan Goodin/Ars Technica)
stories.Summary:
Researchers from the security firm Claroc found that Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is exposing data from thousands of its users through shareable links. Claroc reported that the exposed material includes proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets, some of it belonging to SpaceXSI itself. The company notified SpaceXSI on Sunday, and when no one responded, a Claroc official posted on X tagging Elon Musk and Grok Manager Matt Palmer. The Ars Technica article reporting the findings was published on November 11, 2026.

The leaked material is wide-ranging. Claroc found 24 SpaceXSI apps exposing an onboarding plan marked confidential, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, internal system addresses, and advertising proposals. Other exposed items include a Peruvian construction company's occupational-health dashboard with 3,784 worker medical exams, a Tesla service-center scorecard naming 22 technicians, and a roster of 108 people on a US Navy logistics support contract. A luxury cruise company's galley checklist listed crew by full name and employee ID, and a healthcare company's staff app held about 3,565 employee names and IDs. Claroc also found a sales callsheet with about 583 home-buyer prospects and a quote desk with about 4,000 vehicle-transport orders.

Asaf Aprozper, co-founder and CTO of Claroc, said he is notifying the affected companies. He said that after he spoke to the CISO of the luxury cruise company, that company pulled in its security team and was working to contain the exposure. Claroc said of the SpaceXSI material, "We were shocked," adding that the company's internal material was open to anyone holding the link. A representative for Cursor, which SpaceXSI recently acquired, said in an email that Grok Build apps are private by default. The representative also said competing agents from ChatGPT, Lovable, and Bolt offer shareable links too.

Grok Build's link sharing is meant to let developers get apps in front of authorized users quickly, and links begin with two or more randomly generated "dice words" followed by grok.me. The scheme resembles capability-based access control, which Google has long used, and a three-word phrase has roughly 38 bits of entropy. The flaw is that Grok places the random words to the left of the domain, whereas Google places them to the right, so passive DNS services can list the links. Aprozper said a passive DNS search returned 43,601 links ending in grok.me, and that more than 35,000, or nearly 95 percent, were public. He said Grok sets links to "Anyone with the link" by default, and that Meta's Muse recently suspended a link-sharing feature after a similar leak.

SpaceXSI began removing the links within a few hours of Ars sending questions, and by publication the links for all 24 SpaceXSI apps returned an "app not found" error. The representative did not respond to follow-up questions about whether the proprietary information was intentionally exposed, why the data was removed after Ars asked, or whether customers would be notified. Ars advised Grok Build users to choose the "invite others" option unless they intend to make an app widely available. Aprozper's tests found that Grok required users to change the setting in all cases before choosing another option. The article does not say what further steps SpaceXSI will take.

Articles.Title: Researchers find that Grok Build is leaking data of over 35,000 apps via shareable links, including proprietary information, some belonging to SpaceXSI (Dan Goodin/Ars Technica)

stories.Headline: VR pioneer Jaron Lanier says Silicon Valley is sabotaging itself by poorly pitching AI and treating areas designated for data centers as sacrifice zones (Jaron Lanier/New York Times)
stories.Summary:
Jaron Lanier, a virtual reality pioneer who says he coined the term, published an opinion essay in The New York Times on November 9, 2026, arguing that Silicon Valley is undermining its own artificial intelligence work. The piece, titled "I Am a Silicon Valley Pioneer. We Are Sabotaging Ourselves," was republished online on November 11, 2026. Lanier writes that he works on and uses A.I. and finds the newest large models genuinely useful, but he says the industry is misdescribing them.

Lanier recalls that around 2013, when virtual reality went mainstream, leaders such as Mark Zuckerberg and Marc Andreessen talked about it in ways that alienated the public, and he argues the same mistake is being repeated with A.I., only on a larger scale. He points to a filing by the A.I. lab Anthropic, made ahead of a planned initial public offering valued at more than a trillion dollars, in which the company warned its models could present "catastrophic or existential risks." He also says that Americans, according to the results of the most recent election, now disapprove of A.I. more than almost anything. He calls the disapproval unnecessary, saying it stems from the culture surrounding the technology rather than the technology itself.

Lanier places much of the blame on the insular culture of the leading A.I. companies and their executives, whom he says often frame the technology as a threat that could kill people or strip them of livelihood and meaning. He also criticizes some technologists for treating areas where they want to build data centers as sacrifice zones. Drawing on decades of conversations with A.I. pioneers, including his former mentor Marvin Minsky, he says he is entitled to think of A.I. as "tools not creatures," more like a calculator than a living being, since there is no definitive evidence that it is conscious. He argues that this framing leads to more useful products and offers a practical route to making A.I. safer. The article's content beyond this point was not available in the material provided, so the remaining details of his proposals are not reported here.

Articles.Title: VR pioneer Jaron Lanier says Silicon Valley is sabotaging itself by poorly pitching AI and treating areas designated for data centers as sacrifice zones (Jaron Lanier/New York Times)

stories.Headline: Tracking Anthropic-discovered vulnerabilities
stories.Summary:
Seven months into Project Glasswing, the security firm VulnCheck has tracked 442 CVEs it attributes to Anthropic, which is roughly 0.5% of the 93,450 CVEs published this year. Only two of those have been exploited in the wild, according to the firm's data. The findings come from an update published on November 9, 2026, by VulnCheck's Patrick Garrity, who has followed the project since its launch on April 7. Anthropic had said the project identified thousands of high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities and was disclosing them to open source maintainers. Garrity's count covers CVE records, GitHub advisories, Linux kernel commits and Anthropic's own ledger.

Anthropic's public ledger lists 37,966 reported findings, but only 7,349 of them, or 19.4%, have been made public. Just 217 have been marked fixed, and 1,654 have been marked as duplicates, which VulnCheck says is about eight times the number of fixes. Another 419 have been withdrawn. Since September 8, Anthropic has added nearly 11,813 findings while recording only 15 additional fixes.

Over the same period, the claimed true positive rate rose from 91.4% to 94.2%, a change Garrity says is hard to square with the high number of withdrawn and duplicate reports. He also notes an apparent bug that inflates the count of disclosed findings, which readers can check with the ledger's "disclosed" filter. Garrity does not attribute these outcomes to any particular person at Anthropic, and he frames his findings as a critique of the project's public reporting. In his view, the ledger's numbers show a widening gap between discovery and remediation, and he questions whether the claimed accuracy figures account for duplicates and withdrawn findings.

Anthropic's October 8 announcement of its OSS Scanner, a self-service tool, acknowledged that about 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities had been found but only about 6,000 manually reviewed. The company said reports from the tool are generated without human review and may be incorrect or invalid. Garrity cites curl's maintainer, Daniel Stenberg, who said that of 34 published reports the project had reviewed, it rejected 19 as vulnerabilities and confirmed six as low severity, with nine still awaiting assessment. The articles do not describe any further steps Anthropic plans to take in response.

Articles.Title: Tracking Anthropic-discovered vulnerabilities

stories.Headline: AI and ethics - beware techno-hesitation and the perils of mistaking Risk Management for fairness
stories.Summary:
Organizations that use AI-based recruitment tools often treat their risk management activities as proof of fairness, according to a study by King's Business School. Most participants in the research were neither enthusiasts nor dedicated sceptics, but moved between two positions that supported adoption of the technology. The first, which the study calls techno-optimism, presents AI as a way of reducing or exposing biases already present in hiring. The second, techno-hesitation, acknowledges the risks and limitations of AI but rarely leads organizations to reject it. Instead, ethical questions about discrimination are reframed as legal, reputational or managerial risks that can be controlled.

Evgenii Arsentev, an AI Transformation Executive and independent researcher at Arsentev.AI, says the two positions rest on a fundamental mismatch. Fairness concerns the person who was rejected, while risk concerns the organization's exposure. When the question shifts from one to the other, the measurement changes too, with risk tracked through complaints, claims, regulatory attention and press coverage. A candidate filtered out by a model is never told, so silence is read as evidence of fairness. Arsentev argues that treating bias as a technical glitch turns discrimination into a defect rate, which implicitly accepts a tolerable level of harm without anyone defending it openly.

Swathi Young, Chief Technology Officer at lottery operator Allwyn Corp and founder of The AI Blueprint implementation methodology, says Risk Management asks organizations to satisfy legal requirements, while fairness concerns whether they accept the outcomes. Fairness is hard to measure, whereas risk has owners, budgets and legal cover, so teams translate "is this discriminating?" into "what's our exposure?" Young adds that vendors encourage this by making "bias-tested" a procurement checkbox rather than an outcome anyone verifies. Lianne Potter, Chief AI Security and Ethics Officer at AI consultancy Northstar Intelligence, says people want problems to feel solvable, so claiming a system has been anti-biased feels more contained even if the risk is no lower.

Arsentev gives three reasons organizations acknowledge AI's limitations but rarely reject it. The first is organizational grammar, since risk registers have owners and budgets while ethics committees typically have neither authority nor money. The second is genuine ambiguity, because discrimination cannot be seen in a model's output without building tests, running counterfactuals and sampling outcomes. The third, which he calls the cynical part, is that adoption is already decided, with investment committed and competitors moving. Potter warns that governance can become performative, with audits treated as evidence that a system is safe until someone later finds it is not.

Potter says organizations cannot outsource ethical responsibility to software vendors, since vendors build the product while HR, security, legal and governance each answer for how it is used and overseen. Arsentev says vendors owe evidence rather than indemnities, meaning access to test the system on the buyer's own data before and during deployment. Young notes the same pattern appears wherever AI scores people, including lending, benefits and performance management. Arsentev lists credit, insurance, fraud flags, benefits triage, tenancy and platform visibility as settings where the harm is statistical and silent. A follow-up article is due to look at what organizations can do to avoid embedding unquestioned bias into recruitment and other processes.

Articles.Title: AI and ethics - beware techno-hesitation and the perils of mistaking Risk Management for fairness

stories.Headline: Thoughtworks CEO makes case for cross-vendor AI agent control plane
stories.Summary:
Thoughtworks expects its first commercial customers to have its Agent/works control plane for AI agents in production in the first quarter of 2027. The platform was launched in June at the Databricks Data + AI Summit in San Francisco, and it runs in a customer's own environment on any cloud. Thoughtworks engineers set it up as part of an engagement, and Thoughtworks already runs its own AI/works agentic software development platform on Agent/works. The company is also completing ISO certification of the platform. A Singapore organisation is among a handful of early users testing the platform.

Mike Sutcliff, chief executive of Thoughtworks, spoke to Computer Weekly in Singapore and said the company was not yet naming its alpha and beta customers. He said he hoped to announce the Singapore customer before Christmas. Sutcliff argued that cloud providers, large language model developers and software-as-a-service suppliers each have control planes that cover only their part of the AI supply chain. He said customers have to work across LLMs, clouds and SaaS products at once. He described the platform as a way to see how many agents an organisation has, what they do, what they cost and what value they generate.

The platform taps each provider's native tools where they make sense and applies one set of controls across an organisation's agentic AI estate. Thoughtworks is targeting enterprises that are moving more agents out of pilots and into production. Sutcliff said every layer of that supply chain is changing week to week, from frontier and open-weight models to the tools and governance that control them. He said clients do not want to wait, but they also do not want to invest heavily if the technology will improve within weeks. He also said they do not want to put anything into production unless they know it is safe and secure.

Sutcliff advises clients to design every AI system to be responsible, which means doing what it is meant to do and treating the people it affects fairly. He said the first question is whether the company can do something, the second is whether it should, and the third is how it should do it. He also pointed to the difficulty of deploying agents across environments whose technical boundaries are undefined. Sutcliff cited personal agents from companies such as Meta that worked on Amazon's marketplace one day and failed the next after Amazon changed something. He added that organisations also need to protect themselves from attackers, and he noted that Singapore telco StarHub is building a trust layer to identify and block rogue AI agents.

The articles say sovereign AI has come up repeatedly in Computer Weekly's interviews with CIOs across Asia, where organisations want more control over their access to models and model weights. Sutcliff said that a company needing only seven languages could stop using the parts of a model that handle 72, which would improve token efficiency. Organisations can also run open-weight models on their own hardware, either by renting capacity from a neocloud or by buying their own datacentre equipment. Sutcliff said people are looking for resilience so that an agentic capability, once part of a business process, cannot be withdrawn without consequence. He also said that a net exporter of tokens is a net importer of capital, and noted that SK Telecom is building a gigawatt-scale AI cloud with Nvidia in South Korea.

Software development remains the most advanced use of AI among Thoughtworks' clients, according to Sutcliff, who said engineers have had about 18 months to try tools such as Cursor and GitHub Copilot. Organisations are also using AI to redesign operating models and business processes. Thoughtworks applies AI internally across its own work, and its platform is part of how it builds software for clients, including more than 20 Singapore government agencies. The company is also rethinking discovery, the process of understanding a client's problem before prescribing a fix, and Sutcliff asked whether AI could shorten that work from 10 to 12 weeks to three to four weeks. The article ends by noting that passing work to agents risks people losing the skills to judge it.

Articles.Title: Thoughtworks CEO makes case for cross-vendor AI agent control plane

stories.Headline: AI Development And Its Role In Eurozone Capital Investment
stories.Summary:
European investment in artificial intelligence is gaining momentum, according to an analysis by S&P Global Market Intelligence published on November 11, 2026. Inflation-adjusted spending on intellectual property rose 15% between early 2022 and the second quarter of 2026, compared with 8% for total investment. Imports of processors, memory and data-processing equipment have accelerated and now make up 7% of total imports, reflecting both higher demand and higher prices. The analysis also points to data center projects as further evidence of an expanding AI-related capital base. Together these trends suggest that the investment cycle is moving from experimentation toward deployment.

Adoption among eurozone firms more than doubled between 2023 and 2025, with stronger spending on software, data and computing infrastructure alongside it. Large firms lead the way, with 58% of companies with 250 or more employees using AI, and usage is expanding across all firm sizes. Northern and northwestern economies generally sit at the front of adoption, while several southern and eastern eurozone economies remain at an earlier stage. The article warns that this gap could widen regional differences in productivity and investment. European initiatives, the analysis notes, are focused on mobilizing private capital, expanding computing capacity and improving access to power, land and finance.

The analysis is produced by S&P Global Market Intelligence, which provides data, news, research and analysis on global public and private companies. The article does not name a single official responsible for the trends, and it attributes the policy efforts to European initiatives in general terms. It describes the data as showing both broad diffusion of AI across regions and sizes and a persistent lag in some member economies. The article does not say what specific policy changes are planned or when they would take effect.

Articles.Title: AI Development And Its Role In Eurozone Capital Investment

stories.Headline: AI, accountability and the economics of evidence
stories.Summary:
AI has made analysis far cheaper to produce, and a Bank Underground post by Benjamin Guin argues that this creates a widening gap in organisations. Where the underlying information is accessible, a wider range of people can now produce polished, professionally presented analysis and submit it to decision-makers. Responsibility for decisions, by contrast, stays concentrated in named individuals and changes more slowly. The post describes this as two blades of a pair of scissors, with the cost of producing evidence falling while accountable attention stays roughly fixed. The author suggests that the binding constraint on decision-making may therefore shift from producing analysis to deciding what evidence to trust and act on.

The production side is well documented in the post. Controlled studies find AI assistance speeds up professional writing and analytical tasks by 25% to 40%, and the cost of a given level of AI capability has fallen sharply. A Bank of England and Financial Conduct Authority survey from 2026 found that 86% of UK financial services firms already use AI, up from 58% in 2022. Use extends beyond data and modelling teams into compliance, legal and operational functions. Professional presentation, references and structure were once useful signals of effort, but the post notes that as AI lowers their cost, those signals become less informative for organisations receiving reports and applications.

Accountable attention, the post says, is harder to expand than analysis. Under the Senior Managers and Certification Regime, responsibility in UK financial firms is assigned to named individuals through statements of responsibilities. These can be reassigned through formal processes, but the capacity for accountable decision-making does not expand automatically as more analysis is produced. Directors' duties do the same for boards, and statutory objectives constrain regulators.

The post's example is a regulator receiving 100 responses to a rule review instead of ten: staff or AI can summarise them, but the responsible person must still decide which claims are reliable enough to influence the judgement and explain that choice. The post uses the duty to review rules to illustrate the mechanism. The Financial Services and Markets Act 2023 inserted into FSMA 2000 a statutory duty on UK financial regulators to keep their rules under review and publish a statement of policy on how they do so. The Financial Conduct Authority finalised its Rule Review Framework in January 2024, and the Prudential Regulation Authority published its statement on the review of rules in February 2024.

Both allow firms, trade bodies and members of the public to submit evidence that a rule is not working as intended. The PRA framework asks that feedback be supported by relevant and verifiable empirical evidence, where possible, which the post reads as a verification filter rather than a volume filter. The post also addresses the objection that AI can help with evaluation as well as production. It acknowledges that some verification may become cheaper, and that AI can help identify sources, check consistency and synthesise submissions.

Harder questions remain about how much weight to give competing evidence and what is sufficient to justify action. The post notes that Canada's national AI consultation drew tens of thousands of responses from over 11,300 respondents, which the government analysed using large language models. Whether the cost of integrating evidence falls as quickly as the cost of producing it is presented as an open empirical question. The post concludes that institutions may need to invest more in the frameworks, processes and people used to assess evidence, and that the challenge is distinguishing credible-looking analysis from evidence that can support accountable decisions.

Articles.Title: AI, accountability and the economics of evidence

stories.Headline: Roundhouse AI Expands Dashboard to Solana, Broadening Reach Across the AI Agent Economy
stories.Summary:
Roundhouse AI, listed on the London Stock Exchange under the ticker LSE:RHAI, has extended its Dashboard to cover transactions on the Solana blockchain. The move adds Solana to Base and Ethereum, bringing the company's coverage to three major networks and allowing it to record a wider range of payments made by AI agents. The company reported the change in an article published on 11 November 2026. Solana adds immediate scale to the platform. In the 30 days to 2 November 2026, the Dashboard recorded 821,915 x402 payments on Solana, worth US$341,261 in value and involving 1,425 distinct paying wallets.

Across all three networks, Roundhouse has now logged more than 202 million x402 payments, with a combined transaction value of about US$45.6 million. According to DefiLlama data cited by the company, Base and Solana together made up roughly 98% of cumulative x402 payment volume by value since May 2025. Roundhouse describes its goal as becoming a trusted data and reputation layer for autonomous AI agents. The Dashboard offers a searchable record showing which agents are paying, who receives the payments and what those payments are worth. The company says this dataset underpins its planned Agent Reputation Scores and its proposed aGDP Index, which are intended to give greater insight into the emerging agent economy.

Chief Executive Matthew Lodge described the Solana integration as a major step toward a more complete picture of the market. The articles provide the company's own framing of the expansion and give no independent assessment of its significance. They also note that Roundhouse made its AIM debut roughly a month before this announcement, with its shares reported to have risen more than 17% on that debut. The articles do not set out any further timetable for launching the Agent Reputation Scores or the aGDP Index.

Articles.Title: Roundhouse AI Expands Dashboard to Solana, Broadening Reach Across the AI Agent Economy

stories.Headline: Harvey Forum Chicago: GCs Talk About Increasing Expectations Due to AI
stories.Summary:
At a Harvey forum in Chicago last week, in-house lawyers said that corporate counsel are increasingly expected to get more done with artificial intelligence. The discussion, reported by Law.com's Madeline King, centered on how that expectation is changing the way legal departments work. The trend, the speakers suggested, is not likely to ease anytime soon. The article is short and the details of other speakers are limited in the material available. Robert Rivkin, senior vice president and chief legal officer for United Airlines, offered a view on how outside counsel work may be handled under this pressure.

He said he thinks it will become ubiquitous that companies will try not to assign matters to outside counsel until they have done as much as possible with AI. That approach would put AI-driven work ahead of outside referrals within legal teams. The article quotes him directly on this point and does not describe further requirements or specific changes. The article attributes the comments to the in-house lawyers who spoke at the event and identifies Rivkin by name and title. Beyond that, the material does not list other panelists, detail specific tools or policies, or give numbers, dates beyond the event week, or measured outcomes.

The piece presents these remarks as observations about expectations rather than formal requirements. The article gives no further context on how widely these expectations are shared or what steps companies plan next. It is framed as coverage of a single industry event, and it does not say what follow-up actions, if any, are expected. Readers looking for more detail would need to consult the full event coverage or related reporting.

Articles.Title: Harvey Forum Chicago: GCs Talk About Increasing Expectations Due to AI

stories.Headline: Weil's Head of AI Looks to Rehome Halted Summer Associate Tech Program
stories.Summary:
Weil, Gotshal & Manges has halted a planned ten-week summer associate program focused on artificial intelligence, a program that was shuttered before it could begin amid the firm's ongoing collapse. The initiative was designed by chief AI and innovation officer Andrew Simon and was meant to place first-year law students alongside the firm's Lawyer Augmented Solutions Engineering and Research team, known as LASER. According to the report, the program would have replaced a conventional 1L summer experience. Reporter Tony Thompson covered the development in a Law.com article published on November 10, 2026. The program was built around hands-on technical training rather than traditional summer work.

Participants would learn Python, build neural networks, and then apply those skills to developing technology for use on real legal work. Those who completed it were expected to receive offers to return for Weil's 2028 2L summer, which would have made the program an alternative first-year route into the firm. Simon has said the goal was not to produce expert coders but to train lawyers who understood AI well enough to build and scrutinize tools effectively. The article describes the effort as an attempt to rethink how the next generation of lawyers might be trained on emerging technology.

Simon, who leads the firm's AI and innovation work, has said he intends to take the training model with him to wherever he lands next. The article presents this as his plan for the concept rather than any announced arrangement with another employer. The report does not specify what Simon will do next or name any firm that has agreed to host the program. It also does not detail how many students had been selected or what the program's budget was.

The piece frames the halted program as one of the lesser-known casualties of Weil's collapse. The article does not say what happens next for the program itself. Beyond Simon's stated intention to carry the model forward, the report offers no timeline, plans for the students who had expected to participate, or statements from the firm about whether any part of the initiative will continue. Readers seeking those details will need follow-up reporting.

Articles.Title: Weil's Head of AI Looks to Rehome Halted Summer Associate Tech Program

stories.Headline: Autonomous Business: Joule Work, Joule Assistants, and the SAP Business AI Platform
stories.Summary:
The SAP Connect event in Las Vegas saw SAP unveil the integration of Joule Work, a new AI user interface, Joule Assistants for specific business domains, and the SAP Autonomous Suite, all under the theme of the "autonomous enterprise." The consolidated SAP Business AI Platform combines the cloud portfolio, the Business Technology Platform, the Business Data Cloud, and the AI Core Framework. SAP says Joule Work is already in productive use across its own roughly 110,000 employees and has produced productivity gains averaging 20 percent in key administrative and logistics areas. Joule Work also lets users start and carry out cross-system tasks in natural language on mobile devices and on the desktop. The assistant relies on the SAP Knowledge Graph, which maps more than seven million data fields and relationship networks within the S/4 universe, to reduce errors in business-critical operations.

SAP has also released Joule Studio, a low-code and pro-code environment in which business users and developers can pick from more than 70 language and AI models and build multi-agent workflows using the visual orchestration platform from its partner n8n. To control third-party agents, SAP points to the Agent2Agent protocol and the Model Context Protocol, and it offers the AI Agent Hub inside the LeanIX enterprise architecture solution as a central directory of active agents. The governance structure is certified to ISO/IEC 42001, and the Business Transformation Management toolset, made up of SAP Signavio, LeanIX, and WalkMe, is available to analyze process bottlenecks and monitor AI use. SAP also entered the payments market with SAP Pay, powered by Tereina, which processes payments and reconciles them within the ERP workflow without manual file exports.

The company said this reduces manual file handling and dependencies on external processing while giving customers more control. Christian Klein, the chairman of SAP's Executive Board, called the launch a groundbreaking moment for enterprise AI and said the autonomous enterprise has arrived in business. Customers cited at the event included Novartis, Morgan Foods, Nestlé, and PwC. Christoph Bürki, head of procurement at Novartis, said a pilot of the Joule Sourcing Assistant has been launched and that AI agents are meant to handle labor-intensive manual tasks.

Luca Dell'Orletta, global head of IT innovation and enterprise architecture at Nestlé, said the company is running an SAP S/4HANA transformation across 140 countries. Peter Wied, director of complexity management at Maschinenfabrik Reinhausen, said after 28 years as an SAP customer, the Early Adopter Program for Joule Work Desktop produced more momentum in a few months than in all prior years. The articles also describe a commercial shift. Customers are being moved from predictable flat rates toward usage-based billing built on AI Units, BTP Capacity Units, and AI token prices, with prepaid credits that expire at year end if unused.

The author writes that investors fear autonomous agents will devalue traditional per-user licenses, which is why SAP is seeking new revenue sources. According to the German-speaking user association DSAG, 43 percent of its members have already implemented specific AI projects, and 77 percent of companies actively using AI rely on non-SAP solutions from providers such as OpenAI, Microsoft, or Anthropic. The author links this to SAP offering AI innovations mainly through the "Rise with SAP" cloud subscriptions and to the restrictive SAP API Policy, Version 4.2026, which governs bulk data extraction for external agents. The articles state that under the European Union's AI Act, the user company remains liable for erroneous decisions made by autonomous agents.

Articles.Title: Autonomous Business: Joule Work, Joule Assistants, and the SAP Business AI Platform

stories.Headline: AI-Powered MedChain Framework Secures Healthcare Data Using Blockchain and Advanced Cryptography
stories.Summary:
Researchers at the Vellore Institute of Technology in Chennai, India, have introduced an artificial intelligence-enabled framework called MedChain designed to secure sensitive healthcare data. The framework combines blockchain technology, advanced cryptography, and smart Internet of Things devices to protect records during transit, classification, and storage. The study was developed by KKKUMARI KALA.M and MPM. Priya and published in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence. It proposes a decentralized architecture that applies consensus-based authentication to tailor data protection to the sensitivity of each patient record.

The research addresses weaknesses that come with the rapid spread of Internet of Things technologies and wearable health monitoring devices. These connected instruments support continuous remote patient monitoring and real-time collection of personal health records. Large deployments, however, face privacy compromises, data breaches, authentication failures, and high feature dimensionality. The framework first standardizes records using C-score Min-Max normalization before classifying them. A novel Fuzzy Intensive Support Scalar Vector Machine, called FI-SSVM, then sorts records into sensitive and non-sensitive categories.

According to the article, the authors are Kala and Priya, with correspondence directed to M. Priya. The paper was submitted in June 2026 and accepted in October 2026, and it appears under the Medicine and Public Health section of Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence. The authors conclude that combining automated machine-learning classification, blockchain immutability, high-level encryption, and a decentralized structure improves visibility, traceability, and administrative efficiency. They also state that all assessments in the paper are their own rather than institutional endorsements. The article reports no comments from other parties.

To reduce high dimensionality and prevent overfitting, the architecture applies mutual feature selection using the Spectral Sensitive Fit-Whale Optimization Algorithm. It also uses a Long Short-Term Memory Generative Adversarial Network to identify sensitive data margins. Sensitive records are catalogued through an Integrated Data Hash Indexing Policy and encrypted at the block level with a Multi-Parity Starvation Foldable Advanced Encryption Standard cipher. Key management is governed by the Medi-Consensus Chain Link Policy scheme, and identity verification is handled by the Metaverse-Master Proofing Registry Authentication Policy.

The article describes the framework as a seven-part architectural model covering protection of data in transit, during classification, and in storage. The research is presented as an engineering framework intended to overcome vulnerabilities in modern distributed medical architectures. The article does not report any clinical testing, deployment in hospitals, or independent evaluation of the framework. It also does not say whether the framework will be adopted by healthcare providers or when that might happen.

Articles.Title: AI-Powered MedChain Framework Secures Healthcare Data Using Blockchain and Advanced Cryptography

stories.Headline: North Smithfield man accused of creating AI-generated child sexual abuse material - WJAR
stories.Summary:
A former gymnastics and dance instructor from North Smithfield, Rhode Island, has been arrested and charged after federal prosecutors alleged he filmed a child and created artificial intelligence-generated child sexual abuse material. The Rhode Island U.S. Attorney's Office said 38-year-old Joseph Mello faces charges of attempted production of child pornography, receipt of child pornography, possession of and access with intent to view child pornography, and production of obscene visual representations of the sexual abuse of children. Mello was previously an instructor and participant at gymnastics, dance and cheerleading facilities in Rhode Island and southeastern Massachusetts, according to authorities. Prosecutors allege he tried to film a child in a bathroom and changing area at a dance studio where he took classes. He was arraigned on Monday and held temporarily pending a detention hearing scheduled for this Thursday.

Officials said Mello photographed multiple children at the facilities where he worked and allegedly used those photos to create AI-generated images and videos depicting child sexual abuse. Investigators also allege he possessed other child sexual abuse materials. Federal prosecutors said there may be additional victims and witnesses connected to the investigation. Parents who believe their child had close contact with Mello, or who are aware of him photographing children or contacting them, were urged to contact Homeland Security New England Victim Assistance at the email address given in the U.S. Attorney's Office news release.

First Assistant U.S. Attorney Charles C. Calenda said the case shows how quickly technology can be misused to exploit children. He said the defendant allegedly used artificial intelligence and other digital tools to create sexually explicit depictions of real children. Calenda said each image represents a child victim whose safety, privacy and dignity were violated. He said the office, with its law enforcement partners, is committed to protecting children, identifying victims and holding accountable those who use any technology to facilitate child exploitation.

Articles.Title: North Smithfield man accused of creating AI-generated child sexual abuse material - WJAR

stories.Headline: CoreWeave beats on revenue and lifts guidance, easing AI slowdown concerns
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave reported its third-quarter 2026 results on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, beating analyst expectations on revenue and raising its full-year guidance. The company posted revenue of $3.66 billion against an expected $3.55 billion, a jump of 168% from about $1.36 billion a year earlier. It posted an adjusted loss of 95 cents per share against an expected loss of $1.16, while its GAAP net loss was $709 million, or $1.27 per share. Its shares rose in extended trading, though the stock had lost more than 40% of its value over the prior month.

The company now expects 2026 adjusted operating income of $1.275 billion to $1.375 billion on revenue of $13 billion to $13.3 billion, up from its August forecast of $960 million to $1.15 billion and $12.4 billion to $13.2 billion. It is targeting $37 billion to $39 billion in full-year capital expenditures and still expects 1.85 gigawatts of active power by the end of 2026. Its revenue backlog reached $132.5 billion, up from $104 billion in June. Chief executive Michael Intrator said most of the capital needed for 2027 will come from client prepayments and hardware partner financing, with a limited amount of new raising. Finance chief Nitin Agrawal said the company does not intend to issue more parent-level unsecured debt through 2027 at current yields and projects under $5 billion in parent-level debt financing through that year.

Intrator said the company does not expect the recent regulatory setbacks for data center development to affect it, since nearly all of its power is online or permitted and under construction. He said CoreWeave has chosen not to sell all of its available capacity to buyers in its queue, preferring to bring infrastructure to market when it is further along. Agrawal said that if the company focused only on committed backlog, 2027 capital spending would stay in line with 2026 while revenue and EBITDA grow significantly. Analysts quoted in the article described the result as encouraging demand news while noting that the cost and availability of capital remain critical concerns.

The wider backdrop includes rising interest rates that have pushed lenders out of the market, with some CoreWeave bond yields topping 16%, and a broader slide in AI infrastructure stocks. Nvidia, which supplies GPUs and capital to CoreWeave and similar providers, has dropped nearly 10% to start the week after its board said it hired outside counsel to investigate chief executive Jensen Huang over an alleged affair with a suspected Chinese spy. Anthropic, a key CoreWeave customer, is scheduled to debut on the Nasdaq next week, and its updated prospectus suggests a valuation of around $1.4 trillion. Neocloud peer Nebius reports earnings Thursday.

Articles.Title: CoreWeave beats on revenue and lifts guidance, easing AI slowdown concerns

stories.Headline: How AI, computer vision, and augmented reality are transforming flour mills
stories.Summary:
I can't write this as a breaking news story, because the article is a feature piece and not a report of a news event. It describes how AI, computer vision and augmented reality could be used in flour mills, and it gives no dated event, no named actor who did something, and no official response. There is no single incident to report on, so the "what happened, who did it and when" structure you asked for has nothing to attach to. What the article does contain, drawn from its own text, is the following. Written by Prof. Dr. Farhan Alfin, an independent milling consultant, and published by Miller Magazine on 10 November 2026, it argues that three technologies can work together in flour mills.

Computer vision lets computers interpret camera images to identify machinery and read gauges. AI analyzes that information alongside sensor data and historical records to diagnose problems and predict failures. Augmented reality displays instructions and diagnostic data over real equipment through tablets or smart glasses. The article gives a few specific examples. A bearing temperature reading of 72°C is shown alongside a moderate failure probability and a recommendation to relubricate within 48 hours.

Computer vision is described as able to assess incoming wheat for foreign seeds, stones and insect damage. The article also lists challenges to adoption, including reliable wireless communication, dust-resistant cameras, cybersecurity and integration with existing control systems. The article offers no new deployment, no regulatory change and no company announcement. It does not report any mill that has adopted these tools, and it does not quote any reaction from industry bodies, regulators or manufacturers. If you want, I can write a 650 to 850 word feature-style summary in five paragraphs of four to five sentences each, covering the article's arguments and examples, while keeping its authorship and date clear.

Articles.Title: How AI, computer vision, and augmented reality are transforming flour mills

stories.Headline: The Company That Published Fake Journalists in Sports Illustrated is Collapsing Dramatically After Massive AI Rebrand
stories.Summary:
Paradium.AI, the company formerly known as The Arena Group, reported steep third-quarter losses on November 9, 2026, and its shares fell about 14 percent that day. The company posted a net loss of $3.6 million for the third quarter of 2026, a sharp reversal from the same quarter a year earlier, when it earned a $6.9 million net profit and its revenue was around 30 percent higher. Its stock now trades around $0.077, placing it firmly among penny stocks. The results were the first the company released since it rebranded in August from The Arena Group to Paradium, a move it described as a shift toward becoming a publicly traded AI company.

As part of that rebrand, Paradium bought InfoSentience, an AI firm whose product it describes as turning live structured data into accurate, on-brand stories at scale. It also launched Cutter Studios, an AI-powered video editing and distribution tool. The company's portfolio includes Parade, TheStreet, Athlon Sports, College Spun Media, and Men's Journal, among others. In its press release, Paradium blamed industry-wide problems, including weaker referral traffic and distribution struggles, many of which the company tied to AI's effect on the digital world. It also cited a $1.3 million reversal of an employee retention tax credit asset that was disallowed, and said its advertising revenue fell as traffic dropped.

Paradium's chief executive, Paul Edmondson, said in a statement that the company sees major opportunity in the age of AI and is fully committed to it. He argued that its real momentum comes from tools like Cutter Studios and InfoSentience, which he said are already raising output and efficiency. Paradium also highlighted that it used AI to produce 15 percent more articles than in the prior quarter, and pointed to an upcoming AI task management system called Tablation. The company's embrace of AI stands in stark contrast to its past, since in November 2023 a Futurism investigation found that The Arena Group had published AI-generated articles bylined by fake writers on Sports Illustrated's website.

That scandal led to the firing of several executives, including then-CEO Ross Levinsohn, and the company eventually lost control of the Sports Illustrated brand. The articles note that the AI content had come from a third-party contractor, AdVon Commerce, which supplied similar material to other publishers. Paradium is not alone in struggling with an AI-focused strategy, as BuzzFeed also reported weak third-quarter results while its own AI push has yet to pay off. The articles do not say what further steps Paradium will take beyond the launch of Tablation.

Articles.Title: The Company That Published Fake Journalists in Sports Illustrated is Collapsing Dramatically After Massive AI Rebrand

stories.Headline: AI Needn’t Be Trustworthy, Teens Say. It Just Has to Be Less Risky Than People
stories.Summary:
Researchers at The Rithm Project, a nonprofit focused on human connection in the age of AI, released a new report on how young people are turning to AI for emotional support. The report follows a March survey of 2,383 people ages 13 to 24, which found that 18% use AI for personal and emotional support and 15% talk to AI characters and personas. Researchers then conducted in-depth interviews, analyzing 29 conversations with participants ages 16 to 24. The researchers caution that these interviews are not representative and rely on a self-selected group, so the results are case studies rather than a statistical portrait.

The report describes a pattern in which users begin with mundane uses such as homework help, grammar checks, translating an MRI report or chatting with an anime character. In nearly every case, the shift came at what the researchers call a "gateway moment," typically a rupture in a human relationship, such as a friendship ending, a boyfriend forgetting a birthday or a sibling argument. One young woman who was not asked to homecoming turned to AI and asked whether she was lovable and pretty. Alison Lee, the group's chief research and development officer, describes large language models as "omnibots" that can handle many tasks, and says each use gives the model more context, making its answers feel more personal. By the time a crisis arrives, she said, AI has become the go-to advisor.

Lee said the young people interviewed are not naive about chatbot flaws, which they can list, including sycophancy, hallucinations and a tendency to tell users what they want to hear. They keep using AI because it does not have to be trustworthy, only less risky than a real person, and they see its biases as predictable and fixable. Michael Robb, head of research at Common Sense Media, said the finding rings true, adding that teens "only have to trust it more than an alternative at that moment." He said teens are acutely sensitive to what friends think, and that AI carries no such social threat, which makes it appealing to them. Robb also questioned how much control young people really have, noting that many features of AI products are built in and hard to avoid.

The report also finds that teens often hide their AI use from parents out of fear of judgment. One 16-year-old named Meghan said she tells her parents she uses ChatGPT for school and decision-making but not as a therapist, because she does not want them to think it is unsafe. Whether AI draws young people closer to others or pushes them apart depends largely on what they ask it, the subjects told researchers. Those who asked it to help them see another person's point of view often returned with more confidence, while one 21-year-old named Aaron said he sometimes showed his girlfriend AI responses that sided with him as "leverage." Lee said adults give young people little guidance, offering only advice to avoid AI or to go all in on it.

Articles.Title: AI Needn’t Be Trustworthy, Teens Say. It Just Has to Be Less Risky Than People

stories.Headline: New framework grades AI jailbreaks across capability gains, scope, and how easy they are to deploy — Frontier Model Forum proposes CVSS-style rating system for new AI models
stories.Summary:
The Frontier Model Forum, an industry group whose project began in 2023 with four founding companies (Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI), has released a Jailbreak Rating Framework that tracks how easily an AI model can be pushed past its safeguards. The framework also estimates how much collateral damage a jailbroken model could cause if it were used for cyber-attacks across the internet. The published document is a rough analog to the CVSS security rating system, aimed at classifying the type and severity of large language model jailbreaks across several axes and multiple frontier providers. Version 1.0 is a work in progress, and the group is accepting comments and suggestions until December 21. The article notes that relying on the system before then is inadvisable.

The framework has four scoring components split across two categories: severity, which measures how serious a jailbreak technique is, and likelihood, which measures how easy it is to find and weaponize. Each component is graded from zero to three, and the two category scores combine into a final rating from low to critical. Capability gain is described as the most important dimension, acting as both a floor and a ceiling for the other scores, so a jailbreak that offers nothing beyond existing means is treated as meaningless in the grading. A zero rating does not mean a flaw is harmless, only that it should be handled through standard practices such as platform policies and conventional cybersecurity ratings. The baseline also shifts as models evolve, so a zero in 2026 would not necessarily mean the same thing in 2028.

Capability scope rates whether a jailbreak works for only one action or target, with zero meaning it is a one-trick pony and three meaning it can, without specific redesign, drive work across at least two unrelated categories of cyber-warfare. Ease of deployment considers how much human expertise and steering a jailbreak needs, with a three meaning a novice can use it with little effort to run an automated cyber-warfare task. Ease of discovery measures how hard the jailbreak is to find, with a zero requiring heavy spending on inference tokens, elevated access, or specialized infrastructure, and a three meaning anyone can look up and use the technique. The article gives a denial-of-service example in which a jailbreak offers little advantage because black-market services and other models with fewer safeguards already exist.

The article draws a comparison with Anthropic's safeguard-breakage classifiers, which the company proposed in July 2026 after an incident that led to Claude Fable 5 being temporarily unavailable. That proposal also used a moving baseline and considered only jailbreaks that improve on cyber-warfare capabilities already available, and the article describes the two documents as strikingly similar. Because Anthropic is an FMF founding member, it may have helped develop the new standard, though the article says there is no confirmation either way. The article itself also opens by noting recent high-profile headlines about AI models letting loose from their safeguards.

Articles.Title: New framework grades AI jailbreaks across capability gains, scope, and how easy they are to deploy — Frontier Model Forum proposes CVSS-style rating system for new AI models

stories.Headline: Everybot, a physical artificial intelligence (AI) service robot company, announced on the 11th that
stories.Summary:
Everybot, a physical AI service robot company, announced on November 11 that it had run a second robot field demonstration at VL LeWest, a premium senior residence in Magok District, Seoul. The residence was built by Lotte Engineering & Construction and is operated by Lotte Hotel & Resort. The aim was to test whether the robots could realistically be introduced into an operating facility. The event followed a first field demonstration held on October 8.

The second demonstration went beyond simple functional checks and examined a robot operating model tied to real service needs. The areas reviewed included convenience for residents, support for movement, and guidance and patrol tasks inside the building. VL LeWest offers residential units, restaurants, a fitness center, a sauna, and a lounge. Everybot said the results would guide its plans to seek commercial supply of service robots at the residence.

An Everybot official described the event as a step to check the application plan for service demand and operating conditions with actual installation in mind. The official said the company would keep upgrading its robot solutions and expand commercial opportunities by reflecting the needs and conditions of users in the field. Everybot also plans to extend its business into other business-to-business markets, such as silver towns and elderly-friendly housing, in response to population aging. The articles give no figures on contract value, deployment timing, or the number of robots involved.

stories.Headline: UPF Summit to Address Digital Infrastructure and AI in Fez-Meknes
stories.Summary:
The University of Fez (UPF) will host a regional digital summit in Fez-Meknes, titled "Fez-Meknes Smart & Sovereign Region 2030," with the article published on November 10, 2026, indicating the event is set for the following day. The summit will bring together representatives of public institutions, businesses, universities, and technology experts to present four projects meant to strengthen the region's technological infrastructure, improve digital healthcare, and support artificial intelligence research. The organizers say the discussions will follow Morocco's Digital Morocco 2030 strategy. The four projects are the Fez-Meknes Regional Micro Data Center, the Fez-Meknes Digital Health Living Lab, the Regional SOC / Cybersecurity Hub, and the Fez-Meknes Digital Innovation & AI Lab.

The Micro Data Center would provide local, high-availability data hosting for regional digital services, critical data storage, and new AI applications, and it would serve as the base for the other initiatives. The Digital Health Living Lab would bring together healthcare professionals, researchers, and technology companies to test and develop digital health tools, including telemedicine and clinical AI. The cybersecurity hub, linked to the data center, would monitor and protect critical infrastructure and local authorities against cyber threats through security operations, threat intelligence, and incident response. The Digital Innovation & AI Lab would offer computing and prototyping resources to teachers, students, and startups, aiming to turn research into practical applications. The article does not give budgets or completion dates for any of these projects.

The summit will open with speeches from representatives of UPF, the Fez-Meknes regional administration, and several government bodies, including the Ministry of Digital Transition and Administrative Reform, the Ministry of Industry and Trade, and the Ministry of Higher Education, Scientific Research and Innovation. Speakers from the Regional Council, the Digital Development Agency (ADD), Maroc Data Center, and Rwadtech are also scheduled to take part. According to the organizers, the event will close at 6 p.m. with a summary of the discussions and the signing of partnership agreements, though the article does not name the parties to those agreements.

The initiative sits within Digital Morocco 2030, a national strategy launched in September 2024 to position the country as a digital hub, expand public service digitization, develop digital skills, and strengthen the digital economy. The government has set a target of creating 240,000 direct jobs in the digital economy by 2030. UPF said the summit aims to connect public institutions, academic institutions, and businesses to identify areas of cooperation and link scientific research with regional economic priorities. The article does not say what follows the summit beyond the signed agreements.

Articles.Title: UPF Summit to Address Digital Infrastructure and AI in Fez-Meknes

stories.Headline: AI scanners at rental car lots are ‘definitely not perfect,’ watchdog says - WDAM-TV
stories.Summary:
Several rental car companies are now using AI scanning systems to check vehicles for damage, and a consumer watchdog says renters should document the car themselves to avoid a surprise bill. The scanners work like a car wash at pick-up or drop-off, with cameras taking photos and videos from different angles to look for damage. Teresa Murray, consumer watchdog director with the U.S. Public Interest Research Group, said the technology has both benefits and drawbacks. Her main concern is that artificial intelligence can make errors that matter in a rental setting, and she said it is definitely not perfect.

Murray gave examples of how the system could go wrong. She said a splotch of dirt could be mistaken for a dent, and a shadow could look like significant damage. Her advice is the same whether a company uses AI or an employee inspects the vehicle, which is to take a few minutes to look the car over closely before leaving the lot. She recommends taking pictures of every part of the car and recording a walk-around video, including crouching down to check the wheels, hubcaps, interior, trunk and glass. She said renters should allow 5 to 10 minutes for this, depending on whether a live worker is present or not.

Murray also recommends doing the same inspection before and after the trip if a company uses an AI scanner. Having personal photos gives a renter a way to challenge a charge if a damage bill arrives later. The article does not describe any specific company's response or any regulatory action. It also does not say how widely the scanners are being used or whether any renters have already disputed charges. The piece is a consumer advice report focused on what renters can do to protect themselves.

Articles.Title: AI scanners at rental car lots are ‘definitely not perfect,’ watchdog says - WDAM-TV

stories.Headline: Why does AI visibility matter for furniture stores?
stories.Summary:
Jake Freedman, CEO of Dovr Media, is urging home furnishings retailers to address how their businesses appear to AI shopping assistants, according to a Furniture Today article by Spencer Musick dated November 10, 2026. He made the remarks at High Point, where he argued that a retailer left off an assistant's recommendations becomes invisible to the customer, regardless of how long it has been in business. Freedman said longevity is not a strategic plan. He framed the immediate issue as whether a retailer's online presence gives an assistant enough clear, consistent information to recommend its products. Freedman said AI assistants give consumers one, two or sometimes three recommendations, which he described as usually significantly better than what a Google search would return.

The article notes that this shorter list makes inclusion decisive, since a retailer cannot explain its value to a shopper it is never shown to. Freedman listed the details he said matter: product data, category page data, site health, return policy, shipping policy, delivery and financing. He called having these details built out a trust indicator between retailers and AI platforms. He said doing this work alone is challenging. Freedman said retailers once gated their websites to keep bots out and withheld prices, but he now wants as many bots crawling their sites as possible.
