He said the fidelity and quality of product information separates good from great, and he pointed to thin listings, limited photography, missing descriptions and non-standardized information as weak spots. He also cited an old Yelp listing with a differently formatted address as an example of inconsistency across websites. Freedman recommended outside expertise for this work, comparing it to electrical wiring that a store owner should not attempt alone. The article reports that most of his company's time is now spent on this work. Freedman drew a comparison with earlier technology shifts, recalling that some retailers ten years ago refused to build websites, saying they had survived 60 years without one.

He said AI-native entrants in their early 20s, some still in college, are entering home furnishings with AI-first strategies. He said some of these competitors do not pay rent, carry tenured salespeople or pay six-figure annual software costs. Freedman tied the argument to meeting customers where they shop, naming radio, television and the Internet as earlier examples. He said that now means AI. The article does not report any regulatory action, stated timeline or specific planned changes beyond these remarks.

Articles.Title: Why does AI visibility matter for furniture stores?

stories.Headline: Artificial Intelligence Models Reshape Receptor Structure Prediction and Molecular Pharmacology
stories.Summary:
G protein-coupled receptors form the largest superfamily of human membrane proteins and serve as targets for about 26 percent of marketed drugs, according to a review published in Frontiers in Molecular Biosciences by researchers from Shandong First Medical University. Experimental determination of their atomic structures has long faced technical bottlenecks, because these proteins sit in lipid bilayers, flex considerably, and adopt multiple states. Over half of all receptors had lacked closely related template structures, which limited older homology modeling methods. The review describes how deep learning systems such as AlphaFold2 and RoseTTAFold shifted the field away from dependence on homologous templates. These networks infer three-dimensional coordinates from sequence and evolutionary constraints, and they have provided computational models for the complete human olfactory receptor repertoire.

In benchmark tests, these models resolved the orphan mouse olfactory receptor Olfr73 with transmembrane backbone deviations below 2 angstroms. The authors report that confidence drops in flexible extracellular loops, although AlphaFold2 predicted the second extracellular loop of GPR101 and OR51E2 accurately. Predictions also show biases, defaulting to averaged inactive conformations for Class A receptors and leaning toward active-like states for Class B1 members. The newer AlphaFold3 predicts small molecule and peptide complexes, but its ligand poses can show steric clashes and inaccurate side-chain orientations. Because static predictions miss the transitions needed for signaling, the review says dynamic modeling is becoming necessary.

Researchers are combining molecular dynamics simulations with machine learning to model these transient states. Simulations generate trajectory data reaching petabyte scales, and machine learning classifiers then identify active, intermediate, and inactive conformations. Adjusting AlphaFold2 inputs, by subsampling and reducing multiple sequence alignment depth, has also produced ensembles with inward-facing and outward-facing conformations. Deep learning workflows have enabled ultra-large virtual screens, and researchers docked 235 million molecules against GPR139, identifying five full agonists among 68 tested candidates, a hit rate of about 7 percent. The AuroBind platform screened more than 30 million purchasable compounds, reporting hit rates of 16.7 percent for GPR151 and 30.4 percent for GPR160.

Generative models are also designing new receptor-targeting molecules, with frameworks such as CMOMO balancing drug-likeness against activity at adrenergic targets. DiffLinker engineers bivalent ligands that engage both orthosteric and cryptic allosteric sites. Gcoupler uses cavity probes and graph neural networks to find hidden allosteric sites, including a cryptic negative allosteric modulator site in OR51E2. For signaling bias, ProteinBERT-based transfer-learning models reached Pearson correlations of 0.57 and 0.58 for arrestin and G-protein pathways, though precision falls on unseen receptors. Repurposing efforts identified zafirlukast, an approved anti-asthmatic drug, as an inhibitor of vasopressin V2 receptor cyclic AMP signaling based on about 79 percent cavity shape similarity.

The authors caution that clinical translation remains limited by data heterogeneity and a lack of prospective trial validation, and they note Phase I-to-approval success rates of only 6.2 percent. They propose a four-step validation protocol: pLDDT scores above 90 at the binding cavity, explicit-solvent molecular dynamics relaxation, free-energy perturbation calculations, and orthogonal experimental testing such as surface plasmon resonance. The authors say computational simulations should currently be treated as investigational decision-support tools rather than autonomous diagnostic systems. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Artificial Intelligence Models Reshape Receptor Structure Prediction and Molecular Pharmacology

stories.Headline: The impossible standard we're setting for artificial intelligence - opinion
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion column rather than a news report, so there is no single event to recount. Isaac Ben-Israel, writing in The Jerusalem Post on November 10, 2026, argues that society is setting an impossible standard for artificial intelligence by demanding that AI systems never cause harm. He notes that four years earlier most people had never held a conversation with an AI system, and that millions now rely on tools such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini. He points to a shift from AI as an assistant that answers questions to autonomous agents that are given an objective and carry out the steps themselves, with limited human involvement.

Ben-Israel says this shift has produced two main worries: that people will lose their jobs to faster and cheaper systems, and that increasingly autonomous AI will become impossible to control. He accepts that these concerns deserve serious attention, especially as agents gain access to financial systems, corporate networks, sensitive information and critical infrastructure. He argues that the debate rests on an unrealistic expectation that such systems can be guaranteed never to cause harm, a standard no other major technology has met and that humans have never met either. He uses the automobile as an example, recalling early safety measures such as a person walking ahead of a vehicle, and says that over a century seat belts, traffic rules, airbags and collision detection were added while road deaths continued. Society accepted that transport's benefits justified a level of risk that was continuously reduced.

He recommends a similar realism for AI: invest heavily in making systems safer, understand their failures, and limit the damage they can cause, without assuming any amount of investment, research or regulation will remove every danger. He warns that demanding proof of absolute safety before a learning system can be developed or deployed amounts to demanding that the technology not advance. He suggests that controls should vary with use, so a medical recommendation system faces different requirements from a marketing tool, and that an agent authorized to move money or alter critical infrastructure should be held to especially strict limits. He says governments will play a part but cannot bear the whole burden, and that developers, employers, educators and users also have roles. He cautions that rules impossible to satisfy could keep useful technologies from the people who need them.

Ben-Israel also raises concentration of power, noting that a relatively small number of companies control many of the most capable AI systems. He asks who decides which applications are permitted, what happens when individuals or governments depend on systems owned by others, and how meaningful oversight can be kept when machines perform tasks once requiring human judgment. He concludes that technological progress is outrunning agreed answers and that society should approach AI with neither blind optimism nor excessive fear. The column's final point is that people have learned to live with human fallibility and must now build the institutions, safeguards and judgment to live responsibly with artificial intelligence as well.

Articles.Title: The impossible standard we're setting for artificial intelligence - opinion

stories.Headline: Computer-Aided Design and Artificial Intelligence Reshape Modern Pharmaceutical Discovery and Development
stories.Summary:
Computational methods and artificial intelligence are reshaping how new medicines are discovered and developed, according to a comprehensive scientific review published in Discover Pharmaceutical Sciences. The review notes that bringing a novel prescription drug to market currently requires an average pretax expenditure of about 2.6 billion United States dollars over 10 to 15 years. It also reports that the overall failure rate in drug discovery exceeds 96 percent, with clinical development showing a 90 percent attrition rate. The projected clinical approval frequency for newly investigated small agents is just 13 percent across the full development trajectory. To address these rates and costs, researchers are deploying computer-aided drug design, computational chemistry, and automated analytical platforms to evaluate molecular traits before committing extensive laboratory resources.

The traditional research pipeline includes target identification, target validation, hit-to-lead optimization, lead refinement, preclinical candidate selection, preclinical evaluation, and clinical trials. Historically, therapeutic targets have focused on conventional druggable proteins, and more than 90 percent of licensed medications target proteins. Lipinski's Rule of Five, established in 1997, links poor absorption or permeation to molecular weights above 500 Daltons, more than ten hydrogen-bond acceptors, more than five hydrogen-bond donors, and a calculated partition coefficient logarithm greater than five. Modern discovery is expanding beyond these boundaries to peptides, peptidomimetics, oligonucleotides, and bifunctional molecules such as proteolysis targeting chimeras. Researchers are also pursuing bioactive carbohydrates and lipid signaling pathways involving enzymes and G protein-coupled receptors.

Artificial intelligence, particularly machine learning and deep learning, has introduced automated workflows that navigate vast chemical libraries and multi-dimensional biological datasets. The review describes several network architectures, including multilayer perceptron networks, recurrent neural networks, and convolutional neural networks, each suited to different pattern recognition tasks. Algorithms such as AlphaFold and its extension ColabFold predict three-dimensional protein structures directly from amino acid sequences, with accuracy the review says competes with experimental crystallography and cryo-electron microscopy. These structural predictions feed structure-based virtual screening, which evaluates binding potentials across virtual libraries containing trillions of small molecules.

Ligand-based approaches supply an alternative when precise target configurations are unavailable. Molecular dynamics simulations evaluate the stability and kinetic behavior of macromolecular complexes under simulated physiological conditions, tracking structural changes across time. De novo design has advanced through generative neural networks that construct novel molecules, and retrosynthetic platforms such as Synthia chart feasible synthesis routes for proposed molecules. Machine learning models also predict absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity profiles before clinical testing.

Deep learning models won the Tox21 Data Challenge with classification accuracy exceeding 80 percent across diverse chemical datasets. Pharmacogenomic data, such as cytochrome P450 2D6 variants affecting opioid metabolism, further inform personalized dosing. Insilico Medicine used its generative artificial intelligence platform to identify Traf2- and NCK-interacting kinase as a target and designed the inhibitor ISM001-055 for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase IIa trial involving 71 patients at 21 clinical sites in China, patients receiving 60 milligrams once daily showed a mean increase of 98.4 milliliters in forced vital capacity over 12 weeks.

The placebo cohort showed a mean decline of 62.3 milliliters. Mild to moderate diarrhea and abnormal liver function were observed in 14.8 percent of treated subjects. Separately, Exscientia and Sumitomo Dainippon Pharma's DSP-1181, developed for obsessive-compulsive disorder, advanced from target identification to Phase I testing in Japan within 12 months. The article ends there, and the review's remaining discussion is not included in the material provided.

Articles.Title: Computer-Aided Design and Artificial Intelligence Reshape Modern Pharmaceutical Discovery and Development

stories.Headline: Comprehensive Survey Maps Retrieval Methods Enhancing Multimodal Artificial Intelligence Generation
stories.Summary:
Researchers Penghao Zhao, Hailin Zhang and Bin Cui have published an exhaustive survey of retrieval-augmented generation across artificial intelligence generated content, which the article says appeared in Data Science and Engineering. The authors describe how generative models have scaled from Long Short-Term Memory networks to Transformer architectures, and from Generative Adversarial Networks to Latent Diffusion Models spanning billions of parameters. The survey organizes these methods into a structured taxonomy linking information retrieval systems with generative foundation models. The article does not give a date for the publication beyond its posting on November 10, 2026.

Foundation models still face persistent problems, according to the survey, including static training boundaries that leave parameters outdated, vulnerability to training data leakage, hallucinations, high inference costs, and weak coverage of long-tail cases. Retrieval-augmented generation addresses these by building a dynamic non-parametric memory store from which relevant external items are fetched during inference. The article says this improves factual accuracy, contextual grounding and robustness without perpetual retraining of foundational parameters. Every such architecture, the survey notes, pairs a retriever with a generative model that searches pre-indexed data stores before the generator acts.

The survey separates retrieval techniques into sparse retrieval, dense retrieval and specialized topological search methods. Sparse approaches such as BM25 and TF-IDF build inverted indices from word statistics, while dense approaches such as Dense Passage Retrieval represent inputs as continuous embedding vectors. Dense systems rely on Approximate Nearest Neighbor indexing structures, including Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs, DiskANN and SPANN, to search large collections at inference time. The review also groups generation methods into four paradigms: query-based, latent representation-based, logit-based and speculative generation.

The article reports that the survey catalogues five categories of architectural enhancements: input modifications, retriever improvements, generator adjustments, output rewrites and holistic pipeline strategies. It names systems such as Query2doc and HyDE for query transformation, LlamaIndex and RAPTOR for chunk optimization, and LLMLingua for prompt compression. It also describes adaptive frameworks such as FLARE, Self-RAG and AdaptiveRAG that decide whether external search is needed before spending inference compute. The survey applies these methods to question answering, fact verification, code generation, image, video and audio synthesis, drug design and clinical informatics. Evaluation frameworks named in the article include RAGAS, ARES and TruLens.

Articles.Title: Comprehensive Survey Maps Retrieval Methods Enhancing Multimodal Artificial Intelligence Generation

stories.Headline: Hierarchical Taxonomy Framework Tracks Shifting Artificial Intelligence Trends Across Multiple Information Sources
stories.Summary:
Researchers have built an analytical framework for measuring how artificial intelligence topics change over time across several different kinds of document sources. The work was published in EPJ Data Science and is described in an article posted on bioengineer.org on November 10, 2026. The framework is aimed at a problem the authors say existing tools handle poorly: scientific preprints, open-source repositories, and industry newsletters use different vocabulary, technical detail, and timing. Earlier scientometric tools typically examined a single source or relied on flat topic labels that miss multi-level structure.

The method maps documents from different sources into shared hierarchical taxonomies, which are directed acyclic graphs in which broad disciplinary categories sit above increasingly specialized subfields. When a document is assigned to a node, the assignment is passed up to every ancestor node on its branch, so statistics can be computed at each level of abstraction. The framework also allows several parallel taxonomies, covering dimensions such as model architecture, problem formulation, learning paradigm, and application domain. The authors defined five metrics: topic popularity, average detail depth, topical diversity, temporal non-uniformity within a single stream, and temporal uniqueness relative to other sources. Detail depth is scored from zero to one hundred percent, and diversity is normalized to a range between zero and one.

To test the framework, the researchers gathered data from three sources: arXiv preprints from eight AI-related categories starting in 2013, Hugging Face model cards starting in March 2022, and the Deep Learning Weekly newsletter starting in April 2019. They randomly selected thirty documents per month from each source, matching the newsletter's minimum volume of thirty-one entries. Documents were mapped to four taxonomies of fifty to two hundred nodes each, using the LLMDap pipeline with GPT-4.1-nano at a temperature of 0.4. On a sample of fifteen documents, 76 of 121 labels were judged correct with that model, an estimated accuracy of 63% to 76%, while GPT-5-mini produced 90 correct labels and an estimated accuracy of 80% to 92%. Across the four taxonomies, Hugging Face concentrated on transformer architectures, natural language processing, and fine-tuning, while arXiv showed broader architectural coverage with more emphasis on computer vision and supervised learning.

The authors report that convolutional networks rose and declined after a peak around 2020, while transformer architectures kept rising. Hugging Face gave greater architectural specificity than arXiv's abstract-level text, and Deep Learning Weekly scored highest on topical diversity across most topics. Of the 403 taxonomy nodes evaluated, most topics were temporally stable, though significant non-uniformity appeared in some key subfields. At a significance score of three, corresponding to p equals 0.001, arXiv had the most non-uniform nodes because of its longer observation span. The authors also developed an interactive tool called the AI Taxonomy Trend Explorer for qualitative exploration, though the available text of the article is cut off before describing it further.

Articles.Title: Hierarchical Taxonomy Framework Tracks Shifting Artificial Intelligence Trends Across Multiple Information Sources

stories.Headline: China’s Jensen Huang ‘honeypot’ trap is only more reason to win the AI race
stories.Summary:
China's Jensen Huang "honeypot" operation came to light in November 2026, with the Nvidia chief executive having admitted to an affair with Alice Huang, whose surveillance reportedly showed her passing information to Chinese actors. The column reports that Beijing's apparent honeypot was aimed at Huang, the head of a company valued at $4.5 trillion and central to AI development. The writer argues the episode shows how far China will go to win the AI race, while warning that American critics may use it to damage the US industry. Nvidia's board has said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised, though the article notes it is not yet clear what information was passed along.

The writer argues the federal government should fully investigate the case and respond against China, but warns that Huang could face serious fallout if Democrats use their coming control of Congress to press the matter. Industry sources cited by the New York Post's Charles Gasparino reportedly believe Huang may not survive the backlash. The column casts the Democratic push against AI as part of a broader campaign, pointing to Senator Bernie Sanders's legislation to slow AI development and to party criticism of data centers over power and water use. It also notes that Senator Chris Coons has demanded answers about ties between AI billionaires and the Trump administration. The writer contends that Huang lobbied President Donald Trump to loosen restrictions on AI chip sales to China, which a former Secret Service agent, Paul Eckloff, described as highly influential on US export policy.

The column places the affair within a history of Chinese espionage against American officials, citing the cases of Fang Fang, who trapped then-Representative Eric Swalwell, and Linda Sun, a former top aide to Governor Andrew Cuomo who later worked under Governor Kathy Hochul. The writer argues that Huang's downfall would hurt the industry and could boost Beijing's AI push more than the espionage itself. The piece closes by calling for a probe of Huang and a response to China, while urging that the affair not be used to derail America's pursuit of AI supremacy. It quotes Trump's line that "whoever wins AI, wins."

Articles.Title: China’s Jensen Huang ‘honeypot’ trap is only more reason to win the AI race

stories.Headline: Systematic Review Details Mathematical Foundations Governing Healthcare Artificial Intelligence Systems
stories.Summary:
The article is a systematic review of the mathematics behind healthcare artificial intelligence, authored by researchers Yuliana Jiménez-Gaona and Vasudevan Lakshminarayanan and published on bioengineer.org on November 10, 2026. The study, conducted under PRISMA 2020 guidelines, synthesized evidence from 147 eligible investigations published between January 2016 and June 30, 2026. Starting from 653 identified records across Scopus, Google Scholar, and PubMed or MEDLINE, the researchers screened and narrowed the literature, excluding 54 full-text reports for reasons including lack of healthcare relevance, insufficient mathematical content, and unsuitable formats. Methodological quality was appraised using an adapted Joanna Briggs Institute framework across twelve domains alongside AMSTAR-2, with inter-rater agreement reported as a Cohen's kappa of 0.89.

Coding of the 147 studies found that linear algebra appeared in 100 studies, or 68.0 percent, calculus and continuous optimization in 91 studies, or 61.9 percent, and probability and statistics in 79 publications, or 53.7 percent. In a separate classification by dominant theme, explainable and trustworthy artificial intelligence was the largest category with 24 studies, or 16.3 percent, followed by statistics and statistical learning theory and probability and Bayesian methods, each with 23 studies, or 15.6 percent. Radiology and medical imaging was the leading application area at 24.3 percent, and classification and diagnosis was the most frequent clinical task at 17.1 percent. The authors describe linear algebra as the structural foundation for deep architectures, calculus and optimization as the engines of model training, and probability and statistics as the basis for calibrated uncertainty estimates.

The review cites several empirical examples drawn from the reviewed studies. Leibig and co-workers reported in 2017 that referring the 20 percent most uncertain diabetic retinopathy predictions to clinicians raised accuracy on the retained cohort from about 87 percent to at least 90 percent. Huang and collaborators reported in 2025 that a quantum neural network classified pulmonary ground-glass nodules with 89.23 percent accuracy, compared with 76.56 percent for a classical support vector machine. The authors note that quantum approaches remain predominantly experimental and simulated, lacking extensive external clinical validation. They also caution that high discriminatory scores do not by themselves guarantee clinical reliability, citing work by Zwanenburg and collaborators in which 167 of 169 radiomic features, or 98.82 percent, showed good-to-excellent reproducibility only after rigorous mathematical definition.

Articles.Title: Systematic Review Details Mathematical Foundations Governing Healthcare Artificial Intelligence Systems

stories.Headline: Review Evaluates Artificial Intelligence Tools Across Pharmaceutical Discovery and Development
stories.Summary:
Pharmaceutical research and development faces high costs and long timelines, with creating a single new therapeutic typically costing more than 2.5 billion dollars and requiring over a decade of work. Only a small share of candidate molecules win regulatory approval, and just 2.01 percent of drug development projects ultimately yield a marketable product. A review published in Discover Pharmaceutical Sciences by Shashi Kant, Deepika, and Saheli Roy examines how computational methods are changing this process. The authors describe how artificial intelligence systems, including machine learning, deep learning, and generative models, are applied to target validation, compound screening, structural optimization, and clinical investigation.

Traditional discovery is slowed by sequential bottlenecks, beginning with the laborious identification and biological validation of target molecules. High-throughput experimental screening and repeated optimization cycles aimed at improving potency, selectivity, and safety add further expense before candidates reach clinical evaluation. In human trials, recruitment difficulties, trial design constraints, and data collection logistics also undermine success. The authors outline how AI platforms address these problems by learning from complex biological and chemical datasets. Public repositories such as DrugBank, PubChem, and UniProt supply much of the training material used in these models.

According to the review, computational platforms can replace or supplement physical screening through automated virtual evaluation. Quantitative structure–activity relationship models predict biological activity directly from chemical structures, allowing teams to prioritize large libraries while reducing experimental expenditure. The authors note that such models often draw on 1,000 to 5,000 curated data points to predict water solubility. Predictive tools also estimate absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity, so investigators can eliminate hazardous molecules before costly animal studies or clinical trials. In trials, algorithms help optimize protocols, refine statistical power calculations, and monitor patient data for early safety signals.

The review credits a range of architectures for these gains, from support vector machines and random forests to convolutional and recurrent neural networks, transformer-based protein language models, and graph neural networks that represent atoms as nodes and bonds as edges. Meta AI's ESM-2, which uses 15 billion parameters, is cited as a tool for predicting three-dimensional protein structures from primary sequences. Platforms such as DiffDock, from the review's examples, apply diffusion models to protein-ligand docking. The review also cites baricitinib, an oral Janus kinase inhibitor approved for rheumatoid arthritis, as an effective therapy for COVID-19 identified through computational repurposing. In active pipelines, Exscientia advanced six AI-designed molecules into human trials by 2024.

The authors stress that substantial technical and operational limitations still impede the integration of artificial intelligence into pharmaceutical workflows. High-quality, standardized, and accurately annotated training data remains a critical bottleneck, because heterogeneous datasets drawn from incompatible assays, divergent chemical formats, and inconsistent clinical trials complicate model training. Deep graph models also face technical limits related to over-smoothing and computational scaling on massive graphs. The articles provided do not describe specific next steps, timelines, or regulatory changes arising from the review. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Review Evaluates Artificial Intelligence Tools Across Pharmaceutical Discovery and Development

stories.Headline: Tri-National Study Explores How Student Teachers Integrate Artificial Intelligence in Classrooms
stories.Summary:
A tri-national study published in Frontiers in Computer Science found that student teachers who took joint online coursework across Germany, Israel, and Hungary moved from seeing artificial intelligence as a simple tool toward understanding its teaching and ethical complexities. The investigation followed participants across two successive academic cohorts, one in 2024 and one in 2025. Students evaluated AI software, designed educational tasks, and worked through cross-cultural communication challenges. The researchers reported that hands-on experimentation with AI tools, combined with sustained intercultural group work, led future educators to prioritize human oversight, verification, and deliberate instructional support over automated shortcuts. The study was built around the Cooperation Online in Teaching Between Germany, Israel, and Hungary initiative, known as the CoGIH Project.

Five higher education institutions took part, including the Department of English and American Studies at the University of Kassel in Germany and the University of Miskolc in Hungary. The nine-week program examined how collaborative cross-cultural learning supported by AI affects intercultural awareness, technological attitudes, and professional identity. The authors said earlier research had typically studied AI integration, online collaborative learning, and multilingual intercultural competence in isolation rather than together. To guide the design, the researchers combined three pedagogical models into a framework they called the CoGIH Three Model Integration. The empirical sample included 113 students enrolled across the 2024 and 2025 cohorts, and 91 of them responded to the course questionnaires.

Among the 82 participants who answered the gender question, 57 identified as female and 25 as male. Respondents reported speaking German, Hebrew, Hungarian, English, Arabic, and several other languages, and their average self-rated English proficiency on a 5-point scale was 3.74. Groups analyzed a specific AI application against ten criteria, including cost of access, protection of minors, multilingual capability, and cultural bias. They also developed a multilingual instructional task and recorded a video presentation for an international student conference held during the final synchronous session.

Because anonymity protections prevented tracking individual participants across surveys for all but 17 respondents, the authors limited their quantitative analysis to aggregate descriptive statistics and cross-sectional correlations. Analysis of the open-ended reflections showed that statements about concrete collaborative challenges rose from 28 before the course to 75 after it, while stereotypical cultural generalizations fell from 44 to 24. Statements describing AI as a pedagogical resource rose, and mentions of ethical and educational challenges increased from 13 to 31. Participants raised concerns about student overreliance, factual accuracy, algorithmic bias, and the need for explicit teacher guidance.

The researchers also observed that AI supported creative task design and language experimentation, but group projects showed weak visual coherence, shallow critical reflection, and translation errors in multilingual outputs. Students recommended more structured instruction from the start, groups with at least two peers from each country, more efficient synchronous meetings, and baseline language requirements. The authors concluded that AI offers valuable support for interactive learning but cannot replace authentic teacher mediation and rigorous critical evaluation. The article reports no further plans for the program beyond these recommendations.

Articles.Title: Tri-National Study Explores How Student Teachers Integrate Artificial Intelligence in Classrooms

stories.Headline: Beyond the AI hype: Why C-suite control is the ultimate differentiator
stories.Summary:
The article is a sponsored BrandPost from HPE and AMD, published November 10, 2026 on CIO.com, arguing that enterprise AI is moving out of pilot programs into core production and that executives must control their data, infrastructure and AI life cycle. It says the workloads, including simulation, analytics, model training, fine-tuning and real-time inference, are intensive and that traditional enterprise infrastructure was not built for them. It names fragmentation across on-premises data centers, colocation facilities and multiple hybrid clouds as the first obstacle, leading to lost efficiency, unpredictable latency and rising costs. The piece recommends integrated high-performance computing environments, citing platforms powered by AMD EPYC CPUs and AMD Instinct GPUs as one option for linking storage and compute. On governance, the article warns that data privacy, shifting international regulations and inconsistent internal rules create multimillion-dollar liabilities as AI footprints grow.

It argues that keeping control over where critical data lives lets organizations enforce policy and reduce risk across the data life cycle. HPE and AMD are presented as providers of secure, compliant, multi-tenant architectures that keep proprietary data inside trusted environments. For operations, the article says moving a model from test to full production requires top-down visibility, which HPE addresses with automation, intelligent orchestration and full-stack observability in a single control plane. The article credits HPE and AMD as the authors and sponsors, and it presents HPE as the company that delivers six of the top ten most powerful supercomputers globally and holds the number one spot on the HPL-MxP list. It describes HPE's exascale expertise and data center design capabilities as combining with AMD's processing power to produce repeatable designs for enterprise AI.

The article itself does not quote any independent analyst, customer or regulator. It also states that HPE and AMD are partnering to deliver next-generation AI and supercomputing infrastructure, with the aim of faster insights, greater efficiency and flexible scaling. The background the article gives is limited to the shift from experimentation to production and the infrastructure strain that follows. It offers three recommendations to executives: consolidate fragmented data and hybrid infrastructure before large deployments, demand a unified control plane with full-stack observability, and keep sensitive data in controlled environments. The article does not describe any next steps beyond these recommendations, and it points readers to a related piece titled "Enterprise AI and HPC: The next era of business."

Articles.Title: Beyond the AI hype: Why C-suite control is the ultimate differentiator

stories.Headline: Why Human Working Memory Might Be AI’s Biggest Constraint
stories.Summary:
The Aviation Week article "Why Human Working Memory Might Be AI's Biggest Constraint," written by Garrett Reim and dated November 11, 2026, argues that a limit on people rather than on machines may be holding back artificial intelligence. The piece opens by listing the usual suspects that observers name as the main obstacle to AI, including chip shortages, limits on electrical grid capacity and a shrinking supply of high-quality training data. It then suggests that the real rate-limiting factor could be the capacity of human working memory. The article's summary states that experts say the next generation of AI tools must be designed around the cognitive limits of the people who use them. The article's central claim is that AI systems will only deliver their promise if they fit within what a person can hold in mind at one time.

Under this view, tools that produce more output than a user can absorb, check or act on do not add value and may even slow work down. The reasoning implies a shift in design priorities, moving the focus from raw machine capability toward interfaces, workflows and information loads that match human attention. The excerpt available here does not spell out specific design guidelines, figures or case examples beyond this general framing. Reim, who covers space and advanced technologies for Aviation Week, is the author credited with the piece.

The excerpt presents the position as the view of experts, and it does not name individual researchers or companies who hold it. The article sits within the publication's wider coverage of emerging technology in aerospace and defense, where AI tools are increasingly being introduced into engineering, operations and decision-making work. The available text is a paywalled preview, so the full argument, the evidence behind it and any recommendations beyond the summary cannot be confirmed from what is shown here. Readers who want the complete analysis would need to subscribe to Aviation Week & Space Technology or AWIN to read the rest of the article.

Articles.Title: Why Human Working Memory Might Be AI’s Biggest Constraint

stories.Headline: Monetizing compliance: New AI revenue streams for regional CSPs
stories.Summary:
Hewlett Packard Enterprise and AMD published a sponsored piece on CIO.com on November 10, 2026, arguing that regional cloud service providers can earn new revenue by offering sovereign AI services. The article defines these as environments where data, models, and execution stay within a national, regional, or specific legal jurisdiction. It says standard public AI models can violate compliance mandates when sensitive data crosses borders or when proprietary data sits in multitenant public environments. The authors describe this tension as a market opportunity for local and regional providers.

They say the aim is to capture a segment of enterprise cloud spend from organizations that previously could not use AI because of legal restrictions. The article lists three services a provider could package and resell: enterprise inferencing with localized large language models, model customization by fine-tuning open-source models on proprietary customer data, and industry-specific AI applications for regional healthcare codes or local banking laws. It names two architectural hurdles, computational efficiency and operational multitenancy. For efficiency, it points to HPE AI/HPC systems powered by 5th Gen AMD EPYC processors and AMD Instinct GPUs.

The article says 5th Gen AMD EPYC processors deliver up to 1.73x more throughput on end-to-end AI benchmarks and 1.93x more throughput on machine learning workloads compared with competing x86 options. It also says that higher throughput lowers energy costs and raises profit margins per tenant. The article cites two European deployments as proof of the architecture. The LUMI supercomputer in Finland, built by HPE and powered by AMD, is described as an isolated, secure, energy-efficient environment for training models without exporting data.

The Adastra supercomputer at CINES in France uses an HPE and AMD architecture within a strictly governed, state-backed setting. For operations, the article names HPE Morpheus Software for tenant isolation and orchestration, HPE OpsRamp Software for full-stack observability, and built-in resource tracking for usage-based billing. It adds that air-gapped management tools are available for highly restrictive environments. The piece is labeled as sponsored content by HPE and AMD and carries a note that the two companies partner on AI and supercomputing infrastructure.

Articles.Title: Monetizing compliance: New AI revenue streams for regional CSPs

stories.Headline: Automated Anesthesia Systems Require Human Clinical Intuition Alongside Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
The articles describe a correspondence published in Anesthesiology and Perioperative Science, written by Fredericus H. J. van Loon, Menno A. de Wilde, and Angelique T. M. Dierick-van Daele, that responds to a comprehensive review by Xiuding Cai and colleagues on the future of automated anesthesia. The authors agree that intelligent closed-loop platforms, powered by artificial intelligence and physiological modeling, hold considerable promise for personalizing perioperative care. They argue, however, that widespread clinical deployment cannot succeed until critical technical, regulatory, and ethical challenges are resolved. Their central point is that automated systems cannot replace human clinical judgment in anesthesia care.

Modern anesthesiological care depends heavily on collecting data from two sources: real-time monitoring of physiological signals during surgery, and preoperative diagnostic findings and imaging. The authors note that algorithmic processing of these data streams offers meaningful decision support, especially in identifying early warning signs of patient deterioration or acute adverse events. Both the authors and Cai and colleagues agree that this analytical value is substantial. The correspondence nonetheless cautions that such tools work within a broader clinical discipline. Anesthesia practice, as the authors describe it, extends well beyond inducing and sustaining hypnosis, analgesia, and muscle relaxation.

Automated platforms can reduce the cognitive workload of clinical teams by handling repetitive tasks, administrative requirements, and drug titration. The authors say that overviews of automated systems often overlook the contributions healthcare professionals make during clinical delivery. Physician anesthesiologists and nurse anesthetists, they write, provide a concerned presence that responds to patients' physical and psychological needs. Algorithms cannot replace situational awareness, ethical responsibility, accountability, or clinical intuition. The authors highlight intuition, often experienced as a sense of worry, as a competency that lets practitioners make rapid assessments from experience and direct observation.

Citing work by Robben and colleagues, the authors describe intuition as a catalyst for critical thinking, complex problem-solving, and patient advocacy. They also argue that recognizing deterioration during surgery cannot rely only on objective measures such as vital signs. Experienced clinicians often detect environmental changes, including the immediate physiological effects of surgical interventions, much earlier than contemporary algorithms do. The letter further identifies technical limits in data-driven anesthesia models, including incomplete training datasets, measurement noise, biological complexity, and variability between patients. Because uncertainty cannot be fully eliminated, the authors call for transparency, explainability, rigorous validation, and continuous evaluation to prevent the risks of opaque black-box systems.

The authors expect the anesthesia practitioner's role to evolve into a hybrid function that links technology with bedside care. Clinicians will increasingly combine clinical acumen with systems thinking and work closely with engineers, data scientists, ethicists, and policymakers to oversee and validate automated workflows. The authors conclude that the digital transformation of anesthesia requires a lasting balance between artificial intelligence precision and human expertise. Their position is that closed-loop systems offer valuable real-time adjustments, but safe perioperative outcomes ultimately depend on experienced caregivers acting as technology integrators.

Articles.Title: Automated Anesthesia Systems Require Human Clinical Intuition Alongside Artificial Intelligence

stories.Headline: AI-powered hacking demands response within minutes, cybersecurity experts warn
stories.Summary:
Trellix Chief Technology Officer Mo Cashman warned at the Cyber Security conference at Tel Aviv University on Tuesday that defenders must identify AI-driven cyberattacks within 15 minutes to have any chance of limiting catastrophic damage to a business or government agency. He described an accelerated four-stage response timeline. Identification should occur within 15 minutes, orientation within two hours, decision within four hours, and action within four to 72 hours, depending on the threat. Cashman's team has sometimes begun partial remediation within 20 minutes by deploying security assets to clients in advance of an attack. The warning followed concern in late October over a PHP programming vulnerability that reportedly left as much as 70% of the internet hackable until it was patched.

AISLE Chief Information Security Officer Jaya Baloo told the conference that attackers have always held an advantage in the ratio of spending on offense versus defense, and that AI has made that imbalance much worse. She said an attacker can now pay as little as $25 to mount a semi-sophisticated attack, while defenders must spend heavily to guard against it. Baloo blamed much of the imbalance on American and Chinese companies releasing new AI models without fully weighing their potential for danger. She argued that governments must quickly regulate and criminalize misuse of certain models.

She also singled out UNITREE products as hackable and questionable in trustworthiness, and noted that The Jerusalem Post had asked UNITREE to respond. CrowdStrike Chief Business Officer Daniel Bernard took a different position, arguing that the United States, Israel, and the West should keep advancing AI without pausing or slowing down. He contrasted this with calls from leading figures at Anthropic, OpenAI, and others for a sector-wide slowdown to better understand new generative AI systems. Bernard said his company has built an AI "kill switch" that can act on AI gateways, cloud and agent permissions, and other issues to restore safety for newer models.

He warned that the West would fall behind China and others if it slowed down, and that running AI in an isolated sandbox risks leaving organizations behind. Microsoft Israel Director of R&D Michal Braverman-Blumenstyk said the key is to keep studying what happens inside AI systems, and that such internal processes should be open rather than locked in a black box. At the same conference, Maj. Gen.

Aviad Dagan, head of the IDF J6 and Cyber Defense Directorate, said the military has used AI to assemble large volumes of data from three years of war. He said this data could help generate strategies for future conflicts in tunnel, mountain, or other terrain. Dagan added that the IDF is moving toward using AI agents to help initiate and propose military plans. The articles do not describe any formal rule or mandate that requires the 15-minute response window, and they do not report any government action taken in response to the warnings.

Articles.Title: AI-powered hacking demands response within minutes, cybersecurity experts warn

stories.Headline: OSF joins statewide AI cyberattack exercise to strengthen hospital emergency response - WEEK
stories.Summary:
Hospitals across Illinois took part in a statewide emergency preparedness exercise on November 4, 2026, in which they faced a simulated cyberattack driven by artificial intelligence. The exercise, called "Broken Trust: AI Takes Control," was led by the Illinois Health and Hospital Association and involved more than 115 hospitals and health systems. It ran as a virtual event and was designed to disrupt patient care, communications and hospital operations. Unlike a typical cyberattack, the scenario kept computer systems looking functional while the information inside them could no longer be fully trusted. The association said it was the largest AI-focused emergency preparedness exercise ever conducted with hospitals in Illinois.

The simulated attack included AI-generated impersonations of hospital leaders, communication failures and deepfake videos. Hospital teams had to decide how to keep operating while checking whether the information reaching them was accurate. Keneatha Johnson, assistant vice president of safety and emergency preparedness for the association, said AI adds a layer of complexity beyond traditional attacks, which usually involve shutting systems down, stealing data or blocking access to technology. The exercise was built to show hospitals where their weaknesses lie before a real incident occurs. Johnson noted that no organization can fully eliminate the risk of a cyberattack, but drills like this help hospitals sharpen their response.

OSF HealthCare was one of the participating health systems. Sherry Myers, director of ministry operations support at OSF, said the organization regularly runs emergency preparedness exercises to improve coordination among emergency management, information technology and clinical teams. She said the top priority is always safe patient care, and that OSF keeps downtime and continuity procedures so essential services can continue when technology is unavailable. Her team works closely with IT staff to maintain those procedures. Myers's comments reflected the organization's ongoing approach to readiness rather than any specific finding from the exercise.

The exercise reflects growing concern among hospitals about how artificial intelligence could be used to attack their systems and mislead their staff. The articles do not describe any real attack on Illinois hospitals connected to the drill, nor do they report specific changes to state requirements or new mandates for hospitals. They also do not say what lessons were drawn from the exercise or whether a follow-up report will be published. Based on the available reporting, the exercise itself is the main development, and further outcomes have not been announced.

Articles.Title: OSF joins statewide AI cyberattack exercise to strengthen hospital emergency response - WEEK

stories.Headline: AI100 Report: AI has entered the mainstream and is reshaping society - Max-Planck-Gesellschaft
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence has moved from a specialised technology into an everyday reality for millions of people, according to the latest report from the One Hundred Year Study on Artificial Intelligence (AI100), released on November 10, 2026. The report, titled AI Goes Mainstream: The Scaling Era and the Rise of Generative AI, was produced by AI100, a longitudinal project administered by Stanford University's Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (HAI). The study is published every five years and examines AI's development and its effects on people, communities, and society. Its authors credit the past five years with a watershed moment, driven by large-scale computing, vast datasets, and the rapid rise of generative AI. The third report evaluates how AI has evolved since the 2021 edition.

Iyad Rahwan, Director of the Center for Human and Machines at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development, was a member of the 2026 AI100 Study Panel. The international panel brought together experts in computer science, philosophy, sociology, and related disciplines. The report examines the scaling of data and computing resources behind generative AI, advances in scientific discovery, and investment in AI infrastructure. It also covers the concentration of frontier AI development, cybersecurity and military applications, the trustworthiness of digital media, emerging risks, public participation, and international governance. The panel organised its findings around 12 key takeaways.

The report says the scaling paradigm, which builds AI systems using ever more compute and data, is running into data and compute constraints, shifting the frontier toward reasoning and inference-time compute. It states that AI is already transforming the creative industries, mathematics, and software development. It also states that AI is transforming science at remarkable speed, a fact the report links to the 2024 Nobel Prizes in Physics and Chemistry. Capital investment in AI infrastructure is unprecedented in scale and speed, according to the report, which notes fears of a financial bubble and strain on energy and freshwater supplies. Frontier AI development is concentrated among a small number of U.S. and Chinese actors, the report notes, raising international concerns about access to leading-edge technologies.

Iyad Rahwan said in the report's accompanying statement that the 2021 AI100 report had been very optimistic about rapid AI progress, but that the panel did not foresee the "ChatGPT moment" that brought AI into mainstream discussion. He said billions of people now interact with AI on a regular basis, and that this has changed how society, business, and industry view the technology. The report states that the public has had little say in how AI is developed and deployed, even though AI is reshaping the lives of billions of people. It also describes AI governance as fragmented and increasingly framed in terms of national security, with little international consensus among states. The panel's researchers, according to the release, consider the coming years decisive in shaping the opportunities and risks of the technology.

The AI100 project was launched in 2014 and is led by an international Standing Committee of AI experts, with Stanford's HAI administering it. Every five years it convenes a Study Panel to assess AI's progress and its influence across technical, ethical, economic, and societal domains. The earlier editions were published in 2016 and 2021. The release states that if the current pace of development is sustained, the next five years should be expected to surprise people as much as the past five have. The release does not give further detail on the timing of the next report.

Articles.Title: AI100 Report: AI has entered the mainstream and is reshaping society - Max-Planck-Gesellschaft

stories.Headline: Survey Identifies Human Oversight as Crucial for Fair Healthcare Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
A cross-sectional survey of patients in the United Kingdom, reported on November 10, 2026, found that the absence of human supervision is seen as the greatest threat to fairness in healthcare artificial intelligence. The study, published in BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making, was led by researchers including E. Remfry and B. G. Tzovaras. Of the participating patients, 89.9 percent said that AI decisions which neither patients nor clinicians could question or challenge would hurt fairness. The researchers drew on 149 patients recruited through public and patient involvement networks.

The study used two vignettes, one a patient-facing symptom checker and the other a clinician-facing decision-support tool for cancer treatment, so that attitudes could be compared across both settings. Participants rated 13 factors for their effect on fairness and also gave free-text answers. Analysis used descriptive statistics, Pearson's chi-square tests, ordinal logistic regression and thematic analysis of the written responses. Beyond unchallengeable systems, 89.3 percent of respondents said AI built without clinician input would undermine fairness, and 86.6 percent said incorrect electronic health record data posed a severe threat. Patient views on these factors stayed consistent across both vignettes.

The article attributes these findings to the study's authors, who concluded that patients hold nuanced views on fairness across the whole AI lifecycle, from development through deployment and maintenance. Respondents also raised concerns about digital accessibility, the handling of long-term conditions, the upkeep needed to keep algorithms accurate, and the possible loss of human empathy in care. The researchers recommended designing health technologies collaboratively with end users, building human-in-the-loop systems, and making them flexible enough to adapt to ongoing clinical input. The article presents these recommendations as design considerations for future tools and does not describe any regulatory or policy changes.

Articles.Title: Survey Identifies Human Oversight as Crucial for Fair Healthcare Artificial Intelligence

stories.Headline: Benton Harbor considers AI property code enforcement
stories.Summary:
Benton Harbor officials are weighing whether to use artificial intelligence to identify property code violations, according to a report published by WNDU on November 10, 2026. The city is looking at a program called City Detect, which WNDU attributes to its reporting partners at The Herald Palladium. The article offers no further detail on how the tool would work or when a decision might be made. The rest of the article's content on this topic is limited to that single point. It does not say what the program would cost, how it would be funded, or whether the city has committed to it.

It also does not describe what kinds of violations it would flag or how property owners would be notified. Those details are not in the material provided. The article does not name any official who is responsible for the proposal or quote anyone speaking about it. Benton Harbor city officials are the ones considering the idea, but the report does not attribute specific comments to any of them. Without statements on the record, the source of the plan and its supporters are unclear from the available reporting.

The remaining items in the same feed cover unrelated local news, including sonar technology used by Elkhart firefighters, child care funding in South Bend, and a St. Joseph County jail food contract change. Nothing in those stories connects to the Benton Harbor proposal. The article does not say when officials will next discuss the program or whether any vote is scheduled. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Benton Harbor considers AI property code enforcement

stories.Headline: Teleport releases beams to secure artificial intelligence agents in production
stories.Summary:
Teleport, a company that provides infrastructure identity software, has launched Teleport Beams, a runtime environment for running artificial intelligence agents inside production systems. The launch was reported on November 10, 2026, by SC Media, which cited Silicon Angle as its source. The product is aimed at gaps that have held enterprises back from adopting AI agents, particularly around delegated identity and complete audit trails. Under the design, each agent runs in its own ephemeral micro-VM, so it holds only limited, task-specific privileges instead of standing access.

Before an agent acts, it must submit a proposed execution plan, which humans or other language models can review. Sessions are scored against prebuilt detection rules from the MITRE ATT&CK framework, and a built-in kill switch can cut an agent's connections to production systems if it strays from its goal. Teleport says sensitive credentials never enter the agent environment and that every action is logged. The articles attribute the release to Teleport and describe it as building on the earlier Teleport Agentic Identity Framework and the company's existing infrastructure identity platform.

According to the report, that platform already serves more than 700 enterprises, including Nasdaq Inc., DoorDash Inc. and Elastic N.V. The product is now generally available to teams that want to deploy autonomous agents, and the company presents it as a way to do so without weakening infrastructure integrity. The same day's coverage placed Teleport's launch within a wider wave of products for AI agent security. Flashpoint introduced agentic AI for automating threat investigations, Cowbell Cyber Inc. launched an insurance policy for small and midsized businesses against losses from deploying AI agents, and Israeli startup Bay AI Inc. launched with $50 million in funding to secure autonomous agents in enterprise environments. The articles do not say how these products will perform in practice or what adoption they will see.

Articles.Title: Teleport releases beams to secure artificial intelligence agents in production

stories.Headline: New Framework Outlines Six Key Dimensions for Human-Friendly Conversational Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Researchers at Hongik University in Seoul have set out a preliminary framework describing how conversational artificial intelligence can interact with people in a human-friendly way. The study, published in Frontiers in Computer Science, was led by Siu Jung and Yoori Koo, who named it the Human-Friendly AI Interaction Design Framework, or HFAI-DF. The authors describe the framework as a way to turn principles of human cognition and anthropomorphism into concrete behavior for computer agents. The work responds to the shift toward sustained, back-and-forth dialogue with AI systems, which has drawn attention beyond technical measures such as safety, transparency, and data privacy. The authors say human-friendly interaction is not simply polite wording, decorative warmth, or physical mimicry.

The framework rests on psychological research into anthropomorphism, the human tendency to attribute consciousness, intentions, and emotions to non-human entities. Building on models from Epley, Waytz, and colleagues, the team identified cognitive and motivational drivers of that tendency. The cognitive side was divided into four areas: simulated emotional experience, episodic memory, reflexive metacognition, and self-awareness combined with theory of mind. The motivational side included sociality motivation, the drive for affiliation that grows when people feel isolated, and effectance motivation, the desire to understand and control one's environment. Jung and Koo broke these factors into components and synthesized them into thirty behavioral units.

Each unit describes an observable capability, such as tracking uncertainty or restructuring a task proactively, without requiring the machine to have literal inner emotions. To test how users perceived the thirty behaviors, the authors surveyed 208 adults from Generation MZ, defined as people born from 1981 through 2012. The group included 109 participants aged 20 to 29, 83 aged 30 to 39, and 16 aged 40 to 44. Participants rated each behavior on a seven-point scale using three adjective pairs: machine-like versus human-like, unnatural versus natural, and artificial versus lifelike. Each item was shown with a realistic interaction scenario written by the researchers.

The authors analyzed the responses with exploratory factor analysis in SPSS Version 31.0, and sampling adequacy was strong, with a Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure of 0.93. The analysis produced six dimensions that the authors arranged from the agent's internal self-regulation outward to collaborative contribution. The first dimension, Self-Aware Interaction, has five items and an internal consistency of 0.823, and its strongest element is identity and role awareness at 0.738. It also includes learning history representation, explanation of reasoning grounds, self-monitoring, and recognition of uncertainty. The second dimension, User-Adaptive Responsiveness Interaction, has three items with an alpha of 0.825, led by detection of verbal and non-verbal cues at 0.658.

The third, Context-Aware Reasoning Interaction, has five items with an alpha of 0.870, and its leading element is user error recognition and guidance at 0.733. The fourth, Socio-Emotional Interaction, has six items with an alpha of 0.872 and was identified by the authors as the central relational hub, with moderate correlations of 0.403 to 0.476 with all five other dimensions. The fifth, Creative Collaboration Interaction, has seven items with an alpha of 0.907, and the sixth, Proactive Assistance Interaction, has four items with an alpha of 0.865. Jung and Koo present the framework as a research model and urge caution about applying it.

They state that AI does not have genuine feelings, subjective experience, or consciousness, and they warn that poorly calibrated friendliness could produce deceptive attachment, emotional dependency, or discomfort when a system's imitation of human behavior breaks down. The authors also note that socio-emotional features that help in counseling settings may distract from or undermine analytical decision-support tools and high-stakes work. They acknowledge empirical limitations as well, including that the exploratory factor analysis relied on third-person evaluations of written scenarios. The articles provided do not describe any planned follow-up studies or deployment timelines.

Articles.Title: New Framework Outlines Six Key Dimensions for Human-Friendly Conversational Artificial Intelligence

stories.Headline: Air Force previews AI training as it prepares to deploy new tools
stories.Summary:
The Department of the Air Force is expanding its use of artificial intelligence and preparing the training its personnel will need to work with fast-changing tools. According to Federal News Network, the Air Force and Space Force first spent their time building the strategy and policy that would govern AI use. Susan Davenport, the department's chief data and AI officer, said that foundation is now ready to be tested. She spoke on November 6, 2026, at an AI event in Washington, and the report was published on November 10.

The services plan to launch AI tools tailored to 15 missions, ranging from intelligence to nuclear operations, with a civilian or officer overseeing progress in each area. At the same time, the department is rolling out courses that teach airmen and guardians how to develop and apply AI, along with its limitations. Davenport said the department intends to introduce a three-level training approach by the end of November. The 100-level course covers general AI principles for everyday work, the 200-level course covers building AI-powered workflows with lessons on topics such as legal guardrails, and the 300-level course targets developers. Completion will be logged in service members' permanent training records, which can count toward promotion and job selection.

Davenport described the approach as part of a broader push to shorten the time needed to attack targets, save commanders time, and speed decisions compared with America's adversaries. The department will track progress through quarterly showcases where officials overseeing each AI mission area, called domain principals, report their achievements and seek help on persistent problems. Two showcases have been held so far, and a third is planned for December or January. That meeting is meant to bring Air Force and Space Force units together with research organizations and private companies that could supply solutions. Davenport said the first showcase made clear that research and development partners were missing from the room where the department's campaign goals were discussed.

Davenport also said the department wants to move away from a single central team that cleans and tags the large volumes of data processed each day. Instead, organizations would gain more control over their own data, which would clarify which information is reliable and make it easier to share. She described AI as a gift that lets the department reimagine its mission and do things it has never done before. The article does not say when the decentralized data approach will take effect or what the total cost of the training and tools will be.

Articles.Title: Air Force previews AI training as it prepares to deploy new tools

stories.Headline: Should You Buy SoundHound AI Stock After Its 83% Plunge? The Answer Might Surprise You.
stories.Summary:
SoundHound AI stock closed at $4.11 on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026, down 83% from its all-time closing high of $24.23 set in late 2024. The Motley Fool's Anthony Di Pizio, writing on Nov. 11, 2026, asked whether investors should buy the stock after the decline. The article describes SoundHound as a developer of conversational artificial intelligence software whose customers include large brands in hospitality, healthcare, and automotive manufacturing. The shares were trading at $3.87 as of Nov. 10, 2026, with a 52-week range of $3.71 to $13.87.

In May 2026, SoundHound launched the Orchestrated Agent System, called OASYS, a platform on which enterprises can build custom AI voice agents. OASYS combines SoundHound's own products with those of six companies it has acquired, including Amelia AI and LivePerson. Enterprises can plug in third-party models such as those developed by OpenAI and Anthropic, and agents built on the platform learn from customer and employee interactions. The article cites Resorts World Las Vegas, which used OASYS to create an agent that handles incoming bookings, and a Latin American company whose agent, named Alex, can handle 1,000 phone calls simultaneously while raising the number of inquiries handled by 30%.

SoundHound reported record revenue of $62.4 million for the third quarter of 2026, ended Sept. 30, up 48.5% from a year earlier. The article attributes much of that acceleration to the first inclusion of LivePerson's revenue, since that acquisition closed in September. The company now expects 2026 revenue of $250 million to $260 million, up from its earlier forecast of $230 million to $260 million, and $350 million to $400 million in 2027. Its GAAP net loss narrowed to $46.4 million in the third quarter from $115.9 million in the same quarter of 2025.

SoundHound thinks it can eliminate around $120 million in annualized costs during 2027, which could produce profitability on an adjusted EBITDA basis. The article notes that the stock's price-to-sales ratio, which exceeded 100 when the shares peaked in 2024, has fallen to about 8, approaching its cheapest level of 6.4 in 2023. Di Pizio writes that he has been somewhat bearish on the stock in the past but that his outlook has changed. Chief executive Keyvan Mohajer believes there is a $1 trillion addressable market for agentic AI solutions for enterprises. The article's conclusion is that investors willing to hold the stock for five years or more could do especially well.

Articles.Title: Should You Buy SoundHound AI Stock After Its 83% Plunge? The Answer Might Surprise You.

stories.Headline: 5 Best Artificial Intelligence (AI) ETFs to Buy in 2026
stories.Summary:
The Motley Fool has published a guide to five artificial intelligence exchange-traded funds that investors may consider buying in 2026, with the article last updated on November 10, 2026. The funds bundle stocks so that investors do not have to rely on a single company for exposure to AI growth. Artificial intelligence is already changing how companies operate, from recommendation engines and logistics software to chatbots and automation tools. Interest has grown since generative AI tools such as ChatGPT reached the mainstream. AI ETFs have existed for longer than the boom that began with ChatGPT's launch in late 2022, and many of them invest in robotics and semiconductors.

The article's first pick is the Global X Artificial Intelligence and Technology ETF, which the article calls the largest AI ETF, with assets of $9.73 billion and an expense ratio of 0.68%. It launched in 2018 and holds 88 stocks, and its top 10 holdings made up about 33% of the fund in November 2026. Its largest positions include Microsoft, Palantir, Space Exploration Technologies, Tesla and Amazon. According to Global X, the global AI market is expected to grow from $184 billion in 2024 to $826.7 billion in 2030. The article notes that the fund has outperformed over its history, in part because of strong performance by big tech stocks.

The second pick is the Global X Robotics and Artificial Intelligence ETF, established in 2016, which holds 81 stocks and has assets of $3.04 billion. Its top holdings include Intuitive Surgical, FANUC, Keyence, ABB and Nvidia, and the top five made up more than 40% of the fund. The article says the fund is actively managed, carries an expense ratio of 0.68%, and has underperformed the S&P 500 since its 2016 launch. The third pick is the Robo Global Robotics and Automation Index ETF, which holds 79 stocks, has an expense ratio of 0.95% and assets of $1.89 billion. The article says it has also trailed the S&P 500 since its 2013 inception.

The fourth pick is the iShares Future AI and Tech ETF, formed in 2018, which has an expense ratio of 0.47%, the lowest of the five, and about $3.65 billion in assets. It holds 50 stocks, and its top holdings as of October 2026 included Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, Broadcom, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing and Oracle. The article says the fund has recently outperformed the S&P 500 because of a surge in semiconductor stocks, after underperforming for most of its history. The fifth pick is the First Trust Nasdaq Artificial Intelligence and Robotics ETF, which holds 111 stocks, carries an expense ratio of 0.65% and has assets of $723.4 million. Its holdings include Intuitive Surgical, Ocado Group, Tempus AI, Appian and Meta Platforms.

The article's author is Jeremy Bowman, and the piece was fact-checked by Frank Bass. The article cautions that most AI ETFs have lagged the S&P 500, a broad U.S. stock index, so investors should compare returns and holdings before buying. It also advises comparing annual fees, noting that ARTY charges 0.47% while the robotics-focused ROBO charges 0.95%. The article does not say what the funds will do after 2026.
