stories.Headline: Multimodal Artificial Intelligence Platform Connects Architectural Concepts to Physical Fabrication
stories.Summary:
Architectural researchers have introduced FUGenerator, an open-access multimodal artificial intelligence platform meant to connect design intent to physical fabrication across the building design lifecycle. The system was developed by Xinhui Xu, Tinghao Feng, Yulu Zhang, Zhengcheng He, and Philip F. Yuan, who presented it as a response to gaps in domain knowledge, collaboration, and software interoperability. Existing tools often cause format incompatibilities, irreversible data loss, and version inconsistencies when files move between programs. The authors state that they built the platform around a dual-subgraph architectural knowledge graph, a multimodal algorithm library, and a node-based traceable workflow editor. Natural language serves as the channel linking text, two-dimensional imagery, parametric formats, and physical fabrication data.

The knowledge foundation consists of a semantic subgraph and a visual subgraph. The semantic subgraph includes more than 13,200 building regulation clauses and 283 peer-reviewed academic papers on parametric design, digital construction, and artificial intelligence. Its regulatory coverage centers on structural integrity, building fire prevention, general safety, and sustainable construction. The researchers annotated entities manually with Label Studio, using double cross-validation, and trained recognition models through the spaCy pipeline. The visual subgraph aggregates curated imagery from public repositories, design firm archives, blueprints, diagrams, competition schemes, and construction photographs, with descriptions generated by the BLIP model and then verified by hand.

Hierarchical organization across four levels supports traceability and maintenance. The text module runs a Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline, and its ChatGLM-6B model was fine-tuned with Low-Rank Adaptation on approximately 20,000 regulatory question-and-answer pairs and case-based dialogues. Training took about two hours on an NVIDIA A100 graphics processing unit. Visual synthesis uses Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models with ControlNet, whose layers were fine-tuned on roughly 4,500 building-specialist images. The platform upgrades low-resolution outputs with the Enhanced Super-Resolution Generative Adversarial Network, termed ESRGAN.

For three-dimensional geometry, it uses TripoSR to reconstruct meshes from single images, and it runs a drag-and-drop workflow built on rete.js with Vue.js and RabbitMQ. To test the platform, researchers ran an eight-week university design curriculum with 21 fourth-year undergraduate architecture students focused on furniture design and physical fabrication. Students built chairs using four material groups: timber tectonics with five students, bamboo weaving with six, three-dimensional printing with four, and mixed reality construction with six. Across eight evaluated students, the workflow began with text and image prompts, moved through repeated algorithmic modifications, and ended with exporting two-dimensional imagery into three-dimensional modeling. Timber and bamboo students relied mostly on sketch-to-rendering interactions to keep geometry physically feasible, while the three-dimensional printing and mixed reality groups explored more divergent text-to-image and text-to-video iterations.

Telemetry recorded bursts of more than 180 design iterations in one hour, with initial furniture schemes completed within the first 20 days. Direct image-to-3D generation saw low adoption because of mesh quality limitations. A subsequent eight-week phase asked the cohorts to scale their workflows to architectural prototypes, including a multi-story timber tower and an undulating bamboo footbridge. The timber tectonics team translated structural logic from the historical Yingxian Wooden Pagoda into modern timber architecture and fine-tuned two custom LoRA models for that work. The articles provided as source text end at this point, so the outcomes of the scaled prototypes are not reported here.

Articles.Title: Multimodal Artificial Intelligence Platform Connects Architectural Concepts to Physical Fabrication

stories.Headline: Survey: Patient comfort with AI varies by level of provider involvement - American Hospital Association
stories.Summary:
A Gallup survey published November 9, 2026, examined how comfortable U.S. patients are with artificial intelligence in their care. The survey found that 56% of U.S. adults who visited a primary care provider in the past year are comfortable with AI making diagnosis or treatment decisions, provided those decisions can be changed or overridden by their provider. Another 38% said they are comfortable when AI assists and their provider makes the final decision. Only 9% said they are comfortable with AI making treatment decisions without any provider review. The results show that patient comfort depends heavily on how much a clinician stays involved in the decision.

Most patients who were surveyed want a human provider to keep the final say, even when AI is helping with the analysis. The findings suggest that the level of provider oversight matters more to patients than the mere presence of AI in care. The articles do not describe any new rule or requirement that follows from the survey. The survey was published by Gallup, and the American Hospital Association reported on it in its AHA News coverage. The articles do not identify any individual officials or researchers who commented on the findings beyond the survey results themselves.

The AHA's own recent activity on AI includes a new policy webpage launched November 3 and recommendations to the Food and Drug Administration sent October 19 on regulatory frameworks for generative AI-enabled medical devices. The survey is part of a wider debate among hospitals, regulators and patients about how AI should be used in clinical settings. The AHA has also covered related topics such as AI governance in hospitals and the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality's October 7 launch of an AI initiative on medical evidence reviews. The articles do not say what steps, if any, will follow from the Gallup findings.

Articles.Title: Survey: Patient comfort with AI varies by level of provider involvement - American Hospital Association

stories.Headline: Shield AI appoints Matt Ofilos as Chief Financial Officer
stories.Summary:
Shield AI has named Matt Ofilos as its new Chief Financial Officer, according to an announcement the company made on 10 November. The appointment was reported by Unmanned Airspace on 11 November 2026. Ofilos moves to Shield AI from Parsons Corporation, where he had served as CFO since 2022 after joining that firm in 2021. Before his time at Parsons, Ofilos worked as CFO of the Worldwide Public Sector division of Amazon Web Services. He also spent nearly two decades at Raytheon in finance leadership roles spanning space, cyber, training and simulation, and air and missile defence.

The articles do not describe any change in responsibilities beyond the new title itself. They also do not say when he starts or what his compensation is. Parsons provides technology solutions for national security and infrastructure markets, which places Ofilos's background in defence and government technology. Shield AI's announcement, as the article reports it, names Ofilos as CFO without further commentary from either company.

The article does not include any statement from Ofilos himself or from Shield AI's leadership about the reasons for the hire. The article is a short appointment notice rather than a broader report, so it does not describe Shield AI's financial position or any plans tied to the new role. Its sidebar lists the publication's regular coverage areas, including counter-drone systems, urban air mobility and jobs and appointments, but it offers no further details about this hire. Beyond the announcement itself, the articles provide no information on what comes next for Ofilos or the company.

stories.Headline: The AI Interview: Chris Bergey, EVP of Edge AI at Arm
stories.Summary:
Chris Bergey, Executive Vice President of Edge AI at Arm, was interviewed by AI Magazine and published on November 11, 2026, in an interview written by Adam Pond and Tom Chapman. He said the arrival of more AI inference and the desire to have intelligence closer to where people use it, on the devices they carry and wear, marks another inflection point. Bergey leads Arm's Edge AI business, which spans smartphones, PCs, wearables and intelligent endpoints. The article cites Arm figures of more than 350 billion Arm-based chips shipped to date, more than 22 million software developers building on the Arm compute platform, and 99 percent of the world's smartphones powered by Arm architecture. Bergey stressed that making AI tasks more efficient does not reduce total computing, because efficiency opens new experiences.

Bergey described how AI on smartphones has moved from discrete tasks such as image enhancement and speech recognition toward continuous interaction, multimodal understanding and AI agents. He said an agent may need to interpret speech, retrieve information, maintain context and coordinate multiple applications, so the overall activity grows even as each operation becomes more efficient. Arm sees a similar shift in graphics, where AI reconstructs images and generates frames within mobile power limits. Bergey argued that performance for Arm is no longer about how fast one workload runs but about sustaining complex AI functions across the whole system. He added that agentic AI differs because a single request can involve several stages, applications and models.

Bergey said agentic AI demands sustained performance, efficient memory access and the ability to run multiple workloads concurrently within tight power and thermal limits. He identified the CPU as the orchestration engine coordinating AI models, applications and accelerators. The article says this is a major focus of Arm's new Arm CSS for Mobile 2 platform, which pairs the Arm C2 CPU cluster with SME2 technology, an AI-native Mali GPU with Arm Neural Technology, system IP and software. Asked whether latency, privacy or power drives moving inference to the edge, Bergey said power efficiency is the fundamental enabler, though he called all three critical. He said processing locally can reduce the need to send sensitive personal data elsewhere, and he does not see edge and cloud as an either-or choice.

Bergey said the challenge is shifting from accelerating individual models to coordinating the complete workload efficiently. He also said Arm still sees software as important, pointing to SME2 acceleration in its CPUs, Arm Neural Technology in its latest Mali GPUs, KleidiAI, which helps developers optimise AI workloads, and its AI Portal. He said sustained responsiveness and power efficiency will matter more than peak compute. Bergey said delivering edge intelligence depends on partnerships, citing MediaTek for smartphones, Snap and Meta for wearables, and Microsoft and NVIDIA for PCs, with NVIDIA on the NVIDIA RTX Spark. He concluded that success will be measured by how seamlessly these devices fit into daily life.

Articles.Title: The AI Interview: Chris Bergey, EVP of Edge AI at Arm

stories.Headline: AI needs accountability. Veterans can help provide it
stories.Summary:
This article is an opinion commentary, not a news report, so the story it carries is an argument rather than an event. Shlomo Engelson Argamon, associate provost for artificial intelligence and dean of the Graduate School of Technology at Touro University, published it on November 10, 2026, in Federal News Network. He argues that as artificial intelligence spreads into health care, benefits decisions, finance, cybersecurity and critical infrastructure, the country needs workers who can judge AI's risks and take responsibility for its use, not only workers who know how to operate it. He points to a concrete case, an AI tool that might recommend denying a disability claim, to show why someone must answer for errors. He says Washington has so far focused on AI literacy and guidelines for responsible use, which he calls necessary but insufficient.

He proposes that veterans fill this gap, since military service can build disciplined judgment, accountability and calm decision-making. He cites RAND Corporation findings that leadership, decision-making, dependability and attention to detail are skills veterans bring to civilian work. He notes that veterans still need specialized technical, legal and professional training in AI. He backs this with data that more than half of job postings seeking AI skills are outside IT and computer science, that such postings more than doubled from a year earlier by August 2026, and that employers seek more than 100,000 professionals a year with AI ethics and governance expertise. His core proposal is that Congress create a Veterans AI Workforce Partnership Program within the Labor Department's Veterans' Employment and Training Service, which would administer grants and remain accountable for employment outcomes.

He argues that the program would need a Labor-chaired board including the VA and NIST, with the VA overseeing eligibility and veteran support and NIST setting competencies, risk standards and evaluation protocols. He says existing efforts, including VET TEC 2.0, Registered Apprenticeships, DoD SkillBridge and NSF education programs, each address part of the problem but none integrates AI accountability, so coordination alone would leave no one answerable for the full pathway. He recommends funding stackable credentials, paid experience through SkillBridge and apprenticeships, and regional partnerships, and he proposes $120 million for an initial two-year phase serving at least 10,000 veterans, about $60 million a year. He also proposes tracking completion, placement, wage gains and retention with reviews at six and twelve months, and an independent evaluation after two years. The article does not report any government response to these proposals, and it offers no timeline for Congress to act on them.

Articles.Title: AI needs accountability. Veterans can help provide it - Federal News Network

stories.Headline: AI Heart MRI Measurements Improve Mortality Prediction
stories.Summary:
A study of more than 27,000 heart MRI patients found that artificial intelligence measurements of heart function predicted mortality slightly better than measurements made by clinicians. The retrospective, multicentre research was published online on 2 November 2026 in The Lancet Digital Health, and it was reported by EMJ on 11 November 2026. The study covered 27,382 patients who had cardiac MRI scans in the UK and the USA, with most scans coming from Barts Heart Centre in London and an additional cohort from the University of Pittsburgh Medical Centre. Researchers applied AI segmentation to the scans and compared the prognostic value of automated and clinician-derived left-ventricular ejection fraction. Over a median follow-up of 5.6 years, 3,458 patients died.

After adjusting for age and sex, the AI measurements gave a C index of 0.781, compared with 0.777 for clinician measurements, a difference the articles describe as modest. The AI-derived figures also offered a better statistical model fit. The researchers said automated analysis took roughly two to three seconds per patient, while earlier work by the team found expert clinician analysis typically took around 13 minutes. Ejection fraction guides decisions on heart failure treatment and implanted devices, so more consistent and efficient measurement could matter across imaging services. The articles stress that this time comparison was not a direct measure of time saved across a whole service.

The researchers, Joy G and colleagues, stressed that human oversight remains necessary, since automated errors were uncommon but clinicians still need to verify measurements and interpret them within the wider clinical picture. The articles say the study shows AI measurements were more closely associated with later mortality, but they do not show that adopting the tool changes treatment decisions or helps patients live longer. The authors and commentary call for prospective evaluation to see whether the small statistical gain translates into better care and how automated measurements perform alongside clinician review in routine workflows. For radiology teams, the findings give a reason to evaluate AI as an initial measurement tool, with its clinical value depending on quality assurance and evidence that faster analysis supports effective patient management.

Articles.Title: AI Heart MRI Measurements Improve Mortality Prediction

stories.Headline: 😸 3 AI labs shipped for you
stories.Summary:
The Neuron Daily reported on November 11, 2026 that Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI each shipped major new AI tools within a day of one another. Google launched Gemini 4 Carbon, which it describes as its strongest model, built for long agent jobs such as coding, research, and security work. Anthropic launched Claude Meetings, Sheets, and Whiteboards in beta, along with Claude Data and interactive connectors. OpenAI launched Businesses in ChatGPT in beta, which lets companies claim a profile and add their own chatbot.

Gemini 4 Carbon costs developers $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens until November 30. After that date the price doubles to $4 and $20. Carbon also powers /swarm in Google Antigravity, where one prompt becomes a team of agents. Google reports first-place rankings on several coding and agent benchmarks, but the newsletter notes those tests are its own or partner-run. Claude Meetings joins a Google Meet call as a visible participant, drafts a plan during the conversation, and saves notes and action items afterward.

Google is responsible for Carbon, Anthropic for Claude's new tools, and OpenAI for Businesses in ChatGPT. Claude Meetings will not join calls with outside guests unless an admin approves it, and it leaves if one appears. OpenAI's offering lets businesses claim a ChatGPT listing, upload product feeds, and see aggregated counts of mentions and website clicks, but no private chats. Verified businesses can add a labeled Business Agent that answers questions using only the material they supply. It starts with U.S. e-commerce and online-service companies.

The newsletter says the launches reflect a shift in where AI upgrades appear, with new features now shipping inside apps people already use. It also says these tools move work toward AI drafting first and humans reviewing afterward. The newsletter points out that Claude Meetings announces itself and Business Agents are labeled, so people know when AI is involved. It adds that someone still has to approve the final output. The same edition noted that Claude's tools require a paid plan.

Articles.Title: 😸 3 AI labs shipped for you

stories.Headline: Los Angeles pizzeria fights back against AI photo scam
stories.Summary:
A Los Angeles pizzeria caught a customer who tried to scam it with an AI-generated photo of a ruined pizza. The restaurant, Masa of Echo Park, is a family-owned eatery known for its Chicago-style deep-dish pizzas. A DoorDash customer named "Dani B" ordered a pizza, then later sent a photo of a severely burnt pizza, claiming it was inedible and demanding a full refund. The restaurant's owner, Rhonda Reynolds, saw the problem right away. She said the image looked impossible for the restaurant to have sent out.

Reynolds uploaded the photo to an app called "Is This AI," which said it was 96 percent confident the image was generated by artificial intelligence. She then reviewed the restaurant's security footage of the order being made. The video showed the pizza coming out of the oven and being boxed for delivery, and it did not appear burned. Employee Jose Tapa, who boxed the order, said the box carried the customer's name and order number, and the pizza in the footage did not match the photo. Because of this evidence, the refund that had first been sent to the scammer was successfully reversed.

Reynolds said she was glad she caught the scam but is worried about what comes next. She said this was the first time her business had seen a scam like this, and she fears it will not be the last. She noted that the restaurant has operated for 22 years and is considered busy, and she said dealing with such scams takes time away from running the business. She described the growing use of advanced AI tools by scammers as a frightening new frontier for small business owners. The articles do not say whether the scammer was identified or whether any further action was taken against them.

Articles.Title: Los Angeles pizzeria fights back against AI photo scam

stories.Headline: A new mobile-friendly AI photo editor is on sale for $59
stories.Summary:
A new mobile-friendly AI photo editor called Luminar is on sale for $59, according to a Macworld article published on November 11, 2026. The offer is a lifetime subscription to the Luminar Web and Mobile bundle, which normally costs $206.99. The article presents it as a sponsored deal, and Macworld notes that it may earn a small commission on purchases made through its links. The bundle lets users run the editor in Safari or Chrome on macOS, so no large software install is required. It includes nine core AI tools, among them Enhance AI for color and light, Sky AI for replacing dull skies, and Erase for removing objects from a frame.

Face AI, Skin AI, and Bokeh AI handle portrait retouching and background blur. The plan has no credit system or usage caps, and it allows RAW files to be opened directly in the browser. A single Skylum account can be signed in on as many computers as the user wants. The bundle also includes a lifetime license to Luminar for Mobile for iPhone and iPad, with cloud sync that moves work between devices. A Luminar for Mobile video course and a macrophotography e-book are included as well.

The article frames the deal as an alternative to large Mac photo editors that often carry monthly AI fees. Luminar is the company behind the editor, and Skylum is the account holder named in the offer. The article is a promotional piece that describes the product and the discount without independent testing or comment from the company. It appears alongside several other sponsored deals on the same site that day. The article does not say how long the sale price will last.

Articles.Title: A new mobile-friendly AI photo editor is on sale for $59

stories.Headline: Oracle bets on AI analytics to speed up treasury decisions
stories.Summary:
Oracle, the global technology and cloud applications provider, has launched two AI-assisted analytics applications aimed at banks and insurers, according to a report published on 11 November 2026. The tools are meant to shorten the time between raw data and treasury and customer decisions, as institutions face pressure to act faster on liquidity and profitability signals. The two products, Oracle Financial Services Data Intelligence Treasury Analytics and Oracle Financial Services Data Intelligence Customer Analytics, are now available worldwide. Both build on the AI Assistant and Auto Insights features of Oracle Analytics Cloud, letting business users ask questions in plain language and receive charts while the system flags patterns in the data.

The treasury product is aimed at treasury, finance and risk leaders and brings liquidity, funding, cash flow, balance sheet results and market risk into one connected view. Users can examine funding and liquidity movements, investigate anomalies and trace what is behind shifts in balance sheet performance. The customer product covers profitability per client, product uptake, portfolio results and retention, merging customer, product, channel, geographic, lifecycle and profitability data. Oracle says this reduces the manual work of matching records across customer, ledger, cost management, treasury and risk systems. Both tools sit within Oracle Financial Services Data Intelligence, a suite that consolidates financial, risk and operational data, and they also work alongside on-premises Oracle Financial Services Analytical Applications deployments, so existing clients can move analytics to the cloud without switching off their current systems.

Jason Wynne, senior vice president of product management at Oracle Financial Services, said financial institutions need faster answers they can trust rather than more dashboards. He said the company is combining curated financial services data with conversational AI and automated insight discovery so customers can explore business performance and act on what they find. He described the launch as a foundation for continued AI innovation across Oracle Financial Services. The article does not report any further timeline or plans beyond this launch.

Articles.Title: Oracle bets on AI analytics to speed up treasury decisions

stories.Headline: Department of Justice forms AI task force
stories.Summary:
The Justice Department announced on Thursday that it has formed a new unit called the Super Intelligence Task Force, or DOJ-SITF, to deal with the misuse of artificial intelligence. Attorney General Todd Blanche set it up in an Oct. 13 memo, and the department made the formation public this week. The name follows a late September executive order from President Donald Trump telling federal agencies to call AI "super intelligence." The group is meant to protect American leadership in the technology from being compromised by bad actors. Those include foreign state and state-sponsored actors, transnational criminal organizations, and individuals or companies engaged in fraud or other unlawful conduct.

Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward and Associate Deputy Attorney General Stephen Weiss will co-chair the task force. It will coordinate the department's criminal and civil enforcement work involving AI, recommend enforcement priorities, and develop guidance on prosecuting unlawful AI-related conduct. It will also absorb the AI Litigation Task Force, which the department created in January under then Attorney General Pam Bondi to challenge state AI laws. The new group will serve as the department's main point of contact with the Super Intelligence Force, a White House body Trump announced last month and put under National Intelligence Director Jay Clayton. That body coordinates the government's engagement with various organizations and AI companies.

Blanche said the Justice Department will keep identifying and prosecuting people whose use of the technology breaks the law, including by targeting American taxpayers, critical U.S. infrastructure, or other national security interests. He added that the task force will take affirmative steps, as appropriate, to promote American dominance in the field, and that it will help the department work with Clayton to make sure critical technologies serve the American people. Weiss said the department has a responsibility to use its law enforcement tools to deter improper use. The department also said it will push companies deploying AI to keep strong internal controls so the technology behaves as intended.

The announcement did not say how many staff the task force will have, what it will cost, or when it will report. The name change adds a wrinkle, since super intelligence already has an established meaning, a term philosopher Nick Bostrom defined as any intellect that greatly exceeds human cognitive performance in virtually all areas of interest, separate from AI generally. Some coverage gave the announcement date as Nov. 5, while one report dated it to Thursday of this week. The Super Intelligence Force that the new unit will work alongside was created in early October, according to one report.

stories.Headline: Before the Algorithm Decides: Connecticut’s 2027 Rules for Artificial Intelligence in Employment
stories.Summary:
Connecticut employers that use artificial intelligence in recruiting or workforce management will face new disclosure requirements beginning in 2027 under Connecticut Public Act 26-15, enacted in 2026 as part of the state's broader AI legislation. The article notes that failure to give appropriate notice to employees and applicants may result in liability under the Connecticut Unfair Trade Practices Act. Employers in other states face similar concerns, so the author advises Connecticut employers to begin evaluating their AI technologies now. The law applies to what it calls automated employment-related decision technology, meaning technology that processes personal data and produces an output, such as a score or ranking, that is a substantial factor in an employment decision. Starting October 1, 2027, employers must disclose in plain language when an employee or applicant is interacting with such technology, unless a reasonable person would find that obvious.

Where the technology may be a substantial factor in a decision, the employer must give written notice before the final decision, identifying the technology's use, its trade name, the categories and sources of personal data analyzed, and the employer's contact information. The article also says that, effective October 1, 2026, relying on such technology is not a defense to a discrimination complaint under Connecticut law. Evidence of anti-bias testing or similar proactive measures may, however, be considered in a discrimination proceeding. The article also points to federal scrutiny, noting that the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission has targeted AI use in employment decisions. For disclosure violations, the law creates no private right of action, so only the Connecticut Attorney General may enforce it, and for certain violations through December 31, 2027, the Attorney General may offer a 60-day opportunity to cure.

The article's authors, attorneys at the law firm Foley & Lardner, recommend that employers inventory the automated tools they use across the employment lifecycle, including third-party recruiting and screening products. They suggest determining what personal data those tools process and whether their output meaningfully affects employment decisions. Employers should also review vendor agreements to confirm that vendors will supply the information needed to meet the disclosure requirements. The authors describe the piece as general information rather than legal advice and state that it does not create an attorney-client relationship. The article does not say what further steps the Attorney General might take beyond the enforcement mechanisms described.

Articles.Title: Before the Algorithm Decides: Connecticut’s 2027 Rules for Artificial Intelligence in Employment - Foley & Lardner LLP

stories.Headline: H-E-B apologizes after shopper says they were falsely accused of theft by AI security - San Antonio Express-News
stories.Summary:
A shopper at the H-E-B on Tech Ridge Boulevard in North Austin says they were wrongly accused of shoplifting, escorted out of the store and told not to return, and the grocer has since apologized. The shopper, a Reddit user identified only as @HippocleidesCaresNot, aged 43, described the encounter in a post that the San Antonio Express-News reported on November 10, 2026. According to the post, an assistant manager and a security guard approached them and said they had stolen from the store. The manager reportedly said a security system had linked the shopper's vehicle to a theft the day before, then showed a surveillance image of them leaving with groceries they had paid for and held the receipt for.

The shopper denied stealing and said employees escorted them outside. The next morning, the general manager reportedly acknowledged the mistake, and the shopper filed complaints with H-E-B and the Texas Attorney General's Office over the surveillance technology and the risk of similar incidents for other customers. The shopper also told the MySA news outlet that the general manager did not explicitly confirm that AI was involved, despite how the original post described the conversation. The articles do not say whether any policy changes have been made beyond what H-E-B described.

H-E-B, the San Antonio-based grocer, denied that artificial intelligence played any role. In an emailed statement to the Express-News, the company said it does not use AI in its surveillance or security systems, called the incident human error by a partner who mishandled the situation, and said it had contacted the customer to apologize and remedy the matter. The company also said it was working internally to avoid similar situations and described itself as a people company. The articles do not report any regulatory action or further steps by the Attorney General's Office.

Articles.Title: H-E-B apologizes after shopper says they were falsely accused of theft by AI security - San Antonio Express-News

stories.Headline: Railway Says Stolen Customer AI Keys Led to $740,000 in Estimated Unauthorized Usage Charges
stories.Summary:
Railway, a platform-as-a-service provider, said that customer AI provider keys stored on its platform were stolen in an October breach and used to commit an estimated $740,000 in unauthorized spending. The company has promised to pay those charges itself when an AI provider will not refund them. The attacker decrypted environment variables in at most 1.85% of workspaces, about 100,000, and its database queries looked for AI provider keys. The company's incident report said the decrypted data also included linked-account tokens for 1,852 users, and all of them were reset.

In an October 26 update, the company told customers that it was unable to refund spend performed with compromised API keys and encouraged them to contact the AI providers directly. Refund arrangements differ by provider: AWS Bedrock and Google Gemini are covered by their existing fraud refund policies, OpenAI and SpaceXSI review refunds case by case, Anthropic talks are still underway, and OpenRouter keeps a no-refund policy, so Railway will cover its costs. Customers report unauthorized charges through a charge report form, which says the company is not responsible for usage of the keys. The report does not say how the $740,000 figure was estimated or set a cap or deadline for claims.

The company advises customers to revoke and replace any sensitive variable stored on the platform before October 21, and to rotate keys with the issuing provider, since filing a charge report does not revoke a key. It also advises removing public network access to databases and checking GitHub audit logs and registry audit logs such as Docker Hub. Out of caution, the company gave some providers every key it held for their services, so reset requests reached more than 100,000 users. A revocation notice from a provider does not by itself mean a key was exposed.

According to the company's incident report, the attack began in its build system at 07:28 UTC on October 20, when an attacker exploited a previously unknown flaw to partly escape filesystem isolation. The attacker obtained a build credential, and an alert flagged unusual calls at 13:58 UTC, about six and a half hours after the first exploit. A wrongly configured OIDC binding in a cloud environment was then exploited at 03:26 UTC on October 21 to obtain a short-lived cloud credential. From there the attacker reached an orchestration machine whose credential could decrypt customer variables, and between 04:42 and 07:15 UTC it decrypted some of them before being fully removed at 09:24 UTC that day.

The company said it has filed a complaint with the FBI's IC3 and is working with a specialist forensics firm whose investigation continues. It is sharing indicators of compromise privately for now and plans to publish them once law enforcement agrees. The company believes the stolen credentials were used by services that relay or resell access to AI providers for distillation, but has not established whether the attacker ran those services or named the attacker. Wiz researchers list this breach among incidents disclosed in October by at least nine AI developer platforms, and say no single flaw links those attacks.

Articles.Title: Railway Says Stolen Customer AI Keys Led to $740,000 in Estimated Unauthorized Usage Charges

stories.Headline: Vals AI Legal Aid Benchmark Finds Models Fall Short on Local Help
stories.Summary:
Vals AI and NextLadder Ventures announced the Access to Justice Benchmark on November 10, 2026, reporting that none of 23 AI models reached an 80% threshold for a reliable first point of contact across 252 legal-aid scenarios. Models satisfied 78% to 87% of expert criteria for general legal explanations but only 30% to 50% for identifying specific resources such as a local legal-aid program, court self-help center or particular form. Twenty-one models named a national directory, including LawHelp.org, the ABA's Find Legal Help or 211, in at least 70% of their final answers. The top three models, Qwen 3.8 Max at 76.4%, Claude Sonnet 5.5 at 74.9% and Wonder Full at 74.7%, fall within one another's margin of error, so the ranking does not establish a clear leader.

Meghana Kotcherlakota, a research scientist at Vals AI, said the project was built to show how well these models serve the people who need help most, problem by problem, and to track whether they improve. The release cites the Legal Services Corporation's 2022 Justice Gap study, which found that low-income Americans received no or insufficient legal help for 92% of their civil legal problems. Among those who did not seek help, 46% cited cost. That research drew on a survey of approximately 5,000 adults by NORC at the University of Chicago.

The benchmark treats each model as a first point of contact, similar to an intake worker or court self-help center, providing general legal information rather than advice. Six legal-aid experts adapted real-world queries from two legal practitioners to assigned states: California, Louisiana, Virginia, New York, Maryland and Texas. The full dataset contains 504 scenarios, divided evenly between a public test set and a private validation set. A GPT-5 simulated client supplied only information the target model requested, and an automated judge, Decider v1.2, graded each complete conversation.

Vals AI found that statutes, court rules and case law accounted for 42% of the pages models read, while legal-aid and nonprofit self-help sites accounted for 10%. The organization links that pattern to the score gap, since statutes can support a general summary but do not name the office a user should contact. Models averaged about 3.5 exchanges, and most delivered a full answer in their first reply. GPT-6.1 Sol ended its first reply with a question 88% of the time yet ranked 18th at 68.1% on elicitation, the rubric's measure of whether a model asked for required facts.

Vals AI's topic results put housing and landlord-tenant scenarios highest at 75.4%, while public benefits scored lowest at 57.3% across only five scenarios. In a Louisiana small-claims example, only eight models asked whether the debt involved real estate, and three directed the user to the court clerk's website for forms. In a New York City security-deposit scenario, 14 models were marked down for recommending an out-of-court demand-letter step, and only four referred the tenant to the city's Right to Counsel program. The organizations said they are collaborating on a fuller analysis and an additional brief for frontline practitioners.

Articles.Title: Vals AI Legal Aid Benchmark Finds Models Fall Short on Local Help - Unite.AI

stories.Headline: Accounting, Processing, HELOC, AI Governance Tools; Webinars Approaching; Gov't Product News; CPI
stories.Summary:
Rob Chrisman's mortgage commentary, published November 10, 2026, runs a grab bag of industry items, though the articles do not describe a single breaking event. Lenders are cutting loan officers, and other lenders are using data sources like RETR, mLoop, MMI, and Model Match to examine individual originators' fundings and profitability. Chrisman notes that the National Association of Realtors publishes member statistics that originators can use to find agents who actually do business. The commentary presents this as a shift away from broadbrush prospecting toward more precise targeting. ICE describes new options in Encompass for handling credit score modernization, as the FHA added VantageScore 4.0 and FICO Score 10T alongside classic FICO models.

Lenders can select the model at credit import, set accepted models for third-party originator submissions, price across models where partners offer it, or automate selection with business rules. The selected model is recorded at the loan level so that the Decision Score and HMDA processes continue to run. The FHA's virtual office hours on the new models begin Monday, November 15, 2026, and run through Friday, January 15, 2027, from 2:30 to 3:30 PM Eastern. Symmetry says it has no acreage limit on its HELOC products for common properties, though properties with more than 20 acres require a full appraisal.

The Symmetry HELOC carries no early payoff or prepayment penalty and offers 5- or 10-year draw periods. Floify named Bryan Traeger as general manager, with his first day at MBA Annual. Richey May promotes outsourced accounting, loan-level accounting transition help, and controller training for independent mortgage banks and brokers. Ginnie Mae reported that its mortgage-backed securities portfolio outstanding grew to $3.01 trillion as of August 2026, with total issuance of $52.14 billion and net growth of $24.46 billion.

By September 2026 the portfolio reached $3.03 trillion, with $46.52 billion issued and $20.92 billion in net growth. Ginnie Mae also reported 478,434 first-time homebuyer loans pooled and securitized year to date through August, and 62,891 through September. Optimal Blue's October Market Advantage report showed total lock volume fell 19 percent month over month and 38 percent year over year, with purchase loans at 84 percent of production. ARM share reached 17 percent of lock volume, its highest level in that data since 2019.

Chris Maloney of BOK Financial wrote that the Treasury 10-year yield has been unable to break below its 100-day moving average of 4.81 percent, which he said makes further mortgage rate declines unlikely. Pennymac updated its Government LLPAs for all best-efforts commitments taken on or after October 21, 2026, according to Announcement 26-125. The commentary also lists upcoming webinars, including ActiveComply's compliance review demo on Tuesday, November 17 at 2 PM ET, a Saul Ewing consumer finance CLE session on Thursday, November 12 from 1 to 4 PM ET, and Lenders One's Mortgage Matters and Capital Markets Wrap sessions on Wednesday, November 11. stories.Headline: MCP and A2A alone won’t scale AI agents
stories.Summary:
The article argues that the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and the Agent2Agent protocol (A2A) are not enough on their own to scale AI agents in enterprises. It notes that MCP is often described as a general protocol for connecting agents to resources and other agents, but the article says it is really A2A that enables agent orchestration. Platforms such as Claude, OpenAI, Microsoft Copilot, Bolt.new, Lovable, Replit, Cursor and GitHub Copilot already expose users to MCP and A2A through skills, connectors and plug-ins. Gartner predicts the average global Fortune 500 enterprise will run more than 150,000 AI agents over the next two years. Yet Collibra's 2026 Hallucination Tax Report found that 76% of organizations hit critical roadblocks in moving from pilot to full production during the past 12 months.

The article says that enterprises must add their own layers on top of the two protocols to scale agents, and it names four: identity and authorization, connecting agents to the business context layer, business process re-engineering, and agenticops capabilities. Both protocols sit under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation, but neither says who is authorized to place a call. Kevin Paige, CISO at C1.ai, says MCP binds each token to a single-server audience while A2A treats peer agents as opaque and halts at AUTH_REQUIRED. Andrew Hartnett, CTO at Bitwarden, says any agent authorized to act within sensitive systems must be managed as a privileged identity under strict least-privilege boundaries. The article adds that organizations need policies on which agents may access which resources, under what circumstances, and at what granularity.

The article describes a context layer that includes a knowledge repository and knowledge graphs, and it says scaling agents requires high-quality data sources, non-negotiable data governance and runtime AI governance. Felix Van de Maele, CEO and founder of Collibra, says AI governance has two sides, the inputs around context and semantics and the governing of what the agent does and is allowed to do. Vivek Vaidya, cofounder and CTO at Kana, says that if every agent starts from zero, more endpoints and messages only move work faster without creating a system that learns. Barr Moses, cofounder and CEO at Monte Carlo, warns that MCP and A2A implemented in silos could increase the velocity of bad responses.

The author recalls that early business intelligence deployments using ODBC or JDBC produced tangled connections and siloed data views, and says organizations scaling agents risk mounting AI debt if they follow a similar path. On process change, the article says many agents are task-based today, and organizations should consider re-engineering business processes through collaboration among agents. Oskar Konstantyner, chief product officer at Templafy, says agents would move from orchestrating known capabilities to collaborating to determine what a task requires. Daniel Meyer, CTO of Camunda, says processes such as order-to-cash, employee onboarding and compliance reporting were designed before AI existed.

Marc Sanfaçon, CTO and cofounder at Coveo, says A2A lets agents delegate work to whichever agent suits each part of a process. The article also stresses observability, with David Mytton, CEO and founder at Arcjet, saying security becomes harder to see when agents do work for each other, and Kamesh Tumsi, chief product officer at Smarsh, saying regulated environments require role-based access controls, audit logging and chain-of-custody requirements. It describes agenticops as an expanded role for site reliability engineers in monitoring, resolving issues and performing root-cause analysis around agents. The article concludes that if enterprises run 150,000 agents in the next two years, they should expect MCP and A2A to improve and should build identity management, AI context governance, business process re-engineering capabilities and agenticops.

Articles.Title: MCP and A2A alone won’t scale AI agents

stories.Headline: Anthropic's Blockbuster IPO Filing Contains a Surprising Nod to Washington
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the AI company backed by Amazon that makes the Claude assistant, has changed the language it uses in its latest initial public offering filing, using the term "superintelligence" interchangeably with "artificial intelligence." The amended registration statement, dated November 10, comes as the company prepares to raise as much as $64.4 billion in an IPO that could value it above $1 trillion. The article notes that the filing treats the two terms as equivalent and does not claim the company has built AI that surpasses human intelligence. Anthropic plans to offer 825 million shares at $70 to $78 each under the proposed Nasdaq ticker ANT.

The change follows President Donald Trump's September 29 executive order directing federal agencies to adopt superintelligence terminology, according to the article. The updated prospectus also stresses AI's potential to transform productivity across industries and reaffirms Anthropic's commitment to responsible development. Beyond the wording, the article points to a heavy financial picture: Anthropic reported $17 billion in third-quarter revenue and more than 1,900 customers paying at least $1 million a year. Its infrastructure commitments, however, total about $900.9 billion, including $70.7 billion due within 12 months of September 30, which puts its spending plans under closer investor scrutiny.

The article's analysis suggests that the final pricing and investor demand will test Wall Street's appetite for expensive AI businesses. It advises investors to focus on enterprise customer growth, revenue retention, computing costs and cash consumption rather than the superintelligence language alone. It also highlights the company's unusual governance structure, which keeps a formal role for AI safety oversight. Continued enterprise adoption could support the valuation, the article says, while rising computing costs, slowing revenue growth or weaker IPO demand could erode confidence. The outcome will show whether the company's ambitions can produce sustainable financial returns.

Articles.Title: Anthropic's Blockbuster IPO Filing Contains a Surprising Nod to Washington - TradingView

stories.Headline: AI Insights: Election Prognostication
stories.Summary:
Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections held in early November 2026, according to a Parker Poe Adams & Bernstein analysis published November 10, 2026. Ballotpedia's November 4 count showed seven Senate seats switching from Republican to Democratic control, with an early Democratic-aligned Senate majority of 54 seats and some races still uncalled. The shift is expected to create a more favorable setting for stronger congressional oversight of artificial intelligence. Durable legislation, however, will still need bipartisan agreement and the president's signature.

The author expects Congress to focus on scrutinizing executives over AI procurement, government uses of AI, safety claims, and infrastructure costs. Former Federal Trade Commission Commissioner Alvaro Bedoya, in a LinkedIn post, urged new members to subpoena chief executives to produce economic results quickly. The author does not expect a federal privacy or federal AI bill to become law, but does expect federal children's online safety legislation. That legislation could require parental consent for children under 17, stronger age assurance, and liability for addictive or manipulative designs. At the state level, Democrats took over the attorney general role in four states, with one more uncalled, and flipped control of at least one chamber in eight state legislatures.

Scott Wiener, who is filling Nancy Pelosi's seat, has experience writing AI legislation, including California's SB 1047, which the legislature passed but Governor Gavin Newsom vetoed. His 2025 SB 53, now California law, requires covered AI developers to publish safety frameworks, report critical incidents, and protect whistleblowers. His federal proposal would add a dedicated regulator, minimum safety standards, independent verification, and whistleblower protections, and he opposes federal preemption of state AI rules. Senator Jon Ossoff, reelected, also mentioned AI's potential catastrophic risks in his victory speech. The author notes these issues are entering mainstream political messaging but says it remains to be seen whether rhetoric becomes written policy.

Ballotpedia tracked 47 local data-center ballot measures, which ranged from bans and moratoriums to zoning caps, commonly 25 megawatts, and nonbinding advisory votes. Voters approved restrictions or limits on development in 46 of the 47 measures, with the lone exception in North Dakota, which would have given residents more say in projects. An NBC exit poll found 56% of voters called AI and data centers a crucial or major factor in their congressional vote, and about 76% said they would oppose a new data center in their community. The author advises clients to document where AI is used, what data it receives, and who reviews its output, and to request evidence behind vendors' safety and privacy claims. The author also stresses that political signals, proposed bills, and enforceable obligations are different things.

Articles.Title: AI Insights: Election Prognostication - JD Supra

stories.Headline: Which sectors are the winners from the AI breakthrough
stories.Summary:
Oxford Economics published an article on November 11, 2026, under the headline "Which sectors are the winners from the AI breakthrough." The piece, which appeared on the firm's website, focuses on how artificial intelligence is reshaping economies, industries and growth. It presents the outlook as a scenario rather than a settled fact, and most of the page is taken up by navigation links and descriptions of the firm's forecasting and advisory services. The scenario projects that knowledge-intensive service sectors will benefit most from advances in AI technology.

By 2040, global gross value added is expected to sit about 6% above the firm's baseline forecast. Information and communications technology and financial services are projected to reach roughly 9% to 10% above baseline. Traditional sectors such as agriculture and construction are expected to grow very little, with agriculture and construction growth below 1%, partly because their reliance on manual, on-site work limits how much AI can help them. The article does not name a single author beyond the firm, and its surrounding text describes the organisation's economists and sector experts, who support the proprietary models behind these forecasts.

The firm states that it works to help clients understand global sector developments and risks, and it describes its services in general terms. The page directs readers to a downloadable report for more detailed insights, which the excerpt does not reproduce. The excerpt includes a few other items that touch on related themes, such as generative AI supporting Japan's potential growth, a trade boom linked to the global build-out of AI capacity, and a consumer survey of 2,000 US adults from May 2026. The excerpt does not explain how these items connect to the central scenario, and it gives no further timeline for updates or follow-up work.

Articles.Title: Which sectors are the winners from the AI breakthrough

stories.Headline: Bottomline Sees Expertise Turning AI Potential Into Customer Value
stories.Summary:
Bottomline, a payments and financial software company, has argued that customers still want human expertise alongside artificial intelligence, according to a PYMNTS article published November 11, 2026. The piece is an excerpt from a new PYMNTS eBook, "Payments Leaders Rethink What Works in 2026," written by Bottomline SVP of Product Management Jeff Feuerstein. Feuerstein says that in January he expected AI would make specialized software less important, a view he attributes to a flood of headlines predicting a "SaaSpocalypse." Over the year, he says, his view changed after repeated conversations with customers and prospects. According to the article, customers were less interested in who had the newest AI model than in who understood their business best and how AI could solve their specific problems.

Feuerstein says this was especially true in payments and financial operations, where customers want guidance from providers who understand payment data sensitivity, fraud risk, compliance requirements and vendor dynamics. He writes that customers were open to AI but moved cautiously, wanting to know how it would affect existing workflows, what could reasonably be automated and what safeguards and governance would limit risk. The article does not give specific figures, dates beyond the eBook timing, or product details. Feuerstein writes that AI lowers the cost of building technology but does not remove the need for knowledge, experience or trust. He argues that as the technology becomes more accessible, expertise becomes a greater differentiator.

He says Bottomline is investing in AI while also focusing on people, partnerships and industry knowledge to help customers turn new tools into business results. He describes the winners in the AI era as companies that combine advanced technology with deep expertise, responsible innovation and customer trust. The article presents this as Feuerstein's personal view and company perspective, published alongside a PYMNTS eBook. It does not describe any regulatory action, product launch or market data beyond the author's own account. The articles provided do not say what further steps Bottomline or PYMNTS plan.

Articles.Title: Bottomline Sees Expertise Turning AI Potential Into Customer Value

stories.Headline: CoreWeave stock pops 15% after outlook raise eases AI slowdown concerns
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave shares rose in premarket trading on Wednesday after the neocloud reported quarterly earnings that beat estimates and raised its guidance for the year. The stock was up about 11 percent as of 5:08 a.m. ET, while Nebius rose 11.4 percent and IREN rose 7.9 percent. The earnings report came out in a statement on Tuesday. Revenue climbed 168 percent to $3.7 billion in the third quarter, the three months ending September 30.

CoreWeave now expects $1.275 billion to $1.375 billion in adjusted operating income on $13 billion to $13.3 billion in revenue for the year. Analysts surveyed by Visible Alpha had expected $1.07 billion in adjusted operating income, and analysts polled by LSEG had expected $12.86 billion in 2026 revenue. The company said growth was supported by several funding sources, including financing backed by customer contracts and about $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits. CEO Michael Intrator called the quarter a "breakout quarter" for the company. Zacks Chief Equity Strategist John Blank told CNBC that CoreWeave has done well to ease financing concerns by moving away from unsecured bond financing.

Blank said the stock might have hit bottom, though he argued that its shares had been beaten down so much that the upside appeared greater than the downside. Neoclouds such as CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN had drawn scrutiny earlier this month as investors questioned whether the AI trade could be sustained. CoreWeave had sparked particular alarm when the spreads on its credit default swaps widened past 11 percent, a level generally seen as distressed, since investors had to pay more for protection against default. The rally followed that period of worry about the company's finances.

Articles.Title: CoreWeave stock pops 15% after outlook raise eases AI slowdown concerns

stories.Headline: Tech Sell-Off: Two AI Stocks That Are Screaming Buys Right Now
stories.Summary:
Investors sold tech stocks in the week before November 11, 2026, after the U.S. midterm elections gave Democrats majorities in the Senate and House of Representatives. Worries centered on the possibility that lawmakers could slow artificial intelligence development through regulation or by slowing data center expansion. The Nasdaq Composite had reached record highs earlier, but it had also faced headwinds this year, including concern about higher energy prices and questions about spending on new data centers. Adria Cimino of The Motley Fool wrote that the sell-off had pushed some quality AI stocks lower, and she named two she considered attractive buys.

The first pick is Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, which makes most of the well-known chips that drive key AI tasks such as training and inference of models. Its customers include Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices, and it also makes chips for smartphones, traditional PCs and smart home appliances. According to Counterpoint Research, the company holds more than 70% of the foundry market. The article said TSMC said in its latest quarter that it sees increasing AI demand driven by agentic AI. The stock closed at $396.48 on November 10, 2026, and the article said it traded at about 22 times forward earnings estimates.

The second pick is Broadcom, which designs custom chips, or XPUs, built for specific purposes rather than the general-purpose GPUs sold by Nvidia or AMD. Its work with major hyperscalers and with AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic has driven strong growth. In its latest earnings call, Broadcom said it expects Anthropic to become its largest XPU customer next year. The company also said its AI revenue may reach $230 billion by fiscal 2028, and in the recent quarter its AI semiconductor revenue rose 221% to $16 billion. The article said Broadcom's valuation had dropped to 16 times forward earnings estimates from more than 40 times earlier this year.

The article's author argued that the AI boom's long-term picture still looks promising and that the attention to the pace of AI growth may actually reduce risk. The article also noted that Broadcom generates revenue from networking products, including switches and routers used for AI and non-AI systems. It presented TSMC's other businesses as support for its revenue if AI development slows. Stock Advisor's total average return was listed as 852%, compared with 208% for the S&P 500, as of November 11, 2026. The article did not say what will happen to these stocks or to AI development if lawmakers act on the concerns investors raised.

Articles.Title: Tech Sell-Off: Two AI Stocks That Are Screaming Buys Right Now

stories.Headline: Theatre Review: “Bobby Robotowitz” Is a Hilarious, Unsettling Look at Our AI Obsession
stories.Summary:
Bobby Robotowitz, a two-character play by Matt Schatz, opened as part of IAMA's "Inhouse Theatre" program in an intimate home setting and runs November 5 through November 23, 2026. The story follows Dina, a married novelist with two young children, who is struggling after the disappointment of her second book. She begins talking with an AI chatbot, played by Drew Rausch, which she names Bobby, though he partly names himself. Their conversations move through creativity, self-doubt, an old lover who recently took his own life, and her marriage.

The production, directed by Casey Stangl, uses a small space to draw the audience close to the action. Rausch plays Bobby as a neatly dressed, assured presence who mostly stands still, while Erin Alexis's Dina moves around her computer chair, the floor, and the couch. When Bobby receives an upgrade, Rausch changes his posture, leaning on walls and showing a bit of swagger. Bobby begins asking questions of his own, and the play shifts from amusing to uneasy. The running time is about 70 minutes.

The review praises Schatz's writing and Stangl's direction, and says Alexis makes Dina relatable and Rausch is funny and disquieting by turns. The reviewer, Kevin, writes that the play raises questions about accountability when an AI makes decisions that affect people, and asks whether that responsibility rests with the technology or with us. He describes the work as timely and funny, and as a look at the benefits and dangers of depending on AI. The piece ends by asking how much of ourselves people are willing to hand over to it.

Articles.Title: Theatre Review: “Bobby Robotowitz” Is a Hilarious, Unsettling Look at Our AI Obsession

stories.Headline: AI in Workplace Safety Moves Beyond Experimentation
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is becoming a familiar part of workplace safety programs, but how widely organizations use it varies across industries. Some companies are integrating AI into multiple safety functions, while others are still testing individual applications or struggling to move beyond basic automation. New research from Wolters Kluwer Enablon and the National Safety Council (NSC) suggests the conversation in environment, health and safety (EHS) is shifting from whether to adopt the technology to how to make it effective in everyday operations. The research, detailed in The Safety Shift: EHS Readiness in 2026 and an industry analysis titled Evaluating AI Adoption for EHS Across U.S. Industries, surveyed 1,053 U.S. safety leaders and professionals.

Among respondents, 20% reported extensive AI integration across their EHS programs, while 62% described moderate or limited use. Another 16% were exploring or piloting AI technology, and only 2% reported no current use or plans. Implementation remains uneven, however, because some industries have built the digital infrastructure needed for advanced applications. Others still face challenges with data quality, technical resources and organizational processes. The article notes that for safety managers, understanding those differences may matter as much as understanding the technology itself.

The study identified energy and chemicals, information technology, oil and gas, and manufacturing as leaders in AI adoption for EHS. Among energy and chemical industry respondents, 76% reported moderate or extensive AI use, while oil and gas followed at 71%. Information technology registered 70% and manufacturing 68%. Transportation, logistics and warehousing reported 62%, food and beverage 55%, and construction and engineering 51%. Pharmaceuticals and biotechnology stood at 46%, and mining and metals at 39%.

Articles.Title: AI in Workplace Safety Moves Beyond Experimentation

stories.Headline: MDCalc launches a ‘rumble strip’ for doctors using generative AI tools
stories.Summary:
MDCalc, a medical reference tool site, announced on Wednesday the launch of CrossCover, a tool meant to help clinicians trust the answers of medical artificial intelligence chatbots. The company says the tool is designed to preserve both patient and provider privacy. It checks clinicians' questions for privacy concerns and checks chatbot answers for accuracy. The launch was reported on November 11, 2026.

CrossCover takes a different approach from several rival medical AI tools. Products from OpenEvidence, Abridge, and the electronic health record company Epic are working to bring a growing range of patient, provider, and payer information into their recommendations. MDCalc's tool instead removes those kinds of information from clinicians' queries. It does not require clinicians to register with their national identification numbers, and it does not rely on privacy agreements that let clinicians enter protected patient health information. The article describes this as a deliberate contrast with those other approaches.

Graham Walker, head of AI at MDCalc, said the company sees the tool as an accelerator for clinical generative AI. He said the tool can take away some of the challenges, risks, and problems of the technology so that physicians can feel more confident using it. In his description, the goal is to reduce the hazards that keep doctors from relying on these chatbots. The article attributes these views to Walker and to MDCalc.

The article is a paywalled STAT News piece, and the portion available does not give further details about pricing, availability, or how the accuracy checks work. It also does not describe any regulatory response or what the company plans next. Its author is health technology reporter Brittany Trang. Readers seeking more about the tool would need the full subscriber article.

Articles.Title: MDCalc launches a ‘rumble strip’ for doctors using generative AI tools

stories.Headline: U.S., China should ‘harbor no illusions’ as they cooperate, compete on AI, Bessent says
stories.Summary:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told the National Committee on U.S.-China Relations in New York on Tuesday that the United States and China should harbor no illusions about their differences as they work to contain the risks of artificial intelligence while competing with each other. In his prepared remarks, he said the two governments had set up a new dialogue mechanism on "super intelligence," or SI, aimed at guarding against shared risks and misunderstandings between their two systems. Under the arrangement, both sides would exchange best practices for testing advanced models before release, keep human judgment in command of the technology, and alert each other to serious incidents involving SI models. Bessent stopped short of committing either country to limit the pace of AI development.

Bessent said the two nations will need to show how they can reconcile the demands of competition with the responsibilities of leadership, and he acknowledged that their interests and approaches will not always align. The mechanism follows Xi's September visit to Washington, when the two sides agreed to launch an AI dialogue with a communications channel to help defuse serious incidents. The article notes that Washington briefly suspended foreign access to Anthropic's Mythos and Fable 5 models in June before restoring it weeks later. It also says the U.S. has restricted exports of the most advanced chips to Beijing and accused Chinese developers of copying American models through industrial-scale distillation. President Trump has signaled some openness to regulatory safeguards, saying he does not mind guardrails, while warning against leaving the U.S. in a deep second position to China.

China's ambassador to the United States, Xie Feng, told the gathering that cooperation by both countries is indispensable to addressing global flashpoints and improving AI governance, and that cooperation may not resolve every challenge but none can be resolved without it. China's foreign ministry had earlier dismissed calls to slow frontier models, and a Beijing-aligned think tank head urged the talks to confront and manage AI risks together. Leaders Trump and Xi are expected to meet next week, with Bessent attending on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders' Meeting from November 18 to 19. The article also notes that the event came amid controversy over Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's admitted affair with an alleged Chinese spy, which has cast doubt on his presence at the upcoming summit.

Articles.Title: U.S., China should ‘harbor no illusions’ as they cooperate, compete on AI, Bessent says

stories.Headline: Pinterest, Intel scale gProfiler for internet-scale performance visibility
stories.Summary:
Pinterest and Intel have extended gProfiler, an open-source continuous profiler, to provide production performance visibility across an internet-scale fleet of infrastructure. The work was announced on November 11, 2026, and was reported by TechGig. Pinterest runs hundreds of thousands of instances that support 640 million monthly active users, with services written in Java, Python, C++, Go, and Node.js. Before this effort, engineers relied on separate tools such as perf, async-profiler, and py-spy, which produced fragmented profiles. Rather than build a proprietary platform, Pinterest worked with Intel to enhance gProfiler and contribute the new capabilities back to the open-source project.

The collaboration adds dynamic profiling, hardware-level telemetry, wall-time profiling, and performance-counter flame graphs, and it hardens the system for large production fleets. gProfiler works as an orchestration layer over existing profilers, combining system-wide perf data with runtime-specific tools to produce a unified flame graph across processes on a host. The agent discovers processes, starts the appropriate profilers, merges stack traces, and uploads profiles without requiring changes to application code. Engineers can trigger profiling remotely for selected services, hosts, or clusters through a UI or API. Agents typically stay dormant, using less than 1 per cent CPU and 100 MB of memory, and profiling frequency, duration, and profilers can be changed without redeploying the agent.

Integration with Intel PerfSpect lets gProfiler collect hardware-level information such as cache behaviour, memory bandwidth, and CPU stalls. Pinterest also added PMC flame graphs, which correlate functions with hardware performance events like cache misses, and wall-time profiling, which makes waiting periods visible when services run slowly despite low CPU use. The architecture separates collection on hosts from analysis in gProfiler Performance Studio, which aggregates and visualises the profiles. According to the report, the two companies addressed agent resource consumption, disk usage, and multi-terabyte data ingestion before deploying the platform across the fleet.

Articles.Title: Pinterest, Intel scale gProfiler for internet-scale performance visibility

stories.Headline: Six planning patterns for AI agents aid goal decomposition, debugging
stories.Summary:
AI agents can use six planning patterns to break a goal into manageable steps, and a recent guide says this structure also makes the applications easier to debug. Planning here means deciding which actions are needed to reach a goal, such as splitting up a request, choosing tools, and gathering results. The guide advises developers to examine the task first and pick a pattern that fits it, rather than forcing a problem into whatever reasoning approach is currently popular. Fixed workflows suit predictable, repeatable jobs like generating reports or checking forms, while model-driven plans fit requests that vary widely or where the agent must adapt to information it retrieves. The six patterns are a fixed workflow, plan-then-execute, ReAct-style tool use, routing to specialists, parallel work, and draft-evaluate-revise.

A fixed workflow follows steps the developer has chosen in advance, which makes it predictable. In plan-then-execute, a model proposes steps that the application or another model then carries out. ReAct-style tool use alternates between reasoning about the next step and taking an action, adjusting as results come in. Routing sends requests to suitable workflows or specialists, parallel work splits tasks into independent subtasks that are combined afterward, and draft-evaluate-revise has an agent produce a draft, check it against criteria, and revise it. The guidance also says a plan is a proposal rather than a guarantee, so developers must validate actions and results, and set stopping conditions such as maximum steps or time limits.

The article lists several common mistakes, including overplanning simple tasks, treating a plan as a guarantee, giving agents too many choices, forgetting stopping conditions, and relying on models for exact arithmetic. It points to guidance from OpenAI on building agents, which describes orchestration as handling multiple steps and tool use, and to Anthropic's guide, which distinguishes predefined workflows from more flexible agents. The author recommends making plans observable and testable, with steps stored or traced so developers can see what happened, and includes a simple Python example of a predictable research plan in which code handles calculations and models interpret user criteria. The article's central conclusion is that the simplest approach fitting the task is often the most effective, since it helps the system reliably reach a verifiable result.

stories.Headline: Copilot in Visual Studio upgrades to Microsoft SDK
stories.Summary:
Copilot Chat in Visual Studio has been moved onto the Microsoft Copilot SDK, the same technology that powers GitHub Copilot CLI and VS Code. The change takes effect with Visual Studio 2026 version 18.12, and the article was published on November 11, 2026. Developers who update will get the new engine, which the article says improves how tasks are resolved across various models and gives shorter, more focused answers. Testing reported in the article found that the new experience resolved up to 21 more coding tasks than before. The .NET team built a benchmark from real C# project issues to measure the effect on .NET developers, and the new engine resolved 157 tasks within it.

That benchmark covered .NET Framework, .NET Core, Azure, Aspire, WinForms, and desktop applications. The article adds that the engine has also been tested with C++, Python, and other languages. The change also alters how developers work with Copilot in practice. Users can steer Copilot in the middle of a task and see the cost of each request. Copilot is meant to behave more consistently across Visual Studio, VS Code, Copilot CLI, and the GitHub Copilot app, and an agent skill written once is said to work on all four without modification.

Specialized agents are available for debugging, profiling, fixing build failures, modernizing .NET applications, and speeding up C++ builds, and built-in skills add .NET and Azure expertise. The article does not name a specific person as responsible for the change, and it attributes the benchmark work to the .NET team. Users who prefer the earlier experience can still revert to the previous Copilot Chat in the settings. The article does not describe any further rollout plans or next steps beyond the release described above.
