stories.Headline: Validation architect crucial for AI in software testing
stories.Summary:
AI agents can generate hundreds of tests in minutes, but they cannot decide which of those tests truly matter, according to Donovan Brady, vice president of developer relations at Leapwork. He made the point during the SD Times Live! AI in Test Supercast on November 5, and the article was published on November 11, 2026. Brady argued that organisations can hand testing work to agents without giving up accountability for quality. Vaclav Vincalek, a virtual CTO and founder of Recurrent Patterns Podcast and Media Services, also spoke at the event and questioned the wider push to treat AI as a teammate.

Brady described three ways AI agents can go wrong. They may generate incorrect tests because they lack business context, run tests at the wrong moment, or make what he called silent repairs, where an agent rewrites a failing test so it passes and hides a defect. He gave the example of asking an AI for 500 tests when perhaps only 100 are needed or tied to critical customer journeys. To address this, he proposed a "validation architect" role, a QA professional or SDET who would own business intent, critical journeys, risk priorities, coverage expectations, escalation rules, and release decisions. Agents would handle execution, such as proposing and maintaining tests, selecting suites, running them in CI/CD pipelines, and gathering evidence.

The architect would review what ran, failed, was skipped, or remained unproven, while a person keeps the final release call. Brady's advice is to begin with standing policy, requirements, approved outcomes, mandatory evidence, and escalation rules to decide what agents may do on their own. He said mechanical repairs, such as a moved button, can be left to agents, but changes to expected outcomes should be flagged for the requirement owner. He also cited a case where a 1 per cent failure rate might be acceptable on an ordinary day but not during an event like Black Friday, a judgment he said agents do not inherently make.

Brady called this approach "continuous validation," sitting between continuous integration and continuous deployment, and recommended starting small with one critical journey such as checkout. The article reports that Microsoft reportedly uses Leapwork for Dynamics 365 and Power Platform testing in Azure DevOps pipelines, cutting regression cycles from weeks to hours. Vincalek was more sceptical about the returns from AI. He compared using AI in code to driving a fast car one cannot explain, warning that it can cause harm quickly.

He said that if companies produced ten times more with AI, profits should be ten times higher, which he has not observed, and he noted that model makers still sell tokens to software firms rather than building their own ventures. He urged measuring quality over quantity and seeking technology that helps skilled people deliver better results. Brady also stressed that workflows must be re-engineered rather than having agents attached to old processes. The article notes that Leapwork Play, a Playwright-based tool with built-in agents and MCP support, became generally available on September 30.

Articles.Title: Validation architect crucial for AI in software testing

stories.Headline: Jaeger previews AI-assisted troubleshooting, GenAI trace visualisation
stories.Summary:
Jaeger, the distributed tracing project that has graduated from the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, has begun previewing its first AI-assisted troubleshooting and generative AI observability features. The announcement was published on November 11, 2026, by TechGig, and the features are available as experimental options in Jaeger v2.22. The preview is aimed at engineers who need to find faults in systems spread across many services. It is described as the project's first integrated work of this kind.

The main addition is Ask Jaeger, a natural language assistant built into the product, which lets engineers investigate traces through conversation. A separate opt-in Model Context Protocol endpoint offers nine tools for discovering services and traces, examining errors, mapping service topology, identifying critical paths, and inspecting individual spans. The preview also includes built-in diagnostic skills for root-cause analysis of errors and for detecting N+1 query problems, which give AI agents repeatable investigation workflows. Teams can enable these capabilities after downloading Jaeger and following the project's AI sidecar integration guide.

The article also describes new views built on OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions. These views are meant to help teams study model interactions, agent activity, retrieval operations, token usage, system instructions and tool execution within distributed traces. The features are presented as experimental, and the article does not name specific individuals responsible for the release. It also does not say how the features will move from preview to general availability or when that might happen.

stories.Headline: ChatGPT to offer verified AI business agents for brands
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced that ChatGPT will offer verified "Business Agents," AI assistants that represent specific brands and help users with tasks such as comparison shopping. The feature was reported on November 11, 2026, and it is rolling out in beta. It is initially limited to eligible e-commerce and online service businesses in the United States. Conversations with these agents will be clearly labeled and kept separate from ordinary ChatGPT chats. The articles do not say how many businesses will be included at launch.

Businesses can set up their agents with particular instructions and context to shape how the agents respond. Companies will also be able to claim their organization through a feature called the Business Hub and go through a verification process. The Business Hub will give participating businesses insights, including how often they are mentioned in ChatGPT responses and the top "discovery topics" where they appear. The articles describe these tools as a way to make businesses' presence in ChatGPT more formal and visible. The reporting does not specify the verification criteria or any fees.

OpenAI is the company responsible for the feature, and it has described the change as an early step toward integrating businesses more deeply into ChatGPT. According to the company, the aim is to help users make better decisions while giving businesses a new way to take part in the platform. The articles do not include any further statements from OpenAI or from brands about the rollout. They also do not say when the beta will expand beyond the United States or when it will be broadly available.

stories.Headline: Google finds technical debt derails AI coding agents
stories.Summary:
Google researchers have reported that outdated code comments and references to closed bugs can pull AI coding agents off course, a problem they call "agent distraction." The findings were highlighted in an article by Google senior staff software engineer Sam Saccone and senior staff data scientist Madhuri Garikapati, reported on November 11, 2026. According to the authors, stale technical debt such as old TODO comments and obsolete bug references gets read by agents as context, which can misdirect their work. At best this raises token consumption and execution time, and at worst it can lead agents to flawed logic and decisions. The study focused on TODO(bug/...)

comments, which often outlive the bugs they point to. Google analysed distributed traces from thousands of engineers and hundreds of millions of agent steps. About 13 per cent of sessions exposed agents to inline TODO or FIXME references, and agents acted on the referenced bug in 6 per cent of those cases. In 41 per cent of these unprompted detours, agents worked on tickets that were already closed, while in 57 per cent they addressed open bugs outside the developer's request, which the researchers classed as scope creep. These detours added 70 per cent more steps, 77 per cent more tokens, and 105 per cent more wait time per session.

Most prompts did not mention the referenced bug at all. To counter the problem, Google built scanner agents that search its codebase for obsolete TODOs, sometimes examining years of git history to confirm a comment is out of date. Once confirmed, the agents submit a pull request to remove the reference. Over six months this approach removed thousands of obsolete references, and human reviewers accepted over 95 per cent of the resulting changes.

The researchers concluded that presubmit analyzers, codebase scanners, and automated agents can reduce agent distraction and improve the effectiveness of AI coding agents. Reactions on X and LinkedIn echoed the findings, with one user noting that "comments are context too" and another comparing the behaviour to junior developers working at machine speed while raising token costs. A LinkedIn user took the high human acceptance rate as evidence that cleanup automation can work without losing human judgment. The articles provide no further details on whether Google plans to extend the cleanup tools beyond its own codebase.

Articles.Title: Google finds technical debt derails AI coding agents

stories.Headline: Airbnb CTO details multi-party AI agents for customer support
stories.Summary:
Airbnb's Chief Technology Officer, Ahmad Al-Dahle, discussed the company's deployment of multi-party AI agents to handle customer support, according to a Stack Overflow blog post republished by TechGig on November 11, 2026. The report describes how Airbnb is using several AI agents working together to manage support requests. Al-Dahle's remarks were covered in a short news item that gives few further details about the system's design or rollout. The available account is brief and does not describe the scale of the deployment or its results.

The coverage says that rigorous evaluations help engineers balance latency and accuracy in AI systems. That balance matters because a support agent must answer quickly without giving wrong responses. Al-Dahle also said that AI coding tools require a higher level of judgment from software engineering teams. The articles do not state specific figures, thresholds or timelines for these requirements. They also do not describe any formal change to Airbnb's policies or processes beyond the engineering shifts described.

Al-Dahle is identified as the speaker, and the account of his views comes from a Stack Overflow blog post that TechGig summarized. According to the report, Airbnb is reshaping its engineering organization to put generative AI into use across its platform. The item does not describe any response from outside parties or any criticism of the approach. It also gives no indication of the company's intentions beyond the general effort to adapt its engineering teams.

The item places Airbnb's work within a wider industry move toward generative AI in software and customer service. It does not say what follows next, such as product launches, follow-up statements, or further evaluations. The available information therefore stops at Al-Dahle's comments and the company's stated direction. Readers should treat the account as a summary of one interview or post rather than a full description of the company's systems.

stories.Headline: Platform ownership shapes AI infrastructure strategies, CNCF report finds
stories.Summary:
The Cloud Native Computing Foundation and SlashData released their Q3 2026 Technology Radar report on November 11, 2026, at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026. The research looked at how developers view observability, infrastructure as code, and storage technologies. Its central finding is that the way an organisation structures its platform engineering is closely tied to how it approaches AI infrastructure. The report covers tools across these three areas and tracks which of them earned an "Adopt" position.

The report ties platform ownership to AI choices. Among organisations where individual teams manage their own tooling, 54 per cent of developers use hybrid approaches for AI workflows, compared with 43 per cent where multiple teams collaboratively provide platform capabilities. Only 5 per cent of organisations building custom internal developer platforms use hybrid approaches. Among those building custom platforms, 38 per cent use a separate dedicated AI platform, while 33 per cent extend their existing developer platform.

Where platform teams curate third-party tools, 25 per cent rely primarily on AI vendor platforms. Liam Bollmann-Dodd, principal market research consultant at SlashData, said that centralised teams tend to make deliberate decisions about extending existing platforms or building dedicated AI environments. He added that distributed teams are more likely to adopt hybrid approaches. The report's findings on technology adoption were drawn from developer ratings and recommendations gathered by CNCF and SlashData.

Prometheus and OpenTelemetry earned "Adopt" positions in observability, with 80 per cent of developers rating Prometheus four or five stars for maturity. Ninety-two per cent of current and former OpenTelemetry users said they would likely recommend it, and Fluent Bit was the most recommended observability tool at 99 per cent. In infrastructure as code, OpenTofu and OpenFeature earned "Adopt" positions, and 96 per cent of OpenTofu users said they would likely recommend it. Carina earned the "Adopt" position in storage, while Crossplane, Atlantis, and cdk8s landed in "Trial."

stories.Headline: New Relic launches AI agent for Kubernetes troubleshooting
stories.Summary:
New Relic, the observability company, announced the New Relic Autopilot Kubernetes Agent, an AI tool meant to simplify troubleshooting of Kubernetes clusters, according to a TechGig report published on November 11, 2026. The agent is aimed at site reliability engineers and platform engineers who manage these clusters. It is described as a domain-specific extension of New Relic Autopilot, the company's suite of SRE agents. The report says it was unveiled that day and is currently available in public preview.

The agent runs more than 90 specialised diagnostic detectors across Kubernetes events, object descriptions, logs and APM traces to isolate root causes. It then generates context-aware remediation code, which engineers review and execute themselves. The article notes that the tool connects to New Relic's Ground Truth context engine, which is built on OpenTelemetry. It is designed to diagnose common and complex infrastructure failures such as noisy neighbours, compute resourcing problems, scheduling failures, network errors and cloud misconfigurations, including issues with Application Load Balancers and ingress.

Human-in-the-loop options are included so engineers can keep oversight during investigations. Brian Emerson, chief product officer at New Relic, said the agent brings specialised, agentic AI directly into the engineer's containerised workflows. He said the aim is to remove guesswork from complex cluster incidents while engineers stay in control. The article presents this as the purpose of the launch and does not include further assessments from outside the company.

It does not say how the agent will be priced, when it will reach general availability, or how widely it has been tested. The report describes the agent as fitting into standard SRE and platform engineering workflows rather than replacing them. It also notes that the agent works within New Relic's existing observability platform, which is why it draws on the company's telemetry data. Beyond the public preview, the article gives no timeline or next steps.

Articles.Title: New Relic launches AI agent for Kubernetes troubleshooting

stories.Headline: AttriSwarm: Orchestrating Agent Swarms for Cross-Page Visual Attribution
stories.Summary:
Researchers Suifeng Zhao, Zida Liu, Lei Sun, Xun Wang, Daojian Zeng, Jun Gao and Sujian Li have published a paper describing AttriSwarm, a framework for cross-page visual attribution in multimodal large language models. The work appeared on doi.org on November 11, 2026, and it addresses answers that are synthesized from evidence spread across several document pages. The authors say that when such answers are assembled from many pages, the connection between a conclusion and its supporting visual evidence becomes hard to see, which makes verification and trust difficult. Their system is built to restore that connection.

According to the abstract, cross-page attribution requires two steps: identifying the pages that support an answer and locating fine-grained evidence regions within those pages. Existing methods either process multiple pages jointly or refine evidence step by step in a single trajectory, which the authors say can pollute context across pages and add heavy sequential overhead in interactive settings. AttriSwarm separates these tasks among distinct roles, with a leader agent handling global reasoning across pages and subagents performing page-by-page attribution in isolation and in parallel. To support training and evaluation, the authors also built AttriDoc, a cross-page question-answering dataset that links supporting pages to annotated evidence regions.

The authors report that role-specific training on AttriDoc improved AttriSwarm over its training-free version. Averaged across three open-source backbones and three datasets, the gains were 18.94 percentage points in answer accuracy, 29.34 percentage points in page-level F1, and 23.04 percentage points in region-level IoU. The paper itself is credited to the seven named authors, and the abstract describes the results as the authors' own findings. The article content does not say how the work will be used beyond the research setting, nor does it describe any further releases or follow-up steps.

Articles.Title: AttriSwarm: Orchestrating Agent Swarms for Cross-Page Visual Attribution

stories.Headline: DreamRealm: Exploring and Materializing Hallucination Worlds for Trustworthy Vision-Language Models
stories.Summary:
DreamRealm is a post-training framework for multimodal large language models, introduced in a research paper posted to arXiv and listed on doi.org on November 11, 2026. The authors, Benlei Cui and eight co-authors, say the work addresses visual hallucinations, where a model gives wrong answers when correct responses depend on subtle visual details. The paper describes an approach that explores latent hallucinated responses, makes minimal edits to original images so the responses become valid, and trains the model to match each response to its supporting image. A data pipeline named RealmForgePipe mines hallucinations from a target model and materializes them through image editing. The authors built a dataset called the Realized Hallucination Dataset, or RealmSet, using hallucinations mined from Qwen3.5-9B.

Their training objective, named RealmMatch, builds a likelihood score matrix across image and response combinations and combines supervised learning with bidirectional contrastive losses. The aim is to reinforce correct matches and suppress mismatches between images and responses. The paper says these steps are meant to make supervision target the model's own perceptual confusions rather than generic visual contrasts. According to the paper, DreamRealm improves performance over the original Qwen3.5-9B model across six visual perception and hallucination benchmarks. The reported gains include 7.26 percentage points in HallusionBench accuracy and 11.34 percentage points in MMVP pair accuracy.

The authors also present ablation studies on their data construction and training methods, which they say support the conclusion that hallucination assignment is a promising paradigm. The paper runs 28 pages including supplementary material, and the authors have released code and a model. The article does not describe any independent review, outside reaction, or deployment plans beyond the released code and model. It also does not indicate whether the results have been peer reviewed or published in a conference or journal. The authors frame their findings as a promising direction, and any further validation would depend on follow-up work by the research community.

Articles.Title: DreamRealm: Exploring and Materializing Hallucination Worlds for Trustworthy Vision-Language Models

stories.Headline: 'Reverse Engineer Anything': AI Companies Crack Down on the Coolest Thing People Were Doing With AI
stories.Summary:
Anthropic's Claude and OpenAI's Codex have begun blocking or restricting users who try to use them for AI-assisted reverse engineering, a practice that had grown popular for tasks such as unbricking internet-of-things devices and removing surveillance ads from smart TVs. Users reported triggering "safety checks" in Claude Code, and one user, log4j, said his OpenAI account was banned for violating rules on "cyber abuse" after he used Codex to reverse engineer Samsung TVs. Other users said they had been warned or had their accounts restricted, and a project called Decomp.wtf, which made it easier to reverse engineer software and games, shut down in recent days. The restrictions came after a trend in which people used AI tools to replace manufacturers' software with open source or custom operating systems on smart TVs, baby monitors and older hardware.

An OpenAI engineer, Tarun Gogineni, said on X that the blocks were mostly accidental, stemming from difficult decision boundaries, and that there was no prohibition on reverse engineering with Codex and the problem was being fixed. Matt Brown, a security consultant who uses AI to reverse engineer devices, told 404 Media that his blocks have closely tracked the "cyber" category, and he suggested the labs may be erring toward strict guardrails to avoid criminal hacking. Brown said he is moving toward open weight models from mostly Chinese developers, which he described as improving, because he does not want to build his work around an ecosystem that could lock him out. Brown recently showed how he found hidden Bluetooth commands in a gas monitor on his propane tank using the open weight model GLM 5.3.

The article argues that the restrictions show big AI companies protecting other big companies, since AI scraping of the internet for training is tolerated while consumers using similar tools to free their own devices is not. A paper from researchers at Cornell Tech, Columbia University and New York University, published last month, argued that cheap AI-assisted reverse engineering is challenging manufacturers' control over their devices and existing intellectual property law. The article also points to camera hacking, where a YouTuber, Breno Loves Cameras, said camera makers rely on holding features back for newer models and would lose money if such hacks spread. The author concludes that this kind of work will likely move toward open source, local and uncensored models, which are less accessible to ordinary users.

Articles.Title: 'Reverse Engineer Anything': AI Companies Crack Down on the Coolest Thing People Were Doing With AI

stories.Headline: Who can be licensed as a physician? Not AI
stories.Summary:
The American Medical Association has stated that artificial intelligence cannot be licensed as a physician, cannot hold professional titles reserved for doctors, and cannot be certified to practice medicine. The position was adopted by the AMA House of Delegates at its 2026 Interim Meeting and was reported on November 10, 2026. The policy frames AI as a tool that can support clinical work but not stand in for a physician. It also calls for AI-enabled technologies to be built into physician-led care teams and used at the direction of the treating physician.

The policy sets out several requirements. AI tools used for diagnosis, prescribing and care management should have transparent, auditable evidence of their safety and efficacy, and they should be subject to appropriate regulation, documentation and liability rules. The AMA will push for legislation that sets a framework for physician oversight of AI decisions, protects physicians' independent judgment, and shields them from liability for declining to use an AI tool or for not following its recommendation. Separate model legislation would distinguish authorizing a medical technology from licensing a professional and would bar giving nonhuman entities titles reserved for physicians. The AMA also wants safeguards stopping AI developers from using patients' clinical data for proprietary or research purposes without explicit authorization.

AMA President Willie Underwood III, MD, MSc, MPH, said AI can help physicians analyze information, identify patterns and support decisions, but patients deserve to know who is responsible for their care. He added that physicians need the authority, oversight and liability protections to make independent decisions when AI is part of the care team. A companion policy on liability, which the House of Delegates directed the AMA to advocate, holds that when a physician uses an AI product as intended and exercises appropriate clinical judgment, liability for resulting patient harm should rest with the vendor, manufacturer or distributor rather than the physician. The article notes the Food and Drug Administration had authorized more than 1,450 AI-enabled medical devices as of December 2025. It also reports that the AMA released a liability framework last month.

Separate policy adopted at the same meeting addresses AI used in credentialing, privileging, peer review and quality review, and calls for physician-led oversight and transparency in those uses. Delegates also directed the AMA to oppose the use of AI to produce sexual or other exploitative material of minors and to advocate legislation prohibiting it. The article cites figures that at least 1.2 million children across 11 countries have had their images manipulated into sexually explicit deepfakes, and that 36.3% of American adolescents reported experiencing a nonconsensual AI-generated image created of them. The article does not say when any of the proposed legislation would be introduced or passed.

Articles.Title: Who can be licensed as a physician? Not AI

stories.Headline: ModalSearcher: Weaving Visual Evidence into Autonomous Cross-Modal Deep Search
stories.Summary:
A team of researchers has posted a paper on arXiv, a preprint server, describing a system called ModalSearcher that lets multimodal AI models search for information across text and images. The paper was listed on November 11, 2026, and its authors are Zhihan Yin, Ruyi Li, Chengyu Fang, Yifeng Yao, Nonghai Zhang, Pengfei Xiong, Terry Zhang, Huishuai Zhang and Dongyan Zhao. The work addresses a limitation of current models, whose built-in knowledge is static and incomplete, which hurts performance on questions about new information or those requiring several steps of evidence gathering. The authors describe the approach as autonomous cross-modal search, in which an agent chooses between reasoning on its own, text-to-text search, text-to-image search and reverse-image search.

The system relies on a training pipeline called ModalSearch-Pipeline, which builds an interleaved multimodal knowledge graph of questions with paths of varying depth and mixed modalities. According to the abstract, the procedure hides entity names and image targets that would reveal shortcuts while keeping clues needed to disambiguate the answer. The researchers trained the agent with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning in a live Web environment, and they also built a benchmark called ModalSearch-Bench. The abstract states that the 8-billion-parameter ModalSearcher-8B improves average accuracy by 16.2 points over Qwen3-VL-8B under the same agentic workflow across five multimodal knowledge-intensive question-answering benchmarks. It also reports consistent gains on independently constructed active visual-search benchmarks.

The paper is credited to the nine authors listed above, and the articles do not name any institution, funder or company that sponsored the work. The abstract reports the results as the authors' own experimental findings, and it does not indicate whether independent parties have reviewed them. The articles also do not say whether the code, model weights or benchmark will be released publicly. The research is presented as a preprint, so it has not been described as peer reviewed in the material provided. Any further developments, such as publication in a journal or conference or release of the models, are not covered in the articles.

Articles.Title: ModalSearcher: Weaving Visual Evidence into Autonomous Cross-Modal Deep Search

stories.Headline: BEAKER: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Embodied Brains in Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories
stories.Summary:
A research team led by Fei Lin and 17 co-authors posted a paper on arXiv describing BEAKER, a new benchmark for testing how well multimodal large language models can act as "embodied brains" in self-driving chemical laboratories. The paper's abstract was published on November 11, 2026, and it addresses a gap the authors see in existing tests, which mostly focus on safety, anomaly detection, or general scientific knowledge. BEAKER contains 1,000 question-answer samples spread across 11 image and video task types. The authors say all questions and annotations were manually created and reviewed by chemistry and embodied artificial intelligence experts, without AI-assisted generation.

The benchmark covers the judgments needed to carry out chemical experiments, including affordance grounding, trajectory planning, recognition of equipment, states and safety conditions, apparatus setup, operation and step reasoning, and temporal procedure reasoning. The researchers evaluated 28 models in total, drawn from general-purpose, science-oriented, chemistry-specialized and embodied categories, in an offline, single-turn setting. The results indicate that current models can follow coarse experimental procedures shown in videos. However, the paper reports that they still struggle to turn actions into operable regions and feasible trajectories, to identify fine-grained apparatus, states and safety norms, and to order steps in mid-length procedures.

The paper is credited to the 18 authors listed, with Xue Yang among them, and the abstract does not single out any one author as responsible for the findings beyond that authorship. According to the abstract, the authors frame BEAKER as a diagnostic tool, and they say it exposes a clear gap between coarse procedural understanding and the precise, action-grounded perception that laboratory execution requires. The abstract does not describe any planned follow-up work, release timeline or specific next steps. What the authors hope will happen is that future multimodal models for self-driving laboratories will be measured against this benchmark. The source material offers no further details on how the benchmark will be adopted or what it will change in practice.

Articles.Title: BEAKER: An Expert-Curated Benchmark for Embodied Brains in Self-Driving Chemical Laboratories

stories.Headline: Google broadens its AI hardware portfolio with two new specialized chips
stories.Summary:
Google on Monday unveiled two new variants of its tensor processing units, or TPUs, which are in-house chips built for AI workloads. The two chips, named TPU 8tx and TPU 8i Max, are part of the eighth generation of chips the company introduced in April this year. The launch expands Google's chip lineup to cover new uses, specifically confidential inference and larger memory capacity for heavy workloads. The company is trying to reduce its reliance on chips made by other companies for its cloud computing business.

TPU 8tx was designed with AMD and is based on the TPU 8t chip, aimed at training and running AI models confidentially. Google says the chip builds security into the hardware layer, keeping sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated even while in use. It also includes a custom inferencing network that allows it to run reasoning alongside training, so it can distill and train small models on the fly. According to Google, this could help companies train a model on proprietary data without moving that data between devices. The chip is described as useful for those cases.

TPU 8i Max combines two of the inference-focused TPU 8i chips that Google launched in April into a single package. The combination doubles memory capacity, processing power and bandwidth. The result is a chip that lets AI models handle a broader range of information during queries. The articles present these changes as the main technical differences from the earlier chips.

The launch comes as large cloud providers such as Microsoft and Amazon, along with AI labs like OpenAI and Anthropic, build their own AI-specific semiconductors and software. These companies are seeking to reduce their reliance on Nvidia, which dominates the market. The news also arrives at a sensitive time for Nvidia, whose CEO Jensen Huang admitted over the weekend to having an affair with someone alleged to be a Chinese spy. The articles do not say how that matter will affect Nvidia's business or Google's plans.

Articles.Title: Google broadens its AI hardware portfolio with two new specialized chips

stories.Headline: From Pilot to Production: The Intelligence Powering Agentic AI in Capital Markets
stories.Summary:
Agentic AI, which refers to systems that carry out tasks with some degree of autonomy, is moving from pilot projects into production across the financial services industry. A sponsored HBR webinar, produced with AWS and Moody's and dated November 10, 2026, presents the shift as a matter of enterprise readiness rather than model capability alone. The piece says success depends on trust, auditability, high-quality data, and context. It describes the shift as already under way without giving figures on how many firms have made it. The article says the stakes in finance are high, since mistakes carry severe risks and costs.

Organizations must balance accuracy, latency, and cost efficiency while meeting regulatory demands for open questioning and sourcing of outputs. They are also expected to keep full audit logs of what their systems do. The piece presents these requirements as the reason production deployment is harder than a pilot. The article argues that leaders cannot build every part of agentic AI alone and should look to partners with subject matter expertise and a reliable platform. It recommends starting small with discrete tasks suited to AI.

It also advises organizing data, prioritizing governance, and involving risk teams early. The piece is written as advice from the sponsor side and names no outside regulator or firm in connection with these recommendations. The article frames this as a general industry trend and does not describe a specific event, deadline, or regulatory action. It points readers to a Moody's webinar and a specialist contact for further discussion. Beyond the webinar invitation, the piece does not say what comes next for the sector.

Articles.Title: From Pilot to Production: The Intelligence Powering Agentic AI in Capital Markets

stories.Headline: Helping caregivers use AI in everyday life
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced on November 10, 2026, that it is running free, in-person ChatGPT workshops for caregivers during National Family Caregivers Month. The workshops, called the AI Skills Jam for Caregivers & Community Health, are hosted by OpenAI Academy in collaboration with Caregiver Action Network, Alzheimer's Association, and American Diabetes Association. The events will take place across five U.S. cities and are aimed at family and individual caregivers, caregiver support organizations, and people living with chronic or serious health conditions. No coding or technical background is needed to take part.

The workshops are meant to show participants how ChatGPT can help with tasks such as resource navigation, peer support, and caregiver support. Participants will also learn to use AI responsibly, including how to protect personal information and recognize the limits of these tools. The company says the tools should complement, not replace, medical, legal, or financial advice, and participants will learn when to consult healthcare professionals. OpenAI facilitators and mentors will provide hands-on help throughout each session. The company cites an internal analysis estimating that more than 40 million weekly ChatGPT messages about U.S. healthcare ask about care for someone else.

OpenAI's Chief Global Affairs Officer, Chris Lehane, said AI can give families more control over their lives, reducing time spent organizing schedules and searching for information. Caregiver Action Network CEO Marvell Adams Jr. said the goal is to make caregiving more manageable without replacing human connection, and that the tools must be built around caregivers' needs. Alzheimer's Association Chief Programs and Mission Engagement Officer Katie Evans said responsible AI tools could make everyday tasks more manageable, and American Diabetes Association CEO Charles "Chuck" Henderson said the association is working with AI platforms to ensure they draw on its latest guidelines. The AI Skills Jam is part of OpenAI Academy's wider work, which has already included events with nonprofits, small businesses, K–12 educators, and older adults.

Articles.Title: Helping caregivers use AI in everyday life

stories.Headline: How Allina Health decides where hospital AI can help
stories.Summary:
Allina Health, a 12-hospital health system serving Minnesota and Western Wisconsin, has described in an interview published November 10, 2026, how it decides where artificial intelligence can help its hospitals. The account comes from Dominica Tallarico, the system's chief operating officer, who explained the approach to Healthcare IT News. The system starts by asking which problems the technology is best suited to address, and it measures ideas against four goals: whether they improve quality and safety, make care more accessible, support clinicians, or create a better patient experience. Allina's digital officers and IT leaders guide strategy and implementation, while Tallarico's role is to enable that strategy and connect people, processes and care settings across the organization.

The article gives several examples of the work so far. Allina uses a sensor in every recovery room that lets the care team alert environmental services when a patient has left, which reduces disturbances and helps time cleaning. The system partnered with Qventus, an AI and machine learning software company, to test early-stage tools on operational problems, and Tallarico said this work has unlocked 689 hours of robotics capacity and produced a nearly six-times annualized return on investment from the vendor's Surgical Growth Solution. Allina has set goals to reduce surgery cancellations within 72 hours and to better estimate same-day discharges, noting that a cancelled surgery costs between $3,350 and $8,600 in administrative rework, operating room time and surgeon downtime. The system is also in early stages of auto-populating discharge plans, which the article says has brought discharge times earlier, improved mobility and shortened length of stay across the organization.

Tallarico said the system views AI as foundational rather than as a layer added to the electronic health record, and that it looks for partners willing to learn the details of frontline challenges and who are focused on security and protecting patients. She said Allina is applying AI mainly to intake, scheduling and discharge, which she called administrative areas in need of refinement across the industry. She also said the system does not see the technology as a replacement for clinical judgment and is working to guard against automation that is unnecessary or overrides human decisions. The article does not describe any specific next steps beyond continuing the phased rollout and expanding discharge planning efforts.

Articles.Title: How Allina Health decides where hospital AI can help

stories.Headline: U.K. to Develop North Atlantic Network of Drones, AI Systems to Find Russian Subs
stories.Summary:
The U.K. Ministry of Defence announced on Tuesday that it will invest in a network of drones, sensors and artificial intelligence systems to help the Royal Navy counter Russian submarines in the North Atlantic. The project, called Atlantic Net, is meant to help the navy better protect undersea cables and energy networks from Russian threats. The ministry's release describes a £90 million investment, while a separate report on the project gives a figure of $120 million. U.K. company Ocean Infinity Solutions was selected to deliver the network.

Atlantic Net will bring together maritime systems, underwater sensing, communications, remote operations and data services into a single capability directed by the Royal Navy. It is the first phase of the navy's Atlantic Bastion program, a plan to build a hybrid naval force that can hunt and track enemy submarines. The new systems include advanced sensors to detect Russian submarines and illegal activity, along with uncrewed systems that can patrol underwater. The ministry did not disclose when the network will enter service.

Luke Pollard, the U.K. Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said the threats beneath the North Atlantic are changing and the country is changing with them. Ocean Infinity, named the Commercial Mission Partner for Atlantic Net, said the project would apply its robotics experience to anti-submarine warfare. Joe Robinson, president of Solutions at Ocean Infinity, described the project as a move beyond heavily crewed fleets toward robotic and lean-crewed platforms. Ocean Infinity operates a 14-ship fleet of minimally crewed vessels and has previously carried out several well-known underwater searches.

The announcement comes as NATO began Dynamic Merlin 26, an anti-submarine warfare exercise, in the Baltic Sea off Sweden on Monday. The exercise tests participating ships against submarine, anti-ship missile and drone threats, and includes submarines from Germany and Sweden. NATO officials said the exercise reflects growing concern about threats in the Baltic region. The articles do not say whether Atlantic Net is linked to the NATO exercise beyond the shared focus on undersea threats.

Articles.Title: U.K. to Develop North Atlantic Network of Drones, AI Systems to Find Russian Subs

stories.Headline: GREP: Grounding Generated Room Evaluation in Principles
stories.Summary:
A new research paper titled GREP, short for Grounding Generated Room Evaluation in Principles, was posted on November 11, 2026, by a team of seven authors led by Mohan Cao. The work addresses a gap in how computer-generated furnished rooms are judged, since existing evaluations look only at narrow perspectives or fixed questions. The authors say this leaves no reliable way to assess overall scene quality. They describe the paper as one of the cs.CV, cs.AI and cs.GR categories on arXiv, a preprint server. The core of the approach is a three-tier philosophy rather than a set of predefined questions.

The first tier, basic physical validity, checks whether a scene obeys physical constraints. The second, visual coherence, examines whether objects agree in scale, style and composition. The highest tier, human-use logic, requires that object arrangements match everyday human habits. Guided by these principles, an evaluation agent identifies issues from the scene context, gathers evidence, and produces scores and reports. According to the authors, GREP reached 87% agreement with the majority preferences of human judges, which they say substantially outperforms baseline evaluators.

They also report that GREP's written reports, when used to refine scenes, improved scene quality, while score-only and no-feedback baselines showed slight declines. The paper further suggests that as planning ability improves, recent models such as GPT-5.6 Sol can begin to challenge the pipelines and guidance imposed on them, yet still lack the ability to resolve the resulting conflicts. The authors expect stronger models to plan well and also adapt more flexibly to external guidance and constraints. The paper is available as a PDF and HTML version, with a project page linked by the authors. The articles do not say what follow-up work, adoption or peer review is planned.

Articles.Title: GREP: Grounding Generated Room Evaluation in Principles

stories.Headline: This New Linux-Based Desktop Operating System Is Built for AI Nerds
stories.Summary:
Kora, a new desktop operating system built on the Linux kernel, was announced on a Tuesday by its startup company, with Wired reporting on the launch on November 10, 2026. The company's chief executive and cofounder, Kirt McMaster, says the product is aimed at what he calls "the AI native, not mass market," meaning creators and developers rather than the general public. The central idea is to bring multiple AI models together at the system level, so that users can work with different providers without bouncing between desktop apps and browser tabs. Kora is scheduled to launch sometime in 2027.

The system is designed around a "neural file system" that indexes files by meaning, so a user can search for a document by a small remembered detail rather than an exact file name. Kora runs directly on hardware and is being brought to Snapdragon PCs through a partnership with Qualcomm next year, and it also supports x86-64 processors, so it may install on current Intel- or AMD-based machines. Built-in compatibility layers are meant to let users run standard Windows apps, and the company is developing its own apps for contacts, calendar and email along with a software development kit for third-party developers. The product grew out of McMaster's earlier startup Playtron, and its GameFrame component carries over the architecture of Playtron's GameOS so users can run PC games, provided their hardware can keep up. The company is optimizing Kora for desktop machines with at least 64 gigabytes of RAM, twice the memory of the top Googlebook laptop.

McMaster, who also cofounded Boost Mobile and the Android fork Cyanogen, leads a company of under 100 people alongside cofounders Franck De Girolami and John Lagerling. De Girolami helped develop Playtron's GameOS, and Lagerling previously worked on Android at Google. McMaster has said that the company can change faster than Windows and macOS, which he describes as hard to alter given their billion-user bases. He has compared his targeting of creators to how Steve Jobs focused on creators when pushing the Mac into desktop publishing.

Kora is not the first desktop system rethinking the operating system for the AI era, since Google launched its Googlebook OS and compatible laptops in October, built around Gemini. McMaster does not believe that product, with its Android support, will satisfy power users who need serious chip power to run demanding AI models. The article does not describe any further pricing, release date beyond 2027, or independent testing, so the company's claims remain untested. More to follow.

Articles.Title: This New Linux-Based Desktop Operating System Is Built for AI Nerds

stories.Headline: Why Relying on AI for Medical Diagnoses Can Be Risky
stories.Summary:
Cedars-Sinai chief medical informatics officer Yaron Elad, MD, a cardiologist, told Becker's Clinical Leadership that patients increasingly bring AI-generated diagnoses, treatment ideas and questions to their doctor appointments. He said patients tend to trust AI more than they trusted their earlier internet searches, because AI tools usually draw on cited sources while search results can lead to information that lacks evidence. Some patients arrive with printed AI queries, while others bring a list of generated questions to discuss. Elad said patients often apologize for this, worried that they are challenging their doctor.

His main concern is accuracy, since physicians are trained to spot flawed AI output but patients may not be able to tell when advice is unsuitable for their situation or is simply wrong. He said that AI can produce hallucinations, meaning invented or incorrect content, and patients may not notice them. Elad also addressed patients who use personal AI tools to record appointments, noting that California law requires a doctor's consent for this. He said he would not object himself, but warned that AI-generated notes often contain errors that need physician review, and that a patient using such tools loses the benefit of that review.

Elad said he encourages patients to share their AI findings with their physicians, adding that he knows of no clinician at Cedars-Sinai who is offended by a patient doing their own research. In his view, physicians can help filter out inaccuracies when they see what patients have found. The article presents this as a practical approach rather than a rejection of AI. The piece is published on the Cedars-Sinai website and summarizes an interview first published by Becker's Clinical Leadership.

Articles.Title: Why Relying on AI for Medical Diagnoses Can Be Risky

stories.Headline: Improper AI use leads to another data incident, more patient notifications
stories.Summary:
Weill Cornell Medicine says that protected health information from a radiology research project at NewYork-Presbyterian was entered into artificial intelligence tools and processed using machine learning without authorization. The incident occurred during a radiology research study in June, and the institution discovered it on September 6 and launched an investigation. Patients are now being told that some of their information may have been breached. The notice to patients was sent in the week before the report, and the health system described the matter as an unauthorized use of an AI model.

The data involved was limited, according to the health system, and officials said there is no indication that any patient information has been misused. The exposed information included medical record numbers and radiology accession numbers, which are internal tracking identifiers for images. It may also have included dates and times of radiology services, the locations where patients received care, and clinical details such as diagnoses, treatment, surgical and procedural histories, and medication information. Names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, Social Security numbers, and patient-specific financial information were not included, officials said.

Weill Cornell leaders said they suspended the research activity once the problem was found and asked that all involved data be deleted. They also said they have provided additional education to reinforce compliance with the institution's requirements for appropriate AI use and patient privacy. The health system said it has not so far found evidence that unauthorized individuals accessed patients' protected health information. Leaders expressed regret for any concern the incident may cause and said they are expanding security measures and providing additional training.

The report places this case alongside a recent breach at Johns Hopkins, where a staff member at Bayview Medical Center reportedly uploaded a spreadsheet to a public AI website that had not been approved for use, exposing data of more than 3,000 patients. The article notes that as generative and agentic AI tools spread through healthcare, IT and security teams must stay vigilant about which technologies are used and how. It argues such third-party tools call for more robust oversight and staff education. The article does not say what further regulatory steps or patient follow-up will occur.

Articles.Title: Improper AI use leads to another data incident, more patient notifications

stories.Headline: Brazil's AI Development Strategy Needs an Edge Layer
stories.Summary:
Brazil's government announced in August that it will invest 2.3 billion reais ($444.2 million) in two AI projects, including a supercomputing partnership with China's Huawei and iFlytek and a tender for a second supercomputer. These systems are meant to run on centralized data gathered and entrusted to the government, supporting public services such as digital public tools, automated procurement assistance, and telehealth transcription. Esther Dweck, Brazil's Minister of Management and Innovation in Public Services, has described a strategy called "Base de Dados Brasil" that would centralize, integrate, and protect citizens' data for use in AI training. The article argues this focus overlooks edge AI, in which inference runs on local hardware instead of distant data centers.

The article contends that many public and private AI uses in Brazil do not need frontier capabilities and instead need reliable, bounded, locally controlled inference along with workers who can maintain it. It gives examples of edge AI in industry, such as defect detection on textile or footwear lines, predictive maintenance in packaging and food processing, and structural monitoring on mining sites. It also says local edge infrastructure is an industrial policy choice that trains people to maintain hardware that cannot be offshored. By contrast, a July 2026 Getulio Vargas Foundation study estimated that for a 100-megawatt data center, 85% of jobs are tied to construction and only about 4% become permanent operation and maintenance roles. The author adds that a 2025 WEF and Accenture review describes China organizing industrial AI by sector needs, with provinces building clusters around their own strengths.

The author states that Brazil's Nova Indústria Brasil policy, launched in January 2024, sets aside 300 billion reais (about $58 billion) in financing through 2026 for six missions with targets for 2033, and that it has yet to incorporate regional integration or local AI policy. Andrew Ng, co-founder of Google Brain and former chief scientist at Baidu, has argued in a 2022 IEEE Spectrum interview that small, specialized models trained on good data, sometimes with as few as 50 examples, can serve manufacturing better than giant models. The article notes that the policy's fourth mission concerns digital transformation on the factory floor, while Minister Dweck's public remarks have centered on national data infrastructure and a unified digital identity. It also points out that the Redata regime (Lei 15.504/2026, signed September 2026) suspends federal taxes on electronic components and IT equipment only for companies with approved data center projects, excluding Simples Nacional enrollees.

The article describes Brazil's large, mostly informal repair workforce, where informality likely exceeds the national rate of 37.5% reported by IBGE. It estimates roughly 480 million computers, tablets, and smartphones are in active use in the country, and argues that this repair market sustains specialized technical labor that edge AI policy could formalize and extend. It says that repair workers are sometimes treated as targets by police rather than as technicians. The author also cites Brazil's Pix payment system as an example of centrally standardized digital public infrastructure. As a concrete edge case, the CESAR innovation center's Manaus unit and UCB Power developed a computer vision system for inspecting battery components at UCB Power's factory in the Amazon, using a 4K camera and local processing.

The article also reports education and labor figures that it presents as limits on the centralized path. According to Brazil's Ministry of Labor and Employment, 84% of employed young Brazilians work in jobs that do not require specific qualifications, and only 1 in 7 holds a technical or higher-level post. A 2025 CIEE and Instituto Locomotiva survey found that only 12% of high school students want to pursue engineering. In the PISA 2025 results published in September, Brazil again scored below the OECD average in math. The article argues the scarce resource in edge AI is technicians rather than silicon.

Articles.Title: Brazil's AI Development Strategy Needs an Edge Layer

stories.Headline: Incremental prognostic value of CT radiomics and deep learning beyond complete tumor volume in non-small cell lung cancer: a reanalysis of LUNG1
stories.Summary:
A reanalysis of the publicly available LUNG1 dataset, published in BMC Medical Imaging by Qiang Zhao, Shanwu Ma, F. Chen and colleagues, tested whether CT radiomics and deep learning add to survival prediction in non-small cell lung cancer beyond a simple measure of tumor volume. The team worked with 420 patients from the NSCLC-Radiomics collection, 372 of whom had died, and the work was shared early as an accepted, citable article before final typesetting. The study compared complete gross tumor volume alone, 107 radiomic features extracted from original images, a fixed pretrained 3D convolutional neural network, and a fusion of radiomic and deep learning features. Model evaluation used repeated five-fold cross-validation, with preprocessing and model fitting restricted to training patients to avoid data leakage.

The researchers also checked whether a fixed 96-millimeter cubic crop covered each tumor fully, and found that it cut off part of the tumor in 64 of the 420 patients. On the initial fold assignment, the mean concordance index was 0.585 for tumor volume, 0.567 for volume plus radiomics, 0.571 for clinical plus radiomics, 0.514 for the frozen network and 0.569 for fusion. Across 20 repetitions, the mean concordance index was 0.588 for volume alone, 0.577 for volume plus radiomics and 0.568 for fusion. The authors reported that the confidence intervals for the radiomics-minus-volume and fusion-minus-volume differences crossed zero, and that harmonizing scans across reconstruction kernels with ComBat in a 295-patient subset gave no clear improvement. A separate 46-patient cohort from NSCLC Radiogenomics, with 14 deaths, was too small for comparative validation.

The authors, affiliated with the Center for Precision Cancer Medicine and Translational Research at Tianjin Cancer Hospital Airport Hospital in Tianjin, China, concluded that in this cohort the complete-volume radiomic and fusion models did not show a stable gain in held-out survival prediction over complete tumor volume. They said their findings support measuring the full tumor contour, validating without leakage, and replicating the work in an independent, population-matched cohort. The study was funded by the China Association for Promotion of Health Science and Technology, and the authors declared no competing interests. The articles do not describe any planned follow-up study beyond that recommended replication.

Articles.Title: Incremental prognostic value of CT radiomics and deep learning beyond complete tumor volume in non-small cell lung cancer: a reanalysis of LUNG1

stories.Headline: Adaptive Neural Subspaces with Geometry-Aware Quadrature for Interface Problems
stories.Summary:
The articles here are a single preprint abstract posted on Research Square, a platform where manuscripts appear before any journal peer review, with a timestamp of November 11, 2026. The preprint describes a new machine learning method for solving interface problems, which are mathematical problems involving boundaries where material properties change abruptly. The authors combine neural networks, numerical quadrature schemes, and adaptive subspace approximation, and they say the neural network is used to build the basis functions of a finite-dimensional subspace on which the discrete solution is then computed. They also say the method can handle singularities that arise at such interfaces when paired with high precision integration. The abstract reports that the approach achieves high accuracy in simulations, though it gives no specific figures.

The method includes an a posteriori error estimator derived from the hypercircle technique within the subspace approximation framework. According to the abstract, this estimator serves as the loss function used to adaptively refine the neural network parameters. The authors say the design of these loss functions depends on a high precision numerical integration scheme to reach the reported accuracy. The source does not provide the names of the authors, the institutions involved, the specific test problems, or any quantitative error comparisons against other methods.

The preprint lists no competing interests. Because it has not yet been peer reviewed by a journal, its claims about accuracy and singularity handling have not been independently checked. The articles do not say whether or when the work will be submitted to a journal or what follow-up the authors plan. Details on those points would need to come from the full text or from later publication.

Articles.Title: Adaptive Neural Subspaces with Geometry-Aware Quadrature for Interface Problems

stories.Headline: AI Takes Center Stage at Tech-Forward AFM With Innovation Hub and AFM House Expansion
stories.Summary:
The American Film Market, the five-day independent film marketplace in Los Angeles produced by the Independent Film and Television Alliance, is putting artificial intelligence at the center of its 2026 edition. The market is expanding its Innovation Hub, a space where exhibitors show off new technologies reshaping Hollywood, and is opening its first AFM House, a 15,000-square-foot venue across from the AFM headquarters at the Fairmont Century Plaza. Nearly 20 companies are now set to take part in the Hub, and a new run of panels will discuss AI's impact on the industry. The Hub began last year in collaboration with the Marché du Film, the Cannes Film Festival's marketplace, which also leaned heavily into AI this year.

The growth reflects a wider change in how Hollywood views the technology in production, sales and distribution. Jackie Brenneman, who is leading her first AFM after becoming IFTA president in January, says technology will be a key driver whatever people think about AI. She draws a distinction between AI as a creative tool, which draws more debate, and AI used to analyze data and make predictions, which she says has been in use for a long time. Among the returning participants is Largo.ai, a Swiss firm backed by Sylvester Stallone, which uses AI to help determine whether an idea is producible and offers tools such as simulated focus groups. Its CEO, Sami Arpa, says the company is data-assisted rather than eager to bring AI into the creative process, and he acknowledges that some tools go further and replace human creativity.

Other companies are pushing further into fully AI-generated work. Oxen.ai, founded in 2022 by former IBM veteran Greg Schoeninger, operates as both a platform for building AI shots and a studio that produces them for clients. Its founder says the company publishes the token cost of each model before users pay, a transparency he believes sets it apart from competitors that rely on monthly subscriptions. Schoeninger says AFM approached the company after its September summit, and he describes the industry as reaching a tipping point where more executives are willing to discuss their use of AI openly. AFM panels will also cover the topic, including a Producers Guild of America session on the AI decisions facing film and television leaders and a discussion hosted by the Cine Group.

The approach carries some risk, as seen when the Urbanworld festival lost a longtime sponsor, the Writers Guild of America, after hosting an AI program. Major festivals such as Cannes exclude AI-generated films from their official selections. Brenneman says the market is not a festival and makes no selections, leaving those judgments to buyers, whose role is to decide which films reach audiences. Her stated job is to provide a forum where that can happen. The articles do not report how attendance or deals at this year's market turn out.

Articles.Title: AI Takes Center Stage at Tech-Forward AFM With Innovation Hub and AFM House Expansion

stories.Headline: Anthropic heads for lower than expected $1.3 trillion valuation in stock market debut
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the artificial intelligence company behind the Claude chatbot, is heading for a stock market debut that could value it at around $1.3 trillion, below the $2 trillion some backers predicted in the summer. The loss-making firm plans to list its shares on New York's Nasdaq exchange this month, offering them at between $70 and $78 each and raising up to $64 billion. Anthropic will trade under the symbol ANT from 19 November, and it will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public. The listing is set against a volatile period for big technology firms, after the Nasdaq fell sharply following last week's US midterm elections over concerns that a Democrat-led Congress could slow AI development and the building of data centres.

The company's latest results for the six months to the end of June show revenue rising to $16.2 billion from $1.1 billion a year earlier. Its pre-tax loss, however, grew to $80.7 billion from $12.9 billion over the same period. Anthropic has told investors that its future success depends largely on developing the most advanced AI models, and that any failure to do so could hurt its business. The valuation range is also below that of SpaceX, Elon Musk's rocket, satellite and AI company, which listed in June at a value of nearly $1.8 trillion.

Fiona Cincotta, a senior market analyst at City Index, described the $64 billion fundraising as fairly bullish given the recent volatility and concerns about AI. She said it suggests the company remains upbeat about AI demand. Anthropic has also acknowledged in a recent warning that advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity if they were misused or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy without proper safeguards. The company has said it remains committed to developing AI that benefits people. The company was co-founded in 2021 by Dario and Daniela Amodei and five others, all of whom previously worked at OpenAI, the rival behind ChatGPT, which plans its own listing early next year.

Articles.Title: Anthropic heads for lower than expected $1.3 trillion valuation in stock market debut

stories.Headline: 8 questions for the Wells Fargo wealth unit’s AI chief
stories.Summary:
Wells Fargo's wealth and investment management unit has been using an AI assistant called AI Teammate, according to an interview with Andre Mansour, the bank's head of artificial intelligence, published by Banking Dive on November 10, 2026. Mansour joined Wells Fargo about six months earlier from Google and helped launch the tool, which was rolled out in the most recent quarter. The assistant works as a conversational layer over Advisor Gateway, a single platform with more than 200 tools that advisers use daily. Mansour said it has handled hundreds of thousands of interactions, and tasks that once took hours now take minutes.

The main gains, he said, come from reducing the clicks and time advisers and client associates spend gathering information and building client materials. Meeting preparation is the clearest example, since the assistant can combine investment research, client relationship notes and to-do items into an agenda in a prompt or two. Mansour also described using it to summarize daily investment insights from the Wells Fargo Investment Institute instead of reading each report. He framed the change as making advisers faster while leaving the job's outcomes unchanged.

Mansour said Wells Fargo intends to move quickly but not at the expense of safety, and he pointed to protections for client data and investment guidance kept within set guidelines. He also addressed the expected transfer of wealth to millennials and Gen Z, describing two channels: a consumer AI product called Fargo, which he said has logged over a billion interactions, and advisers who review what clients get from their own AI agents. He argued that experienced advisers remain essential and imagined a future where AI agents handle monitoring and research while humans make the decisions. The interview was edited for clarity and brevity.

Articles.Title: 8 questions for the Wells Fargo wealth unit’s AI chief

stories.Headline: As AI Anxiety Grows, UVA Symposium to Examine What Human Flourishing Looks Like in an AI-Driven World
stories.Summary:
The University of Virginia's Contemplative Sciences Center will host AI Anxiety + Human Flourishing, a public symposium on November 18 and 19, 2026, at the Contemplative Commons. The event asks how the future generation can be prepared for artificial intelligence and brings together students, technologists, thought leaders and contemplative practitioners. Its focus is on emerging adults and the stresses that rapid AI adoption places on them. The Contemplative Commons opened to the public in fall 2024 as a space for contemplative research and practice.

The program will address AI's effects on work and higher education, youth mental health, AI ethics and the wider social consequences of new technologies. Its proceedings will form the basis of an undergraduate course on AI Anxiety at UVA, and a model of that course will be available to other universities. Speakers named in the announcement include Anton Korinek of Anthropic, who is on leave as a UVA economics professor, Bethany Teachman of UVA's Thriving Youth in a Digital Environment initiative, Father Michael Baggot of the Pontifical Athenaeum Regina Apostolorum and Paul Tudor Jones of Tudor Investment Corporation. The symposium is organized around four themes: AI anxiety, human agency, contemplative interventions and possible futures. Registration and the full program are posted on the center's website.

Michael Sheehy, research associate professor and director of research at the Contemplative Sciences Center, said that young people feel existential dread about their jobs, relationships and how they will raise their children, and that the center feels compelled to respond. He argued that the emergence of AI also invites people to reflect more deeply on what it means to be human, and that difficult human experiences can inform how people relate to AI. UVA President Scott Beardsley said AI should serve humanity and that the university is well placed to bring together experts across disciplines. The symposium falls under the university's AI + Human Flourishing Initiative, which studies how AI can support human wellbeing and how lived knowledge of flourishing can guide the design of AI systems.

Articles.Title: As AI Anxiety Grows, UVA Symposium to Examine What Human Flourishing Looks Like in an AI-Driven World | Newswise

stories.Headline: The AI boom could shift diesel generators from backup to everyday use
stories.Summary:
During mid-October 2026, when the grid is normally in a slack season, a spell of unseasonable warmth led the U.S. Department of Energy, at PJM Interconnection's request, to issue an emergency order from October 13 to 16 to avoid blackouts. The order allowed PJM to direct backup generation at large loads such as data centers to run. Earlier, on July 2, PJM recorded its highest-ever unrestricted demand at 168 GW during a heat dome over the Mid-Atlantic. Utility executives in Northern Virginia said they came within minutes of calling on the backup generator fleets at data centers. Similar emergency authority was invoked 13 times this year, seven of them in PJM, after DOE in January authorized grid operators to tap as much as 35 GW of idle backup generation.

The authors, from Inlyte Energy, argue that this shift could turn diesel generators built for emergencies into a routine source of grid capacity. Diesel units emit nitrous oxides and particulate matter, and a study of Northern Virginia data centers found that running them up to permitted limits would raise the region's total nitrous oxide emissions by 45 percent. That study also found the most exposed census blocks tend to have lower household incomes. Residents in Loudoun County described continuous generator noise during an earlier emergency as like airplanes landing for more than 24 hours. Virginia has directed regulators to review the cumulative impact of backup generation and to consider batteries, load flexibility, fuel cells and other non-diesel options.

The authors say that batteries can cut a data center's grid demand during short stress periods, but today's lithium-ion systems typically last only two or four hours. Once those run out, they say, the default fallback is diesel or natural gas generation, which would make a clean resource dirty. They recommend long-duration energy storage lasting 24, 48 or even 72 hours, which could replace diesel backup while also supporting the grid every day. They also urge policymakers to avoid simply defaulting to diesel, and to reward behind-the-meter long-duration storage through capacity accreditation, procurement mandates and rebate changes that now favor shorter durations.

The article describes these as the authors' views and notes that new battery chemistries are emerging that use more abundant materials and need less land. The authors frame their case against a backdrop of public backlash that shaped last week's midterm results, and new state data center rules signed in September in Virginia, Massachusetts, Maryland and California. They argue that if regulators do not act, diesel reliance could become the default for the U.S. grid. The piece also notes that PJM has sought emergency approval to curtail data centers and large loads during hot weather, and that PJM is weighing reliability requirements for data centers and crypto loads after 3.8 GW of load tripped offline.

Articles.Title: The AI boom could shift diesel generators from backup to everyday use

stories.Headline: New York’s Hochul launches nation’s first state AI testing program
stories.Summary:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul has launched what her office calls the first state program to independently test artificial intelligence systems, and she announced it publicly on a Tuesday after first sharing it with Decoded by POLITICO. The program also aims to train a new generation of AI safety experts. The move follows public concern about the technology, including hacks involving AI models and warnings from researchers at leading labs. It comes as President Donald Trump has declined to pursue federal safeguards for AI, having earlier called AI safety fears a hoax and instead backing a voluntary safety framework that has only been shared with companies.

Hochul, a Democrat, said the federal government is failing to act while New York is leading on AI safety and holding large technology companies accountable. She told POLITICO that the stakes are too high to simply take AI companies at their word. The new center is funded by a $30 million gift from Tom Secunda, a co-founder of Bloomberg, and a $25 million research investment from the State University of New York and the state. It is set to open before the state's major AI safety law, the RAISE Act, takes effect on January 1.

That law will require AI companies operating in New York to submit detailed safety frameworks, which Hochul's office hopes researchers at the center will scrutinize. The articles present Hochul as the official driving the initiative, with her office describing the effort as a response to federal inaction. Her quoted remarks frame the program as a way to check claims made by AI companies rather than rely on them. The articles do not describe any federal or company response to the program.

They also do not give details on how the testing will be carried out, what staff the center will have, or what consequences companies could face from its findings. The launch sits within a broader debate over who should set rules for artificial intelligence, with states moving ahead while Washington has not adopted binding federal safeguards. The articles do not say what happens next beyond the center opening and the RAISE Act taking effect on January 1. More to follow.

Articles.Title: New York’s Hochul launches nation’s first state AI testing program

stories.Headline: AI agents promise to do everyday tasks. Uber, DoorDash, and Airbnb say barely anyone is using them
stories.Summary:
Executives at Uber, DoorDash, and Airbnb have reported that AI agents, which AI companies promote as tools that can handle everyday errands such as booking trips, ordering food, and shopping, are barely being used for those tasks. Uber's chief financial officer, Balaji Krishnamurthy, said on the company's November 4 third-quarter earnings call that AI agents booked only four rides and 500 Uber Eats deliveries during the week of Halloween, out of 320 million combined rides and deliveries. DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said on the company's October 29 earnings call that agents had generated "maybe several hundred orders" since launching. Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots both launched in September.

Airbnb's situation is similar. CEO Brian Chesky told analysts on the November 5 earnings call that a "very non-material number" of the company's nearly half a million daily bookings come through AI agents, including Muse and Instinct. Meanwhile, all three companies are building their own AI tools for customers. Uber Eats offers Cart Assistance, which fills a basket from an uploaded grocery list or recipe screenshot, and Khosrowshahi said baskets built this way are roughly twice the average size. DoorDash offers Ask DoorDash and Text DoorDash, and Airbnb plans to roll out its own trip-planning agent early next year.

The executives and outside experts offer several explanations. Uber's Khosrowshahi noted that ordering a ride takes a median of 50 seconds and ordering food takes 90 seconds, so customers have little reason to hand those jobs to an agent. Matt Maher, founder and CEO of M7 Innovations, said big tech firms are overcomplicating simple tasks, and Chesky said travelers enjoy researching trips, which general-purpose agents do not handle well. Michael Klein of Talkdesk added that shoppers want to know how their data and payment details will be used before they trust agents with them. Uber's Khosrowshahi also said the company is negotiating terms with third-party AI systems and sees them as another way to reach its platform.

Articles.Title: AI agents promise to do everyday tasks. Uber, DoorDash, and Airbnb say barely anyone is using them

stories.Headline: UA regents delay statement of intent on AI amid feedback
stories.Summary:
The University of Alaska Board of Regents has postponed the release of a statement of intent that would govern how the university system uses artificial intelligence. The delay came after the board received feedback on the draft, and the regents chose to hold the document back rather than publish it on schedule. The Alaska News Source reported the postponement on November 10, 2026. The articles available describe the delay itself but do not spell out the specific contents of the statement or a new release date. The regents' decision means the university system has not yet made public its formal position on AI, which is the purpose the statement was meant to serve.

Because the document was pulled back for further input, the wording and scope of any eventual version remain unsettled.
