At the event he also described a hypothetical scenario in which a software update or cyberattack causes a million robots from one manufacturer to perform the same dangerous action at once. A humanoid robot developed in the laboratory of Professor Yuval Elovici appeared on stage during the address.

Karadi's warning follows a series of Iranian cyber campaigns against Israel. In March he said the Shin Bet and the National Cyber Directorate had thwarted Iranian attempts to gather intelligence on security personnel, defense companies and their relatives, including attempts to take control of surveillance cameras. The Directorate counted 50 attempts to penetrate public camera systems since the start of the war, plus another 50 cases in which attackers entered organizational systems and deleted critical data. It also reported issuing 2,304 targeted cyber alerts to organizations in 2025, an increase of nearly 350 percent over the previous year. Microsoft's annual cyber defense report, published in October, ranked Israel as the second most targeted country for cyber activity between July 2025 and June 2026, behind only the United States, and identified Iran as the leading state-backed source of operations against Israel.

Karadi had already urged Israeli company executives and board members in May to prepare for a new generation of AI models able to find security vulnerabilities and carry out complex attack sequences. He warned that skills once limited to highly trained specialists were becoming more accessible and that traditional defenses alone would no longer suffice. The articles do not describe any specific new Iranian AI-driven attack or any new regulatory requirement. They also do not say what further steps Israel or other governments plan to take in response to the warning.

Articles.Title: Israel warns Iran is seeking AI-powered cyberattack capabilities

stories.Headline: Where AI Can Strengthen Clinical Research, and Where Patient Input is More Important
stories.Summary:
Stacy Hurt, chief patient officer at Parexel, discussed how artificial intelligence can be used in clinical research in an interview with Pharmaceutical Executive, published November 10, 2026. Her central point is that the question facing the pharma and biotech industries is less whether AI should be used and more when it should be used. She says AI can make trials faster and smarter, which matters to patients with advanced cancer or rare disease. The article notes that the technology can be applied across many workflows, but that doesn't guarantee good results.

Hurt argues that patient input is needed from the very beginning of a study, because lived experience cannot be replaced. She describes the side effects of chemotherapy, including nausea, fatigue, constipation and diarrhea, to make the point that AI cannot substitute for what patients endure. She also explains that AI learns from the prompts it is given, so patients asking the right questions can help train these systems. When AI is used poorly, patients may face badly designed research and weak communication, but she says proper use can deepen understanding of patients' viewpoints. Her approach treats AI as complementary to patient experience rather than a replacement for it.

The article is an interview feature rather than a report on a specific event, and it does not describe any new regulation, rule or product change. It sits among related PharmExec coverage on tumor testing, COVID-19 prevention and clinical data infrastructure, though those pieces are not tied to Hurt's remarks. The article does not describe any next steps or timelines for how AI should be adopted in clinical trials. Its main takeaway is Hurt's view that patient involvement should remain central as the industry adopts these tools.

Articles.Title: Where AI Can Strengthen Clinical Research, and Where Patient Input is More Important

stories.Headline: Anthropic says a key AI safety alarm has been triggered, days before its IPO
stories.Summary:
Anthropic said on Tuesday that one of its key AI safety alarms has been triggered, in the same amended prospectus that set a price range for its record-setting IPO. A week earlier, the company had told would-be investors that AI speeding up its own research might "imminently" trigger the alarm. The filing said the threshold has now been met, and the company wrote that it made the determination "rather than on what we have observed from current models." The safety threshold is part of Anthropic's Responsible Scaling Policy, which sets out tougher safety measures as its AI grows more powerful. It is triggered when AI does enough of Anthropic's research to roughly double how fast its models improve.

The policy says that pace would fit two years of AI progress, measured at the 2018-2024 rate, into a single year. Crossing the line brings more safeguards, not a shutdown, and the filing says AI "has already been accelerating our research and development." Anthropic set its IPO price range at $70 to $78 per share on Tuesday as it began its roadshow, valuing the company at as much as about $1.4 trillion. Trading could start as soon as Nov. 19, according to reports.

Nvidia and Google are each buying $10 billion of Anthropic stock at the IPO price, part of a $26 billion private placement that also includes AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft and Taiwan Semiconductor. Anthropic says humans remain in charge and that it does not expect to safely use Claude "to fully autonomously design and build successive generations of frontier models without meaningful human supervision or understanding." The filing says the company is weighing policy changes "to keep humans in control." METR, an independent nonprofit that tests AI systems, estimated last week that Anthropic's models have been improving nearly twice as fast since October 2025, and in a separate review called Anthropic's August argument that it was still below the threshold "overstated."

The filing also changed some terminology. Anthropic swapped in "super intelligence" for "AI" in places, citing President Trump's Sept. 29 executive order telling federal agencies to use the term, and mentions of "AI" fell by about a quarter from the Nov. 2 version, by Yahoo Finance's count. Anthropic said it is still weighing what crossing the threshold means and will release further reports. It also warned that "our organization may lose visibility across certain processes" as it increasingly uses Claude to accelerate progress within the company.

Articles.Title: Anthropic says a key AI safety alarm has been triggered, days before its IPO

stories.Headline: AI Fraud and Risk Intelligence to Protect Revenue and Conversion
stories.Summary:
Riskified, an ecommerce risk intelligence company, and Emerj Artificial Intelligence Research published a sponsored article on November 10, 2026, arguing that online fraud is growing more costly and that companies need to protect revenue while stopping it. The piece draws on a webinar series that included Riskified executives Jeff Otto and Danielle Dzbanek, Adobe's Robert Rose and MoneyGram's Debjit Saha. It cites Federal Trade Commission testimony to Congress in March 2026 that consumers reported losing $15.9 billion to fraud in 2025, up from just over $12 billion a year earlier. It also notes that the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center logged more than one million complaints and nearly $21 billion in losses that year, and for the first time devoted a section of its annual report to AI-enabled schemes.

The guests recommend four practices. Companies should resolve identities across networks so that controls fall on the small group of actors driving most losses, and should monitor behavior inside trusted accounts, since attackers increasingly exploit accounts that legacy controls treat as safe. They should also match verification friction to rising risk so that low-risk and high-value customers face minimal interruption, and build a shared policy framework so that risk, customer experience, finance, bots and human agents make consistent decisions. Otto says identities linked to losses can represent roughly 20 basis points of a merchant's customer base, and that one person may operate dozens of accounts. Ring, the Amazon-owned home security company, reportedly lost about $4 million to refund abuse traced to 600 people who created tens of thousands of accounts.

The article's principal voices are Otto, Dzbanek and Saha, who describe the shift from transaction-level checks to identity and behavior. Dzbanek argues that no single business can see enough of modern fraud using only its own data, and Saha says that greater focus on new customers has left established accounts comparatively weakly controlled, which makes aged accounts more valuable to fraudsters. Otto adds that analysts monitoring fraud forums noticed about a year ago that aged accounts were selling for higher prices. The article presents these views as those of the guests and is labeled as sponsored content. It does not describe any specific regulatory deadline or next step beyond the continuing webinar series.

Articles.Title: AI Fraud and Risk Intelligence to Protect Revenue and Conversion

stories.Headline: QSAN and JetStor to Showcase 3U60 NVMe All-Flash Storage for On-Prem AI at SC26
stories.Summary:
QSAN Technology Inc. announced on November 11, 2026, that it will take part in SC26 (Supercomputing 2026), held November 15 to 20 at McCormick Place in Chicago, Illinois. Together with its U.S. distribution partner, JetStor, QSAN plans to show its 3U60 NVMe All-Flash Array, which uses an OCP card-based design. The companies present the showing as part of QSAN's work on on-premises AI infrastructure. The announcement was issued from Taipei, Taiwan.

The 3U60 array accommodates up to 60 NVMe SSDs within a 3U chassis, which the article says maximizes storage capacity while minimizing data center footprint. The OCP card-based design is described as a modular approach that allows high-density hardware integration and greater architectural flexibility. The platform is also described as offering low-latency, high-throughput data access for AI data pipelines, large datasets and HPC applications. QSAN says selected NVMe platforms support NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage.

The article also lists uses for its broader NVMe portfolio, including retrieval-augmented generation, vector databases, and enterprise data protection. QSAN describes the array as a product of its in-house hardware engineering, and the partnership with JetStor is described as combining that engineering with JetStor's established U.S. market presence. JetStor is described as a U.S.-based provider of enterprise data storage solutions that brings QSAN's technologies to customers across the United States. Steven Lin, General Manager of QSAN Technology Inc., said that storage infrastructure must evolve to deliver greater density, performance, and efficiency as enterprises bring AI workloads into their own data centers.

QSAN invites enterprise AI architects, HPC professionals, system integrators, and IT decision-makers to meet its representatives at SC26 through one-on-one consultations. The article describes SC26 as the largest international HPC conference, attracting more than 18,000 attendees from around the world. Separately listed event details say Women in HPC will host a full-day workshop, a Rising Stars early-career program, and a networking reception at SC26 on November 16 in Chicago. The article gives no further background on QSAN's prior conference activity or on how the array has performed in deployments.

Articles.Title: QSAN and JetStor to Showcase 3U60 NVMe All-Flash Storage for On-Prem AI at SC26

stories.Headline: Dartmouth provost resigns over undisclosed AI use
stories.Summary:
Dartmouth Provost Santiago Schnell has resigned and is leaving the university after a faculty-led committee found he used artificial intelligence in his writing without properly disclosing it. President Sian Leah Beilock announced the resignation on Oct. 28 in an email to the campus community. She wrote that the decision was Schnell's own and was made out of respect for his colleagues and the institution. Beilock had formed the committee on Sept. 25 after news reports questioned his AI use, including an August Semafor article about AI-written opinion pieces that named his Washington Post column.

The committee's report, dated Oct. 27, concluded that Schnell used AI in ways that broke at least one publication's disclosure rules and that he was not forthcoming about it. It did not use AI detection tools, relying instead on his logs from Dartmouth's enterprise tool, Claude, and his emails. In one journal paper, it found he used Claude to substantially edit a manuscript, troubleshoot code and generate figures without the disclosure the journal required. Schnell told Semafor he used ChatGPT to refine arguments and check grammar in a Post submission, which the committee called a clear violation of the paper's policy. The report also said he did not provide logs of his personal AI accounts when asked, though he did hand over his Dartmouth laptop.

The committee was led by former provost David Kotz and included Hany Farid, Peter Orner, Lindsay Whaley and Odette Harris. It said it was not recommending any disciplinary action. Schnell did not respond to a request for comment, and Dartmouth's media relations director did not immediately reply. Beilock wrote that leaders must model the transparency and human judgment expected of students and scholars. History professor Matthew Delmont will serve as interim provost through June 2028.

Articles.Title: Dartmouth provost resigns over undisclosed AI use

stories.Headline: Russia’s AI Ambitions Take a Hit With Ukrainian Data Center Strikes
stories.Summary:
Ukrainian drone strikes in October hit data centers operated by Sber and Yandex, adding to the difficulties Russia's AI industry already faced in securing chips and electricity. The facilities struck accounted for roughly 11% of Russia's data center capacity. While most services have been restored, Kommersant reported that full repairs could take up to six months. Yandex said on Tuesday that it had restored access to about 97% of the affected cloud customer data, and that the remaining 3% was permanently lost.

The Kremlin is counting on AI to raise productivity and offset a labor shortage driven by demographic decline, the war in Ukraine and an exodus of skilled workers. President Vladimir Putin has put AI at the center of his push to revive investment and spur long-term growth, calling for Russia to build its own "sovereign" infrastructure and standards. Moscow and St. Petersburg together host about 80% of Russia's data centers, and their power grids are nearing capacity. Russia faces an estimated annual shortfall of up to 300 megawatts in new data center capacity. The Moscow region is expected to add just 66 megawatts in 2026, down from 199 megawatts originally planned, while St. Petersburg is expected to add about 15 megawatts.

Yandex, which develops the YandexGPT model, said last year it was struggling to secure enough electricity to expand its AI infrastructure. Herman Gref, CEO of Sber, which developed the GigaChat AI model, said at a September AI conference that infrastructure constraints put Russia at a disadvantage against China. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov acknowledged in July that Russia "cannot compete with the leading American language models," though he said it was "among the five countries in the race." David Martirosov, CEO of Rostelecom's data center subsidiary RTK-TSOD, said Russia's output of server racks fell to 5,000 in 2025 from 14,000 the previous year. Data center developers are already squeezed by high borrowing costs, and one option under discussion, building underground, would cost 40% more than conventional construction, according to Kommersant.

Sanctions have complicated imports of foreign equipment, while a weaker ruble has driven up costs. Russia lacks large-scale domestic production of advanced processors, including graphics processing units, and Russian-made equipment accounts for just 15% to 20% of the engineering equipment used to build data centers, according to CNews. Russia has an estimated 1.8 gigawatts of data center capacity, according to Kommersant figures, compared with 50.4 gigawatts in the U.S., 30.9 gigawatts in China and 3 gigawatts in Germany. Russia falls outside the top 10 in both Stanford's AI Vibrancy ranking and a UN assessment of countries' capacity to use AI, and Russian models are absent from the Artificial Analysis leaderboard.

An IT specialist at a major Russian bank said Russia has the expertise to develop its own AI systems, but that the war makes it hard for companies to plan multibillion-dollar investments. He said planning such a strategy may be difficult given the current international environment. Companies must also weigh how much to spend protecting facilities against Ukrainian attacks while keeping construction and operating costs under control. Building farther inland in Siberia or the Urals could ease pressure on the two cities' grids and reduce exposure to strikes, but those sites can have weaker network connections, sit farther from major internet hubs and have fewer specialists to service equipment. Asked how long the conflict will last, he said, "No one knows how long the armed conflict will last and how intense it will be."

Articles.Title: Russia’s AI Ambitions Take a Hit With Ukrainian Data Center Strikes

stories.Headline: AI Accelerates Agricultural Biotechnology as Crop Innovation Becomes More Predictive and Data-Driven
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is reshaping agricultural biotechnology, according to a market research report published by BCC Research LLC in Boston on November 10, 2026. The report, titled AI Impact on Agricultural Biotechnology - BCC Pulse Report, examines how AI is being used across seed design, precision agriculture, livestock vaccine development, and digital farming platforms. BCC says AI is shortening research and development timelines and speeding the creation of climate-resilient crop varieties. The release was distributed as a paid press release through GlobeNewswire and carried on Yahoo Finance.

The release describes several areas of growth tied to this shift. It reports that venture capital in AI-focused agri-tech startups exceeded $6 billion in 2022, and that Inari raised $103 million in 2024 and $144 million in 2025, bringing its total funding above $720 million. It also says AI-powered farming systems can increase crop yields by up to 30 percent and reduce input costs by 15 to 20 percent. Government programs are adding support, including India's Digital Agriculture Mission, with a total investment of about $338 million, and the EU's AGROBOOST project, which deploys €6.5 million in robotics and AI. The release also notes that Cytotrait raised about $3.8 million in seed funding in March 2026, and that Corteva Catalyst led a $10.3 million Series A into Resurrect Bio in May 2026.

BCC Research is the author of the report and the release, and the material was written by the company itself rather than by an independent newsroom. The release also names a range of companies active in the field, including Inari, Greeneye Technology, Cropin, Bayer AG, Syngenta Group, Corteva, and BASF. Among the headwinds it lists, the release says only about 15 to 20 percent of large U.S. farms have adopted AI technologies, and it cites data governance rules under GDPR and the EU AI Act as added friction. It also points to infrastructure gaps in Latin America and Africa and the technical difficulty of combining genomic, environmental, and soil data.

The release presents the trend as a long-term opportunity tied to food security and climate adaptation, and it advises investors to weigh gene-edited crop approval timelines and infrastructure limits in emerging markets. It does not say when or how any of these trends will move from forecast to measured result. Readers should note that the figures come from the company's own promotional material and have not been independently verified in the release. Further developments are not described in the article.

Articles.Title: AI Accelerates Agricultural Biotechnology as Crop Innovation Becomes More Predictive and Data-Driven

stories.Headline: The AI industry's week from hell
stories.Summary:
Anthropic announced on Tuesday, November 11, 2026, that it plans to raise as much as $64.4 billion in an IPO that targets a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion. The offering fell short of earlier expectations, as the valuation sits roughly $600 billion below what investors envisioned just months ago. Slowing revenue growth, soaring infrastructure costs and a sharp market selloff all contributed to the lower target. The article describes the move as one of the largest IPOs in history, and the timing added to a difficult week for the wider AI industry.

The reset came after a series of setbacks for AI companies that began with last week's midterm results. Voters in 40 of 41 local ballot measures nationwide favored restrictions on data-center development. Congress will also gain AI-skeptical Democrats who may use subpoena power to look into the industry's safety record and political influence. Nvidia has shed more than $1 trillion in market value since New York Times reports on October 29 linked CEO Jensen Huang to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, and the FBI, the company's board and Congress are investigating. The Nasdaq also lost $2.5 trillion in value on Thursday, its worst session since April 2025.

Anthropic's own figures show the strain. Its annualized revenue reached $81 billion in October, but its long-term commitments to chips, data centers and computing infrastructure have climbed to nearly $901 billion. Other financial warning signs appeared as OpenAI scaled back its fundraising ambitions and SoftBank reported a $3.7 billion write-down on U.S. data-center equipment. The article also notes that lenders are growing wary of financing the industry's infrastructure spending. Still, Google, Nvidia and other technology giants have committed another $26 billion in private investment alongside the public offering.

The article suggests the outcome will depend on whether Anthropic can post a strong debut and keep its share price up after trading begins. It points to SpaceX, whose stock surged after its record June IPO but later fell below its offering price within weeks. If Anthropic completes the offering, the company could bring in roughly $85 billion in net new capital. The article argues that even a valuation of $1 trillion or $1.5 trillion may not reassure investors who expected as much as $2 trillion only weeks ago.

Articles.Title: The AI industry's week from hell

stories.Headline: Camille Roberts’ AI Comedy Show Comes to Silver Spring
stories.Summary:
Improbable Comedy will present "Sounds Like Something I'd Do," a semi-educational comedy hour about artificial intelligence and what art and humanity can hold onto in its presence, at the Silver Spring Black Box Theatre in January. The show blends a coming-of-age story about a comedian with nine years of experience and a robot built by an engineer who graduated a decade ago with no practical experience. Both roles are played by Camille Roberts, a New York-based comedian, producer, biomechanical engineer, college writing professor, and Human-Computer Interaction graduate student. She has performed at more than 40 clubs and eight festivals across the United States, the United Kingdom, and Ireland, and has sold out the D.C. Drafthouse and Caveat in New York City.

In the hour, Roberts explains what happened when she trained a small language model on more than 600 pages of her own transcripts, jokes, and ideas. The result, according to the announcement, is a clearer picture of how AI actually works, though the show is driven by a narrative built from her stand-up and the life stories that have shaped her. After the first run last March, audience members from several fields left post-show feedback. Becca, a physician, said the show teaches complex technology in simple, approachable ways while staying funny. Zach, a human factors engineer, described the work as profoundly human, and Olivia, an actor and comedian, said it balances stand-up and education well.

Improbable Comedy founder Kim Levone framed the production as a way to address AI through humor. Levone said that while everything seems to be about AI right now, Roberts uses the subject to explore what she believes remains deeply human, which is humor. Improbable Comedy, based in Silver Spring, was founded in 2011, has produced hundreds of shows, runs the free Comedy in the Parks series with Montgomery Parks and the SPRUNG! Comedy Festival, and is known for presenting underrepresented groups and talent. The company's background is part of why the production is being presented locally.

The performance is scheduled for 7:30 p.m. on Saturday, January 9, 2027, at the Silver Spring Black Box Theatre on Colesville Road in downtown Silver Spring, with doors opening at 7 p.m. Tickets start at $29.37 and are available for purchase online through improbablecomedy.com. The article describes the show as a first-run production that has already been staged once, and it presents the January date as the next scheduled presentation.

Articles.Title: Camille Roberts’ AI Comedy Show Comes to Silver Spring

stories.Headline: Contributor: Cute faces like Muse Charm are a Trojan horse for exploitative AI tech
stories.Summary:
Meta has released a new AI assistant called Muse Charm, a keychain-sized gadget designed to look soft and approachable, like a toy from a child's bedroom. According to a November 10, 2026 opinion column by victims' rights attorney Carrie Goldberg in the Los Angeles Times, the device's friendly appearance hides how much access it can gain. The product encourages users to connect email, messages, photographs and financial accounts, building detailed records of their private lives. Goldberg argues that this cheerful packaging can lead people to hand over sensitive information without weighing the risks.

Goldberg draws a comparison to earlier industries that used cartoon characters, candy flavors and playful packaging to attract young consumers to harmful products like tobacco, vaping and alcohol. She writes that AI is seeing a similar pattern with little scrutiny from regulators or lawmakers. Her concern is that intimate details, once shared, can fall into the wrong hands and be used for harassment or abuse. She also notes that people who never use Muse could have their information exposed if someone else connects their accounts to the product. Her argument rests on her firm's work with survivors of sexual exploitation, stalking and technology-facilitated abuse.

Goldberg is critical of Meta and of technology companies generally, which she says have historically introduced products, encouraged adoption and addressed harms only after people were hurt. She points to reassuring branding at Meta and Google as a tactic that offers little comfort to survivors. Her firm is suing xAI, the maker of Grok, over allegations that its technology enabled sexualized images of a real person without consent. She also argues that companies can be held responsible under established legal principles when their dangerous products cause foreseeable harm, citing her firm's lawsuits against Amazon over its sale of sodium nitrite. Meta, according to the broader coverage summarized alongside the column, says Muse includes safeguards such as isolated user environments, secure credential storage, adjustable permissions and confirmation prompts for sensitive actions.

The column's call for accountability faces legal uncertainty, since courts have not yet settled how existing rules, including Section 230, apply to claims based on generative AI outputs. Supporters of personal AI agents counter that access to private accounts can offer practical benefits such as help with correspondence, shopping and bill-paying. Goldberg's piece frames the debate as one in which powerful systems with access to intimate details of people's lives should not be trusted merely because they look friendly. The article does not report any specific regulatory action on Muse Charm, and it leaves open how courts and lawmakers will respond.

Articles.Title: Contributor: Cute faces like Muse Charm are a Trojan horse for exploitative AI tech

stories.Headline: Otter AI can now follow conversations across 30+ languages
stories.Summary:
Otter.ai, the AI note-taking company, announced on Tuesday, November 10, 2026 that it is expanding its multilingual capabilities. The company is adding support for 27 languages, its largest expansion to date, bringing its total to 31 once the rollout finishes. A new multilingual transcription feature can detect when speakers switch languages during a meeting and keep transcribing without users changing any settings. Thirteen of the new languages are available now, including Mandarin Chinese, Korean, German, and Polish, while the other 14 are coming soon.

The company says the update is meant to help global teams whose language differences make meetings and collaboration harder. Otter gave an example of a call moving from English to Korean to Portuguese, with the tool following the conversation throughout. The newly added languages run on Otter's own speech models, which the company says were trained on publicly available datasets. Native-speaking volunteers reviewed transcripts to check accuracy. Otter's spokesperson described the goal as helping any company, wherever it is based, keep a record of decisions made through voice AI communication.

The expansion comes as Otter moves beyond transcription into other workplace tools, following $320 million in funding from General Catalyst. Its recently introduced Work Mode uses meeting history and connected apps to help users prepare for upcoming calls, pulling in prior customer conversations, outstanding action items, and recent Google Drive files. Another recent addition, Live Assist, offers real-time suggestions during meetings based on what has already been discussed and what is happening at the moment. The articles do not describe any further rollout timeline beyond the languages marked as coming soon.

Articles.Title: Otter AI can now follow conversations across 30+ languages

stories.Headline: "AI has caused an insane inflation in the number of games; it’s becoming harder to capture a player's attention."
stories.Summary:
AI has caused what Anat Horvitz, a director at Google Israel, called an insane inflation in the number of games, making it harder than ever to capture players' attention. She said this during a panel at the Gaming Conference hosted by Calcalist, Google, and Playtika, where Eitan Reisel, managing partner at investment fund vgames, also spoke. The panel was moderated by Meir Orbach of Calcalist, and the discussion took place on 11 November 2026. The two discussed how artificial intelligence has made game development faster and cheaper while intensifying competition for players' attention. Horvitz described an 11% decline in game downloads over the past year, although revenue rose 1.5% this year, the third consecutive year of revenue growth.

She said the industry once focused on attracting new customers, but the battle is now centered on market share and retaining existing players. Reisel said games can be released much faster but still require significant capital. He cited five-person teams building games that generate hundreds of millions of dollars in annual revenue. Horvitz said the bottleneck has shifted from production to attention, since tools such as those provided by Google let even small studios produce games in days. She projected 136,000 new games would be released in 2026, a massive increase over 2025.

She said only 6% of total playtime goes to games released within the past year, with the rest going to older titles. Winning attention, she said, requires AI, creative strategy, and in-depth data analysis. Reisel said that where a $5 million seed investment once bought two attempts at casual games, he now expects a company to launch 12 games with the same amount, which reduces risk. He added that faster production does not make running a gaming company easier, because companies must constantly create new content and invest heavily in marketing. Horvitz said studios now want to determine quickly whether a game's economics work, and Reisel said competitors' ability to clone games has reached an extreme level.

Reisel described vgames' financing model, which has raised $500 million with backing from The Phoenix and in partnership with General Catalyst. The fund covers user acquisition costs and is repaid from revenue generated by the users it helps acquire, rather than taking equity. Horvitz said similar financing is emerging among companies that fund smaller studios, and that M&A activity is high because companies can acquire existing titles instead of developing every game themselves. Reisel said his portfolio company is generating 800 creative assets a week, and Horvitz said Israeli companies think globally from day one. More to follow.

Articles.Title: "AI has caused an insane inflation in the number of games; it’s becoming harder to capture a player's attention."

stories.Headline: AI startup Spines raises $64m., challenging traditional publishing industry
stories.Summary:
Israeli AI company Spines announced on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, that it had completed a $64 million funding round, made up of $29 million in Series A equity and $35 million in debt, bringing its total investment to $86 million since it was founded. The equity portion was led by Zeev Ventures, the fund of Oren Zeev, with participation from Aleph, NordStar, M-Fund, LionTree, and angel investor Dan Senor, while the debt came from the American investment firm and financing platform Twelve Grow. Spines has built a platform meant to replace traditional publishing houses, and it says its AI agents can cut the time to publish a book from 12 to 18 months to about three to four weeks. Authors need only upload their manuscript, after which the platform handles genre analysis, editing, proofreading, layout, cover design, metadata, and distribution and marketing. The company says it can translate books into seven languages, with plans for about 20, and produce print, digital, and audio editions, and it estimates direct costs to authors could fall by up to about 90 percent compared with a traditional publisher, before royalties.

The company takes a 20 percent share of author royalties, which it presents as more modest than the 75 to 90 percent of the retail price that the Authors Guild attributes to traditional publishers and distributors. Spines consolidates sales and royalty data in one place and distributes books across about 100 channels worldwide, while also letting authors manage reader communities. Founded in 2021 by Yehuda Niv, who serves as CEO, the company reports growth of about 400 percent over the past year, with roughly 8,000 American authors publishing through it and about 400 new authors joining each month. It employs 350 people, 90 of them in Israel and the rest in the United States, Eastern Europe, and South America. Niv, who founded Niv Publishing in 2013, told Walla Money that the US publishing industry generates about $40 billion a year, and that most of the roughly 4 million books published there annually are paid for by authors out of pocket.

Niv described the company's aim as empowering authors rather than writing books for them, saying Spines runs no process for AI-generated books and works only with human-created manuscripts. He argued that the platform removes the gatekeeping role of publishers in deciding who gets published. Investors and others involved made similar points: Zeev compared the opportunity to his early investment in Audible, and Michael Eisenberg of Aleph, who has published nine books himself, said the goal is to open publishing to more people and more voices. Market research cited in the article puts the global publishing market at about $307 billion a year, growing toward roughly $391 billion by 2033, though the article does not say what the funding will be used for or describe next steps beyond the company's stated plans for more languages.

Articles.Title: AI startup Spines raises $64m., challenging traditional publishing industry

stories.Headline: "Everybody has access today. I think that's beta": PE investors say AI's edge is in data and judgment
stories.Summary:
Executives from three private equity firms said at a panel that AI models are now widely available, so a firm's real advantage lies in its proprietary data, workflow context and human judgment. The discussion took place on Tuesday at the Israel Private Markets Summit, the main annual conference of Israel's institutional alternative investment market, held at the Peres Center for Peace and Innovation in Tel Aviv. Moderator Ofir Reiner Sigler, head of direct and PE investments at Menora Mivtachim Group, framed the debate as a split between "AI alpha" and "AI beta." Nicolas Schaufele, managing director at Veritas Capital, said that access to models is now commonplace and will commoditize over time, while the real edge comes from proprietary data inside portfolio companies. Hannah Dolgin, senior vice president at Vista Equity Partners, said the differentiators are access to context, trust and scale, and pointed to Duck Creek, a Vista portfolio company supporting underwriting for property and casualty insurers, which does not give that information to general-purpose models.

Panelists agreed that the bottleneck has shifted from the technology to the firms themselves. Schaufele said hallucinations were a concern a year ago but are now mostly solved, and that what is lacking is the firms' workflows, willingness to adopt AI and data structure. Dolgin said adoption has moved much faster than the technological changes Vista saw over its 25 years. Cécile Mayer-Lévi, head of private debt at Tikehau Capital, said AI is now part of underwriting, with every deal assessed for whether AI is a risk or an opportunity.

She warned that cost savings are not automatic, citing a large insurer that switched off a copilot tool after seeing no efficiency gains. Schaufele described a Veritas manufacturing portfolio company where AI helped cut the time to launch new products from two years to six months and raised yields by up to 30%. Cost reduction is the more established gain, and Dolgin said all Vista portfolio companies run AI cost-saving initiatives. The growth opportunity, she said, lies in tapping labor spend as a new market and turning existing software into agentic products through what Vista calls its "agentic factory," which places engineers inside portfolio companies.

Schaufele was more cautious, saying revenue is accelerating where companies hold data assets but that it is unclear how much of that growth is driven by AI as opposed to other innovations. On junior staff, Mayer-Lévi said the era of long hours spent on presentations hardly anyone read is ending. Schaufele argued that juniors may gain earlier exposure to management meetings and judgment as number-crunching shrinks. The panel closed by returning to human judgment as the real source of advantage.

Dolgin noted that models produce probabilistic rather than deterministic outcomes, which makes a human in the loop essential. Schaufele said Veritas uses models as a red team that challenges the firm's assumptions, and reviews past mistakes together. He cautioned that firms must not rely on the models blindly. The panel was reported by Ctech, where Zachy Hennessey published the article on November 10, 2026.

Articles.Title: "Everybody has access today. I think that's beta": PE investors say AI's edge is in data and judgment

stories.Headline: U.S. Democrats likely to seek China AI cooperation: Stimson Center expert
stories.Summary:
Democrats, who will control both chambers of Congress when the new legislature convenes in January, are likely to pursue artificial intelligence regulation and safety standards, according to Stimson Center researcher Robert Manning. He said the backlash against AI and data centers helped shape the midterm results and may push Democrats toward tighter oversight. Manning also suggested they could be more open to adopting safety standards with China to control what he called runaway AI. He told Kyodo News in a written interview that the U.S. elections will likely have a large effect on AI policy.

Manning said Democrats may also press the administration of President Donald Trump to carry out at least part of a planned $14 billion arms sale to Taiwan. More broadly, he expects Democrats to work on repairing damage he attributed to Trump to alliances and allies, though their role will be limited. He said Democrats will also want to appear tough on Taiwan so they are not seen as soft. On Ukraine, he expects Democrats to push for more military aid, investigate Trump's dealings with Russia and oppose efforts to force Ukraine to yield to Russian President Vladimir Putin's demands.

Manning said Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi should maintain her ties with Trump while also strengthening ties with Congress. He described the elections as a net plus for Japan and the U.S.-Japan alliance, expecting continuity and perhaps less erratic pressure from Trump. He also said Elon Musk and other tech executives spent heavily to stop Democrats but failed, underestimating public resentment over the market dominance of major technology companies. He added that there is considerable uncertainty after the elections about whether Trump will become a lame duck or an angry one.

Manning said the large Democratic majority could constrain Trump's domestic agenda and roll some of it back. He said Trump could take a combative stance that deadlocks domestic policy or instead seek to build his legacy through deals with Democrats. Manning advised senior government officials on global issues while serving at organizations under the Office of the Director of National Intelligence and at the State Department. He is now a distinguished fellow with the Strategic Foresight Hub and the China Program at the Stimson Center, where he works mostly on China, emerging technologies and great power competition.

Articles.Title: U.S. Democrats likely to seek China AI cooperation: Stimson Center expert

stories.Headline: Teleperformance's latest results spotlight Africa's AI opportunity
stories.Summary:
Teleperformance, the French multinational now operating under the TP brand, published its third-quarter results on November 5, 2026, and Business Insider Africa covered them on November 10. The company revised its 2026 revenue outlook to a decline of 1.5% to 2.5% on a like-for-like basis, reflecting pressure on traditional activities, particularly content moderation. Outside those activities, however, TP recorded 2% like-for-like revenue growth during the quarter once Trust & Safety was excluded. The results are presented as a sign of how artificial intelligence is reshaping the global business services industry. The article frames the company's African expansion as part of that same shift.

TP operates in 11 African countries with more than 50,000 employees and over 50 delivery sites. Egypt is the article's main example, where the company employs about 26,800 people and generates 90% of its local revenues from exported services. Those exports reached €280 million in 2025 and are projected to reach €344 million in 2026. TP has also outlined plans to create 18,000 additional jobs in Egypt under its expansion programme. The article presents these figures as evidence of how African economies are becoming more closely integrated into global technology and business services value chains.

On the AI side, the company reported at the end of September roughly 1,400 AI projects worldwide, more than double the previous year's level. It recorded over 300 new production-grade deployments during the third quarter, and more than 35% of its global client portfolio now uses TP.ai solutions. The article says AI-enabled operations increasingly require multilingual specialists, technical supervision, data expertise and employees able to manage complex interactions. It also notes that automation raises questions about the future of routine roles and about reskilling.

The article describes the group as having maintained its 2026 profitability and cash-flow targets while accelerating its AI transformation. The article concludes that Africa's outsourcing advantages, which include multilingual talent, competitive costs and proximity to European markets, may increasingly depend on combining those strengths with technological capabilities. It argues that future competitiveness will rest on skills and infrastructure rather than labour supply alone. The piece presents TP's African footprint as a substantial platform for taking part in that transition.

Articles.Title: Teleperformance's latest results spotlight Africa's AI opportunity

stories.Headline: AI Investment Risk Demands Vigilance by Retirement Plan Managers
stories.Summary:
The article, published by Bloomberg Law on November 10, 2026, examines how retirement plan managers should respond to the heavy weight that a small group of large technology companies carries in public stock markets. Benefits attorneys said that Americans with retirement accounts invested in public markets are increasingly exposed to these firms, which have been lifted by the boom in artificial intelligence, often without participants realizing it. The piece notes that this exposure has raised concern that retirement savings could suffer if an AI bubble were to burst and push the market lower. It also points to a historic tech selloff that followed speculation about the effects of the November 3 election. The article frames the issue as one that calls for close attention from fiduciaries, the people responsible for overseeing retirement plans and protecting participants from a downturn.

In that framing, concentration in a few large companies means that plan managers have less room for error when markets turn. The available text is cut off before it sets out specific steps, figures or rule changes, so it does not say what new requirements, if any, managers would face. Readers should treat the piece as a call for vigilance rather than a report on a formal change in policy. Benefits attorneys are the sources quoted for the warning about participant exposure, and the article presents their view that many savers do not know how much of their money rides on these technology firms. The article attributes the broader concern about a possible AI bubble to the same discussion of market risk.

The excerpt available does not name any regulator, company or official who has taken a position beyond those attorneys. The article places this discussion against a recent market shock, the historic tech selloff linked to speculation over the November 3 election, which showed how quickly concentrated holdings can fall. The available text does not describe what fiduciaries are expected to do next, and it ends before providing further detail. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI Investment Risk Demands Vigilance by Retirement Plan Managers

stories.Headline: McDonald’s AI Price-Fixing Suit Fuels Legal Risk Over Franchises
stories.Summary:
A proposed class action filed on October 2 accuses McDonald's Corp. of improperly using an algorithmic pricing tool to push its franchise restaurants toward higher menu prices. The complaint is described as one that is expected to prompt a wave of similar AI price-fixing cases involving franchisee relationships. Several similar cases have already been filed since then. The articles say the lawsuit heightens antitrust risks for companies that want to deploy this kind of technology.

On November 2, Senator Elizabeth Warren and Representative Becca Balint demanded answers from McDonald's President and CEO Chris Kempczinski. Their letter asked how the company uses artificial intelligence to set prices. The articles present this request as a sign of growing political scrutiny of the issue. They do not describe any response from the company.

The articles attribute the allegations to the lawsuit's plaintiffs, who claim the company pressured franchisees into adopting the pricing tool. The articles do not include a company statement rejecting or addressing these claims. Kempczinski is named as the executive to whom the lawmakers directed their questions. Beyond that, the articles offer no further detail on who is responsible for the tool's design or use.

The broader context is a legal environment in which regulators and lawmakers are watching how companies use AI to set prices. The articles suggest that franchise arrangements could expose more companies to similar claims. They do not say what the court will decide or when. More to follow.

Articles.Title: McDonald’s AI Price-Fixing Suit Fuels Legal Risk Over Franchises

stories.Headline: China touts tech, AI cred at world Web Summit
stories.Summary:
China is using the Web Summit in Lisbon, which opens its program on Tuesday, to showcase its technology and artificial intelligence sector. The event's founder, Paddy Cosgrave, said at Monday's opening ceremony that the future's leading figures are increasingly coming from China rather than California. Organizers expect at least 70,000 participants from 164 countries, including 10,000 startups and 1,500 investors, at the conference, which runs until Thursday. Chinese firms are showing off dancing and tai chi-performing humanoid robots, along with low-cost AI models.

The Chinese presence includes speakers from more than 50 leading AI labs, robotics startups, carmakers, quantum computing startups and energy startups. Among them are Tao Zhang of Manus AI, who is due to demonstrate Manus 2.0, an agent that can carry out a sequence of tasks on its own. Representatives from the robotics firms Unitree and Agibot will speak, while Galbot and Ubtech Robotics plan to demonstrate their humanoid robots. Pony.ai, Xpeng and other companies will also present, and Xpeng displayed a prototype flying car at Monday's opening events.

The timing is shaped by a scandal engulfing Nvidia, the US company that dominates the market for chips used in leading AI systems. Its chief executive, Jensen Huang, has acknowledged an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials reportedly suspect of spying for China, a claim Beijing has denied. The articles also report that Nvidia has announced a probe into Huang and that the company faces a class-action lawsuit over the affair. Chinese open-weight AI models, which can be downloaded free and partly modified, are drawing interest from European firms including Orange, Renault, Revolut and Siemens.

The articles frame the push as part of China's search for new markets amid weak domestic demand and US restrictions on much of its market on national security grounds. The summit gives Beijing a stage to present its firms to European buyers and investors at a time when the Nvidia controversy has drawn attention to China's AI ambitions. The articles do not say how the Nvidia matter will be resolved or what commitments, if any, the Chinese firms will make in Lisbon. More to follow.

Articles.Title: China touts tech, AI cred at world Web Summit

stories.Headline: Ron Daniels: Exploring the Ethical Frontiers of AI in Cancer Care
stories.Summary:
Ron Daniels, president of The Johns Hopkins University, posted on LinkedIn on November 10, 2026, about a recent Next Conversations event on artificial intelligence in cancer care. The panel included Hopkins researchers Ashani Weeraratna and Vasan Yegnasubramanian, along with Pulitzer Prize-winning author Siddhartha Mukherjee, who spoke with NPR's Steve Inskeep. The discussion focused on the ethics of AI tools in oncology and the next stage of their development. Daniels shared his opening remarks and encouraged readers to listen to the full conversation.

In his post, Daniels described how cancer tools have grown more powerful and how each advance brings both hope and new questions about using them responsibly. He said the event returned to questions that have long shaped medicine but now feel more pressing. Those questions include how to use technology in a humane way, how to make sure these tools benefit all patients, and how to keep the human connection, clinical judgment, and trust between doctor and patient at the center of care. The article does not describe specific policies, rules, or changes that the discussion called for.

Daniels is the one responsible for the message, and the article presents his views as an invitation to the conversation rather than as a set of conclusions. The panelists' individual remarks are not reported in the article, so their positions are not described. The piece also points readers to a related article about AI in oncology by Yan Leyfman, which offers a further look at the field. The article does not say whether any follow-up events or outcomes are planned.

Articles.Title: Ron Daniels: Exploring the Ethical Frontiers of AI in Cancer Care

stories.Headline: A New AI Tool From Google DeepMind Proved the Signal Protocol Is Secure
stories.Summary:
Google DeepMind researchers used an agentic AI system to mathematically prove several of the Signal protocol's key cryptographic guarantees, a result WIRED reported on November 10, 2026. The work was a proof-of-concept project completed in just four weeks, and it used a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code. The effort matters for two reasons: it independently validates the cryptography that protects large volumes of communications on Signal, Google Messages, and WhatsApp, and it showcases DeepMind's formal verification capabilities. Formal verification uses mathematics to check that software works as intended and lacks critical vulnerabilities.

Before AI, turning a description of software behavior into formulas and then building a proof took a great deal of time, and agentic AI can significantly shorten that process. The analysis was limited in scope, however, because it did not formally verify the entire Signal mobile app. The DeepMind team did not find new vulnerabilities in the portions it examined. When the researchers ran AlphaProof Code on older Signal versions with known, long-fixed vulnerabilities, the tool correctly flagged them and showed that those versions could not be formally verified. The researchers are releasing the specification and proof they developed to help other formal verification efforts.

Swarat Chaudhuri, a DeepMind research scientist, said the result is exciting but that a long road remains before the approach can scale to all the world's software. Ehren Kret, Signal's chief technology officer, said in a statement that the DeepMind approach enables significant expansion beyond prior formal verification, which focused on smaller portions of code. Kret added that rigorous verification gives Signal greater confidence in its privacy guarantees as AI-driven security threats grow. Pushmeet Kohli, chief scientist at Google Cloud and DeepMind's vice president of research, said such verification could give banks and other companies a way to prove that their software has certain properties.

The analysis was conducted free of charge as a research project, and Google declined to disclose its cost. The company also declined to say whether it plans to release a commercial formal verification product or service. The researchers highlighted a human-AI collaboration process in which agents contribute and self-correct at most phases while still seeking human input and review at key points. Chaudhuri said the team wants to avoid a situation where AI generates the goals, the proofs, and the tests on its own. The open question across the tech sector is whether AI-automated formal verification can truly scale at a workable cost.

Articles.Title: A New AI Tool From Google DeepMind Proved the Signal Protocol Is Secure

stories.Headline: Sysmex and Hologen form Saibogen for blood test AI analysis
stories.Summary:
Sysmex Corporation and Hologen have set up Saibogen, a joint venture that uses artificial intelligence to draw clinical insights from routine blood tests. The venture was announced in an article published on November 10, 2026. Its generative AI models will work on the diagnostic data that Sysmex haematology hardware produces, and its first commercial products are planned exclusively for research use. Saibogen will deliver its software directly through Sysmex haematology analysers. Laboratories therefore will not need to buy extra instruments, chemical reagents or patient samples.

The platform pairs Sysmex test data with Hologen's large medicine models, which are configured to analyse biological mechanisms within real-world healthcare datasets. Under this arrangement, the companies intend to turn standard laboratory equipment into analytical platforms that supply biological information without reducing test accessibility. The aim is to help healthcare providers with predictive, preventive and personalised patient care. Haematology testing is among the most widely conducted laboratory assessments worldwide and often serves as the first evaluation in a patient's care pathway. Sysmex analysers process around three billion of these tests each year, producing standardised metrics for clinicians across international healthcare systems.

Sysmex, which is based in Kobe, Japan, is contributing haematology technical knowledge, proprietary datasets, diagnostic product development and an established worldwide distribution network. Hologen, which is based in the UK, is contributing more than ten years of fundamental scientific research into medical AI deployment carried out by its co-founders. Saibogen's chief executive, Leila Luheshi, said that every routine blood count measures tens of thousands of cells with great precision and that much of that information goes unused. She added that the company is building AI to read that information in full so that researchers, laboratories and clinicians can learn more from a test already part of everyday care. The article does not give a launch date beyond the research-use plan.

Articles.Title: Sysmex and Hologen form Saibogen for blood test AI analysis

stories.Headline: AI's potential in cancer treatment, cures debated at first New Haven Oncology Summit
stories.Summary:
AI's role in cancer care was the focus of New Haven's first Future of Oncology Summit, held Monday, November 9, 2026, at the 101 College bioscience building. The event was hosted by Yale Cancer Center and the biotech industry group BioCT and drew more than 500 people on its first day. Speakers described AI as already in routine use, with oncologists using it to take visit notes, arrange appointments and research treatment options, while scientists use it to analyze large data sets and help design clinical trials. David Scheer, a local biotech entrepreneur and co-chair of BioCT's board of directors, called the present a golden age of intersection between technology and cancer research.

Experts also raised concerns about the technology. Dr. Sarah Goldberg, chief of thoracic oncology at the Yale School of Medicine, said some trainee doctors struggle to diagnose patients without help from devices and AI tools, and that training must adapt so students learn how to think about a patient. Keynote speaker Dr. Clifford Hudis, CEO of the American Society of Clinical Oncology, said AI shows little promise in controlling costs, which neared $200 billion for oncology drugs alone in the U.S. in 2025. He added that the field has averaged almost one new drug label per week over the last two years. State First Lady Annie Lamont, a venture capitalist, warned that AI could threaten New Haven's network of biotech startups and that Chinese biotech firms have grown to draw about 50% of outside pharma investment in research and drug development.

Speakers from large drugmakers stressed the value of independent startups, including those spun out of Yale. Eli Lilly's Chief Medical Officer, David Hyman, said the company has made 31 acquisitions of smaller companies in the last year and needs external innovation to scale its research budget. Dr. Eric Winer, director of Yale Cancer Center, said AI could help doctors do less in some breast cancer cases unlikely to become life-threatening, since overuse of chemotherapy and surgery can sometimes cause more harm than good. Katerina Politi, deputy director of the Yale Cancer Center, said AI tools are helping sort growing data to improve lung cancer treatment and may enter the clinic as research advances.

Articles.Title: AI's potential in cancer treatment, cures debated at first New Haven Oncology Summit

stories.Headline: Trimble expands AI capabilities across construction lifecycle
stories.Summary:
Trimble has announced new AI capabilities for its Trimble Connect platform, spanning the design, build and operate phases of construction. The announcement was made at the Trimble Dimensions User Conference and was published on November 10, 2026. The new tools include generative design through Trimble Assist, customer-designed agents through Trimble Agent Studio, and expanded AI governance features. Trimble says the platform natively integrates precision field hardware, machine control telemetry and jobsite data, and that it has more than 55 million cumulative users across more than 35 million projects.

During the design phase, Trimble highlighted generative design that references live as-built point clouds, automated structural modeling that turns natural language prompts into constructible steel models, and design file verification for civil projects. A one-click AI indoor classification tool sorts millions of point cloud scan points into structural regions such as floors, walls and pipes. During the build phase, the company described AI diagnostics for field hardware, 360 reality capture that turns sitewalk videos into 3D point clouds, and an AI punch walk tool that transcribes voice-driven field inspections. During the operating phase, Trimble pointed to AI procurement and invoice matching, contract risk analysis that drafts potential change orders, and a scheduling engine linked to live jobsite data.

Trimble says all currently available AI agents and models in the platform carry standardized AI safety labels documenting safety, security design and data provenance. The company states these labels align with the EU AI Act, its own AI Statement and Principles, and ISO 42001 standards. The announcement presents the platform as a way to link design, estimating, field and financial data while keeping human judgment central to decisions. The company has not described the platform as a replacement for project leaders, who it says retain final decisions.

On availability, Trimble says automated structural modeling, AI indoor classification, 360 reality capture, AI punch walk, AI procurement and invoice matching, and Trimble Connect Scheduling are available now. AI diagnostics for field hardware is offered to select customers, while design file verification and change order automation remain in development. Generative design is currently part of Trimble Labs, an early engagement program for customer feedback. More information is available at trimble.com.

Articles.Title: Trimble expands AI capabilities across construction lifecycle

stories.Headline: Don’t just prompt AI — architect it: Introducing the Professional Agentic Architect Certification
stories.Summary:
Google Cloud has announced a new certification called the Professional Agentic Architect, aimed at proving skill in building production-ready AI agents. The announcement was published on November 11, 2026, by Gary Eimerman, managing director of Google Cloud Learning. The certification is the latest step in the company's Gemini Agent Ready initiative, which nearly one million developers are already using to learn about agents. It was first used internally, where Google trained thousands of forward deployed engineers and strategic partners over the past four months, and is now being opened to the wider developer community and partner ecosystem.

The certification uses a hybrid format rather than a traditional multiple choice test. The first part is a proctored multiple choice exam that tests system design choices, architectural standards, cost optimization, and security governance. The second part is a set of hands-on labs on Google Skills, where candidates build, test, and debug live agentic workflows in an active cloud environment. The curriculum covers building agents with low-code tools, using coding agents for application development, developing custom agents on the Gemini platform with open source frameworks, evaluating and deploying agentic workflows, and securing and governing them. Candidates who pass both parts receive a digital badge.

The announcement was written by Gary Eimerman, who presents the program as a response to enterprise demand for agentic workloads, which the article says has skyrocketed. Google says its forward deployed engineers and partners work directly with customers worldwide, and that standardizing training ensures its own teams follow the same standards it recommends. The article also cites research with Ipsos, reporting that 82% of learners using Google Skills say listing Google Cloud certifications on a resume draws more recruiter responses, and that 90% of cloud professionals say such credentials give them verified know-how for in-demand roles. Ravi, the vice president who manages Google's forward deployed engineers, is also named as a contributor to the program's rollout.

Developers can get started by registering for Gemini Agent Ready, which offers 35 free monthly learning credits on Google Skills. Google Cloud customers can join a no-cost, cohort-based guided certification journey called Get Certified, while partners can register for Partner Certification Kickstart. Candidates are directed to review the exam guide, learning path, and sample questions, complete the hands-on preparation modules, then take the multiple choice exam and the lab requirements. The article does not state the exam fee, pass thresholds, or the number of participants who have completed the certification so far.

Articles.Title: Don’t just prompt AI — architect it: Introducing the Professional Agentic Architect Certification

stories.Headline: How exposed is your portfolio to a single AI model failure?
stories.Summary:
Anthropic's IPO filing, known as an S-1, has drawn attention for a warning about the insurance market's ability to cover AI risk. The filing says that, given how much harm a catastrophic AI-related incident could cause, no single insurer, and possibly the insurance industry as a whole, may have enough capacity or expertise to underwrite coverage at that level. The article treats this as a signal for insurance leaders to look closely at their own books. It frames the central issue as concentration of risk rather than the size of any one claim.

The article's core point is that one failure in a widely used AI model could produce claims from policyholders in many industries and regions at the same time, because they all depend on the same underlying technology. A portfolio that looks diversified on paper can therefore be more tightly linked than the insurer expects. Trevor Jones, a partner in the insurance practice at West Monroe, a global business and technology consulting firm, is quoted in the piece. The article does not give figures for insurer exposure or specific policy requirements tied to this warning.

The article is a feature built around the S-1 language and the views of the consultant, so it attributes the warning to Anthropic's filing and the analysis to Jones. It does not describe any actual AI failure or claims event. Surrounding coverage on the same site covers related topics, including insurers facing liability when AI agents bind policies, Allstate's plans for an AI shopping aide, and the need to budget for AI governance rather than only usage costs. The page does not report any regulatory action or a timeline for how insurers should respond.

Articles.Title: How exposed is your portfolio to a single AI model failure?

stories.Headline: Agent substrate: how Kubernetes became the foundation for AI
stories.Summary:
Kubernetes, the container orchestrator, has grown into what enterprises now rely on to run artificial intelligence agents, according to a SiliconANGLE report published on November 11, 2026. The article frames this as a shift in which Kubernetes acts as the agent substrate, a change that revives older security ideas such as the network perimeter. It also raises the importance of moving workloads smoothly between clouds. The story centers on remarks made at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America, where Broadcom unveiled two open-source initiatives.

Broadcom is pushing two main efforts to make the platform simpler to deploy and safer to run. The company's approach is security in depth, which uses its vDefend firewall at the network perimeter and deeper inside the system to cut off network access when rogue agents appear. Broadcom also isolates agents inside compute boundaries called vSphere Pods, which are micro virtual machines that create a secure runtime. On the portability side, the company is co-chairing a new working group on Kubernetes workload conformance, which aims to end separate validations for each distribution.

Dilpreet Bindra, senior director of engineering in the VCF Division at Broadcom, is the main voice in the report. He said that KubeCon blew open the doors on a project that some had considered stable and less active, because Kubernetes has become the foundation for AI. Bindra also said Broadcom wants Kubernetes to work the same way wherever it runs, so that users do not need separate validations for VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service and other distributions. He described the company's contribution of its VM API project to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation as a way to bring virtual machines into Kubernetes as first-class citizens.

The article places this discussion within a wider debate about how agents change cloud infrastructure, and it notes that the interview was sponsored by Broadcom, which had no editorial control over the content. The report does not describe specific timelines for when the working group will produce results or when the VM API project will reach a particular milestone. It likewise does not say how widely the security approach has been adopted by customers. The piece appears as part of SiliconANGLE and theCUBE's coverage of the conference, with the full video interview included.

Articles.Title: Agent substrate: how Kubernetes became the foundation for AI

stories.Headline: How a Teams-Native AI Receptionist Makes Automation Feel More Human
stories.Summary:
Heedify, a voice AI company, has released an AI receptionist built to work inside Microsoft Teams, and CX Today reported on the product in a November 10, 2026 article. The company's CEO and co-founder, Mefteh Werghemmi, spoke with the publication about setting clear limits on what voice AI should handle alone. He argued that even if only 5% of customers have a poor experience because an escalation is weak or badly timed, that is still a significant number of people. The article frames this as a shift in how success is measured, away from autonomous resolution alone. The article says voice AI now needs to do more than give information.

It should understand a request, pull up the relevant details, apply the business's rules, and take action in the system, while asking follow-up questions and responding naturally rather than following a rigid script. Regulated organizations, the piece notes, need extra controls around authentication, data access, and the actions an AI agent can take. Werghemmi said customers should know from the start that they are speaking with AI and should have a clear route to a human when they need one. Heedify's receptionist connects to a knowledge base and to a CRM so it can identify callers and see their account details, open tickets, and history. Heedify says its receptionist is among the first solutions certified under Microsoft's Teams Unify Integration Model for voice agents, which allows third-party voice agents to work with Teams Phone.

Calls can be routed to users or queues with caller context preserved, and Teams presence can help find an available employee for a handover. Werghemmi said keeping AI and human service on one platform lets organizations report on both together and see how calls move between them. He also said that a Teams-based model gives partners and system integrators a way to add customer experience features to a Microsoft environment their customers already use. The article presents this as part of a broader move toward a division of work between AI and employees, and it describes Heedify's approach as a practical starting point. The piece does not give adoption figures, pricing, or customer results, and it does not say what further product changes are planned.

Articles.Title: How a Teams-Native AI Receptionist Makes Automation Feel More Human

stories.Headline: Denmark wants its AI supercomputer to power new businesses and jobs
stories.Summary:
Denmark has announced an additional 500 million DKK (about €67 million) for its AI supercomputer Gefion, according to an announcement on Tuesday, 10 November 2026. The funding was disclosed by the Export and Investment Fund of Denmark and is aimed at the machine's infrastructure and operations at the Danish Centre for AI Innovation, which runs it. The new money comes on top of an initial 700 million DKK (about €93.8 million) from Denmark's state investment fund and the Novo Nordisk Foundation, which backs the supercomputer. Gefion was launched in 2024 with 1,528 Nvidia chips, and the centre says it is now nearing full capacity. Details on how the funds will be spent and when the extra capacity will become available have not been revealed.

The government's stated goal is to turn wider access to computing power into economic growth. Martin Lidegaard, Denmark's minister for business and competitiveness, said the funding would give Danish companies and researchers more computing power to turn ideas into new solutions, companies and jobs. He also argued that it strengthens national competitiveness and keeps ownership of future technology from passing to others. A second aim is to help public institutions and businesses adopt AI while keeping sensitive data under their own control. Netcompany, a Danish technology firm that builds and runs public-sector IT systems, is joining the centre's investors and will supply software for access management, monitoring and security.

The announcement sits within a broader European effort to gain more control over the infrastructure used to develop AI. The United Kingdom invested £225 million (about €269 million) in an AI-focused supercomputer in 2023, and Finland hosts LUMI, a supercomputer jointly funded by the European Union and participating countries at a lifetime cost of more than €200 million. In July, the European Commission opened a call for up to seven AI gigafactories, large data centres for training and running advanced AI models, backed by up to €10 billion in EU and national funding. Christina Egelund, Denmark's minister for research, education and digitalisation, said Europe must do much more for itself and that Denmark should contribute to technological independence so that technology can be regulated and developed in line with democratic values. The article does not say what further steps are planned beyond the funding itself.

Articles.Title: Denmark wants its AI supercomputer to power new businesses and jobs

stories.Headline: AI-native applications need distributed cloud, not just GPUs
stories.Summary:
Vultr, a cloud provider operating under the legal name The Constant Company LLC, has been arguing that enterprises building AI-native applications need more than raw GPU capacity. The position was laid out by Kevin Cochrane, chief marketing officer of Vultr, in an interview recorded at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA and broadcast on theCUBE, with John Furrier and Rebecca Knight of theCUBE Research. The article is dated November 11, 2026. Vultr sponsored the segment, a disclosure the article states plainly.

Cochrane said the early wave of so-called neoclouds focused on building large GPU clusters for a small set of buyers, often reselling that capacity to hyperscalers. In his view, the sector lost sight of the fact that companies still need a full cloud to run their workloads. He said the architecture has drifted back toward centralized systems and that the longer direction of computing is toward decentralized, distributed systems built on open standards and open source. The article also says distributed inference is a focus, with Vultr working with partners such as Vast Data Inc. on a global namespace that shares KV cache across nodes. Cochrane argued that networking between data centers, including private networks isolated from other tenants, is the main obstacle to enterprises adopting GPUs from newer cloud providers.

Vultr is also backing the open-source community, according to the article. The company has joined the Cloud Native Computing Foundation as a platinum member and highlighted its Open Source Credits Program, which provides infrastructure to maintainers of new CNCF projects. Cochrane said maintainers cannot be expected to fund compute themselves, and asked how a major CNCF project can be built without it. The article notes that the views are Cochrane's and that neither Vultr nor other sponsors have editorial control over theCUBE content.

Articles.Title: AI-native applications need distributed cloud, not just GPUs

stories.Headline: At 13x earnings, is Qualcomm the most overlooked AI chip stock?
stories.Summary:
This is an opinion and investment-analysis piece, not breaking news, so the one-or-two-paragraph breaking format does not apply. The article is a Yahoo Finance republication of an Investing.com commentary, published 10 November 2026, arguing that Qualcomm trades at a low multiple despite a broadening of AI into on-device processing. It reports Qualcomm at $165.41, about 12.98 times trailing earnings, and says Arm trades above 200 times earnings. The piece is promotional for the InvestingPro ProPicks AI service, and I have kept that framing clear below.

The article's central claim is that Qualcomm has been overlooked as artificial intelligence spending concentrates on cloud data center chips. It says the AI rally has been dominated by hyperscaler silicon, while on-device processing for laptops, phones and cars is gaining ground. Qualcomm is presented as supplying both chips and the patent portfolio used in that shift, with its Snapdragon X Elite processors cited for AI personal computers. The author treats the stock's low valuation as a gap between steady licensing cash flow and a multiple tied to smartphone skepticism.

The article cites several figures for the company's recent performance.
